0.title: Everyone Did What Was Right in His Own Eyes: The Book of Judges
0.overview:
The book of Judges is the bridge between conquest and kingdom, and it is the record of a steady decline. Joshua ends with the people at Shechem, swearing covenant loyalty to the LORD who had given them the land. Judges opens with that loyalty already crumbling and, near its end, shows a Levite dismembering the body of his murdered concubine and shipping the pieces across Israel. Judges is an unflinching exposure of what the human heart will do when it is left to itself. It does not name its author; Jewish tradition credited Samuel, and the refrain about Israel having no king suggests it was finished once there were kings. Its worst chapters record violence against women in order to condemn it: the book does not look away, and neither does God.

The book is built on a repeating cycle that follows the warnings of Deuteronomy 28: Israel abandons the LORD and serves the Baals, the gods of Canaan; God hands them over to oppressors; they cry out; God, moved by compassion, raises up a judge who delivers them; the land has rest; the judge dies; and the people sink back, deeper than before. The cycle is a downward spiral, and the deliverers grow more flawed as the book goes on, until by Samson the judge can hardly be told apart from the people he is meant to save.

How do the dates fit? The periods in Judges add up to about 410 years, yet 1 Kings 6:1 gives 480 years from the exodus to the temple. Many of the judges were regional, so their periods overlapped, and “forty years” often stands for a generation. Jephthah’s 300 years (11:26) is often taken to support the early date of the exodus, about 1446 BC; others hold a later date and read these numbers differently, and the question remains debated.

Why does Hebrews 11 name Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah? Hebrews commends their faith at the moment they trusted God’s promise, not their whole lives. Judges records their failures without approving them; they are monuments to God’s grace in using flawed people, and they all point to the true Deliverer.

Judges does not merely tell us that Israel needed better leaders; it tells us that Israel needed a different kind of King. The refrain of the final chapters, 'In those days there was no king in Israel' (17:6; 18:1; 19:1; 21:25), is not a wistful plea for a monarchy like David's, for even David and his sons would fail. It is a cry, whether the writer fully knew it or not, for the true King, the Lord Jesus Christ: the Judge who does not die, the Deliverer who does not fail, whose reign breaks the cycle for ever.

So we read Judges as Christians, watching each rescuer rise and fall, Othniel the ideal, Ehud the unlikely, Deborah the bold, Gideon the doubting, Jephthah the outcast, Samson the wasted, each a partial shadow of the Saviour to come. The judges deliver from Moab and Midian for a generation; Jesus delivers his people from sin and death for ever. The darkness of Judges, honestly faced, makes the gospel shine. Only those who feel the weight of 'everyone did what was right in his own eyes' will fall to their knees in gratitude for the King who does what is right in the eyes of his Father, and gives that righteousness to us.

1.title: The Incomplete Conquest

1.overview:
The book opens as the last one did, at a funeral, and for eighteen verses it sounds like a sequel. Israel inquires of the LORD before acting, the strong tribe invites the weak one along, giants fall at Hebron, Jerusalem is taken and burned, and a young woman gets off her donkey and asks her father for springs.

Then verse 19 says two things that do not fit together: the LORD was with Judah, yet Judah could not take the plain. There the chapter turns.

From there the chapter is a list, and one phrase tolls through it eight times: did not drive out. The reason given in verse 28 is not weakness but profit.

By verse 32 the wording is reversed, so that Israel is living among the Canaanites, and the chapter ends with Dan pressed back into the hills by the people it was sent to dispossess. Not one person in this chapter rebels against God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The book opens on a grave and a right instinct: after the death of Joshua, Israel asks the LORD who should go up first (v. 1), and the answer names Judah with the promise attached, I have given the land into his hand (v. 2). Judah invites Simeon along (v. 3), and the campaign goes well: ten thousand at Bezek (v. 4), Adoni-bezek captured and confessing that God has repaid him (vv. 5-7), Jerusalem taken and burned (v. 8), the giants of Hebron cut down (vv. 9-10), Othniel winning a town and a wife (vv. 11-15), the Kenites settling among them (v. 16). Then at verse 19 the chapter turns, and verse 21 records the first of the failures that fill the rest of it.
verseByVerse.theology: The first eighteen verses are the longest stretch of good news in the book. It is downhill from verse 19, and the book never fully recovers.
verseByVerse.examples: Verses 10-15 and 20 are lifted almost word for word out of Joshua (Josh. 15:14-19; 14:13). Judges begins by re-running Joshua's best material, and then goes somewhere Joshua never went.

verseByVerse.quote: After the death of Joshua, the people of Israel inquired of the LORD, "Who shall go up first for us against the Canaanites, to fight against them?" The LORD said, "Judah shall go up; behold, I have given the land into his hand." And Judah said to Simeon his brother, "Come up with me into the territory allotted to me, that we may fight against the Canaanites. And I likewise will go with you into the territory allotted to you." So Simeon went with him. Then Judah went up and the LORD gave the Canaanites and the Perizzites into their hand, and they defeated 10,000 of them at Bezek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua began after the death of Moses; Judges begins after the death of Joshua. Twice now the story has restarted at a funeral. The difference is what happens next. When Moses died, God named a successor before anybody asked. Here Israel asks and gets an answer about a tribe, not a man: there is no Joshua to follow Joshua.

What they do is right, and it will not happen like this again. They inquired of the LORD, the very thing the leaders failed to do at Gibeon, with the priest and the Urim and Thummim (the priest’s sacred lots) available in the camp (Josh. 9:14; Num. 27:21). The book of Judges opens on its highest note. The answer speaks of the gift as already made, as God did all through Joshua: I have given. The land is a gift before it is a campaign.

Then Judah, the largest tribe, invites Simeon, whose towns were scattered inside Judah's own land (Josh. 19:1, 9). The strong tribe does not go alone: come with me, and I will come with you. It is the high-water mark of Israelite brotherhood in this book. In twenty chapters' time the tribes will be at war with each other and one of them will nearly cease to exist.
verseByVerse.note: Judges covers roughly three centuries between Joshua and the monarchy. The “judges” were mostly military deliverers rather than courtroom figures.

verseByVerse.quote: They found Adoni-bezek at Bezek and fought against him and defeated the Canaanites and the Perizzites. Adoni-bezek fled, but they pursued him and caught him and cut off his thumbs and his big toes. And Adoni-bezek said, "Seventy kings with their thumbs and their big toes cut off used to pick up scraps under my table. As I have done, so God has repaid me." And they brought him to Jerusalem, and he died there. And the men of Judah fought against Jerusalem and captured it and struck it with the edge of the sword and set the city on fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mutilation is deliberate and it was a known practice: a man without thumbs cannot grip a sword, and a man without big toes cannot balance or run. He is disabled as a warrior and left alive as an exhibit. The text does not say God commanded it, and nothing in the law of Moses prescribed it; Israel is doing what the kings of Canaan did, and the narrator lets the victim’s own words name it as justice on him, not as a model for anyone.

The prisoner's explanation is better theology than most of what Israel will manage in the rest of the book. Seventy kings crawled under his table, and he does not call his fate bad luck: As I have done, so God has repaid me. A Canaanite tyrant, in his own humiliation, states the moral law of the universe without being taught it, the principle Jesus put in a sentence, with the measure you use it will be measured to you (Matt. 7:2), and Paul made unavoidable: whatever one sows, that will he also reap (Gal. 6:7).

The number seventy comes back in chapter 9, where an Israelite named Abimelech murders his seventy brothers on one stone to make himself king. By then it will be Israel doing what the Canaanite king did.

The city Judah could not take in Joshua's day (Josh. 15:63) is captured and burned, and for one verse the unfinished business of the last book is finished. Verse 21 will show it coming undone.

Was it just? This was God’s judgment on peoples whose sin had ripened over centuries (Gen 15:16; Deut 9:4–5), including child sacrifice (Deut 12:31), and Israel was warned that the land would vomit it out too for the same sins (Lev 18:24–28). It was a unique command, carried out through Israel at one moment in redemptive history. It is no pattern for any later war, nation or church: Christ’s kingdom is not of this world (John 18:36), and the church’s weapons are not of the flesh (2 Cor 10:4).

verseByVerse.quote: And afterward the men of Judah went down to fight against the Canaanites who lived in the hill country, in the Negeb, and in the lowland. And Judah went against the Canaanites who lived in Hebron (now the name of Hebron was formerly Kiriath-arba), and they defeated Sheshai and Ahiman and Talmai. From there they went against the inhabitants of Debir. The name of Debir was formerly Kiriath-sepher. And Caleb said, "He who attacks Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give him Achsah my daughter as wife." And Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother, captured it. And he gave him Achsah his daughter as wife. When she came to him, she urged him to ask her father for a field. And she dismounted from her donkey, and Caleb said to her, "What do you want?" She said to him, "Give me a blessing. Since you have given me the land of the Negeb, give me also springs of water." And Caleb gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A reader who has just finished Joshua will find this familiar, and it is meant to be. These verses are Joshua 15:14-19 told again, almost word for word: the same three giants by name, the same challenge, the same kinsman, the same daughter.

Remember Othniel's name. When the nation finally collapses into idolatry two chapters from now, he is the first man God raises up to rescue them (3:9), and the writer records nothing against him.

Achsah gets off her donkey to ask. She has been given land in the Negeb, which is dry country, and a field down there without water is a farm in name only. So she asks for the one thing that makes what she already has worth having, and she asks her father to his face.

She is given more than she requested: the upper springs and the lower springs, both.

It is the last unmixed good thing in the chapter, and it is a woman asking a generous man for water. Everything after verse 19 is about people who settled for less than God had given.

verseByVerse.quote: And the descendants of the Kenite, Moses' father-in-law, went up with the people of Judah from the city of palms into the wilderness of Judah, which lies in the Negeb near Arad, and they went and settled with the people. And Judah went with Simeon his brother, and they defeated the Canaanites who inhabited Zephath and devoted it to destruction. So the name of the city was called Hormah. Judah also captured Gaza with its territory, and Ashkelon with its territory, and Ekron with its territory. And the LORD was with Judah, and he took possession of the hill country, but he could not drive out the inhabitants of the plain because they had chariots of iron. And Hebron was given to Caleb, as Moses had said. And he drove out from it the three sons of Anak. But the people of Benjamin did not drive out the Jebusites who lived in Jerusalem, so the Jebusites have lived with the people of Benjamin in Jerusalem to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Kenites were the clan of Moses' father-in-law, a priest of Midian (Ex. 3:1), foreigners with no allotment and no claim. They are going to matter: in three chapters a Kenite woman called Jael will drive a tent peg through the enemy commander's skull while every Israelite man in the story is somewhere else.

Verse 18 first, briefly: the Greek Old Testament reads that Judah did not take Gaza, Ashkelon and Ekron, which fits verse 19 and the Philistines of later chapters. The Hebrew says it did, which most likely means a raid rather than lasting control. Either way, the coast did not stay in Israel’s hands.

Then the hinge of the chapter: one sentence with two halves that do not agree. The LORD was with Judah: there is nothing higher this book can say about anybody. And then: could not. Set the two side by side and could not cannot be the whole truth. This is the God who put Pharaoh's chariots at the bottom of the sea, dropped a wall flat at Jericho, threw hail down the pass at Beth-horon and stopped the sun over Gibeon. Iron is no difficulty to him. What has changed is not the odds but how Judah looked at them: they counted the chariots and left God out of the sum. Three chapters later God will rout nine hundred iron chariots in a single battle, apparently to settle the question (4:13-15).

This is how it goes with most of us. We confess the presence of God in general and then draw a map of the places where we assume he cannot help: the entrenched habit, the marriage that has been like this for years, the diagnosis. We give him the hill country and concede the plain.

Verses 20 and 21 are the whole book in miniature. Caleb, of the previous generation, drove out the giants. Benjamin, of this one, did not drive out the Jebusites from the city Judah had already burned. The victory of verse 8 was real and it was not held, and to this day says how long: until David took the citadel (2 Samuel 5:6-9).

Was God not strong enough for iron chariots? The LORD had promised victory over chariots (Josh 17:18). The failure was Judah’s faith, not God’s power, which is the theme of this chapter (2:1–3).
verseByVerse.note: “Hormah” means “utter destruction” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–26 — The Man Who Took the Mercy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The house of Joseph goes up against Bethel, and once more the LORD was with them (v. 22). Their scouts offer a man coming out of the city terms: show us the way in and we will deal kindly with you (vv. 23-24). He does, the city falls, and he and his family are let go (v. 25). Then verse 26, the point of the story: he went to the land of the Hittites, built a city and called it Luz, the old name of Bethel.
verseByVerse.theology: The episode is written to remind the reader of Rahab, and then to differ from her at every point that matters. She asked for mercy and joined the people who gave it; this man took the mercy and left.
verseByVerse.examples: The land of the Hittites here probably means the country north of Israel, in Syria, well beyond Israel's reach.

verseByVerse.quote: The house of Joseph also went up against Bethel, and the LORD was with them. And the house of Joseph scouted out Bethel. (Now the name of the city was formerly Luz.) And the spies saw a man coming out of the city, and they said to him, "Please show us the way into the city, and we will deal kindly with you." And he showed them the way into the city. And they struck the city with the edge of the sword, but they let the man and all his family go. And the man went to the land of the Hittites and built a city and called its name Luz. That is its name to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Spies, a city, a local who helps them in, and a promise of mercy in exchange: this is Jericho again, and the bargain is kept exactly. He walks out of a burning city alive with everyone he loves. Up to this point the story is Rahab's.

Then the difference, which is the whole point. Rahab asked for mercy and stayed. She came out of Jericho, lived in Israel, and ended up in the family tree of Jesus. She wanted the God who was doing this. This man takes the mercy and leaves, goes north out of reach, and names his new town after the pagan town he has just betrayed. He rebuilds the thing he escaped from, somewhere safer.

He was rescued and not changed. There are people who accept a rescue from God's people without ever wanting the God who sent it: grateful, unharmed, and gone. Rahab is in Matthew's genealogy. The man of Luz is a footnote with a town named after a place he did not want to leave.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: From here the chapter becomes a list, and one phrase runs through it like a bell. Manasseh did not drive out five named towns (v. 27); when Israel grew strong they put the Canaanites to forced labour instead (v. 28). Ephraim did not (v. 29). Zebulun did not (v. 30). Asher did not (v. 31), and in verse 32 the wording is quietly reversed: now Asher lives among the Canaanites. Naphtali did not (v. 33). And Dan is not merely failing: the Amorites press Dan back into the hills and will not let them come down (vv. 34-36).
verseByVerse.theology: No region is exempt: the failure runs from Joseph's tribes in the centre of the land to Asher and Naphtali in the far north.
verseByVerse.examples: Watch the small change of wording at verse 32: the Canaanites are now the people of the land, and Asher lives among them.

verseByVerse.quote: Manasseh did not drive out the inhabitants of Beth-shean and its villages, or Taanach and its villages, or the inhabitants of Dor and its villages, or the inhabitants of Ibleam and its villages, or the inhabitants of Megiddo and its villages, for the Canaanites persisted in dwelling in that land. When Israel grew strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labor, but did not drive them out completely. And Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer, so the Canaanites lived in Gezer among them. Zebulun did not drive out the inhabitants of Kitron, or the inhabitants of Nahalol, so the Canaanites lived among them, but became subject to forced labor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Five towns are named, and the reason given is almost comic in its honesty: the Canaanites persisted in dwelling in that land. Of course they did. The question was never whether Canaan would object. These are the towns Joshua listed as Manasseh's and unconquered (Josh. 17:11-12). Nothing has moved in a generation.

Verse 28 explains the whole chapter. The excuse used to be weakness: Joshua 17 said Manasseh could not, stated as fact rather than sin. Then Israel grew strong, the excuse expired, and at the moment obedience became possible they found something better to do. Forced labour is not a defeat; it is a business decision. Removing an entrenched population is expensive; keeping it as a workforce is profitable. The command was replaced by a labour policy and everybody did well.

The irony seems to have gone unnoticed: a nation redeemed out of forced labour by God's own hand, within living memory, imposes it on somebody else rather than obey. Ephraim, Joshua's own tribe, leaves Gezer exactly where Joshua's book left it (Josh. 16:10).

verseByVerse.quote: Asher did not drive out the inhabitants of Acco, or the inhabitants of Sidon or of Ahlab or of Achzib or of Helbah or of Aphik or of Rehob, so the Asherites lived among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land, for they did not drive them out. Naphtali did not drive out the inhabitants of Beth-shemesh, or the inhabitants of Beth-anath, so they lived among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land. Nevertheless, the inhabitants of Beth-shemesh and of Beth-anath became subject to forced labor for them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everywhere else the formula is that the Canaanites lived among them: Israel is the household and the Canaanites the lodgers. In verse 32 the phrase turns round. Asher is the minority in his own allotment, and the Canaanites are called, without comment, the inhabitants of the land, the phrase the book uses for the people God said to remove, now simply the name for whoever lives there.

Nobody in Asher voted for that. There was no day on which the tribe agreed to become a minority. It happened the way it always happens, by not doing something for long enough. The next tribe, Naphtali, gets the same wording (v. 33): two northern tribes have become Israelites living in Canaanite country.

The names in Naphtali's list say what that costs. Beth-shemesh is the house of the sun; Beth-anath is the house of Anath, the Canaanite war goddess. Naphtali now lives among towns named after other gods, and takes its rent from them in forced labour (v. 33).

verseByVerse.quote: The Amorites pressed the people of Dan back into the hill country, for they did not allow them to come down to the plain. The Amorites persisted in dwelling in Mount Heres, in Aijalon, and in Shaalbim, but the hand of the house of Joseph rested heavily on them, and they became subject to forced labor. And the border of the Amorites ran from the ascent of Akrabbim, from Sela and upward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends at the bottom. Every other tribe failed to drive somebody out. Dan is being driven: the Amorites push them up into the hills and did not allow them to come down to the plain. The conquest is running backwards. In verse 2 God gave the land into Judah's hand; in verse 34 an Israelite tribe is confined to high ground by the people it was sent to dispossess, and the last verse describes the border of the Amorites, not of Israel.

What happens to Dan next is where the book's darkest chapters come from. In chapter 18 the Danites give up on the allotment, march north, steal an idol and a priest on the way, and take a quiet town that had done nothing to anybody. The turning away from God at the end of this book begins with the pressure recorded here.

Across thirty-six verses Israel began by asking God a question and receiving a promise, and ended with a tribe in the hills and a border drawn for the enemy: the people who were given a country are living in somebody else's.

1.theology:
Nobody rebelled. There is no idol in this chapter, no defiance, no refusal. There is a war that got long, an arrangement that paid, and the words did not drive out repeated eight times. That is the book's diagnosis of how a covenant nation is lost: not by a decision to abandon God but by a series of compromises, each of which seemed reasonable on the day it was made.

Could not. Verse 19 is the hinge, and its two halves do not fit: if the LORD was with Judah, iron was not too much for him. To confess God’s presence in general while marking off areas where we assume he cannot help is not a gap in belief. It is a failure to act on what we already believe.

Profit, not weakness. When Israel grew strong (v. 28), the old excuse expired and the arrangement stayed, because by then it paid.

Who will go up first? The book’s opening question is answered with a tribe, Judah, and a promise, and the tribe goes up and then stops at the plain. The question waits for a better answer. Jacob had said the sceptre would not depart from Judah (Genesis 49:10), and the New Testament names the one in whom that word comes true: the Lion of the tribe of Judah, who has conquered (Revelation 5:5). He is the one who goes up first for his people, as a forerunner on our behalf (Hebrews 6:20), and he does not stop short of a single enemy, for he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:25).

Mercy without conversion. The man of Bethel takes Rahab's terms and leaves Rahab's God behind. He had no quarrel with Israel's God and no interest in him, and used his rescue to start again on his own terms.
1.examples:
A generation that began by asking God a question ended by keeping the enemy as a workforce, with one tribe a minority in its own allotment and another pushed off its land. There was no moment at which anybody chose it.

The phrase to test yourself against is not “I will not” but “I could not”. Name the plain you have conceded, the habit, the relationship, the fear you have quietly decided will never change, and ask what made you decide that. It is unlikely to have been new evidence about God. Then ask what you have kept because it is useful, that God told you to end. The land was given before a battle was fought, and the Lion of Judah has already gone up first; his Spirit is given to his people for exactly the ground they have conceded. Where you have settled, the way back starts with confession, not with a new resolution.

2.title: The Pattern Established
2.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the angel of the LORD went up from Gilgal to Bochim. And he said, "I brought you up from Egypt and brought you into the land that I swore to give to your fathers. I said, 'I will never break my covenant with you,<sup>2</sup>and you shall make no covenant with the inhabitants of this land; you shall break down their altars.' But you have not obeyed my voice. What is this you have done?<sup>3</sup>So now I say, I will not drive them out before you, but they shall become thorns in your sides, and their gods shall be a snare to you."<sup>4</sup>As soon as the angel of the LORD spoke these words to all the people of Israel, the people lifted up their voices and wept.<sup>5</sup>And they called the name of that place Bochim. And there arose another generation after them who did not know the LORD or the work that he had done for Israel.<sup>11</sup>And the people of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baals.<sup>12</sup>And they abandoned the LORD, the God of their fathers, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt. They went after other gods, from among the gods of the peoples who were around them, and bowed down to them. For the LORD was moved to pity by their groaning because of those who afflicted and oppressed them.<sup>19</sup>But whenever the judge died, they turned back and were more corrupt than their fathers, going after other gods, serving them and bowing down to them. 2.overview:
Chapter 1 gave the symptoms; chapter 2 gives the diagnosis and sets out the pattern that will govern the rest of the book. It opens with the angel of the LORD coming up from Gilgal, the place of the twelve stones and the first Passover in the land, to a place about to be named Bochim, "weepers", and delivering what reads like a legal case: a covenant (the binding bond God had made with Israel, with promises on his side and terms on theirs) perfectly kept on God's side, the terms Israel was given, and a seven-word charge, but you have not obeyed my voice.

The sentence is a withdrawal. The people weep and sacrifice, and not one altar comes down.

Then the narrative repeats four verses from the end of Joshua in order to add the sentence Joshua never wrote: another generation arose who did not know the LORD (v. 10).

The rest is the cycle in formula: evil done, God's anger, a selling into enemy hands, a judge raised up, and relapse the moment he dies, each turn ending lower than the last. At its centre stands verse 18, which is why the book is bearable: the LORD was moved to pity by their groaning.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The angel of the LORD goes up from Gilgal to Bochim and delivers what reads like a legal indictment (v. 1). The recital first: I brought you up from Egypt, I brought you into the land, I said I would never break my covenant with you. Then the terms: make no covenant with the inhabitants, break down their altars. Then the charge, in seven words, and a question (v. 2). The sentence follows: I will not drive them out; they will be thorns in your sides and their gods a snare to you (v. 3). The people weep, name the place Bochim, and offer sacrifice (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: The sentence is not an added punishment but a withdrawal. God simply stops doing the thing Israel had already stopped wanting done. They would not drive the Canaanites out; now neither will he.
verseByVerse.examples: The question at the end of verse 2 has been asked before. What is this you have done? is what God said to the woman in the garden (Gen. 3:13), and what Pharaoh said to Abraham about Sarah (Gen. 12:18). It is the question asked when the thing is already done and cannot be undone.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the angel of the LORD went up from Gilgal to Bochim. And he said, "I brought you up from Egypt and brought you into the land that I swore to give to your fathers. I said, 'I will never break my covenant with you, and you shall make no covenant with the inhabitants of this land; you shall break down their altars.' But you have not obeyed my voice. What is this you have done? So now I say, I will not drive them out before you, but they shall become thorns in your sides, and their gods shall be a snare to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two things about the speaker first. He is called the angel of the LORD, and he speaks as God in the first person, without the usual thus says the LORD. He does not report God's words. He uses them as his own.

He comes up from Gilgal, where the twelve stones were set up, the nation circumcised, the reproach of Egypt rolled away and the first Passover in the land eaten. The messenger travels from the place where the covenant was celebrated to a place about to be named for weeping.

The speech is built like a legal case, and the order matters. First what God has done and promised, all of it kept: brought you up, brought you in, and I will never break my covenant with you. Grace comes first, and there is no complaint on that side of the ledger. Then the terms: make no treaties, and pull down the altars. Israel had done neither; chapter 1 is the evidence. Then a question God first asked of a woman standing beside a tree with the fruit already eaten (Gen. 3:13). It is not a request for information.

They would not drive the Canaanites out. Very well: neither will he. The two consequences named are what Moses had warned, almost word for word, thorns in your sides and a snare (Num. 33:55; Deut. 7:16). What was a warning is now a verdict. Thorns wound; a snare catches. The Canaanites will be an irritation, their gods a trap, and the rest of this book is Israel walking into it.

There is a kind of judgment that consists in being allowed to keep what you insisted on having.

A believer who fears this has happened to him may take heart from the fear itself. Those who have been given up do not grieve that God is gone, and this same chapter goes on to show God raising up rescuers for people who had earned nothing (v. 18).

Who is the angel of the LORD? He speaks as God himself and is called “the LORD”. Some take him as a created angel speaking with God’s full authority. The best reading, held by many in the Reformed tradition, is that he is the LORD appearing in person, most likely the Son before his incarnation.
verseByVerse.note: “Bochim” means “weepers” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as the angel of the LORD spoke these words to all the people of Israel, the people lifted up their voices and wept. And they called the name of that place Bochim. And they sacrificed there to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The response looks right. They weep, they name the place after the weeping, and they offer sacrifice. A congregation in tears and an altar smoking: on any ordinary reckoning this is a revival meeting.

Nothing changes. Not one Canaanite is driven out the next morning. Not one altar comes down. The place is given a name that commemorates the emotion, and within a few verses the same people are bowing to Baal.

That is the reason this scene is in the book. It is a warning about a particular kind of religious experience: real feeling, genuine tears, an actual sacrifice, and no change of direction whatever.

Paul makes the distinction exactly. Godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death (2 Cor. 7:10). The difference is not in the intensity of the sorrow but in what happens afterwards, and it is often not visible on the day.

Weeping at what a sin has cost is not the same as hating the sin. Israel had just been told about thorns and snares; they wept at the sentence. It is possible to leave a church service genuinely moved, having felt something true, and to have moved nothing.

The name stuck, and it is the right name. This place is not called "Repentance". Its name means "weepers".

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–10 — A Generation That Did Not Know
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The narrative goes back to fill in what happened after Joshua dismissed the people (v. 6). Israel served the LORD all the days of Joshua and of the elders who outlived him, who had seen all the great work that the LORD had done (v. 7). Joshua dies at a hundred and ten and is buried in his own inheritance (vv. 8-9). And then verse 10, the sentence the whole book turns on: another generation arose who did not know the LORD or the work that he had done for Israel.
verseByVerse.theology: Judges repeats the end of the previous book (Josh. 24:28-31) in order to add the one line Joshua never wrote: what happened next.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 10 is set directly after Joshua's own epitaph, and the contrast is the point.

verseByVerse.quote: When Joshua dismissed the people, the people of Israel went each to his inheritance to take possession of the land. And the people served the LORD all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders who outlived Joshua, who had seen all the great work that the LORD had done for Israel. And Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died at the age of 110 years. And they buried him within the boundaries of his inheritance in Timnath-heres, in the hill country of Ephraim, north of the mountain of Gaash.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrative jumps backwards: Joshua is alive again, dismissing the assembly at Shechem. The writer is not padding. He is quoting the end of the previous book so that he can add a sentence to it.

The clause describing the faithful generation contains the whole problem: they served the LORD all the days of the elders who had seen all the great work that the LORD had done for Israel. Faithfulness lasted exactly as long as the eyewitnesses: not as long as the teaching, or the institutions, or the stones at Gilgal, but as long as the men who had watched the river stop.

The generation that opened this chapter weeping at Bochim is the generation that buried him.

verseByVerse.quote: And all that generation also were gathered to their fathers. And there arose another generation after them who did not know the LORD or the work that he had done for Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the verse the book turns on, and the order of what they did not know is the explanation. They did not know the work that he had done for Israel, and so they did not know the LORD.

These were not pagans. They were the grandchildren of the men who crossed the Jordan, living in the land and knowing the name of their national God. What they had not been given was the account: the river standing in a heap, the wall going down, the hail at Beth-horon, the day that would not end. They had the country and not the story.

Everything in Joshua was built to prevent this. Twelve stones were set up at Gilgal to provoke a child's question: when your children ask in time to come, 'What do those stones mean to you?' (Josh. 4:6). The whole law was read aloud with the women, the little ones and the foreigners present. A stone was set up at Shechem because it had heard. The stones did not fail; they were still standing. What failed was that somebody's father, walking past them for the fortieth time, did not say anything.

It does not say the next generation rejected the LORD or argued with him. It says they did not know him. There was no controversy, only an absence, and the Baals moved into it. The church has never been more than one silence away from this. Faith is not carried in the blood and does not pass on by nearness to a building.

The Bible's final answer to verse 10 is more than better telling. Through Jeremiah God promised a new covenant in which he would write his law on hearts, and they shall all know me (Jeremiah 31:34). Hebrews says that covenant has come in Jesus (Hebrews 8:6-12). Parents and churches must still tell the story, but the knowing of God that no generation could hand on by itself is the gift of the Son and his Spirit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–15 — The Baals, and the Selling
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first two turns of the cycle are stated in formula. Israel did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baals (v. 11); they abandoned the LORD who brought them out of Egypt and went after the gods of the peoples around them (vv. 12-13). So the anger of the LORD was kindled, and he gave them over to plunderers and sold them into the hand of their enemies (v. 14). Whenever they went out, the hand of the LORD was against them for harm, as he had warned, and they were in terrible distress (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: Notice the order in verse 12: they abandoned the LORD first, and then went after the gods around them. The emptiness came before the replacement.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel's defeats in this book are not the failure of their God to protect them. They are his discipline, and verse 15 says they had been warned of it.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baals. And they abandoned the LORD, the God of their fathers, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt. They went after other gods, from among the gods of the peoples who were around them, and bowed down to them. And they provoked the LORD to anger. They abandoned the LORD and served the Baals and the Ashtaroth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The formula that will run through the rest of the book appears here for the first time: in the sight of the LORD. Everything in Judges is measured by it, not by what worked or what the neighbours thought.

Serving the Baals was not a philosophical decision. Baal was the storm god, believed to control the rain, and therefore the barley, and therefore whether a family ate in the spring. Israel had come out of forty years of manna into a farming economy in a country they did not understand, and the locals had a settled body of expertise about this soil. The Baals came with the agricultural advice.

The narrator refuses the sensible description and uses the accurate one, twice: they abandoned the LORD, with the identifying clause attached, the God of their fathers, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt. That is the indictment in a relative clause: they exchanged the God who had verifiably done something for them for gods credited with the weather. Jeremiah puts the trade in a single picture: my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water (Jer. 2:13).
verseByVerse.note: Baal was the Canaanite storm and fertility god; the Ashtaroth were images of the goddess Astarte.

verseByVerse.quote: So the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he gave them over to plunderers, who plundered them. And he sold them into the hand of their surrounding enemies, so that they could no longer withstand their enemies. Whenever they marched out, the hand of the LORD was against them for harm, as the LORD had warned, and as the LORD had sworn to them. And they were in terrible distress.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The writer will not let God stand at a distance from the disaster. God gave them over; God sold them. The raiders were not a geopolitical accident. Sold is the harder word: what a man does with a slave he no longer wants, used of a nation God had bought out of slavery himself.

The clause that keeps this from being cruelty is as the LORD had warned. Deuteronomy had set it out in advance, in public, read aloud to the whole nation with the children present (Deut. 28:25). This is a Father's discipline of a people already his, not the end of the covenant.

Then an observation, not a verdict: they were in terrible distress. The narrator does not gloat. The misery is deserved, announced and self-inflicted, and he still records that it was terrible, which matters, because the God who sold them is about to be described as unable to bear the noise they make.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then the turn that keeps the book going: the LORD raised up judges, who saved them out of the hand of those who plundered them (v. 16). And immediately the qualification: they did not listen even to the judges, but whored after other gods (v. 17). Verse 18 gives the reason any of it happens: the LORD was with the judge, and he was moved to pity by their groaning. And verse 19 closes the loop: whenever the judge died they turned back and were more corrupt than their fathers.
verseByVerse.theology: The word for what the judges did is yasha, to save, the root behind the names Joshua and Jesus.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 18 is among the tenderest sentences in the book, and the reason the cycle does not simply end.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD raised up judges, who saved them out of the hand of those who plundered them. Yet they did not listen to their judges, for they whored after other gods and bowed down to them. They soon turned aside from the way in which their fathers had walked, who had obeyed the commandments of the LORD, and they did not do so.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One word turns the chapter: then. Israel has not repented, has not asked, has not changed. The previous verse ended in distress and this one begins with rescue, and the only thing between them is God. The LORD raised up; the judges saved. Israel is the object of both verbs and the subject of neither.

Matthew explains the name built on that verb when it is given: you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins (Matt. 1:21). Every judge is a small, borrowed, temporary version of that, raised up for one crisis in one region and then buried.

The word for the idolatry is deliberately offensive: they whored after other gods. It is the vocabulary of a betrayed marriage, the settled biblical way of saying idolatry is not an intellectual error but adultery against someone who has a claim. And the timing is the worst part: they did not listen to their judges, so this was happening while the rescue was going on.

verseByVerse.quote: Whenever the LORD raised up judges for them, the LORD was with the judge, and he saved them from the hand of their enemies all the days of the judge. For the LORD was moved to pity by their groaning because of those who afflicted and oppressed them. But whenever the judge died, they turned back and were more corrupt than their fathers, going after other gods, serving them and bowing down to them. They did not drop any of their practices or their stubborn ways.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the sentence that keeps this book from being unbearable. The secret of every deliverance is the phrase that explained Judah's victory in chapter 1: the LORD was with the judge. Never the man's ability; the book will make that unmistakable by choosing the least likely men it can find.

Then the reason God does it at all. Not because they repented, nor because they prayed: The LORD was moved to pity by their groaning. Groaning is not repentance. It is the noise a person makes under a weight picked up voluntarily and warned about in advance. God is moved by the sound of people suffering the exact consequences he told them would come.

Does God change? The verb for moved to pity is the one elsewhere translated relent, and it describes real compassion, not a change of plan. God is not a man, that he should change his mind (Numbers 23:19); what never changes is that he is the kind of God who is moved by his people's misery.

It is the same movement recorded when God heard a different groaning from a different slavery: God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant (Ex. 2:24).

Then the loop closes, and two words give the book its shape. Died: the trigger for every relapse is a funeral, and the deliverance lasted exactly as long as the deliverer. More: they were more corrupt than their fathers. Each turn ends lower than the last.

The diagnosis is structural. The system fails not because the judges were bad, but because they were mortal and the people were not changed by being rescued. Hebrews puts its finger on the same weakness: the former priests were many in number, because they were prevented by death from continuing in office, but he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues for ever (Heb. 7:23-24). Israel did not need a better judge. Every improvement on Othniel would still be buried. It needed a deliverer who would not stay dead.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends with God stating a purpose behind the unfinished conquest. Because this people have transgressed the covenant (v. 20), he will no longer drive out any of the nations Joshua left when he died (v. 21), in order to test Israel by them, whether they will take care to walk in the way of the LORD as their fathers did, or not (v. 22). So the nations were left, not driven out quickly (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: The same nations are two things at once: the consequence of Israel's disobedience (v. 3) and the instrument of God's testing (v. 22).
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 23 looks back as far as Joshua's day: the business was unfinished before anybody now living was born.

verseByVerse.quote: So the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he said, "Because this people have transgressed my covenant that I commanded their fathers and have not obeyed my voice, I will no longer drive out before them any of the nations that Joshua left when he died, in order to test Israel by them, whether they will take care to walk in the way of the LORD as their fathers did, or not." So the LORD left those nations, not driving them out quickly, and he did not give them into the hand of Joshua.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The decision of verse 3 is restated as settled policy, and then a purpose clause changes how the whole book must be read. The same Canaanites are the natural result of a job left unfinished and an instrument deliberately left in place in order to test. Scripture puts those sentences nineteen verses apart and shows no anxiety about it. The thing Israel brought on itself is the thing God is using. A reader who drops either will misread what follows, and most of his own life.

What is tested is not their theology but their walking: whether they will take care to walk in the way of the LORD as their fathers did. The exam is conducted over a lifetime and marked by ordinary behaviour.

And the last clause should not be walked past: he did not give them into the hand of Joshua. The man who left nothing undone of all that the LORD commanded Moses (Josh. 11:15) still died with nations standing, and the writer says this was God's doing, not Joshua's failure.

That is a strange comfort, and a real one. There was never a moment in Israel's story when the ground was entirely held, and there is not one in ours. The Canaanite left standing in a believer's life is not always evidence of a battle lost; sometimes it is the examination room, left standing on purpose by a God who has already made the believer his own and means to see how he walks.

2.theology:
Judgment as withdrawal. God's sentence at Bochim is to stop doing what Israel had already stopped wanting done (v. 3). It is the judgment Paul names three times in one chapter, God gave them up (Rom. 1:24, 26, 28), and its most frightening feature is that it required God to do nothing at all.

One generation. Verse 10 does not say the next generation rejected God; it says they did not know him, because they did not know his work. Faith arrives by somebody telling somebody, and it stops when they stop.

Moved by groaning, not by repentance. Verse 18 gives the reason God keeps raising up deliverers, and it is not Israel's contrition or their prayers. He was moved to pity by their groaning, and that is the only reason this book has more than three chapters.

The flaw is mortality. The trigger for every relapse is a funeral (v. 19). The system fails not because the judges were poor, several were remarkable, but because they died, and because being rescued did not change anybody. Israel needed a deliverer who would not stay dead, and a covenant that changes the heart.
2.examples:
Then: A nation wept at a place they named after the weeping, offered sacrifices, and drove out nobody. A generation later their children knew the name of their God and nothing he had done, and took farming advice from the neighbours about which god sent rain.

Now: Two tests come out of this chapter. The first is Bochim: genuine tears, a real sacrifice, and no Canaanite driven out the next morning. Ask what actually changed after the last time you were deeply moved. Godly grief is not produced by trying to feel worse; it is the Spirit's work, turning us towards the Christ whose sacrifice did what Bochim's could not, and he gives the strength for the altar that has to come down tomorrow. The second is verse 10, aimed at parents and churches. The stones at Gilgal were still standing; what had stopped was somebody answering the question, telling children what the LORD has done before telling them what to do.

3.title: Othniel, Ehud, and Shamgar
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Now these are the nations that the LORD left, to test Israel by them, that is, all in Israel who had not experienced all the wars in Canaan.<sup>2</sup>It was only in order that the generations of the people of Israel might know war, to teach war to those who had not known it before.<sup>3</sup>These are the nations: the five lords of the Philistines and all the Canaanites and the Sidonians and the Hivites who lived on Mount Lebanon, from Mount Baal-hermon as far as Lebo-hamath.<sup>4</sup>They were for the testing of Israel, to know whether Israel would obey the commandments of the LORD, which he commanded their fathers by the hand of Moses.<sup>5</sup>So the people of Israel lived among the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites.<sup>6</sup>And their daughters they took to themselves for wives, and their own daughters they gave to their sons, and they served their gods.<sup>7</sup>And the people of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. They forgot the LORD their God and served the Baals and the Asheroth.<sup>8</sup>Therefore the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of Cushan-rishathaim king of Mesopotamia. And the people of Israel served Cushan-rishathaim eight years.<sup>9</sup>But when the people of Israel cried out to the LORD, the LORD raised up a deliverer for the people of Israel, who saved them, Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother.<sup>10</sup>The Spirit of the LORD was upon him, and he judged Israel. He went out to war, and the LORD gave Cushan-rishathaim king of Mesopotamia into his hand. And his hand prevailed over Cushan-rishathaim.<sup>11</sup>So the land had rest for forty years. Then Othniel the son of Kenaz died.<sup>12</sup>And the people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD strengthened Eglon the king of Moab against Israel, because they had done what was evil in the sight of the LORD.<sup>13</sup>He gathered to himself the Ammonites and the Amalekites, and went and defeated Israel. And they took possession of the city of palms.<sup>14</sup>And the people of Israel served Eglon the king of Moab eighteen years.<sup>15</sup>Then the people of Israel cried out to the LORD, and the LORD raised up for them a deliverer, Ehud, the son of Gera, the Benjaminite, a left-handed man. The people of Israel sent tribute by him to Eglon the king of Moab.<sup>16</sup>And Ehud made for himself a sword with two edges, a cubit in length, and he bound it on his right thigh under his clothes.<sup>17</sup>And he presented the tribute to Eglon king of Moab. Now Eglon was a very fat man.<sup>18</sup>And when Ehud had finished presenting the tribute, he sent away the people who carried the tribute.<sup>19</sup>But he himself turned back at the idols near Gilgal and said, "I have a secret message for you, O king." And he commanded, "Silence." And all his attendants went out from his presence.<sup>20</sup>And Ehud came to him as he was sitting alone in his cool roof chamber. And Ehud said, "I have a message from God for you." And he arose from his seat.<sup>21</sup>And Ehud reached with his left hand, took the sword from his right thigh, and thrust it into his belly.<sup>22</sup>And the hilt also went in after the blade, and the fat closed over the blade, for he did not pull the sword out of his belly; and the dung came out.<sup>23</sup>Then Ehud went out into the porch and closed the doors of the roof chamber behind him and locked them.<sup>24</sup>When he had gone, the servants came, and when they saw that the doors of the roof chamber were locked, they thought, "Surely he is relieving himself in the closet of the cool chamber."<sup>25</sup>And they waited till they were embarrassed. But when he still did not open the doors of the roof chamber, they took the key and opened them, and there lay their lord dead on the floor.<sup>26</sup>Ehud escaped while they delayed, and he passed beyond the idols and escaped to Seirah.<sup>27</sup>When he arrived, he sounded the trumpet in the hill country of Ephraim. Then the people of Israel went down with him from the hill country, and he was their leader.<sup>28</sup>And he said to them, "Follow after me, for the LORD has given your enemies the Moabites into your hand." So they went down after him and seized the fords of the Jordan against the Moabites and did not allow anyone to pass over.<sup>29</sup>And they killed at that time about 10,000 of the Moabites, all strong, able-bodied men; not a man escaped.<sup>30</sup>So Moab was subdued that day under the hand of Israel. And the land had rest for eighty years.<sup>31</sup>After him was Shamgar the son of Anath, who killed 600 of the Philistines with an oxgoad, and he also saved Israel.
3.overview:
The chapter opens by explaining the unfinished conquest twice over: the nations were left to test Israel, and to teach war to a generation that had never fought (vv. 1-2). The enemy left standing is called a school.

They fail the test in one verse: they took wives, they gave daughters, and they served their gods (v. 6).

Then three deliverers, and no two of them alike. Othniel is the model, with forty years of rest, and then the word that ends every judge, died. Ehud, a left-handed man from the smallest tribe, kills Eglon of Moab in a locked room and buys eighty years, the longest peace in the book. And Shamgar gets one verse, an oxgoad and six hundred Philistines.

A younger brother, a man whose sword arm did not work, and a farmer with a cattle prod. It is a fair summary of how God has always gone about it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Left to Teach Them War
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter opens by naming the nations God left and giving two reasons for it. The first is testing (v. 1, restated in v. 4): to find out whether Israel would obey. The second is stranger and is stated as the whole purpose: only in order that the generations of the people of Israel might know war, to teach war to those who had not known it before (v. 2). The nations are listed (v. 3), and then the result: Israel lived among them, married their sons and daughters, and served their gods (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: A generation that had never fought is given an enemy, and the writer calls it an education.
verseByVerse.examples: The peoples named in verse 5 are almost the same list Israel was told to devote to destruction (Deut. 7:1). Now Israel lives among them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now these are the nations that the LORD left, to test Israel by them, that is, all in Israel who had not experienced all the wars in Canaan. It was only in order that the generations of the people of Israel might know war, to teach war to those who had not known it before. These are the nations: the five lords of the Philistines and all the Canaanites and the Sidonians and the Hivites who lived on Mount Lebanon, from Mount Baal-hermon as far as Lebo-hamath. They were for the testing of Israel, to know whether Israel would obey the commandments of the LORD, which he commanded their fathers by the hand of Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first purpose is the testing announced at the end of chapter 2. The second is put as though it were the whole point: only in order that the generations... might know war, to teach war to those who had not known it before.

This is the generation born after the fighting stopped. They grew up in houses their parents had taken, ate from vineyards somebody else had planted, and had never faced an enemy across a field. They had inherited the results of faith without ever exercising any. So God leaves the Philistines and the Canaanites in place, and the writer calls it a school: not a mistake, but a course of instruction for people who had grown up soft in a country won by other men's obedience.

Hold that against the instinct to read every remaining difficulty as a failure. A settled Christian who has never had to depend on God for anything is not in a stronger position than one who has; he is in a more dangerous one, and has no way of knowing it until something is left standing in his way.

The test is not of their doctrine but of their obedience, and the syllabus is already written and published. Nothing new will be asked of them.

verseByVerse.quote: So the people of Israel lived among the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites. And their daughters they took to themselves for wives, and their own daughters they gave to their sons, and they served their gods.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The result of the test uses the wording chapter 1 introduced at Asher: Israel lived among them, the population living in someone else's country.

Then the sequence, in one direction with no pause: they took wives, they gave daughters, they served their gods. Nobody married a Canaanite in order to worship Baal. The worship arrived at the end of a chain that began with an ordinary decision about a wedding.

That is the reason God had given for the prohibition. It was never about ancestry: Rahab married into Judah, Ruth the Moabite is in the same family tree, and a Kenite clan is settled among them in chapter 1. Moses stated the ground plainly: they would turn away your sons from following me, to serve other gods (Deut. 7:4). Paul reasons the same way about being unequally yoked (2 Cor. 6:14): the heart does not stay independent of what it has bound itself to. Israel married the families and ended up at the family altars.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first full turn of the cycle, in textbook form. Israel did evil, forgot the LORD and served the Baals and the Asheroth, images of the goddess Asherah (v. 7); God sold them to Cushan-rishathaim of Mesopotamia for eight years (v. 8); they cried out, and the LORD raised up Othniel, Caleb's younger brother (v. 9). The Spirit of the LORD came on him and God gave the king into his hand (v. 10). The land had rest forty years, and then Othniel died (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Othniel is the model, and the writer gives him no faults. He is from Caleb's family, the Spirit rests on him, he wins, and the land is quiet for a generation. Every judge after this is measured against him, and every one falls short.
verseByVerse.examples: Mesopotamia here is, in Hebrew, Aram-naharaim, "Aram of the two rivers", far to the north-east: the oppressor comes from a long way off.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the LORD. They forgot the LORD their God and served the Baals and the Asheroth. Therefore the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of Cushan-rishathaim king of Mesopotamia. And the people of Israel served Cushan-rishathaim eight years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One verb explains the whole book, and it is not a dramatic one. They forgot. Not rejected, not renounced. There is no record anywhere in Judges of Israel deciding that the God of the exodus was untrue; the writer keeps describing a nation mislaying him. Chapter 2 said the generation did not know him. This one says they forgot him.

Forgetting takes no effort at all. It is what happens to anything not deliberately kept in front of the mind, and Moses spent a whole book warning about it: take care lest you forget the LORD, when you have eaten and are full and have built good houses and live in them (Deut. 8:11-12).

Say the oppressor's name aloud. Cushan-rishathaim reads in Hebrew as something like "Cushan of double wickedness", and it is hard to imagine a king calling himself that. Eight years under a tyrant, and the narrator will not grant him much dignity.
verseByVerse.note: Attempts to identify Cushan with a ruler known from outside the Bible remain uncertain.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the people of Israel cried out to the LORD, the LORD raised up a deliverer for the people of Israel, who saved them, Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother. The Spirit of the LORD was upon him, and he judged Israel. He went out to war, and the LORD gave Cushan-rishathaim king of Mesopotamia into his hand. And his hand prevailed over Cushan-rishathaim. So the land had rest for forty years. Then Othniel the son of Kenaz died.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They cry out. It is not called repentance; they are simply in pain and make a noise about it, the groaning God was described as unable to bear in 2:18.

The man raised up is already known. Othniel took Kiriath-sepher and married Achsah in chapter 1, and belongs to the one family chapter 1 had nothing against: Caleb's.

Then the sentence that will explain every deliverance in this book: the Spirit of the LORD was upon him. Not his lineage, though it was good, nor his record. The book will prove the point by putting the Spirit of the LORD on men with far worse credentials: a frightened farmer hiding in a winepress, a rejected son of a prostitute, a man who could not keep away from Philistine women. The one qualification is the Spirit, and it is given rather than earned.

The prophets carry that line forward to the Deliverer who would not die and leave his people leaderless. Of the coming son of David, Isaiah wrote, the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him (Isaiah 11:2). In the synagogue at Nazareth Jesus read, The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, and said that the Scripture was fulfilled that day (Luke 4:18-21). Othniel had the Spirit for a campaign. Christ has him without measure, and gives him to his people.

Forty years is a full generation of peace, and it is real. Then the hinge word: died. Othniel is the model judge, without a single criticism anywhere in Scripture, and he was mortal, and the rest he won was buried with him. The best available deliverer, doing everything right, could not give Israel anything that outlasted his own funeral.
verseByVerse.note: Othniel was Caleb’s younger brother (some read it as his nephew).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The wheel turns on the word again (v. 12), and this time God strengthened the oppressor: Eglon of Moab, with Ammon and Amalek, takes the city of palms and holds Israel eighteen years (vv. 13-14). Israel cries out and God raises up Ehud, a left-handed Benjaminite, who makes a short two-edged sword and straps it to his right thigh (vv. 15-16). He delivers the tribute, sends the carriers away, comes back with a secret message, and kills the king alone in his roof chamber (vv. 17-22). He locks the doors and walks out; the servants stand outside waiting until they are embarrassed (vv. 23-25). Ehud escapes, sounds the trumpet, takes the fords of the Jordan, and ten thousand Moabites fall, and the land has rest for eighty years (vv. 26-30).
verseByVerse.theology: God's deliverer is a man from the smallest tribe with a disqualified sword arm, carrying a homemade blade to a tribute ceremony. The whole plan depends on the thing about him a guard would have written off.
verseByVerse.examples: Eighty years is the longest rest recorded in the book. It is also, like every other rest here, measured in the lifetime of one man.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD strengthened Eglon the king of Moab against Israel, because they had done what was evil in the sight of the LORD. He gathered to himself the Ammonites and the Amalekites, and went and defeated Israel. And they took possession of the city of palms. And the people of Israel served Eglon the king of Moab eighteen years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Again: Othniel is barely in the ground and the wheel has come round. Then a hard verb: The LORD strengthened Eglon. God does not merely allow the oppressor; he equips him. That is uncomfortable and it is consistent. Israel's troubles in this book come not from God's absence but from his attention, the discipline of a Father who has not let go.

The city of palms is Jericho. The first city God gave them, whose walls fell at a shout, is now a Moabite forward base. Cushan held them eight years; Eglon holds them eighteen. The oppressions are getting longer, as chapter 2 said the spiral would run.

And Moab was family, descended from Lot, and Israel had been forbidden to attack them in the wilderness because of it (Deut. 2:9). The people God brought out of the greatest empire on earth are paying tribute to their distant cousins.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the people of Israel cried out to the LORD, and the LORD raised up for them a deliverer, Ehud, the son of Gera, the Benjaminite, a left-handed man. The people of Israel sent tribute by him to Eglon the king of Moab. And Ehud made for himself a sword with two edges, a cubit in length, and he bound it on his right thigh under his clothes. And he presented the tribute to Eglon king of Moab. Now Eglon was a very fat man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrator gives one physical detail about this man, the one the whole story turns on. The Hebrew says something like "bound" or "restricted as to his right hand": a man whose sword arm does not work as a sword arm should. In a world where every soldier drew from the left hip with his right hand, that is a defect on a military record. Many think, though, that the phrase describes a skill rather than a defect: a man trained to fight left-handed, perhaps with the right arm bound in boyhood (compare 1 Chronicles 12:2). Either way, the enemy did not expect it.

He is also a Benjaminite, and Benjamin means "son of the right hand" (so the ESV note at Gen. 35:18). The trait ran in that tribe: later in this book Benjamin fields seven hundred left-handed men who could sling a stone at a hair and not miss (20:16).

He makes the weapon himself, about eighteen inches, two-edged, small enough to hide under a cloak, and straps it to his right thigh. If he was searched at all, a guard would look on the left, and the blade goes in through the front door on the body of a man officially disarmed.

The last sentence of verse 17 is loading a gun: now Eglon was a very fat man. His name is probably part of the joke, close to the Hebrew for a calf. A king grown heavy on eighteen years of another nation's tribute is about to be dealt with like livestock.
verseByVerse.note: The Hebrew word for this measure occurs only here in the Old Testament; most take it as a short cubit.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Ehud had finished presenting the tribute, he sent away the people who carried the tribute. But he himself turned back at the idols near Gilgal and said, "I have a secret message for you, O king." And he commanded, "Silence." And all his attendants went out from his presence. And Ehud came to him as he was sitting alone in his cool roof chamber. And Ehud said, "I have a message from God for you." And he arose from his seat. And Ehud reached with his left hand, took the sword from his right thigh, and thrust it into his belly. And the hilt also went in after the blade, and the fat closed over the blade, for he did not pull the sword out of his belly; and the dung came out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He sends the delegation home first, so that no other Israelite is near the palace when it happens, and turns back at the idols near Gilgal. The ground where the twelve stones were set up now has idols standing near it. The Hebrew word can also mean carved stones, and some have wondered whether these were the memorial stones themselves, now treated as idols; the text does not say.

Ehud says he has a secret, and Eglon empties the room: the one thing an oppressor cannot resist is intelligence, and he dismisses his own bodyguard to get it. Then: I have a message from God for you. Eglon stands up to receive it. Whatever he believed about the God of Israel, he stood.

The message from God is eighteen inches of iron, and the narrator describes it with a bluntness that has embarrassed readers for centuries. The hilt goes in after the blade, the fat closes over it, and the last clause is as undignified as it sounds. Scripture can write an oppressor's death with dignity and declines to do it here. There is a strand running through the Bible that laughs at tyrants, he who sits in the heavens laughs (Ps. 2:4), and this is the crudest page of it.

Is Ehud’s deception and killing approved? Ehud was raised up by the LORD (v. 15) to free Israel from an occupier in a war of liberation. Scripture records his method without holding it up as a pattern. It gives no Christian licence to deceive or to kill; private persons may not take vengeance (Romans 12:19). Hebrews does not name Ehud, and where it names his fellow judges it commends their faith, not every act (Hebrews 11:32). The deliverers of this book are flawed pointers to a better Deliverer. Ehud carried a hidden blade and a false pretext into a tyrant's room. Christ said he had spoken nothing in secret (John 18:20), and he freed his people from the tyrant behind every tyrant by dying himself (Hebrews 2:14-15).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Ehud went out into the porch and closed the doors of the roof chamber behind him and locked them. When he had gone, the servants came, and when they saw that the doors of the roof chamber were locked, they thought, "Surely he is relieving himself in the closet of the cool chamber." And they waited till they were embarrassed. But when he still did not open the doors of the roof chamber, they took the key and opened them, and there lay their lord dead on the floor. Ehud escaped while they delayed, and he passed beyond the idols and escaped to Seirah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He locks up. A man who has just killed a head of state in his own palace stops, pulls the doors to, turns the key, and walks out through the household.

The servants arrive, find the doors locked, and reach the obvious conclusion. Their king is using the lavatory.

They wait. And the writer, who could have moved straight to the discovery, stops to record their state of mind: they waited till they were embarrassed.

A corridor full of courtiers standing outside a locked door, too well-bred to knock, growing steadily more uncomfortable, while the assassin gets further away by the minute and the man they are protecting has been dead for some time.

The delay is the escape route. What saves the deliverer is not his speed but the manners of his enemies, and the writer's point is not subtle: when God moves against an oppressor, the oppressor's own household becomes part of the arrangement.

Whatever else the court of Moab was that day, it was not formidable. Eighteen years of domination ends with a locked door and a group of embarrassed men who cannot bring themselves to interrupt.
verseByVerse.note: The meaning of the Hebrew for “porch” is uncertain (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: When he arrived, he sounded the trumpet in the hill country of Ephraim. Then the people of Israel went down with him from the hill country, and he was their leader. And he said to them, "Follow after me, for the LORD has given your enemies the Moabites into your hand." So they went down after him and seized the fords of the Jordan against the Moabites and did not allow anyone to pass over. And they killed at that time about 10,000 of the Moabites, all strong, able-bodied men; not a man escaped. So Moab was subdued that day under the hand of Israel. And the land had rest for eighty years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The assassination was not the deliverance; it was the opening. Ehud blows a trumpet in the hills and the same Israelites who have paid tribute for eighteen years come down after him. The oppression was never as solid as it looked; what was missing was somebody to move first.

His speech is two clauses, and the second is the whole theology of the book: the LORD has given, perfect tense again, as at Jericho and in 1:2. The killing of Eglon did not create the victory; it acted on one already granted.

The tactics are sound too. The fords of the Jordan are the only way home for a Moabite army on the wrong side of the river, and Israel takes them first.

Eighty years, twice what Othniel achieved, came out of one day in a locked room. The Moabites had let him in armed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: One verse: Shamgar the son of Anath killed six hundred Philistines with an oxgoad, and he also saved Israel (v. 31).
verseByVerse.theology: No cycle, no years, no oppression narrated and no rest recorded: a name, a farm implement, a number, and the same verb used of Othniel.
verseByVerse.examples: This is the first time the Philistines appear as an enemy in this book. The whole Samson cycle is against them, and they are still there when Saul dies.

verseByVerse.quote: After him was Shamgar the son of Anath, who killed 600 of the Philistines with an oxgoad, and he also saved Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is no cycle here: no apostasy, no crying out, no years of rest. Even the name is a puzzle: Anath was a Canaanite war goddess, and some think Shamgar was not an Israelite at all, or came from a town such as Beth-anath. God's rescues are not limited to the people one would expect.

The weapon is the point. An oxgoad is a wooden pole eight feet long or so, with an iron spike for driving cattle and a flat blade for scraping a ploughshare. It is what a man has in his hand when he is working, and it is not a sword.

Set the three deliverers side by side, as the writer has arranged them. Nothing in that list is what a nation would choose. God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong, and what is low and despised, so that no human being might boast in his presence (1 Cor. 1:27-29).

And the last clause: and he also saved Israel, the same verb used of Othniel and of Ehud, the word behind the names of Joshua and Jesus. A man with a stick is entered in the record with the same word as everybody else, and God did not need better equipment than what was already in his hand.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of Anath” may name his father, his home town, or even mark him out as a warrior; the text does not say which.

3.theology:
The enemy as curriculum. Verse 2 says the nations were left to teach war to a generation that had never fought. The difficulty still standing in a Christian life is not automatically evidence of a battle lost; it may be the very place where a believer learns to depend on God.

They forgot. The verb in verse 7 is the ordinary one, and it takes no effort at all. Judges never once records Israel deciding that the God of the exodus was untrue, and Moses located the danger in prosperity rather than persecution.

The one qualification. What explains Othniel is not his family, though it was the best in the book, but one clause: the Spirit of the LORD was upon him (v. 10). The book will put the Spirit of the LORD on a frightened farmer hiding in a winepress, the rejected son of a prostitute, and a man who could not keep away from Philistine women. The qualification is given, not earned.

Improbable instruments. Ehud's deliverance turns on the trait a recruiting officer would have written off, and Shamgar's weapon is what happened to be in his hand at work. It is the pattern Paul states outright: God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong, so that no human being might boast (1 Cor. 1:27-29).
3.examples:
A generation that had never fought a battle married into the neighbours and ended up at their altars. Then God raised up a model judge who died, an assassin whose disability was the plan, and a farmer with a stick, and every deliverance was real and every one wore off.

Two things carry over to us. Verse 6 is the sequence to watch, because nobody in it chose to change gods; they chose relationships, and the worship followed. And verse 7 is the honest description of most spiritual decline: not rejection but forgetting, which requires no decision. The remedy is not a stronger grip but remembering what God has done, which is why he gives his word, the Lord's Supper and his people, and his Spirit, who brings to remembrance what Christ has said (John 14:26). And when you find you have forgotten, the God of this chapter still answers the cry of people who had forgotten him.

4.title: Deborah and Barak
4.text: <sup>1</sup>And the people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD after Ehud died.<sup>2</sup>And the LORD sold them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor. The commander of his army was Sisera, who lived in Harosheth-hagoyim.<sup>3</sup>Then the people of Israel cried out to the LORD for help, for he had 900 chariots of iron and he oppressed the people of Israel cruelly for twenty years.<sup>4</sup>Now Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time.<sup>5</sup>She used to sit under the palm of Deborah between Ramah and Bethel in the hill country of Ephraim, and the people of Israel came up to her for judgment.<sup>6</sup>She sent and summoned Barak the son of Abinoam from Kedesh-naphtali and said to him, "Has not the LORD, the God of Israel, commanded you, 'Go, gather your men at Mount Tabor, taking 10,000 from the people of Naphtali and the people of Zebulun.<sup>7</sup>And I will draw out Sisera, the general of Jabin's army, to meet you by the river Kishon with his chariots and his troops, and I will give him into your hand'?"<sup>8</sup>Barak said to her, "If you will go with me, I will go, but if you will not go with me, I will not go."<sup>9</sup>And she said, "I will surely go with you. Nevertheless, the road on which you are going will not lead to your glory, for the LORD will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman." Then Deborah arose and went with Barak to Kedesh.<sup>10</sup>And Barak called out Zebulun and Naphtali to Kedesh.
