And 10,000 men went up at his heels, and Deborah went up with him.<sup>11</sup>Now Heber the Kenite had separated from the Kenites, the descendants of Hobab the father-in-law of Moses, and had pitched his tent as far away as the oak in Zaanannim, which is near Kedesh.<sup>12</sup>When Sisera was told that Barak the son of Abinoam had gone up to Mount Tabor,<sup>13</sup>Sisera called out all his chariots, 900 chariots of iron, and all the men who were with him, from Harosheth-hagoyim to the river Kishon.<sup>14</sup>And Deborah said to Barak, "Up! For this is the day in which the LORD has given Sisera into your hand. Does not the LORD go out before you?" So Barak went down from Mount Tabor with 10,000 men following him.<sup>15</sup>And the LORD routed Sisera and all his chariots and all his army before Barak by the edge of the sword. And Sisera got down from his chariot and fled away on foot.<sup>16</sup>And Barak pursued the chariots and the army to Harosheth-hagoyim, and all the army of Sisera fell by the edge of the sword; not a man was left.<sup>17</sup>But Sisera fled away on foot to the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, for there was peace between Jabin the king of Hazor and the house of Heber the Kenite.<sup>18</sup>And Jael came out to meet Sisera and said to him, "Turn aside, my lord; turn aside to me; do not be afraid." So he turned aside to her into the tent, and she covered him with a rug.<sup>19</sup>And he said to her, "Please give me a little water to drink, for I am thirsty." So she opened a skin of milk and gave him a drink and covered him.<sup>20</sup>And he said to her, "Stand at the opening of the tent, and if any man comes and asks you, 'Is anyone here?' say, 'No.'"<sup>21</sup>But Jael the wife of Heber took a tent peg, and took a hammer in her hand. Then she went softly to him and drove the peg into his temple until it went down into the ground while he was lying fast asleep from weariness. So he died.<sup>22</sup>And behold, as Barak was pursuing Sisera, Jael went out to meet him and said to him, "Come, and I will show you the man whom you are seeking." So he went in to her tent, and there lay Sisera dead, with the tent peg in his temple.<sup>23</sup>So on that day God subdued Jabin the king of Canaan before the people of Israel.<sup>24</sup>And the hand of the people of Israel pressed harder and harder against Jabin the king of Canaan, until they destroyed Jabin king of Canaan.
4.overview:
Ehud dies, the cycle turns, and the oppressor this time is Jabin king of Canaan, reigning in Hazor, the city Joshua had burned (Josh. 11:10-11).

His commander has nine hundred chariots of iron: the thing Judah would not face in 1:19, now multiplied.

Deborah is already in place before the rescue begins, a prophetess settling disputes under a palm tree, and her word to Barak is a question, not a commission. He already had his orders.

He will go if she goes. She goes, and tells him what it costs: the LORD will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman. Then a flooded river, an abandoned chariot, a tent pitched near Kedesh for no stated reason, and a woman with the tools of her own trade.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Nine Hundred Chariots, and a Woman Under a Palm
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel does evil again after Ehud died (v. 1), and God sells them to Jabin king of Canaan, who reigns in Hazor, with Sisera commanding his army (v. 2). Sisera has nine hundred chariots of iron, and he oppresses Israel cruelly for twenty years (v. 3). Then the narrator introduces the person God has already put in place: Deborah, a prophetess, judging Israel, sitting under a palm between Ramah and Bethel while the people come up to her for judgment (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: What a generation declines to face does not stay the same size.
verseByVerse.examples: Twenty years is the longest oppression yet, and it is called cruel: each turn of the cycle runs lower than the last.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD after Ehud died. And the LORD sold them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor. The commander of his army was Sisera, who lived in Harosheth-hagoyim. Then the people of Israel cried out to the LORD for help, for he had 900 chariots of iron and he oppressed the people of Israel cruelly for twenty years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The trigger is named without comment: after Ehud died. Eighty years of rest ended at a funeral, exactly as chapter 2 said.

Then a detail that should stop a reader: there is a king in Hazor. Joshua took it, killed its king and set fire to the city, the only town in the northern campaign he burned, because it had been the head of all those kingdoms (Josh. 11:10-11). A century or so later there is a Jabin reigning there with a standing army. Nothing had to be conquered for that to happen; the site was left empty and somebody moved back in. What God's people do not occupy does not stay unoccupied.

Readers sometimes ask how a Jabin can reign in Hazor when Joshua killed a king of that name (Joshua 11:10). The likeliest answer is that Jabin was a dynastic name, used by more than one king of Hazor, much as Pharaoh was used in Egypt.

And nine hundred chariots of iron. In 1:19 the LORD was with Judah, and he could not drive out the inhabitants of the plain because they had chariots of iron. That excuse sounded practical at the time. It has now multiplied into a twenty-year occupation described as cruel, the longest oppression yet: eight years under Cushan, eighteen under Eglon, twenty now.
verseByVerse.note: Hazor lay north of the Sea of Galilee and was one of the largest cities in Canaan.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time. She used to sit under the palm of Deborah between Ramah and Bethel in the hill country of Ephraim, and the people of Israel came up to her for judgment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the deliverer is raised up, the narrator introduces someone already there, and three things said about her are unusual. She is a prophetess, the only judge in the book also called that: the others are given the Spirit for a campaign; she is given words. She is the wife of Lappidoth, in an ordinary household. And she was judging Israel in the plain sense: people brought disputes and she settled them. Elsewhere in this book judge usually means rescuer; Deborah is the one who actually judges, and she is doing it before any of this starts.

Israel is under occupation, with no army worth the name and no king, and there is one fixed point in the country where the word of God is applied to ordinary disputes, day after day, by a woman under a palm tree. The nation has a court.

The song in the next chapter tells us how she read it herself: the villagers ceased in Israel, until I arose; I, Deborah, arose as a mother in Israel (5:7). When the men who should have led did not, God did not stop governing his people. He put somebody else under the tree.

Does Deborah’s leadership mean women may lead and teach men in the church today? Some hold that she is a precedent for women in every office. But Deborah was a prophetess raised up in an extraordinary time, and her role exposes the failure of the men: Barak will not go without her, and the honour goes to a woman (v. 9). She never served as a priest, and she gave her word to a man to lead the army. The New Testament governs church office directly: elders are men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7). Women served God with great honour in Israel, as they do in the church, but Deborah does not overturn that order. That is the reason this commentary holds the complementarian view: Deborah’s office was a prophet’s, given by God in a crisis, while the New Testament gives standing rules for the elders who teach and govern the church. Many faithful Christians read Deborah differently, out of real love for Scripture, and the question deserves patience rather than suspicion. Both can agree on what the chapter plainly honours: God gave his people a woman who knew his word and applied it faithfully when the men had failed, and he still gives his church such women.
verseByVerse.note: Lappidoth means “torches”, and some have taken the phrase as “a woman of fire” rather than as her husband’s name; most read it as a name.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–10 — Has Not the LORD Commanded You?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Deborah summons Barak and puts the whole thing to him as a question: has not the LORD, the God of Israel, commanded you to gather ten thousand men at Mount Tabor (v. 6)? The promise comes with it: I will draw out Sisera to the Kishon with his chariots, and I will give him into your hand (v. 7). Barak's answer sets a condition: if you go with me I will go, and if not, I will not (v. 8). Deborah agrees and names the price: the road you are going on will not lead to your glory, for the LORD will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman (v. 9). Ten thousand men go up at his heels, and Deborah goes with him (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: Barak's home, Kedesh-naphtali, lay in the occupied north, within reach of Hazor.
verseByVerse.examples: God sold Israel into Jabin's hand (v. 2); now God will sell Sisera into a woman's hand. The transaction is reversed, by the same seller.

verseByVerse.quote: She sent and summoned Barak the son of Abinoam from Kedesh-naphtali and said to him, "Has not the LORD, the God of Israel, commanded you, 'Go, gather your men at Mount Tabor, taking 10,000 from the people of Naphtali and the people of Zebulun. And I will draw out Sisera, the general of Jabin's army, to meet you by the river Kishon with his chariots and his troops, and I will give him into your hand'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is not Deborah handing Barak a new commission. It is Deborah sending for a man who already has one, and asking why nothing has happened. The muster point was chosen, the tribes named, the numbers given, and Barak was at home in Kedesh-naphtali with his orders in his pocket. The problem in the north is not that God has been silent. It is that a man has heard him and stayed where he was.

The command comes wrapped in a promise, and the promise does the harder half of the work. God will draw out Sisera: Israel does not have to find him; the enemy will be brought to the chosen ground. And I will give him into your hand, the promise of this whole history, said before anybody has marched.

The ground God names is the last place a sensible commander would pick. The plain of Jezreel is flat, open, exactly the country chariots were built for. God proposes to fight nine hundred iron chariots on their own terrain, and says he will personally arrange the enemy's attendance.
verseByVerse.note: Mount Tabor rises from the Jezreel valley; the Kishon river runs through it.

verseByVerse.quote: Barak said to her, "If you will go with me, I will go, but if you will not go with me, I will not go." And she said, "I will surely go with you. Nevertheless, the road on which you are going will not lead to your glory, for the LORD will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman." Then Deborah arose and went with Barak to Kedesh. And Barak called out Zebulun and Naphtali to Kedesh. And 10,000 men went up at his heels, and Deborah went up with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Barak's answer is not a refusal, and it is not obedience either. It is a condition.

Be fair to him. He does not deny the word or dispute the odds, and Hebrews lists him among those who by faith conquered kingdoms (Heb. 11:32-33). But he has the command of God through a prophetess the whole country trusts, and what he wants in addition is a person he can see standing next to him.

She agrees at once, without a lecture, and tells him the cost. Not the victory, which is not in question, but the glory. She goes; a man who needed her presence in order to obey is given it, and the ten thousand assemble.

God does not withdraw the commission from a man who asked for a crutch. He gives him the crutch and the commission, and quietly moves the honour somewhere else. It is the kindness of a God who works with weak faith rather than waiting for strong faith, and the reason Barak's name stands in Hebrews is not the quality of his obedience but the faithfulness of the one he finally trusted.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A parenthesis drops in a fact that will matter later: Heber the Kenite has separated from his people and pitched his tent near Kedesh (v. 11). Sisera hears that Barak is on Tabor and brings out all nine hundred chariots to the river Kishon (vv. 12-13). Deborah gives the order, and ten thousand men come down off the mountain (v. 14). The LORD routs Sisera and his chariots; Sisera gets down and runs away on foot; not a man of his army is left (vv. 15-16).
verseByVerse.theology: The verb in verse 15 belongs to God: the LORD routed Sisera, infantry from a hill against armour on the plain where chariots are supposed to win.
verseByVerse.examples: Nine hundred iron chariots had made a nation afraid for twenty years, and the man who commanded them finishes the day running across country on foot like anybody else.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Heber the Kenite had separated from the Kenites, the descendants of Hobab the father-in-law of Moses, and had pitched his tent as far away as the oak in Zaanannim, which is near Kedesh. When Sisera was told that Barak the son of Abinoam had gone up to Mount Tabor, Sisera called out all his chariots, 900 chariots of iron, and all the men who were with him, from Harosheth-hagoyim to the river Kishon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A parenthesis, in the middle of a military narrative, about a man moving house. The Kenites entered this book in 1:16, settling with Judah in the south. (Moses' father-in-law is called Jethro and Reuel elsewhere; the Hebrew word can also mean brother-in-law, and Numbers 10:29 makes Hobab the son of Reuel.) Heber has left them and pitched his tent near Kedesh, precisely where Barak is mustering. Nothing explains why it is here. Six verses later it is the most important sentence in the chapter (v. 17).

Sisera then does exactly what God said he would: I will draw out Sisera... to the river Kishon. He comes of his own initiative, at speed, with everything he has, to the spot named in advance, believing he is responding to intelligence about an outnumbered enemy on a hill. He is right about all of it. Everything Sisera concludes is correct, and it takes him to the place God chose.

verseByVerse.quote: And Deborah said to Barak, "Up! For this is the day in which the LORD has given Sisera into your hand. Does not the LORD go out before you?" So Barak went down from Mount Tabor with 10,000 men following him. And the LORD routed Sisera and all his chariots and all his army before Barak by the edge of the sword. And Sisera got down from his chariot and fled away on foot. And Barak pursued the chariots and the army to Harosheth-hagoyim, and all the army of Sisera fell by the edge of the sword; not a man was left.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The order treats the battle as already decided. This is the day in which the LORD has given: not will give. And then the whole argument as a question: does not the LORD go out before you? Barak is told that somebody has already gone ahead of him into it.

That is the shape of the greatest rescue too. Christians are not sent to win a battle nobody has fought. Jesus went ahead of them into death and out of it, and Hebrews calls him the founder of their salvation and their forerunner (Hebrews 2:10; 6:20).

And he goes down. That should not be undersold: ten thousand men walk off a defensible hill onto flat ground towards massed chariots, because a woman told them the LORD had gone in front.

The LORD routed Sisera. The swords in Israelite hands are mentioned, and they are not the explanation. The next chapter gives it in one line of poetry: the torrent Kishon swept them away (5:21). The river came down, the plain turned to mud, and nine hundred iron chariots became nine hundred heavy objects stuck in a floodplain. What made them unstoppable on dry ground fixed them in place when the ground changed.

Then the detail the writer enjoys: Sisera fled away on foot. The chariot was the reason a nation had lain down for twenty years, and he abandons it in a field. Barak, whatever was wrong with his faith in verse 8, pursues properly, all the way back to their base.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sisera runs to the tent of Jael, wife of Heber, because there is peace between Jabin and that household (v. 17). She comes out to meet him, urges him in, and covers him with a rug (v. 18). He asks for water and she gives him milk (v. 19), and he makes her his sentry: if anyone asks, say no one is here (v. 20). While he lies fast asleep from weariness she takes a tent peg and a hammer, goes softly to him, and drives it through his temple into the ground (v. 21). When Barak arrives she goes out to meet him with the words the whole chapter has been building to (v. 22). God subdues Jabin, and Israel presses harder and harder until he is destroyed (vv. 23-24).
verseByVerse.theology: Heber's household had peace with Jabin (v. 17); Jael breaks with her husband's treaty to side with Israel.
verseByVerse.examples: The last two verses record something that has not happened anywhere else in this book: a job finished. Israel pressed harder and harder until they destroyed Jabin. Chapter 1 is a list of things left standing; this is the one enemy who is not left standing at all.

verseByVerse.quote: But Sisera fled away on foot to the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, for there was peace between Jabin the king of Hazor and the house of Heber the Kenite. And Jael came out to meet Sisera and said to him, "Turn aside, my lord; turn aside to me; do not be afraid." So he turned aside to her into the tent, and she covered him with a rug. And he said to her, "Please give me a little water to drink, for I am thirsty." So she opened a skin of milk and gave him a drink and covered him. And he said to her, "Stand at the opening of the tent, and if any man comes and asks you, 'Is anyone here?' say, 'No.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the parenthesis from verse 11 pays. Sisera runs for the one place in the district where he has a treaty. His reasoning is sound and his information correct.

Everything she says is what an exhausted fugitive most wants to hear, my lord, twice turn aside, and do not be afraid, and the first thing she does is cover him up. He asks for water; she gives him milk, heavier and likelier to send a worn-out man to sleep, and covers him again. Every detail is more hospitable than what was asked, and the hospitality is the trap. A guest under a tent roof was under the host's protection absolutely; that is what Sisera is counting on, and why he does not watch her.

His last recorded words are an order to lie for him. He posts as his sentry the woman who is about to kill him, and goes to sleep.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jael the wife of Heber took a tent peg, and took a hammer in her hand. Then she went softly to him and drove the peg into his temple until it went down into the ground while he was lying fast asleep from weariness. So he died. And behold, as Barak was pursuing Sisera, Jael went out to meet him and said to him, "Come, and I will show you the man whom you are seeking." So he went in to her tent, and there lay Sisera dead, with the tent peg in his temple. So on that day God subdued Jabin the king of Canaan before the people of Israel. And the hand of the people of Israel pressed harder and harder against Jabin the king of Canaan, until they destroyed Jabin king of Canaan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A tent peg and a mallet are not improvised weapons; they are the tools of her trade. Jael had driven pegs into hard ground more times than she could count, and knew the weight of that hammer. The commander of nine hundred chariots is killed in his sleep, by a woman using domestic equipment, and the writer does not soften a syllable of it.

Barak arrives at a run, and a woman steps out of a tent and offers to show him what he is looking for. Deborah's word in verse 9 lands. He will get the victory in the record and the credit in Hebrews, and he will not get this.

The chapter signs off by naming the author of the whole thing, and it is not Barak, Deborah or Jael: God subdued Jabin. Then a sentence unlike anything else in this book: Israel pressed harder and harder until they destroyed Jabin. Set that against the eight-fold did not drive out of chapter 1, and every other victory in Judges ending in a rest that wears off. Here, once, the work is carried through. Hazor is not mentioned again in this book.

It took a woman under a palm tree already doing her job, a man who would not move until she came, ten thousand men who walked onto chariot ground, a river that came down at the right hour, and a housewife with a mallet. God arranged every piece, including the tent pitched near Kedesh ten verses earlier, and then took the credit in a single sentence.

Is Jael praised for treachery against a guest? She took Israel’s side against a tyrant who had oppressed God’s people for twenty years, when Barak’s men held back, and Deborah’s song blesses her for that (5:24). The blessing honours where she stood, as Rahab’s faith is honoured (Heb 11:31); it is not a pattern for breaking faith with a guest in ordinary life. This was war, and Sisera was God’s judged enemy. Hebrews does not name Jael. The deliverers of this period are flawed pointers to a better Deliverer, who defeated the enemy of his people not by deceiving a guest but by giving his own life for them.

4.theology:
What is not faced grows. The iron chariots of 1:19 were an excuse that sounded practical at the time; now there are nine hundred of them, and the burned-out capital Israel did not occupy has a king in it again. Neither required a new decision by anybody. They are what happens to ground that is left.

A question, not a call. Barak is not being commissioned in verse 6 but asked why nothing has happened since he was. The problem in the north was never divine silence.

The transaction reversed. In verse 2 the LORD sold Israel into Jabin's hand; in verse 9 the LORD will sell Sisera into a woman's hand. The same verb and the same seller. Israel's oppression and Israel's deliverance are two entries in one ledger kept by one person.

Ordinary equipment. The chapter's deliverance is carried by a woman already doing her job under a tree, a river doing what rivers do, and a tent peg. Nothing in it was fetched in specially.
4.examples:
A general sat at home with his orders while a woman held court under a palm tree and a foreign army ran the north. When he finally moved, he moved on condition, walked ten thousand men off a hill onto chariot ground, and arrived at the end of the chase to find the war already finished by somebody with a tent peg.

Two questions come out of it. The first is Deborah's, aimed at people who have already been told what to do: has not the LORD commanded you? A great deal of Christian paralysis is not waiting for guidance but sitting on it. But hear the second half of her sentence too: does not the LORD go out before you? The command comes with the promise, and the Spirit who gives the courage to go down the hill is given before the battle, not after it. The second question is about the iron chariots, the thing you decided years ago was beyond reach. It has not stayed the size it was when you decided. And if, like Barak, you have obeyed late and on conditions, the God of this chapter still used him, and has a Deliverer whose obedience was neither late nor conditional, offered in your place.

5.title: The Song of Deborah
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Then sang Deborah and Barak the son of Abinoam on that day:<sup>2</sup>"That the leaders took the lead in Israel, that the people offered themselves willingly, bless the LORD!<sup>3</sup>"Hear, O kings; give ear, O princes; to the LORD I will sing; I will make melody to the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>4</sup>"LORD, when you went out from Seir, when you marched from the region of Edom, the earth trembled and the heavens dropped, yes, the clouds dropped water.<sup>5</sup>The mountains quaked before the LORD, even Sinai before the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>6</sup>"In the days of Shamgar, son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the highways were abandoned, and travelers kept to the byways.<sup>7</sup>The villagers ceased in Israel; they ceased to be until I arose; I, Deborah, arose as a mother in Israel.<sup>8</sup>When new gods were chosen, then war was in the gates. Was shield or spear to be seen among forty thousand in Israel?<sup>9</sup>My heart goes out to the commanders of Israel who offered themselves willingly among the people. Bless the LORD.<sup>10</sup>"Tell of it, you who ride on white donkeys, you who sit on rich carpets and you who walk by the way.<sup>11</sup>To the sound of musicians at the watering places, there they repeat the righteous triumphs of the LORD, the righteous triumphs of his villagers in Israel. "Then down to the gates marched the people of the LORD.<sup>12</sup>"Awake, awake, Deborah! Awake, awake, break out in a song! Arise, Barak, lead away your captives, O son of Abinoam.<sup>13</sup>Then down marched the remnant of the noble; the people of the LORD marched down for me against the mighty.<sup>14</sup>From Ephraim their root they marched down into the valley, following you, Benjamin, with your kinsmen; from Machir marched down the commanders, and from Zebulun those who bear the lieutenant's staff;<sup>15</sup>the princes of Issachar came with Deborah, and Issachar faithful to Barak; into the valley they rushed at his heels. Among the clans of Reuben there were great searchings of heart.<sup>16</sup>Why did you sit still among the sheepfolds, to hear the whistling for the flocks? Among the clans of Reuben there were great searchings of heart.<sup>17</sup>Gilead stayed beyond the Jordan; and Dan, why did he stay with the ships? Asher sat still at the coast of the sea, staying by his landings.<sup>18</sup>Zebulun is a people who risked their lives to the death; Naphtali, too, on the heights of the field.<sup>19</sup>"The kings came, they fought; then fought the kings of Canaan, at Taanach, by the waters of Megiddo; they got no spoils of silver.<sup>20</sup>From heaven the stars fought, from their courses they fought against Sisera.<sup>21</sup>The torrent Kishon swept them away, the ancient torrent, the torrent Kishon. March on, my soul, with might!<sup>22</sup>"Then loud beat the horses' hoofs with the galloping, galloping of his steeds.<sup>23</sup>"Curse Meroz, says the angel of the LORD, curse its inhabitants thoroughly, because they did not come to the help of the LORD, to the help of the LORD against the mighty.<sup>24</sup>"Most blessed of women be Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, of tent-dwelling women most blessed.<sup>25</sup>He asked for water and she gave him milk; she brought him curds in a noble's bowl.<sup>26</sup>She sent her hand to the tent peg and her right hand to the workmen's mallet; she struck Sisera; she crushed his head; she shattered and pierced his temple.<sup>27</sup>Between her feet he sank, he fell, he lay still; between her feet he sank, he fell; where he sank, there he fell—dead.<sup>28</sup>"Out of the window she peered, the mother of Sisera wailed through the lattice: 'Why is his chariot so long in coming? Why tarry the hoofbeats of his chariots?'<sup>29</sup>Her wisest princesses answer, indeed, she answers herself,<sup>30</sup>'Have they not found and divided the spoil?— A womb or two for every man; spoil of dyed materials for Sisera, spoil of dyed materials embroidered, two pieces of dyed work embroidered for the neck as spoil?'<sup>31</sup>"So may all your enemies perish, O LORD! But your friends be like the sun as he rises in his might." And the land had rest for forty years.
5.overview:
They sang it on the day, with the bodies still in the valley, and the first thing the song blesses God for is not the victory but the volunteering (v. 2). After a chapter in which the general had to be sent for, that is where the gratitude starts.

The poem reaches back to the LORD marching north out of Seir with the earth trembling (vv. 4-5). The longest section is an uncomfortable muster roll: six tribes came, and Reuben, Gilead, Dan and Asher stayed with their livelihoods. Then the song says what chapter 4 left out, that the river came down, and its harshest word falls not on Canaan but on Meroz, an Israelite town that stayed at home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The God Who Marched from Seir
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The song opens in praise, reaches back to Sinai, and describes what the occupation had done to Israel before it turns on one line: until I arose; I, Deborah, arose as a mother in Israel (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel's first response to its rescue is a song, as it was at the Red Sea (Exod. 15). Worship comes before analysis, and the song does its thinking in the form of praise.
verseByVerse.examples: When ordinary life shrinks, when the roads empty and people stop going out, the song invites us to ask not only what has gone wrong around us but what has been chosen in place of God (v. 8).

verseByVerse.quote: Then sang Deborah and Barak the son of Abinoam on that day: "That the leaders took the lead in Israel, that the people offered themselves willingly, bless the LORD! "Hear, O kings; give ear, O princes; to the LORD I will sing; I will make melody to the LORD, the God of Israel. "LORD, when you went out from Seir, when you marched from the region of Edom, the earth trembled and the heavens dropped, yes, the clouds dropped water. The mountains quaked before the LORD, even Sinai before the LORD, the God of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They sing on the day itself, not at an anniversary once somebody had time to compose properly. The first thing the song blesses God for is not the victory. It is the volunteering: that the leaders took the lead in Israel, that the people offered themselves willingly. After a chapter in which a general had to be sent for and asked why he was still at home, the poem's opening note of gratitude is that people finally came.

That theme brackets the whole song. It is here in verse 2 and again in verse 9, and everything between is a list of who did and who did not.

The audience summoned is not Israel. It is kings and princes — the class of person who has just been beaten. Deborah sings this at the rulers of the region, and the content is a description of what happens to armies that come against her God.

Before saying a word about Sisera, the song goes back generations, to Sinai. Seir and Edom are the country south of the Dead Sea, on the road up from Sinai. What is being described is the LORD marching north out of the desert with the earth shaking under him — the language of the exodus generation, of the mountain that smoked and the ground that could not hold still.

The poetic move is the whole argument of the song. A skirmish in Galilee is not being reported as a local success. It is being filed as one more episode in a march that started at Sinai, and the same weather is mentioned in both: the clouds dropped water. What is about to destroy Sisera's chariots is a storm, and the song has already told the reader who is walking in it.
verseByVerse.note: “Even Sinai” may be rendered “the One of Sinai” (ESV note). The Hebrew of this song is very old and in places hard, so translations differ more here than in the prose of chapter 4.

verseByVerse.quote: "In the days of Shamgar, son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the highways were abandoned, and travelers kept to the byways. The villagers ceased in Israel; they ceased to be until I arose; I, Deborah, arose as a mother in Israel. When new gods were chosen, then war was in the gates. Was shield or spear to be seen among forty thousand in Israel? My heart goes out to the commanders of Israel who offered themselves willingly among the people. Bless the LORD. "Tell of it, you who ride on white donkeys, you who sit on rich carpets and you who walk by the way. To the sound of musicians at the watering places, there they repeat the righteous triumphs of the LORD, the righteous triumphs of his villagers in Israel. "Then down to the gates marched the people of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is what twenty years of occupation looked like from ground level, and the song describes it in terms of roads.

The highways were empty. Nobody used the main routes, because the main routes were where you were robbed, so traffic moved on tracks and back lanes. Trade slowed to the pace of people travelling scared.

Then the second detail, and it is worse: the villagers ceased. The unwalled settlements emptied. Farming families gave up the open country and moved into towns with gates, which meant the fields went out of cultivation and the nation began quietly starving in its own land.

That is what tyranny does. It does not usually announce itself in massacres; it shrinks ordinary life until people stop going out.

The turn comes in a single line, and the title she gives herself is not judge, prophetess or commander. A mother in Israel.

It is exactly right for what she did. She did not lead an army; she sent for a man who should have gone already, went with him when he would not go alone, and told him when to move. The country was rescued by somebody behaving like a mother to it.

Verse 8 states the causation the prose never quite spelled out. New gods were chosen, and then war came to the gates. The idolatry was not a religious matter running alongside a political one; it was the reason the roads emptied.

And the second half is a rhetorical question with a terrible answer. Forty thousand men in Israel, and not a shield or a spear among them — a nation systematically disarmed by its occupiers, exactly as the Philistines will later keep Israel without a blacksmith (1 Sam. 13:19-22).

Then the summons to remember, and it is aimed at everybody. The people on white donkeys are the wealthy; the people walking are everyone else; and both are told to talk about this at the watering places, where villagers meet every day.

The song is arranging its own retelling. In chapter 2 a generation grew up that did not know what the LORD had done (2:10); here his victories are to be told again at every well.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The roll call (v. 12): Ephraim, Benjamin, Machir, Zebulun and Issachar march down (vv. 13-15a); Reuben, Gilead, Dan and Asher stay home, each with a reason (vv. 15b-17); and Zebulun and Naphtali risked their lives to the death (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: A muster roll is an unusual thing to set to music. The song makes the record of who came part of Israel's worship, so that faithfulness and its absence are both remembered before God.
verseByVerse.examples: Most of us will never be Deborah or Jael. The roll call is where ordinary believers find themselves, among the tribes who came or among those who stayed at home.

verseByVerse.quote: "Awake, awake, Deborah! Awake, awake, break out in a song! Arise, Barak, lead away your captives, O son of Abinoam. Then down marched the remnant of the noble; the people of the LORD marched down for me against the mighty. From Ephraim their root they marched down into the valley, following you, Benjamin, with your kinsmen; from Machir marched down the commanders, and from Zebulun those who bear the lieutenant's staff; the princes of Issachar came with Deborah, and Issachar faithful to Barak; into the valley they rushed at his heels. Among the clans of Reuben there were great searchings of heart. Why did you sit still among the sheepfolds, to hear the whistling for the flocks? Among the clans of Reuben there were great searchings of heart. Gilead stayed beyond the Jordan; and Dan, why did he stay with the ships? Asher sat still at the coast of the sea, staying by his landings. Zebulun is a people who risked their lives to the death; Naphtali, too, on the heights of the field.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Five names come first, and the verbs are all of movement: marched down, came, rushed at his heels. Issachar is described as rushing into the valley — not summoned, not dragged, but running downhill towards nine hundred chariots.

Then the absentees, and the song's treatment of Reuben is the sharpest thing in it. He is not accused of cowardice, treachery or indifference. What he is charged with is great searchings of heart — and the phrase is repeated, before and after the question, so that the reader cannot miss it. Reuben thought about it seriously, at length and with real feeling, and there is no suggestion that the deliberation was insincere. The picture between the two repetitions is devastating in its ordinariness: sitting among the sheepfolds, listening to the whistling for the flocks. That is a man staying within earshot of his own livelihood while the decision goes on inside him.

The other three are given no motive beyond their occupations: Gilead has a river in the way, Dan has shipping, and Asher stays by his landings. Not one of these is a wicked excuse. They are the reasons anybody would give: distance, business, responsibilities that do not pause because somebody else is in trouble. The song simply records what each tribe was doing at the time, and lets the list stand next to the next verse.

Zebulun and Naphtali, the two tribes Barak mustered in 4:6, are given the highest line in the song: they risked their lives to the death on the exposed heights of the field. Set the two halves of the roll call side by side, because that is what the poem is for. Reuben, deliberating within earshot of the sheep. Zebulun, on the heights of the field.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–23 — From Heaven the Stars Fought
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The kings of Canaan fought at Taanach and got no spoil (v. 19); the stars fought and the Kishon swept them away (vv. 20-22); and the angel of the LORD curses Meroz because they did not come to the help of the LORD (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: The song credits the victory to heaven and to the creation together: the stars fought, and the river swept the enemy away. Israel's part was real, but it was not what decided the day.
verseByVerse.examples: Meroz is cursed for staying away from what God was doing. It is worth asking where he is at work around us, and whether we have kept our distance.

verseByVerse.quote: "The kings came, they fought; then fought the kings of Canaan, at Taanach, by the waters of Megiddo; they got no spoils of silver. From heaven the stars fought, from their courses they fought against Sisera. The torrent Kishon swept them away, the ancient torrent, the torrent Kishon. March on, my soul, with might! "Then loud beat the horses' hoofs with the galloping, galloping of his steeds. "Curse Meroz, says the angel of the LORD, curse its inhabitants thoroughly, because they did not come to the help of the LORD, to the help of the LORD against the mighty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kings came for plunder and went home with nothing, if they went home.

Chapter 4 said only that the LORD routed Sisera. The song fills in the mechanism with a storm. The Kishon is a trickle for most of the year and a torrent when rain falls on the hills, and the plain of Megiddo turns to a bog in an afternoon. Nine hundred iron chariots, on flat ground, in mud: the weight that made them irresistible on a dry plain fixed them where they stood, and the army that had terrorised the north for twenty years could not even run. And the line above it is bigger still: whatever the stars fought means precisely, the claim is that the created order itself was ranged against him. Sisera worshipped gods who were supposed to run the weather. The weather killed him.

Then the harshest sentence in the song, aimed not at Canaan but at an Israelite settlement near enough to have come. Reuben was chided and Dan was asked a question; Meroz is cursed, thoroughly, by the angel of the LORD, the figure who delivered the covenant lawsuit at Bochim in chapter 2. The charge is not that Meroz fought on the wrong side, but that they did not come to the help of the LORD against the mighty, as though God needed reinforcements, which he plainly did not. They are held responsible for not turning up to a battle he had already won.

The curse is real, and it is spoken over a town that had stayed home from a deliverance God had given freely. The same God who curses Meroz had come up from Sinai for these people before any of them lifted a spear; the point of the warning is to send his people back to him, not to make them earn the rescue.
verseByVerse.note: The Kishon drains the Jezreel valley and runs north-west to the sea below Mount Carmel; in the dry season it is little more than a stream.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jael is blessed as most blessed of women and the deed told again slowly (vv. 24-27). Then the song moves to a window in Canaan, where Sisera's mother waits and comforts herself (vv. 28-30).
verseByVerse.theology: The song blesses a deed that most readers find hard, and the comment below takes up directly the question of Jael and her guest.
verseByVerse.examples: Even in a victory song, Israel's poet sees the grief on the other side. That is worth learning for the way God's people speak about those they oppose, without pretending that evil was not evil.

verseByVerse.quote: "Most blessed of women be Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, of tent-dwelling women most blessed. He asked for water and she gave him milk; she brought him curds in a noble's bowl. She sent her hand to the tent peg and her right hand to the workmen's mallet; she struck Sisera; she crushed his head; she shattered and pierced his temple. Between her feet he sank, he fell, he lay still; between her feet he sank, he fell; where he sank, there he fell—dead. "Out of the window she peered, the mother of Sisera wailed through the lattice: 'Why is his chariot so long in coming? Why tarry the hoofbeats of his chariots?' Her wisest princesses answer, indeed, she answers herself, 'Have they not found and divided the spoil?— A womb or two for every man; spoil of dyed materials for Sisera, spoil of dyed materials embroidered, two pieces of dyed work embroidered for the neck as spoil?'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The song answers the curse of Meroz with a blessing, and it is put in the strongest terms it can find.

There is only one other person in Scripture greeted in words like these. When Mary comes to Elizabeth's house, Elizabeth cries out, blessed are you among women (Luke 1:42). The two people so described are the mother of the Lord and a Kenite housewife with a mallet, and both blessings are spoken over a woman about something God has done that nobody expected.

The poem tells the deed more slowly than the prose did, and it names the tools twice: the tent peg, and the workmen's mallet. Not a weapon that happened to be lying about — the equipment of a trade, in the hand that used it professionally.

Then the hammering. Read verse 27 aloud and the sound of it is the point: he sank, he fell, he lay still... he sank, he fell... where he sank, there he fell. The lines beat like a mallet on a peg, and the last word in the stanza is the last word about Sisera.

Then the song does something no reader expects. It leaves the battlefield, crosses into enemy country, and stops at a window, where a woman is watching the road for her son. She has waited long enough to start asking out loud why the chariots have not come back. We know why; she does not. It is one of the most humane moments in the Old Testament, written by the winning side on the day of the victory.

Then comes the reassurance she settles on, the ugliest line in the song. The delay is explained, she decides, by the sharing out of plunder, and the first item on the list is women: a womb or two for every man, in the crudest of terms. A mother says this at a window to steady herself, and it shows what such an army did in the villages and what the empty highways of verse 6 were about. In three verses the song makes us pity her and then shows us what she is comfortable with.

Does the song bless Jael for betraying a guest? It blesses her for taking the LORD’s side against a tyrant who had oppressed his people for twenty years, at the hour when whole tribes stayed at home (v. 24). Rahab is honoured in the same way for where she stood (Hebrews 11:31). The song is not a pattern for breaking faith with a guest in ordinary life: this was war, and Sisera was an enemy God had already judged. Hebrews does not name Jael, and even the judges it does name are commended for their faith, not for everything they did (Hebrews 11:32).

One line of the song has long made Christians think further back. She crushed his head (v. 26): many have heard in it an echo of the first promise, that the woman’s offspring would bruise the serpent’s head (Genesis 3:15). The song does not say so, and Jael is no saviour. But each time God breaks an oppressor through the weak he keeps that promise in small, until the God of peace crushes Satan under his people’s feet (Romans 16:20), because Christ was crushed for them first (Isaiah 53:5).

verseByVerse.ref: v. 31 — Like the Sun as He Rises
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The song ends in one sentence of prayer and one of report: the land had rest for forty years (v. 31).
verseByVerse.theology: The closing prayer looks beyond this one battle to the end of all evil and the shining of all who love God, a hope the rest of Scripture takes up.
verseByVerse.examples: The rest is real, it is dated, and it lasts one generation; the reader of Judges knows what the next sentence of the book will be. Peace in this world, however hard won, is always for a time.

verseByVerse.quote: "So may all your enemies perish, O LORD! But your friends be like the sun as he rises in his might." And the land had rest for forty years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The song ends in prayer, and the two halves of it are one wish.

The first half is hard, and it should not be tidied up: so may all your enemies perish. It is asked immediately after a scene of a bereaved mother, by people who have just seen what these enemies did to their villages. It is not the reflex of the comfortable.

Prayers like this run all through the Psalms and they ask for one thing: that evil should stop — not be managed, not be balanced, but end. Anybody who has looked closely at what was happening on the roads of Galilee in verse 6, or heard what Sisera's mother expected her son to be doing, has felt the force of the request. The last book of the Bible contains the same prayer, asked by people under an altar, and it is answered rather than rebuked (Rev. 6:10).

Christians pray it now in the light of the cross. Jesus taught his people to pray for their enemies (Matthew 5:44), and the prayer that evil should end is answered in two ways: some enemies of God are made his friends, as Paul was, and the rest will meet the justice he has promised. Every friend of God was once an enemy, reconciled by the death of his Son (Romans 5:10).

The second half is the one to take away. But your friends be like the sun as he rises in his might.

It is a sunrise: the first minute of full light after a night, when the sky goes from grey to unbearable and everything on the ground is suddenly visible. That is what the poem asks for the people who love God — not safety, not comfort, not even victory, but that they should be like that.

It is nearly the last line of the song, and the New Testament finishes the thought. Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Matt. 13:43).

Then the narrator adds one flat sentence and the singing stops. And the land had rest for forty years.

Forty years of quiet, bought by a woman under a palm tree, a man who had to be fetched, two tribes who went up the heights, a river in spate, and a housewife with a mallet — and every bit of it credited, in the song they sang about it, to the God who came up out of the south with the mountains shaking and the clouds dropping water.

5.theology:
One march, from Sinai to the Kishon. Before a word about Sisera, the song describes God coming up out of Edom with the clouds dropping water (vv. 4-5), and the same weather returns in verse 21 when the river takes the chariots. What happened in that valley was not a lucky storm but an arrival. The same God would one day arrive in person, and at the cross Jesus disarmed the powers behind every Sisera (Colossians 2:15).

What the absent tribes were doing. The song never calls Reuben, Gilead, Dan or Asher cowards. It records their occupations and sets them beside Zebulun, who came. Reuben's charge is the most searching in the book because it is not indifference: he took the matter seriously and stayed within earshot of his flocks.

Meroz. The one community cursed in this song is cursed for doing nothing, by the angel of the LORD who delivered the covenant lawsuit at Bochim. Its entire trace in the Bible is the sentence cursing it for staying home.

Two women at the end. Jael is called most blessed of women, echoed only in Elizabeth's greeting to Mary (Luke 1:42). Then the song stops at the enemy's window, where another woman's comfort tells the reader what had been happening on those empty highways for twenty years.
5.examples:
Then: A nation that had kept off the main roads for twenty years sang, on the day of its rescue, a song that named the tribes who came and those who did not, cursed a village for staying home, blessed a housewife with a mallet, and paused at the window of the enemy commander's mother.

Now: Reuben is the one to sit with, because he is the most respectable figure in the poem. He did not refuse; he deliberated, in earnest, within hearing of his own business, and the moment passed. The song's question to him is one to put to yourself about whatever you are weighing: what are you sitting among while the searching of heart goes on? The God who calls is the one who has already marched out for his people and won; he does not ask us to save him, but to come where he is working. Every reader has been Reuben more than once, and Christ never was: he went all the way into the battle that mattered, and his obedience covers our staying home. So the answer to a Reuben moment is not self-reproach but confession, and the Spirit who stirred Zebulun gives the willingness that verse 2 blesses God for.

6.title: The Call of Gideon
6.text: <sup>1</sup>The people of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD gave them into the hand of Midian seven years.<sup>2</sup>And the hand of Midian overpowered Israel, and because of Midian the people of Israel made for themselves the dens that are in the mountains and the caves and the strongholds.<sup>3</sup>For whenever the Israelites planted crops, the Midianites and the Amalekites and the people of the East would come up against them.<sup>4</sup>They would encamp against them and devour the produce of the land, as far as Gaza, and leave no sustenance in Israel and no sheep or ox or donkey.<sup>5</sup>For they would come up with their livestock and their tents; they would come like locusts in number—both they and their camels could not be counted—so that they laid waste the land as they came in.<sup>6</sup>And Israel was brought very low because of Midian. And the people of Israel cried out for help to the LORD.<sup>7</sup>When the people of Israel cried out to the LORD on account of the Midianites,<sup>8</sup>the LORD sent a prophet to the people of Israel. And he said to them, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: I led you up from Egypt and brought you out of the house of slavery.<sup>9</sup>And I delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of all who oppressed you, and drove them out before you and gave you their land.<sup>10</sup>And I said to you, 'I am the LORD your God; you shall not fear the gods of the Amorites in whose land you dwell.' But you have not obeyed my voice."<sup>11</sup>Now the angel of the LORD came and sat under the terebinth at Ophrah, which belonged to Joash the Abiezrite, while his son Gideon was beating out wheat in the winepress to hide it from the Midianites.<sup>12</sup>And the angel of the LORD appeared to him and said to him, "The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor."<sup>13</sup>And Gideon said to him, "Please, my lord, if the LORD is with us, why then has all this happened to us? And where are all his wonderful deeds that our fathers recounted to us, saying, 'Did not the LORD bring us up from Egypt?' But now the LORD has forsaken us and given us into the hand of Midian."<sup>14</sup>And the LORD turned to him and said, "Go in this might of yours and save Israel from the hand of Midian; do not I send you?"<sup>15</sup>And he said to him, "Please, Lord, how can I save Israel? Behold, my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house."<sup>16</sup>And the LORD said to him, "But I will be with you, and you shall strike the Midianites as one man."<sup>17</sup>And he said to him, "If now I have found favor in your eyes, then show me a sign that it is you who speak with me.<sup>18</sup>Please do not depart from here until I come to you and bring out my present and set it before you." And he said, "I will stay till you return."<sup>19</sup>So Gideon went into his house and prepared a young goat and unleavened cakes from an ephah of flour. The meat he put in a basket, and the broth he put in a pot, and brought them to him under the terebinth and presented them.<sup>20</sup>And the angel of God said to him, "Take the meat and the unleavened cakes, and put them on this rock, and pour the broth over them." And he did so.<sup>21</sup>Then the angel of the LORD reached out the tip of the staff that was in his hand and touched the meat and the unleavened cakes. And fire sprang up from the rock and consumed the meat and the unleavened cakes. And the angel of the LORD vanished from his sight.<sup>22</sup>Then Gideon perceived that he was the angel of the LORD. And Gideon said, "Alas, O Lord GOD! For now I have seen the angel of the LORD face to face."<sup>23</sup>But the LORD said to him, "Peace be to you. Do not fear; you shall not die."<sup>24</sup>Then Gideon built an altar there to the LORD and called it, The LORD Is Peace. To this day it still stands at Ophrah, which belongs to the Abiezrites.<sup>25</sup>That night the LORD said to him, "Take your father's bull, and the second bull seven years old, and pull down the altar of Baal that your father has, and cut down the Asherah that is beside it<sup>26</sup>and build an altar to the LORD your God on the top of the stronghold here, with stones laid in due order. Then take the second bull and offer it as a burnt offering with the wood of the Asherah that you shall cut down."<sup>27</sup>So Gideon took ten men of his servants and did as the LORD had told him. But because he was too afraid of his family and the men of the town to do it by day, he did it by night.<sup>28</sup>When the men of the town rose early in the morning, behold, the altar of Baal was broken down, and the Asherah beside it was cut down, and the second bull was offered on the altar that had been built.<sup>29</sup>And they said to one another, "Who has done this thing?" And after they had searched and inquired, they said, "Gideon the son of Joash has done this thing."<sup>30</sup>Then the men of the town said to Joash, "Bring out your son, that he may die, for he has broken down the altar of Baal and cut down the Asherah beside it."<sup>31</sup>But Joash said to all who stood against him, "Will you contend for Baal? Or will you save him? Whoever contends for him shall be put to death by morning. If he is a god, let him contend for himself, because his altar has been broken down."<sup>32</sup>Therefore on that day Gideon was called Jerubbaal, that is to say, "Let Baal contend against him," because he broke down his altar.<sup>33</sup>Now all the Midianites and the Amalekites and the people of the East came together, and they crossed the Jordan and encamped in the Valley of Jezreel.<sup>34</sup>But the Spirit of the LORD clothed Gideon, and he sounded the trumpet, and the Abiezrites were called out to follow him.<sup>35</sup>And he sent messengers throughout all Manasseh, and they too were called out to follow him. And he sent messengers to Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali, and they went up to meet them.<sup>36</sup>Then Gideon said to God, "If you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said,<sup>37</sup>behold, I am laying a fleece of wool on the threshing floor. If there is dew on the fleece alone, and it is dry on all the ground, then I shall know that you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said."<sup>38</sup>And it was so. When he rose early next morning and squeezed the fleece, he wrung enough dew from the fleece to fill a bowl with water.<sup>39</sup>Then Gideon said to God, "Let not your anger burn against me; let me speak just once more. Please let me test just once more with the fleece. Please let it be dry on the fleece only, and on all the ground let there be dew."<sup>40</sup>And God did so that night; and it was dry on the fleece only, and on all the ground there was dew.
6.overview:
Seven years of Midian, and Israel is living in caves, because the raiders come every harvest and take the year's work and the plough animals with it.

They cry out, and God's first answer is not a rescuer but a preacher. Then the angel of the LORD greets a man hiding his threshing in a winepress as a mighty man of valor. What follows is God's patience, at length: fire out of a rock, peace spoken to a man who expected to die, an altar pulled down in the dark and recorded as obedience anyway, the Spirit clothing himself with Gideon, and then, after all of it, a fleece, twice.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Locusts, Caves, and a Sermon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Seven years of Midianite raids drive Israel into the hills. When they cry out, God sends a prophet before he sends a deliverer.
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter opens with the LORD giving his people into Midian's hand (v. 1). The raids are discipline, and discipline has a purpose: to bring a people back to the God they have left.
verseByVerse.examples: When we ask God to take away a pain, he sometimes deals first with something we did not mention. That is not indifference to the pain; it is care for the whole person.

verseByVerse.quote: The people of Israel did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD gave them into the hand of Midian seven years. And the hand of Midian overpowered Israel, and because of Midian the people of Israel made for themselves the dens that are in the mountains and the caves and the strongholds. For whenever the Israelites planted crops, the Midianites and the Amalekites and the people of the East would come up against them. They would encamp against them and devour the produce of the land, as far as Gaza, and leave no sustenance in Israel and no sheep or ox or donkey. For they would come up with their livestock and their tents; they would come like locusts in number—both they and their camels could not be counted—so that they laid waste the land as they came in. And Israel was brought very low because of Midian. And the people of Israel cried out for help to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Picture what verse 2 describes: God's people, in the land God swore to give them, living underground, not in the walled towns or on the farms but in dens, caves and strongholds up in the hills. A generation earlier the complaint was about towns not taken; now Israelites are digging holes to sleep in on ground that is legally theirs.

The oppression is agricultural, and the timing is the cruelty. This is not an invasion but an annual harvest. Israel is left alone to plough, sow, weed and watch the crop come up. Then, when it is ready to cut, the raiders arrive and camp on it. Everything is taken — the grain, and then the sheep and the oxen and the donkeys, which means next year's ploughing as well.

A whole year of labour, every year, done for somebody else. That is a particular kind of misery: not the terror of a battle but the slow exhaustion of working hard at something you already know you will not keep.

Two details explain how it was possible. The first is the comparison with locusts: not an army but a swarm, arriving in a season, eating everything green and moving on. The second is the camels, and this is probably the earliest record of camels used at this scale in war. A camel raid could cross desert that horses could not, cover ground fast, appear where nobody was watching and be gone before a defence could form. Israel had no answer to it and no way even to find them.

They cry out. As always in this book, it is not called repentance; they are hungry and frightened and they make a noise.
verseByVerse.note: Midian's homeland lay in the desert south-east of Israel, east of the Gulf of Aqaba; the Amalekites and the people of the East (v. 3) were other desert tribes who rode with them.

verseByVerse.quote: When the people of Israel cried out to the LORD on account of the Midianites, the LORD sent a prophet to the people of Israel. And he said to them, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: I led you up from Egypt and brought you out of the house of slavery. And I delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of all who oppressed you, and drove them out before you and gave you their land. And I said to you, 'I am the LORD your God; you shall not fear the gods of the Amorites in whose land you dwell.' But you have not obeyed my voice."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the surprise of the chapter. Every previous cycle has run the same way: they cried out, and the LORD raised up a deliverer. Here God sends a preacher.

The sermon is a recital of what God has done, in the first person, as at Bochim. Four verbs, all his: I led you up, I brought you out, I delivered, I drove them out. And one gift: I gave you their land. Only then the command, I am the LORD your God; you shall not fear the gods of the Amorites, and the charge, the same words the angel used in 2:2. The order matters: the command was never the price of the rescue. It was given to people already brought out, as the shape of life with the God who had done it.

The prophet brings no promise and no comfort. He states the case and stops, and he is never named. That silence is a kindness rather than a cruelty. Israel's cry so far says nothing about Baal, and a rescue delivered into an unchanged situation would only have started the clock on the next seven years. God takes the crying out seriously enough to answer the real problem rather than the stated one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–24 — The LORD Is with You, Mighty Man of Valour
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The angel of the LORD finds Gideon hiding his harvest and calls him to save Israel. Gideon argues, asks for a sign, and receives far more than he asked: fire from the rock, and the word of peace.
verseByVerse.theology: Gideon's call follows the pattern of Moses' call closely: an appearance, an objection, a promise of God's presence and a sign. God is not inventing a new way of saving; he is doing again what he did at the exodus.
verseByVerse.examples: Gideon's complaint in verse 13 is not punished. God lets a frightened man say what he thinks and answers him with a calling rather than a rebuke. Honest prayer, even bitter prayer, is not shut out.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the angel of the LORD came and sat under the terebinth at Ophrah, which belonged to Joash the Abiezrite, while his son Gideon was beating out wheat in the winepress to hide it from the Midianites. And the angel of the LORD appeared to him and said to him, "The LORD is with you, O mighty man of valor."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two men are in this verse and neither is doing what he should be. The angel of the LORD is sitting under a tree; Gideon is threshing wheat in a hole in the ground.

The detail is precise and it needs unpacking. Wheat was threshed on a threshing floor: a flat open place, deliberately sited on a rise, because the whole process depends on wind. You beat the grain out and then throw it up so the breeze carries the chaff away.

A winepress is the opposite of that in every respect. It is a pit cut down into rock, out of the wind, where grapes were trodden. Nothing about it works for threshing wheat, and the writer tells us why he is doing it anyway: to hide it from the Midianites.

So the picture is a man crouched in a stone pit, doing a job badly in the one place it cannot be done well, because the alternative is being seen. He is not fighting anybody. He is saving a few bushels of grain from the swarm.

Both halves of the greeting look wrong. The LORD is with you, said to a man in a hole in an occupied country; and O mighty man of valour, said to somebody hiding his breakfast.

The Hebrew phrase, gibbor hayil, is a real title — used of soldiers of proven courage and of men of substance in a community. It is the last description anybody in Ophrah would have applied to Gideon that day, including Gideon.

God is not flattering him and he is not being ironic. He is naming what this man is going to be, before there is any evidence for it, and the naming is the first act of the making.

Who is the angel of the LORD? In verse 14 the text simply says the LORD turned to him, and in verse 22 Gideon fears for his life because he has seen this messenger face to face. Some take him as a created angel carrying God’s full authority. The best reading, held by many in the Reformed tradition, is that this is the LORD appearing in person, most likely the Son before his incarnation, the one through whom God has always made himself known (John 1:18).

How could Gideon see him face to face and live (v. 22; Exodus 33:20)? God showed himself in a veiled form, and the word Peace be to you; do not fear (v. 23) kept him.
verseByVerse.note: Ophrah, Gideon's home town, belonged to the clan of Abiezer in western Manasseh; its exact site is not known.

verseByVerse.quote: And Gideon said to him, "Please, my lord, if the LORD is with us, why then has all this happened to us? And where are all his wonderful deeds that our fathers recounted to us, saying, 'Did not the LORD bring us up from Egypt?' But now the LORD has forsaken us and given us into the hand of Midian." And the LORD turned to him and said, "Go in this might of yours and save Israel from the hand of Midian; do not I send you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gideon does not thank the messenger for the compliment. He argues with the first half of it, and the argument is the honest complaint of a man who has been reading his circumstances.

Now hold this verse against 2:10, because Gideon is the opposite problem. There the tragedy was a generation that did not know the LORD or the work that he had done. Gideon knows the work. He can quote it — his wonderful deeds that our fathers recounted to us, and he knows the sentence that goes with them: did not the LORD bring us up from Egypt?

The stories got through to him. Somebody answered the question at Gilgal after all. And he has looked at the stories, looked at the winepress, and concluded that they belong to different worlds.

That is a distinct kind of unbelief and a very common one. It is not ignorance and it is not denial. It is a man who believes every word of what God did and has quietly stopped expecting anything of the sort now — who reads his own circumstances as the more recent and reliable evidence.

His conclusion is a serious charge: the LORD has forsaken us. It is also, in this book, precisely wrong. What has happened to Israel is not abandonment; chapter 2 said God gave them over, sold them, was against them for harm. Gideon has mistaken discipline for desertion.

The reply does not answer a single one of his questions.

God does not defend himself, explain the seven years, or produce a theology of suffering. He gives the man a job.

And the phrase is deliberately puzzling: go in this might of yours. What might? The only thing Gideon has demonstrated is the ability to hide grain and complain accurately. The sentence is either mockery or a promise about what is now in him, and the question that follows settles which: do not I send you?

The whole commission rests on the sending. Not on the strength, which is not there, but on the one who is doing the sending.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, "Please, Lord, how can I save Israel? Behold, my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house." And the LORD said to him, "But I will be with you, and you shall strike the Midianites as one man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
His objection is not false modesty. It is an accurate report.

He gives two facts, and each is a step down. Manasseh is a middling tribe; within it his clan is the weakest; within the clan he is the least in his own father's household. He is at the bottom of a small heap, and everything he says is true.

What is wrong with it is the question itself: how can I save Israel? The question assumes the saving depends on his resources, and on that assumption the inventory is decisive.

God does not argue with the inventory. He does not tell Gideon that he has hidden potential, that Manasseh is stronger than he thinks, or that the least in a household often surprises people. Every fact Gideon has stated is allowed to stand.

This exchange has happened before, word for word in substance, at a burning bush on the far side of a desert. Moses said, who am I that I should go to Pharaoh? and God answered, but I will be with you (Ex. 3:11-12). The question was about the man; the answer was about God, and it did not engage with the question at all.

That is the shape of every genuine call in Scripture. The objection is usually correct and always irrelevant. Neither man is told he is capable. Both are told who is coming with them.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, "If now I have found favor in your eyes, then show me a sign that it is you who speak with me. Please do not depart from here until I come to you and bring out my present and set it before you." And he said, "I will stay till you return." So Gideon went into his house and prepared a young goat and unleavened cakes from an ephah of flour. The meat he put in a basket, and the broth he put in a pot, and brought them to him under the terebinth and presented them. And the angel of God said to him, "Take the meat and the unleavened cakes, and put them on this rock, and pour the broth over them." And he did so. Then the angel of the LORD reached out the tip of the staff that was in his hand and touched the meat and the unleavened cakes. And fire sprang up from the rock and consumed the meat and the unleavened cakes. And the angel of the LORD vanished from his sight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He asks for a sign, and then asks the visitor to wait while he goes and gets something.

Take in what he brings out, in the seventh year of raiders who leave no sustenance in Israel. A whole young goat. An ephah of flour, about the amount Abraham had Sarah bake for the three visitors at Mamre.

Gideon has been threshing in a pit to save a little grain, and he takes a large part of what his household has and cooks it for a stranger under a tree. Whatever is wrong with his faith, his hospitality is not calculating.

The instruction turns a meal into an offering. Meat and bread on a rock, and then the broth poured over the lot, which soaks everything and makes it very much harder to burn.

The staff touches it and fire comes out of the rock — not down from the sky, but up through the stone under the food. It burns a soaked meal to nothing, and the visitor is gone.

Gideon asked for proof of identity, and he gets fire out of the ground and an empty space under the tree.
verseByVerse.note: An ephah was about 3/5 bushel (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Gideon perceived that he was the angel of the LORD. And Gideon said, "Alas, O Lord GOD! For now I have seen the angel of the LORD face to face." But the LORD said to him, "Peace be to you. Do not fear; you shall not die." Then Gideon built an altar there to the LORD and called it, The LORD Is Peace. To this day it still stands at Ophrah, which belongs to the Abiezrites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The proof he asked for arrives, and the first thing it produces in him is terror.

He is frightened because he has been talking face to face with somebody he now understands, and the conviction ran deep in Israel that this kills a man. God had told Moses plainly: you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live (Ex. 33:20). Jacob said the same in astonishment at Peniel: I have seen God face to face, and yet my life has been delivered (Gen. 32:30). Gideon's terror is the correct instinct of a man who has just realised who was sitting under the tree while he complained.

Three short sentences, and they are the gospel in the order the gospel always comes: peace first, then the command not to be afraid, then the reason. Nothing in Gideon has changed between his terror and this answer. He has not offered, promised or improved. The word is simply spoken over him.

He names the altar after the sentence that saved his life: YHWH Shalom, the LORD Is Peace. It is a strange name for a man about to fight a war, and the right one. What Gideon has discovered is not that God is on his side against Midian but that God is at peace with him, a frightened man who had just been accusing God of desertion.

The stone was still standing when the book was written, and centuries later Paul would put the same word at the centre of everything, and make it a person rather than an altar: for he himself is our peace (Eph. 2:14).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–32 — The Altar in His Father's Yard
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gideon's first task is at home: the altar of Baal in his father's yard. He obeys by night, and the town turns on him.
verseByVerse.theology: In a nation that cries to the LORD in trouble and lives by Baal the rest of the year, reform has to begin somewhere, and God begins it in one household.
verseByVerse.examples: Most of us have something in our own back garden that we have learned to live with. The chapter suggests that is where God's work in us is likely to start, and that it may be done with trembling hands.

verseByVerse.quote: That night the LORD said to him, "Take your father's bull, and the second bull seven years old, and pull down the altar of Baal that your father has, and cut down the Asherah that is beside it and build an altar to the LORD your God on the top of the stronghold here, with stones laid in due order. Then take the second bull and offer it as a burnt offering with the wood of the Asherah that you shall cut down." So Gideon took ten men of his servants and did as the LORD had told him. But because he was too afraid of his family and the men of the town to do it by day, he did it by night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first assignment is not Midian. It is his father's back garden: the altar of Baal that your father has. Joash, the man who owns the field where the angel sat, maintains a shrine to Baal with an Asherah pole beside it. Israel cried out to the LORD in distress; this is where the family went the rest of the year. There is no chance of Israel being delivered from Midian while the deliverer's own father runs a Baal altar, and God begins where Gideon actually lives.

The command comes the same night as peace be to you, and it comes from the God who has just made peace with him. It is not the condition of that peace but the first thing a man at peace with the LORD does.

The bull is seven years old, born in the year the raids began, and it is burned on the wood of the idol that caused them. The idol heats the offering that replaces it.

The narrator will not tidy him up. He did every instruction, and he did it in the dark because he was frightened of his own family and neighbours. Both halves are recorded and neither cancels the other. This is obedience with the hands shaking, and Scripture calls it obedience. There is no rebuke anywhere in the chapter.

A great deal of Christian courage looks like this from the inside. The command is obeyed and the fear is real at the same time, and the fear does not disqualify the obedience.

verseByVerse.quote: When the men of the town rose early in the morning, behold, the altar of Baal was broken down, and the Asherah beside it was cut down, and the second bull was offered on the altar that had been built. And they said to one another, "Who has done this thing?" And after they had searched and inquired, they said, "Gideon the son of Joash has done this thing." Then the men of the town said to Joash, "Bring out your son, that he may die, for he has broken down the altar of Baal and cut down the Asherah beside it." But Joash said to all who stood against him, "Will you contend for Baal? Or will you save him? Whoever contends for him shall be put to death by morning. If he is a god, let him contend for himself, because his altar has been broken down." Therefore on that day Gideon was called Jerubbaal, that is to say, "Let Baal contend against him," because he broke down his altar.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The town wakes up to find its shrine demolished and a sacrifice already burning on a new altar built out of the wreckage.

They investigate, find him, and come for a death sentence. Look carefully at who these men are. They are Israelites, the same people who were crying out to the LORD in verse 6 because the Midianites were eating their harvest, and they are now demanding capital punishment for a man who pulled down a Canaanite altar.

That is how far it has gone: the nation prays to the God of the exodus when the raiders come and lynches anyone who interferes with Baal.

The defence comes from the last man anybody would expect: Joash, who owned the altar. His argument is unanswerable and it takes one sentence: if he is a god, let him contend for himself. Turn it over and see how much it demolishes. A god who requires a mob to defend his honour has already lost the argument. If Baal is what the town says he is, he is perfectly capable of dealing with one man overnight; if he needs the men of Ophrah to do it for him, he is not worth the altar they are avenging.

It is the same case Elijah will make on Carmel with heavier irony, and the same case Isaiah will make about men who cut down a tree, burn half of it and pray to the other half (1 Kings 18:27; Isa. 44:15-17). A god you have to protect is not a god.

He gets a nickname out of it, and it is a standing dare: let Baal contend. Every time somebody says the name, the challenge is repeated and Baal's silence is noted again. Gideon carries that name for the rest of his life, and his sons carry it after him.
verseByVerse.note: “Jerubbaal” means “let Baal contend.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Midian gathers in the valley of Jezreel, the Spirit of the LORD takes hold of Gideon, and four tribes answer his call. Then he asks God for a sign with a fleece, twice.
verseByVerse.theology: This section holds together the two sides of Gideon: clothed with the Spirit, and still afraid. Both can be true of a believer at the same time.
