verseByVerse.examples: If you are asking God for one more sign about something he has already made plain, this passage does not shame you. Nor does it recommend fleeces. It points you to the God who is patient with the fearful, and to his word, which is clearer than any sign.

verseByVerse.quote: Now all the Midianites and the Amalekites and the people of the East came together, and they crossed the Jordan and encamped in the Valley of Jezreel. But the Spirit of the LORD clothed Gideon, and he sounded the trumpet, and the Abiezrites were called out to follow him. And he sent messengers throughout all Manasseh, and they too were called out to follow him. And he sent messengers to Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali, and they went up to meet them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole confederation crosses over and camps in the great plain — the same valley where the Kishon took Sisera's chariots two chapters ago. They are not raiding this time. They have come to stay.

Here is the sentence that changes him, and the Hebrew is unusual enough to be worth having exactly. It does not say the Spirit came upon Gideon, as with Othniel. It says the Spirit of the LORD "clothed himself with" Gideon — put him on, the way a man puts on a coat. Gideon is not handed an ability to deploy; he is worn.

The same phrase is used twice more in the Old Testament, both times of the Spirit taking hold of a man so that he speaks or acts beyond himself (1 Chron. 12:18; 2 Chron. 24:20). It is the only explanation offered for what happens next.

The man who was hiding grain in a pit blows a trumpet and summons four tribes, and they come. Nothing about his circumstances has altered. His clan is still the weakest in Manasseh and he is still the least in his father's house; the inventory in verse 15 was accurate and remains accurate. What has changed is who is wearing him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Gideon said to God, "If you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said, behold, I am laying a fleece of wool on the threshing floor. If there is dew on the fleece alone, and it is dry on all the ground, then I shall know that you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said." And it was so. When he rose early next morning and squeezed the fleece, he wrung enough dew from the fleece to fill a bowl with water. Then Gideon said to God, "Let not your anger burn against me; let me speak just once more. Please let me test just once more with the fleece. Please let it be dry on the fleece only, and on all the ground let there be dew." And God did so that night; and it was dry on the fleece only, and on all the ground there was dew.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take stock of what this man has already been given before he asks for this. The angel of the LORD has come to him in person and given him his commission and the promise I will be with you. He has seen fire come out of a rock and heard peace be to you when he expected to die. He has built and named an altar, carried out a night raid and survived it, and the Spirit of the LORD is wrapped round him like clothing. Then he lays out a fleece.

Mark how he phrases it, twice: as you have said. He is not asking whether God said it; he is asking whether God meant it. The request is not for information. It is for reassurance.

God does it, without comment: a bowlful of water out of the wool, and dry ground all round it.

He asks again, and the way he asks tells us he knows exactly what he is doing. Let not your anger burn against me is the language of a man apologising in advance, and it is almost word for word what Abraham said when he kept reducing the number for Sodom (Gen. 18:30, 32).

Here is the thing that should slow anybody down before mocking him: his second test is the intelligent one. A fleece of wool left out overnight will draw dew and hold it while the ground round it dries in the first sun; wool does that, and any shepherd knows it. The first test could have happened by itself. The reverse, dry wool on wet ground, cannot. Gideon spotted the flaw in his own experiment and asked for the one result that nature does not produce. He is not being lazily superstitious. He is being careful, and his carefulness exposes how much he still needs.

God does that too, in one sentence, with no rebuke, no lecture about the signs already given and no weary sigh in the text at all. The God who had already done all this for him gets up in the night and does the second experiment.

This is not a method to copy, and the chapter is not recommending fleeces. Gideon was not seeking guidance he lacked; he was seeking confidence in guidance he already had, and every reader who has ever asked God for one more confirmation of something already perfectly clear knows precisely which of the two he was doing.

What the passage is recommending is its God. He does not break a bruised reed or quench a smouldering wick (Isa. 42:3), and here is what that looks like in practice: a frightened man asking for the same assurance twice in two nights, and getting it twice, from the one who had already called him a mighty man of valour while he was hiding in a hole.

Matthew says that sentence from Isaiah describes Jesus (Matthew 12:18-21), and the Gospels show him doing exactly this. Thomas asked for one more proof after the others had seen the risen Lord, and Jesus came back a week later and offered him his hands and his side (John 20:26-27).

6.theology:
Named for what he will be. God calls a man hiding grain in a pit a mighty man of valor, naming what he will become before there is any evidence for it (v. 12).

The objection is correct and irrelevant. God does not dispute a word of Gideon's account of his own weakness. He answers it, as he answered Moses, with his presence: but I will be with you (v. 16).

Knowing the stories is not enough. Gideon can quote the wonderful deeds his fathers recounted, yet he has weighed them against the winepress and concluded that God has forsaken Israel (v. 13). He believes the history and has stopped expecting anything like it now.

Obedience with the hands shaking. Gideon pulls down his father's altar exactly as commanded, and does it at night because he was too afraid to do it by day (v. 27). Both halves are recorded, and there is no rebuke, either for that or for the fleece, asked for twice after everything he had already been given. The God of this chapter does not break a bruised reed or quench a smouldering wick (Isa. 42:3), the words Matthew applies to Jesus (Matt. 12:20), and verse 40 is what that looks like on the ground.
6.examples:
Then: A man from the least family of the weakest clan was crouched in a winepress saving a few bushels of wheat from raiders when somebody sat down under the tree above him and called him a mighty man of valour. Before he was sent against an army he was sent against his own father's shrine, and he did it after dark because he was frightened.

Now: Two things. The first is verse 13: it is possible to know exactly what God has done, to be able to recite it, and to have quietly concluded from your own circumstances that he has stopped. Gideon had the stories; what he had lost was the expectation. The second is verse 27. If you are waiting to stop being afraid before you obey, this chapter records a man who obeyed at night instead, and God did not mention it again. The courage did not come from Gideon, and it does not come from us: the same Spirit who clothed him lives in every believer now, and where our obedience is half-hearted or frightened or late, Christ's was whole, and it is his that stands for us before God.

7.title: Gideon's 300
7.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon) and all the people who were with him rose early and encamped beside the spring of Harod. And the camp of Midian was north of them, by the hill of Moreh, in the valley.<sup>2</sup>The LORD said to Gideon, "The people with you are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hand, lest Israel boast over me, saying, 'My own hand has saved me.'<sup>3</sup>Now therefore proclaim in the ears of the people, saying, 'Whoever is fearful and trembling, let him return home and hurry away from Mount Gilead.'" Then 22,000 of the people returned, and 10,000 remained.<sup>4</sup>And the LORD said to Gideon, "The people are still too many. Take them down to the water, and I will test them for you there, and anyone of whom I say to you, 'This one shall go with you,' shall go with you, and anyone of whom I say to you, 'This one shall not go with you,' shall not go."<sup>5</sup>So he brought the people down to the water. And the LORD said to Gideon, "Every one who laps the water with his tongue, as a dog laps, you shall set by himself. Likewise, every one who kneels down to drink."<sup>6</sup>And the number of those who lapped, putting their hands to their mouths, was 300 men, but all the rest of the people knelt down to drink water.<sup>7</sup>And the LORD said to Gideon, "With the 300 men who lapped I will save you and give the Midianites into your hand, and let all the others go every man to his home."<sup>8</sup>So the people took provisions in their hands, and their trumpets. And he sent all the rest of Israel every man to his tent, but retained the 300 men. And the camp of Midian was below him in the valley.<sup>9</sup>That same night the LORD said to him, "Arise, go down against the camp, for I have given it into your hand.<sup>10</sup>But if you are afraid to go down, go down to the camp with Purah your servant.<sup>11</sup>And you shall hear what they say, and afterward your hands shall be strengthened to go down against the camp." Then he went down with Purah his servant to the outposts of the armed men who were in the camp.<sup>12</sup>And the Midianites and the Amalekites and all the people of the East lay along the valley like locusts in abundance, and their camels were without number, as the sand that is on the seashore in abundance.<sup>13</sup>When Gideon came, behold, a man was telling a dream to his comrade. And he said, "Behold, I dreamed a dream, and behold, a cake of barley bread tumbled into the camp of Midian and came to the tent and struck it so that it fell and turned it upside down, so that the tent lay flat."<sup>14</sup>And his comrade answered, "This is no other than the sword of Gideon the son of Joash, a man of Israel; God has given into his hand Midian and all the camp."<sup>15</sup>As soon as Gideon heard the telling of the dream and its interpretation, he worshiped. And he returned to the camp of Israel and said, "Arise, for the LORD has given the host of Midian into your hand."<sup>16</sup>And he divided the 300 men into three companies and put trumpets into the hands of all of them and empty jars, with torches inside the jars.<sup>17</sup>And he said to them, "Look at me, and do likewise. When I come to the outskirts of the camp, do as I do.<sup>18</sup>When I blow the trumpet, I and all who are with me, then blow the trumpets also on every side of all the camp and shout, 'For the LORD and for Gideon.'"<sup>19</sup>So Gideon and the hundred men who were with him came to the outskirts of the camp at the beginning of the middle watch, when they had just set the watch. And they blew the trumpets and smashed the jars that were in their hands.<sup>20</sup>Then the three companies blew the trumpets and broke the jars. They held in their left hands the torches, and in their right hands the trumpets to blow. And they cried out, "A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!"<sup>21</sup>Every man stood in his place around the camp, and all the army ran. They cried out and fled.<sup>22</sup>When they blew the 300 trumpets, the LORD set every man's sword against his comrade and against all the army. And the army fled as far as Beth-shittah toward Zererah, as far as the border of Abel-meholah, by Tabbath.<sup>23</sup>And the men of Israel were called out from Naphtali and from Asher and from all Manasseh, and they pursued after Midian.<sup>24</sup>Gideon sent messengers throughout all the hill country of Ephraim, saying, "Come down against the Midianites and capture the waters against them, as far as Beth-barah, and also the Jordan." So all the men of Ephraim were called out, and they captured the waters as far as Beth-barah, and also the Jordan.<sup>25</sup>And they captured the two princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb. They killed Oreb at the rock of Oreb, and Zeeb they killed at the winepress of Zeeb. Then they pursued Midian, and they brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon across the Jordan.
7.overview:
Gideon has thirty-two thousand men and God's objection to the army is that it is too many: too many to be a convincing explanation (v. 2). Everything in the chapter serves that sentence. God is arranging not just a victory but an account of it that nobody can misread.

The army is cut twice, first by Israel's own war law and then at the water. God answers Gideon's lingering fear with a companion rather than a rebuke (v. 10), and the attack is made by three hundred men who stand still while the LORD turns the enemy against itself.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God cuts Gideon's army from thirty-two thousand to three hundred, first by sending home the fearful and then by a test at the water.
verseByVerse.theology: Israel's danger was not only Midian but the story Israel would tell afterwards. Pride in a victory can do as much harm as a defeat.
verseByVerse.examples: It is humbling to be made smaller on purpose. When God strips away what we were relying on, it may be so that, when help comes, there is no doubt where it came from.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon) and all the people who were with him rose early and encamped beside the spring of Harod. And the camp of Midian was north of them, by the hill of Moreh, in the valley. The LORD said to Gideon, "The people with you are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hand, lest Israel boast over me, saying, 'My own hand has saved me.' Now therefore proclaim in the ears of the people, saying, 'Whoever is fearful and trembling, let him return home and hurry away from Mount Gilead.'" Then 22,000 of the people returned, and 10,000 remained. And the LORD said to Gideon, "The people are still too many. Take them down to the water, and I will test them for you there, and anyone of whom I say to you, 'This one shall go with you,' shall go with you, and anyone of whom I say to you, 'This one shall not go with you,' shall not go." So he brought the people down to the water. And the LORD said to Gideon, "Every one who laps the water with his tongue, as a dog laps, you shall set by himself. Likewise, every one who kneels down to drink." And the number of those who lapped, putting their hands to their mouths, was 300 men, but all the rest of the people knelt down to drink water. And the LORD said to Gideon, "With the 300 men who lapped I will save you and give the Midianites into your hand, and let all the others go every man to his home." So the people took provisions in their hands, and their trumpets. And he sent all the rest of Israel every man to his tent, but retained the 300 men. And the camp of Midian was below him in the valley.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is called Jerubbaal first — let Baal contend — and the name is a standing dare that Baal has now been ignoring for some time.

Then comes the sentence the whole chapter exists to serve, and it has nothing to do with tactics. Gideon has thirty-two thousand men facing a coalition described as locusts, and God's objection to the army is that it is too many: not too few, badly equipped or poorly positioned, but too many to be a convincing explanation.

Read the reason again: lest Israel boast over me, saying, my own hand has saved me. God is not arranging a victory here; he is arranging an account of the victory that nobody can misread. The reduction is a piece of theology carried out with manpower.

The first cut is not Gideon's invention. Moses had written the rule into Israel's law of war: before a battle the officers shall say, is there any man who is fearful and fainthearted? Let him go back to his house, lest he make the heart of his fellows melt like his own (Deut. 20:8).

Gideon reads out the standing statute, and two thirds of his army goes home. Twenty-two thousand men admit in public that they are afraid and walk away, which tells you what the seven years had done to the country.

Ten thousand remain against a valley full of camels, and the sentence comes again. Then the test at the water, and the temptation to make it clever should be resisted.

A great deal has been written about the alertness of men who scoop water to the mouth and keep their eyes up, as against those who put their faces down to drink. It may be right. The text does not say so, and it does not say the three hundred were chosen for a quality at all.

What the text says is that God sorted them by something arbitrary and kept the smaller group. The point of a test that selects three hundred out of ten thousand is the three hundred. If the lappers had been the alert ones, we would be back at a victory that could be credited to good selection, and verse 2 has already ruled that out.

The men who leave hand over their supplies and their trumpets. That detail is quietly important: three hundred men are about to be issued with an army's worth of trumpets, and the plan in verse 16 depends on it.

Ninety-nine per cent of the army has gone home, and Gideon is standing on a hillside above a valley full of Midianites with a small company, a great many horns, and a promise.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God meets Gideon's fear with an offer, and sends him to the edge of the enemy camp to overhear a dream.
verseByVerse.theology: God knows what we are made of and remembers that we are dust (Ps. 103:14). He provides for his servants as they really are, not as they ought to be.
verseByVerse.examples: The word Gideon needed came from the last place he would have looked. It is worth listening for God's encouragement in unexpected voices, while testing every voice by his word.

verseByVerse.quote: That same night the LORD said to him, "Arise, go down against the camp, for I have given it into your hand. But if you are afraid to go down, go down to the camp with Purah your servant. And you shall hear what they say, and afterward your hands shall be strengthened to go down against the camp." Then he went down with Purah his servant to the outposts of the armed men who were in the camp. And the Midianites and the Amalekites and all the people of the East lay along the valley like locusts in abundance, and their camels were without number, as the sand that is on the seashore in abundance. When Gideon came, behold, a man was telling a dream to his comrade. And he said, "Behold, I dreamed a dream, and behold, a cake of barley bread tumbled into the camp of Midian and came to the tent and struck it so that it fell and turned it upside down, so that the tent lay flat." And his comrade answered, "This is no other than the sword of Gideon the son of Joash, a man of Israel; God has given into his hand Midian and all the camp." As soon as Gideon heard the telling of the dream and its interpretation, he worshiped. And he returned to the camp of Israel and said, "Arise, for the LORD has given the host of Midian into your hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two sentences, and the second is the tenderest line in the Gideon story.

The first is the order and the promise, in the usual form: go down, for I have given it into your hand. The second is God adding, unprompted, a provision for the state he knows this man is in.

But if you are afraid to go down: notice what does not follow. There is no "do not be afraid", and no rebuke for still being frightened after the angel, the fire, the Spirit and two nights of fleeces. God simply grants the fear and works with it: take Purah with you, and go and listen. Gideon is given a companion for the walk and told what he will find when he gets there: afterward your hands shall be strengthened. God is not embarrassed by his servant's nerves and does not require him to pretend; he gives him a plan for them.

Gideon takes the servant, and the narrator lets that stand without comment.

What he sees when he gets down there is not reassuring. The valley is full: locusts again, and camels beyond counting, and the phrase used for them is the one God used to Abraham about his own descendants — as the sand that is on the seashore.

He arrives at the exact moment a man is describing a dream, and the dream is about a cake of barley bread. Barley is the cheap grain, the bread of the poor, what you eat when you cannot afford wheat — and harvests like it are what these men have been stealing off Israelite fields for seven years. In the dream, a loaf of the stuff they have been robbing rolls into the camp and knocks a tent flat.

The second man interprets it exactly right, including the name. Two enemy soldiers, in the dark, in their own camp, telling each other that God has handed them over to a farmer from Ophrah. The one sentence Gideon needed to hear is spoken by the enemy, in the enemy's language, about the enemy's own destruction.

He worships. Standing in the dark at the edge of a hostile camp with one servant beside him, the first thing he does is bow. See what it took: not the angel, the fire, the Spirit or the fleece, but a frightened man overhearing a stranger's nightmare. God knew what would work on Gideon and had it waiting for him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The three hundred go down with trumpets, jars and torches, and at the middle watch the LORD turns the Midianite camp against itself.
verseByVerse.theology: The battle cry names the LORD first and Gideon second (v. 20). God uses human instruments, but the credit is never shared equally.
verseByVerse.examples: The weapons of the three hundred were a light and a sound, carried in clay jars. Paul's picture of the gospel as treasure in jars of clay, so that the power plainly belongs to God and not to us (2 Cor. 4:7), fits this night well, though he does not mention it.

verseByVerse.quote: And he divided the 300 men into three companies and put trumpets into the hands of all of them and empty jars, with torches inside the jars. And he said to them, "Look at me, and do likewise. When I come to the outskirts of the camp, do as I do. When I blow the trumpet, I and all who are with me, then blow the trumpets also on every side of all the camp and shout, 'For the LORD and for Gideon.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the equipment, and it repays counting on the fingers. Each man gets a trumpet and an empty jar with a lit torch inside it, which is what the jar is for: a clay pot over a flame hides it completely until the pot is broken. That is two hands, and there is nothing in either of them that can hurt anybody. No sword is issued to the three hundred. The men are going into a night attack on a valley full of raiders carrying a musical instrument and a pot.

The whole battle order is six words long: look at me, and do likewise. There is no strategy to memorise and no contingency. Three companies take up positions on three sides of a sleeping army in the dark, and every man watches one man on a hillside and copies him.

Hear the shout as it stands, because it names the arrangement exactly: for the LORD and for Gideon. Not for Israel, the tribes or freedom, but for a God and a farmer, in that order.

verseByVerse.quote: So Gideon and the hundred men who were with him came to the outskirts of the camp at the beginning of the middle watch, when they had just set the watch. And they blew the trumpets and smashed the jars that were in their hands. Then the three companies blew the trumpets and broke the jars. They held in their left hands the torches, and in their right hands the trumpets to blow. And they cried out, "A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!" Every man stood in his place around the camp, and all the army ran. They cried out and fled. When they blew the 300 trumpets, the LORD set every man's sword against his comrade and against all the army. And the army fled as far as Beth-shittah toward Zererah, as far as the border of Abel-meholah, by Tabbath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The timing is professional. The middle watch probably began around ten at night, and Gideon moves at the changeover — the moment when the new sentries are settling in, their eyes are not yet adjusted, and the men coming off duty are heading for their blankets.

Then three hundred trumpets sound, and three hundred clay pots are smashed at once.

Consider what this looks like from inside the camp. A man wakes in the dark to trumpets on three sides at once — and in that world a trumpet probably belonged to the leader of a unit, so three hundred horns would mean three hundred companies. At the same instant, three hundred flames appear in a ring where a moment ago there was nothing. And a war cry announces a sword. Nobody in that valley sees three hundred men; everybody in it hears an army that has already surrounded them.

Verse 21 is the sentence to hold on to. Every man stood in his place around the camp. The three hundred do not charge, do not advance, do not engage. They stand still, holding a light and making a noise, and the enemy disintegrates in front of them.

What actually killed the Midianites was each other, in the dark, in a panic, unable to tell friend from enemy. Yet the subject of the verb is God. The LORD set every man's sword against his comrade. Verse 2 said the army had to be small enough that Israel could not claim the credit, and the final arrangement removes even the sword. Three hundred men with pots and horns stood still, and the enemy destroyed itself.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The tribes pursue (v. 23), Ephraim seizes the crossings (v. 24), and the princes Oreb and Zeeb are killed at places that keep their names (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: Ephraim's part here sets up the quarrel at the start of the next chapter, when the tribe complains that it was not called sooner (8:1).
verseByVerse.examples: Places named after a battle keep its story alive. Christians have their own memorial of rescue, the Lord's Supper, kept in remembrance of Christ (1 Cor. 11:24).

verseByVerse.quote: And the men of Israel were called out from Naphtali and from Asher and from all Manasseh, and they pursued after Midian. Gideon sent messengers throughout all the hill country of Ephraim, saying, "Come down against the Midianites and capture the waters against them, as far as Beth-barah, and also the Jordan." So all the men of Ephraim were called out, and they captured the waters as far as Beth-barah, and also the Jordan. And they captured the two princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb. They killed Oreb at the rock of Oreb, and Zeeb they killed at the winepress of Zeeb. Then they pursued Midian, and they brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon across the Jordan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the rest of Israel is recalled — including, presumably, a good many of the twenty-two thousand who had gone home admitting they were afraid.

There is something generous in the arrangement. The part of the work that could only ever be credited to God was done by three hundred men holding crockery. The pursuit, which is ordinary soldiering and takes days, is given back to the tribes.

God arranged an unmistakable miracle and then handed the follow-up to ordinary people doing ordinary work, and that second half is not despised in the telling.

Gideon's own generalship is sound. He sends to Ephraim to seize the fords before the fleeing army reaches them, exactly as Ehud had done at the same river, and the retreat is closed.

Two enemy princes are taken and killed, and the places keep their names afterwards, which is how a country remembers a night like this.

The second location is worth a moment: Zeeb dies at a winepress. The last winepress in this story had a man crouched in it, threshing wheat where the wind could not reach, hiding a few bushels from the very people this prince commanded. The Midianites are now dying in one.

The book makes nothing of it, and there is nothing to make. God took a man out of a pit, let him be given a nickname daring a dead god to answer, reduced his army by ninety-nine per cent so that nobody could get the story wrong, sent him to overhear a stranger's dream about a barley loaf, and had him stand still in the dark holding a jar while the valley emptied.

Isaiah, some four or five centuries later, was still using this night as shorthand for what God does to an oppressor: the rod of his oppressor you have broken as on the day of Midian (Isa. 9:4) — and the verses on either side of it are about a light shining on people who walked in darkness, and a child who is born.

Matthew quotes the opening of that same passage, the light dawning on Galilee, when Jesus begins to preach there (Matthew 4:15-16). The day of Midian was a small rescue in the northern country where the great one would begin.

7.theology:
An explanation, not just a victory. Verse 2 gives the reason for every reduction that follows, and it is theological rather than military. God will not win this in a way that leaves room for my own hand has saved me. The arithmetic runs from thirty-two thousand to three hundred to a battle in which nobody on Israel's side draws a sword at all. The gospel is built the same way: God saves in Christ so that no one may boast in his presence, and the one who boasts must boast in the Lord (1 Corinthians 1:29-31; Ephesians 2:8-9).

God works with the fear rather than against it. The offer in verse 10 is unprompted, and there is no rebuke in it. God gives Gideon what he needs to go, and he goes.

Standing still. The three hundred do not charge; they stand in their places (v. 21), and the LORD does the fighting.

The day of Midian. Centuries later Isaiah uses this night as the standard picture of God breaking an oppressor (Isa. 9:4), in a passage about a child who is born to us (see vv. 23-25).
7.examples:
Then: An army of thirty-two thousand was cut to three hundred on purpose, and the three hundred were sent into a night attack carrying a pot and a horn. They stood still in a ring around a sleeping valley, broke the pots, and watched an army kill itself in the dark.

Now: Verse 10 is the one to keep. Here is what God does with a frightened man who has already been given more assurance than most people get in a lifetime: he does not shame him, does not withdraw the commission, and does not tell him to feel differently. He offers him a companion for the walk down, and the command comes wrapped in a promise already kept, I have given it into your hand. If you are waiting to stop being afraid before you go, this is a chapter about a man who went with somebody else beside him. Christians do not walk down alone either: the Spirit is given to them, and the brothers and sisters God puts beside them are his Purahs.

8.title: Gideon's Failure

8.overview:
The victory is won and this chapter is about what winning did to the man. Ephraim arrives furious about credit, and Gideon soothes them with skilled flattery. The three hundred cross the Jordan exhausted yet pursuing, two Israelite towns refuse them bread, and Gideon comes back to flail one with thorns and kill the men of the other. Verse 19 reveals a private blood feud running under the national deliverance.

The chapter's spine is two consecutive sentences: the LORD will rule over you (v. 23), the finest thing he ever says, and then a request for the earrings from the spoil (v. 24). He refuses the crown, takes the treasury, makes an ephod that Israel whores after, and leaves seventy sons and a boy in Shechem named "my father is king".

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ephraim is furious at not being called to the fight (v. 1), and Gideon answers with flattery about their gleanings and credits them with Oreb and Zeeb (vv. 2-3). Their anger subsides.
verseByVerse.theology: The quarrel is about credit, arriving after the danger has passed. Nobody from Ephraim was at the spring of Harod when there were thirty-two thousand men and God said there were too many.
verseByVerse.examples: Keep this scene. The same tribe will bring the identical complaint to Jephthah in chapter 12, almost word for word — and that time nobody answers softly, and forty-two thousand Ephraimites die at the fords of the Jordan (12:1-6).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the men of Ephraim said to him, "What is this that you have done to us, not to call us when you went to fight against Midian?" And they accused him fiercely. And he said to them, "What have I done now in comparison with you? Is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the grape harvest of Abiezer? God has given into your hands the princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb. What have I been able to do in comparison with you?" Then their anger against him subsided when he said this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fighting is over and the first thing that happens is a row about credit.

The grievance is not what it pretends to be. Ephraim is not angry that Midian ate the harvest for seven years. They are angry that they were not invited to the part with the glory in it, and they arrive after the battle, after the rout, after the two princes are dead.

Gideon's answer is a piece of skilled flattery, and it works. What Ephraim picked up off the ground after the harvest is worth more than my whole clan's vintage: their share of the mopping-up was greater than his share of the victory, which is not true and is exactly what they want to hear.

The proverb says that a soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger (Prov. 15:1). Here is the soft answer, doing its work on men who came looking for a fight over nothing.

The difference between this quarrel and the massacre of chapter 12 was one man's willingness to let somebody else be flattered.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The three hundred chase the last of Midian across the Jordan, and two Israelite towns refuse them bread.
verseByVerse.theology: Succoth and Penuel are Israelite towns, not Midianite ones. The threat in this section comes from inside Israel, and before long so does the cruelty.
verseByVerse.examples: If you are tired in the Christian life, you are in good company here. The three hundred were not chasing in hope of a victory still to be won; they were following up one God had already given, and that is the believer's position too.

verseByVerse.quote: And Gideon came to the Jordan and crossed over, he and the 300 men who were with him, exhausted yet pursuing. So he said to the men of Succoth, "Please give loaves of bread to the people who follow me, for they are exhausted, and I am pursuing after Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian." And the officials of Succoth said, "Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand, that we should give bread to your army?" So Gideon said, "Well then, when the LORD has given Zebah and Zalmunna into my hand, I will flail your flesh with the thorns of the wilderness and with briers." And from there he went up to Penuel, and spoke to them in the same way, and the men of Penuel answered him as the men of Succoth had answered. And he said to the men of Penuel, "When I come again in peace, I will break down this tower."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Carry three words of that verse about with you: exhausted yet pursuing. The three hundred have been awake since before the middle watch, have run a valley and crossed a river, and are following two kings into the desert on empty stomachs. Few phrases in Scripture describe ordinary Christian perseverance better: not fresh, not visibly winning, worn out, and not stopping.

He asks his own countrymen for bread. The request is modest: loaves, for tired men chasing the enemy of the whole nation.

The refusal is a sneer, and underneath it is a calculation that is entirely rational. Succoth sits east of the Jordan, exposed. If Gideon succeeds, they have lost a few loaves. If he fails, Midian is back next harvest and will know exactly which towns fed the raiding party. So they wait to see; their governing word is already. That is a very old form of practical unbelief: not a denial that God can do it, but a refusal to be committed until the outcome is safe, and it is called prudence by everyone who practises it.

And here the chapter turns, in Gideon. His faith is intact: when the LORD has given. What has entered is something else, a promise of torture, delivered to fellow Israelites, over bread. The man who would not tear down an altar by daylight because he was afraid of the town is now threatening to flay two towns for insulting him.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor with their army, about 15,000 men, all who were left of all the army of the people of the East, for there had fallen 120,000 men who drew the sword. And Gideon went up by the way of the tent dwellers east of Nobah and Jogbehah and attacked the army, for the army felt secure. And Zebah and Zalmunna fled, and he pursued them and captured the two kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, and he threw all the army into a panic.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The arithmetic of the night in the valley is given here for the first time. A hundred and twenty thousand dead; fifteen thousand left.

Fifteen thousand is still fifty times the size of Gideon's force, and it is what remains after the disaster. The three hundred are pursuing an army that could still destroy them without difficulty if it turned round and looked.

He takes the caravan route round to the east and comes at them from the desert side, which is the direction nobody watches, and the narrator gives the reason it worked in four words: the army felt secure.

They had put enough distance between themselves and the Jezreel valley to relax. Nobody chases a beaten army that far on foot; it is not done, and it is why it worked.

Both kings are taken alive. The chapter has been building to that, and it will turn out in a few verses that Gideon had his own reasons for wanting them alive rather than dead.

Are the numbers realistic? Either the host was as large as stated and God destroyed it, setting them against one another (7:22), or “thousand” here means a military unit. Either way, the point is that three hundred men won because God fought.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–21 — What He Did on the Way Back
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gideon comes back to punish Succoth and Penuel, then deals with the captured kings, and in doing so reveals a private reason for the whole pursuit.
verseByVerse.theology: Justice and revenge can look alike from the outside. This section shows a judge punishing real wrongs and, at the same time, settling his own scores.
verseByVerse.examples: Parents who have been shown patience by God are called to show it to their children. And anyone who was shamed as a child for being afraid may know that God does not treat his children so: as a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him (Ps. 103:13).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Gideon the son of Joash returned from the battle by the ascent of Heres. And he captured a young man of Succoth and questioned him. And he wrote down for him the officials and elders of Succoth, seventy-seven men. And he came to the men of Succoth and said, "Behold Zebah and Zalmunna, about whom you taunted me, saying, 'Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand, that we should give bread to your men who are exhausted?'" And he took the elders of the city, and he took thorns of the wilderness and briers and with them taught the men of Succoth a lesson. And he broke down the tower of Penuel and killed the men of the city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He comes back, and the first thing he does is compile a list.

The detail is chilling in its ordinariness. He seizes a young man from the town, questions him, and the young man writes out seventy-seven names — every official and elder in Succoth. It is a literate young man doing clerical work under duress, and what he produces is an execution list.

He quotes their own sentence back at them with the kings standing there, and both promises are kept. Desert thorns are not a figure of speech; this is torture, methodically applied to seventy-seven named men who had refused a meal. And at Penuel the tower comes down and the men of the city are killed — Israelites, killed by Israel's judge, for declining to feed his soldiers.

The book records it without comment, and the absence of comment is not approval. This is the same narrator who told us Gideon was afraid to pull down an altar by day, and who will shortly tell us the ephod became a snare. He is showing us a man, and the man is coming apart.

Set the two halves of Gideon side by side. In chapter 6 he says my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house. In chapter 8 he tortures seventy-seven elders and destroys a town for wounding his dignity. What changed between those two chapters was not his theology. It was that he won.

Why, then, does Hebrews list Gideon among the heroes of faith (Hebrews 11:32)? Because it commends what he did by faith: he believed God against impossible odds and went down to the camp with three hundred men. It does not commend Succoth's thorns, the blood feud or the ephod, and this chapter makes sure no reader could think so. Every judge is a flawed pointer to the true Deliverer. Gideon broke an oppressor and then began to act like one; Christ broke the oppressor and was himself broken for the people who had failed him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to Zebah and Zalmunna, "Where are the men whom you killed at Tabor?" They answered, "As you are, so were they. Every one of them resembled the son of a king." And he said, "They were my brothers, the sons of my mother. As the LORD lives, if you had saved them alive, I would not kill you." So he said to Jether his firstborn, "Rise and kill them!" But the young man did not draw his sword, for he was afraid, because he was still a young man. Then Zebah and Zalmunna said, "Rise yourself and fall upon us, for as the man is, so is his strength." And Gideon arose and killed Zebah and Zalmunna, and he took the crescent ornaments that were on the necks of their camels.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A question comes out of nowhere, about an incident the book has never mentioned, and the answer is a piece of flattery from two men in chains: they looked like you. They looked like princes.

Here is the sentence that reorganises the whole pursuit.

Gideon's brothers — his full brothers, the sons of his own mother — had been killed by these two men at Tabor, and he has said nothing about it until now. And then the admission: if you had saved them alive, I would not kill you.

The execution of the Midianite kings is not, in this moment, an act of national deliverance. It is a blood feud, and he says so out loud. Somewhere under the trumpets and the torches and a sword for the LORD and for Gideon, there has been a private account running, and it is being settled now.

None of that makes the deliverance false. God did give Midian into his hand, and the barley loaf did flatten the tent. But the man God used had reasons of his own, and the book is honest enough to let us hear one of them.

Then he tells his eldest boy to do it.

This is a deliberate humiliation of the prisoners — to be executed by a child was probably the most degrading death a soldier could suffer — and it is being arranged by a father for his son to carry out.

The boy cannot. The text says why, plainly and without contempt: he was afraid, because he was still a young man.

There is a terrible echo in that line. The last person in this story who could not do something because he was afraid was Gideon himself, pulling down an altar at night. God met that fear with patience, a companion and a plan. Gideon meets his son's fear by handing the job to somebody else in front of everybody.

The kings ask him to do it himself, and he does. And then the last clause of the verse, which the narrator has put there on purpose: he took the gold off their camels.

Keep that detail. It is about to matter a great deal.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–27 — The Crown Refused and the Gold Requested
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel offers Gideon a crown. He refuses it in words that could hardly be better, then asks for gold, and the gold becomes a snare.
verseByVerse.theology: Refusing a title is easier than refusing what comes with it. Gideon's words are right; his request shows where his heart had drifted.
verseByVerse.examples: Some of the most dangerous moments in a life with God come after a success, not after a failure. The gifts God gives can quietly become objects of trust in their own right.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the men of Israel said to Gideon, "Rule over us, you and your son and your grandson also, for you have saved us from the hand of Midian." Gideon said to them, "I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you; the LORD will rule over you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel offers him a crown, and three generations of it. This is not gratitude; it is a constitutional proposal. They want a dynasty, and they want it for the reason nations always want one: somebody delivered them and they would like the arrangement to be permanent.

It is also the exact error the whole book has been diagnosing. Every rest in Judges ends when the judge dies, and Israel's solution is not to hold on to God but to make the deliverer hereditary.

This is the finest sentence Gideon ever speaks.

He refuses all three generations, one at a time, and gives the reason without any softening: the LORD will rule over you. Israel has a king already, and the offer is not a compliment but a substitution.

It is theologically exact. Generations later, when the nation finally demands a king so that they can be like the other nations, God tells Samuel what is really happening: they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them (1 Sam. 8:7). Gideon saw it clearly, in one sentence, standing in front of the men making the offer.

Whatever comes next, he said this, and he meant it.

The sentence waits for its fulfilment. God's answer in the end was that he himself would rule his people in the person of a son of David. When a crowd tried to make Jesus king by force after he fed them, he withdrew (John 6:15); he took his throne another way, by the cross and the empty tomb. In him, the LORD will rule over you and a man on the throne are at last the same thing.

verseByVerse.quote: And Gideon said to them, "Let me make a request of you: every one of you give me the earrings from his spoil." (For they had golden earrings, because they were Ishmaelites.) And they answered, "We will willingly give them." And they spread a cloak, and every man threw in it the earrings of his spoil. And the weight of the golden earrings that he requested was 1,700 shekels of gold, besides the crescent ornaments and the pendants and the purple garments worn by the kings of Midian, and besides the collars that were around the necks of their camels. And Gideon made an ephod of it and put it in his city, in Ophrah. And all Israel whored after it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and to his family.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the next sentence out of the same mouth. Read verses 23 and 24 together, because nothing separates them. I will not rule over you... the LORD will rule over you... Let me make a request of you: every one of you give me the earrings from his spoil.

He declines the crown and asks for the treasury, and there is no sign that he noticed any distance between the two.

Seventeen hundred shekels is something over forty pounds of gold, and that is only the earrings. The list goes on: the crescents, the pendants, the purple — royal cloth, the most expensive dye in the ancient world — and the collars off the camels.

The man who would not be king now owns the wardrobe of two kings, and with it he makes an ephod. An ephod was a priest's garment. The high priest wore one, and attached to it was the breastpiece with the Urim and Thummim, by which Israel enquired of God. Whatever exactly Gideon made out of forty pounds of gold, it was a priestly object, and he set it up in his own home town.

So the shape of what he has done comes clear. He refused to be king and he made himself a shrine. The tabernacle was at Shiloh; the sanctioned way of enquiring of God was through the priesthood; and Ophrah now has a golden object made from the spoils of the deliverance, standing in the town of the man God used.

The two verbs in that sentence are the two the book has been using all along. Whored after is what Israel does with other gods in 2:17. Snare is the word God used at Bochim about the gods of the nations he would no longer drive out: their gods shall be a snare to you (2:3). Both words are now attached to a thing an Israelite judge made, out of the plunder of a victory God gave him, in the town where he had torn down an altar to Baal.

Gideon began by demolishing a false shrine at night because he was afraid, and ended by building one in daylight because he was asked for gold and did not refuse it. Nobody made him do it. He was never tempted by the crown. The snare came in through the one door he had left open.
verseByVerse.note: Gideon's ephod is the first of several unauthorised shrines in Judges; Micah's household shrine in chapter 17 also has an ephod (17:5).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Midian is broken and the land has forty years of rest. Gideon's household grows like a king's, and when he dies Israel forgets both the LORD and Gideon's family.
verseByVerse.theology: Faithfulness that rests on a man rather than on God ends when the man dies. Israel's loyalty lasted exactly as long as Gideon did (v. 33).
verseByVerse.examples: Gideon's public words refused a crown; the name he let his son carry claimed one. Children usually learn from what is said at home.

verseByVerse.quote: So Midian was subdued before the people of Israel, and they raised their heads no more. And the land had rest for forty years in the days of Gideon. Jerubbaal the son of Joash went and lived in his own house. Now Gideon had seventy sons, his own offspring, for he had many wives. And his concubine who was in Shechem also bore him a son, and he called his name Abimelech. And Gideon the son of Joash died in a good old age and was buried in the tomb of Joash his father, at Ophrah of the Abiezrites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The formula closes the cycle properly. Midian is broken, permanently, and the land is quiet for forty years.

By the standard of this book that is a success, and it should be said before the rest. The raids stopped. A generation grew up who could plant a crop and eat it.

Then the writer tells us what living in his own house looked like, and does it without a word of comment.

Seventy sons and many wives are not a large family but a royal household. Keeping multiple wives at that scale required the income of a king, and the number of sons is precisely the currency of a dynasty — heirs, alliances, a name that cannot be extinguished.

He refused the crown in verse 23 and then lived exactly like the thing he had refused to be called. The title was declined and the life was adopted, which is a distinction that satisfies nobody but the man making it.

Then the name: Abimelech is Hebrew for "my father is king". Whatever Gideon said in public at the assembly, that is the sentence being carried round Shechem by a boy for the rest of his childhood. He was the son of a concubine in a town away from home, walking about with a name that announces a claim his father had formally refused.

He will spend the next chapter acting on it, and one of the first things he does is kill the seventy sons of verse 30.

He dies old and full of years and is buried in his father's tomb — the same father whose altar he pulled down in the dark, and who defended him the next morning.

Was Gideon’s polygamy acceptable to God? The narrator records it without approving it. It went against God’s design (Gen 2:24) and the law for kings (Deut 17:17), and its fruit was Abimelech, who murdered seventy brothers (ch. 9).

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as Gideon died, the people of Israel turned again and whored after the Baals and made Baal-berith their god. And the people of Israel did not remember the LORD their God, who had delivered them from the hand of all their enemies on every side, and they did not show steadfast love to the family of Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon) in return for all the good that he had done to Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As soon as Gideon died. The trigger is a funeral, exactly as 2:19 said it always would be, and this time the narrator does not even leave a decent interval.

The god they choose has a name worth translating. Baal-berith means "lord of the covenant", or "Baal of the treaty". Israel is in a covenant already, with the God who brought them out of Egypt; they have gone and found a Baal who offers the same service.

The verb is the ordinary one again, and by now it is the book's diagnosis: they did not remember. They did not reject him or argue with him; they forgot him, a nation that had watched three hundred men break jars in the dark.

The last verse of the chapter adds a second failure, the human one. The word is hesed, the loyal, covenant kindness that God shows his own people and expects them to show each other. They did not show it to Gideon's family.

The two failures belong together in one sentence for a reason. A people who stop remembering what God has done stop keeping faith with each other very shortly afterwards; the vertical and the horizontal go together, and the writer puts them in consecutive clauses.

This verse is the hinge into what follows. Seventy sons are living in Ophrah, a man named "my father is king" is living in Shechem, the town has just adopted a god called lord of the covenant, and nobody in Israel feels any obligation to the family of the man who saved them.

Everything needed for the next chapter is now in place, and every piece of it was assembled during forty years of rest.

8.theology:
What winning did to him. The man who called himself the least in his father's house now tortures elders for wounding his dignity. His theology has not changed (v. 7); what changed is that he won.

The crown and the treasury. Verse 23 is theologically exact: Israel already had a King. Verse 24 is the next sentence from the same mouth, and the gold became the snare that the crown never was.

The title refused, the life adopted. Gideon declined to be called king and lived like one. The speed with which Israel forgot both the LORD and Gideon's family when he died (vv. 33-35) shows how little of its faith had rested on God himself.
8.examples:
Then: A man who would not move until he had asked for signs twice, and then pulled down an idol after dark because he was frightened, finished his career torturing the elders of an Israelite town over bread, executing two kings for the death of his brothers, refusing a crown in one sentence and asking for forty pounds of gold in the next.

Now: The chapter's question is what happened to him after the success. The snare came not from the enemy, nor from the crown he had the theology to refuse, but from the spoils of a genuine victory everybody agreed was God's. Blessing received is the moment to hold it with open hands, remembering whose it was, and it is the Spirit, not our own vigilance, who keeps the heart from turning gifts into ephods. Where we have already made one, the way back is the one Gideon never took: confession, to the God who, unlike Israel in verse 35, keeps hesed with those who fail him, because the true Judge and King never took what was not his, and his faithfulness is counted to us.

9.title: Abimelech the Bramble King
9.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Abimelech the son of Jerubbaal went to Shechem to his mother's relatives and said to them and to the whole clan of his mother's family,<sup>2</sup>"Say in the ears of all the leaders of Shechem, 'Which is better for you, that all seventy of the sons of Jerubbaal rule over you, or that one rule over you?' Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh."<sup>3</sup>And his mother's relatives spoke all these words on his behalf in the ears of all the leaders of Shechem, and their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech, for they said, "He is our brother."<sup>4</sup>And they gave him seventy pieces of silver out of the house of Baal-berith with which Abimelech hired worthless and reckless fellows, who followed him.<sup>5</sup>And he went to his father's house at Ophrah and killed his brothers the sons of Jerubbaal, seventy men, on one stone. But Jotham the youngest son of Jerubbaal was left, for he hid himself.<sup>6</sup>And all the leaders of Shechem came together, and all Beth-millo, and they went and made Abimelech king, by the oak of the pillar at Shechem.<sup>7</sup>When it was told to Jotham, he went and stood on top of Mount Gerizim and cried aloud and said to them, "Listen to me, you leaders of Shechem, that God may listen to you.<sup>8</sup>The trees once went out to anoint a king over them, and they said to the olive tree, 'Reign over us.'<sup>9</sup>But the olive tree said to them, 'Shall I leave my abundance, by which out from the leaders of Shechem and from Beth-millo and devour Abimelech."<sup>21</sup>And Jotham ran away and fled and went to Beer and lived there, because of Abimelech his brother.<sup>22</sup>Abimelech ruled over Israel three years.<sup>23</sup>And God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem, and the leaders of Shechem dealt treacherously with Abimelech,<sup>24</sup>that the violence done to the seventy sons of Jerubbaal might come, and their blood be laid on Abimelech their brother, who killed them, and on the men of Shechem, who strengthened his hands to kill his brothers.<sup>25</sup>And the leaders of Shechem put men in ambush against him on the mountaintops, and they robbed all who passed by them along that way. And it was told to Abimelech.<sup>26</sup>And Gaal the son of Ebed moved into Shechem with his relatives, and the leaders of Shechem put confidence in him.<sup>27</sup>And they went out into the field and gathered the grapes from their vineyards and trod them and held a festival; and they went into the house of their god and ate and drank and reviled Abimelech.<sup>28</sup>And Gaal the son of Ebed said, "Who is Abimelech, and who are we of Shechem, that we should serve him? Is he not the son of Jerubbaal, and is not Zebul his officer? Serve the men of Hamor the father of Shechem; but why should we serve him?<sup>29</sup>Would that this people were under my hand! Then I would remove Abimelech. I would say to Abimelech, 'Increase your army, and come out.'"<sup>30</sup>When Zebul the ruler of the city heard the words of Gaal the son of Ebed, his anger was kindled.<sup>31</sup>And he sent messengers to Abimelech secretly, saying, "Behold, Gaal the son of Ebed and his relatives have come to Shechem, and they are stirring up the city against you.<sup>32</sup>Now therefore, go by night, you and the people who are with you, and set an ambush in the field.<sup>33</sup>Then in the morning, as soon as the sun is up, rise early and rush upon the city. And when he and the people who are with him come out against you, you may do to them as your hand finds to do."<sup>34</sup>So Abimelech and all the men who were with him rose up by night and set an ambush against Shechem in four companies.<sup>35</sup>And Gaal the son of Ebed went out and stood in the entrance of the gate of the city, and Abimelech and the people who were with him rose from the ambush.<sup>36</sup>And when Gaal saw the people, he said to Zebul, "Look, people are coming down from the mountaintops!" And Zebul said to him, "You mistake the shadow of the mountains for men."<sup>37</sup>Gaal spoke again and said, "Look, people are coming down from the center of the land, and one company is coming from the direction of the Diviners' Oak."<sup>38</sup>Then Zebul said to him, "Where is your mouth now, you who said, 'Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him?' Are not these the people whom you despised? Go out now and fight with them."<sup>39</sup>And Gaal went out at the head of the leaders of Shechem and fought with Abimelech.<sup>40</sup>And Abimelech chased him, and he fled before him. And many fell wounded, up to the entrance of the gate.<sup>41</sup>And Abimelech lived at Arumah, and Zebul drove out Gaal and his relatives, so that they could not dwell at Shechem.<sup>42</sup>On the following day, the people went out into the field, and Abimelech was told.<sup>43</sup>He took his people and divided them into three companies and set an ambush in the fields. And he looked and saw the people coming out of the city. So he rose against them and killed them.<sup>44</sup>Abimelech and the company that was with him rushed forward and stood at the entrance of the gate of the city, while the two companies rushed upon all who were in the field and killed them.<sup>45</sup>And Abimelech fought against the city all that day. He captured the city and killed the people who were in it, and he razed the city and sowed it with salt.<sup>46</sup>When all the leaders of the Tower of Shechem heard of it, they entered the stronghold of the house of El-berith.<sup>47</sup>Abimelech was told that all the leaders of the Tower of Shechem were gathered together.<sup>48</sup>And Abimelech went up to Mount Zalmon, he and all the people who were with him. And Abimelech took an axe in his hand and cut down a bundle of brushwood and took it up and laid it on his shoulder. And he said to the men who were with him, "What you have seen me do, hurry and do as I have done."<sup>49</sup>So every one of the people cut down his bundle and following Abimelech put it against the stronghold, and they set the stronghold on fire over them, so that all the people of the Tower of Shechem also died, about 1,000 men and women.<sup>50</sup>Then Abimelech went to Thebez and encamped against Thebez and captured it.<sup>51</sup>But there was a strong tower within the city, and all the men and women and all the leaders of the city fled to it and shut themselves in, and they went up to the roof of the tower.<sup>52</sup>And Abimelech came to the tower and fought against it and drew near to the door of the tower to burn it with fire.<sup>53</sup>And a certain woman threw an upper millstone on Abimelech's head and crushed his skull.<sup>54</sup>Then he called quickly to the young man his armor-bearer and said to him, "Draw your sword and kill me, lest they say of me, 'A woman killed him.'" And his young man thrust him through, and he died.<sup>55</sup>And when the men of Israel saw that Abimelech was dead, everyone departed to his home.<sup>56</sup>Thus God returned the evil of Abimelech, which he committed against his father in killing his seventy brothers.<sup>57</sup>And God also made all the evil of the men of Shechem return on their heads, and upon them came the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal.
9.overview:
Gideon refused a crown for himself, his son and his grandson. Within a generation one of his sons had taken it, killing seventy brothers on a single stone with money from the temple of Baal-berith, and was crowned at Shechem by the oak where Joshua set up a stone as a witness against Israel (Josh. 24:26-27).

One son escapes, climbs the mountain of blessing, and shouts down the first fable in the Bible: the olive, the fig and the vine all decline to reign, and the bramble, with no shade to offer and the most flammable thing on a dry hillside, accepts at once. His curse runs both ways, fire out of Abimelech to devour Shechem and fire out of Shechem to devour Abimelech (v. 20), and both halves happen before the chapter ends.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Abimelech wins Shechem's backing, murders his brothers, and is crowned king.
verseByVerse.theology: This is Israel's first attempt at a king, and it is a warning. When the nation later asks Samuel for a king (1 Sam. 8), this chapter stands behind the request.
verseByVerse.examples: Jotham survives by hiding, and God preserves him to speak. Even in the worst of times God keeps a witness alive.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Abimelech the son of Jerubbaal went to Shechem to his mother's relatives and said to them and to the whole clan of his mother's family, "Say in the ears of all the leaders of Shechem, 'Which is better for you, that all seventy of the sons of Jerubbaal rule over you, or that one rule over you?' Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh." And his mother's relatives spoke all these words on his behalf in the ears of all the leaders of Shechem, and their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech, for they said, "He is our brother." And they gave him seventy pieces of silver out of the house of Baal-berith with which Abimelech hired worthless and reckless fellows, who followed him. And he went to his father's house at Ophrah and killed his brothers the sons of Jerubbaal, seventy men, on one stone. But Jotham the youngest son of Jerubbaal was left, for he hid himself. And all the leaders of Shechem came together, and all Beth-millo, and they went and made Abimelech king, by the oak of the pillar at Shechem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The campaign opens with a question that has been written so that only one answer is possible, and it contains a lie in the premise. Nobody has offered Shechem seventy rulers. Gideon refused the crown for himself and his sons in as many words (8:23), and there is no suggestion anywhere that his seventy sons had any designs on anything.

The clinching argument is not policy but blood: I am your bone and your flesh. Vote for me because I am one of you.

It works, for exactly the reason offered. He is our brother. Not he is competent, not he is godly, not he has any claim — he is ours.

The money comes out of a temple, and the temple is Baal-berith — the god Israel adopted as soon as Gideon died (8:33). The shrine that Israel set up in place of the LORD funds the murder of the deliverer's family.

Count the coins against the corpses: seventy pieces of silver, seventy brothers. One coin each. The going rate for a son of the man who saved the country was a single piece of temple silver, and it bought a gang of men the narrator describes as worthless and reckless — unemployed, unattached and available.

On one stone. The detail is there because it turns an atrocity into a ceremony. This is not a raid that got out of hand; it is an execution conducted at a single place, one man after another, in the courtyard of the house where the angel once sat under the tree.

One escapes, and the writer says how: he hid. Jotham survives by doing what his father did in chapter 6, which is to get out of sight of people who were looking for him.

Then they crown him, and the place they choose is the worst possible one. Shechem is where Joshua gathered all Israel, made them say three times that they would serve the LORD, and set up a great stone under a terebinth as a witness against us, for it has heard all the words of the LORD (Josh. 24:26-27).

They make a fratricide king at the foot of the stone that was put there to stop them dealing falsely with God.
verseByVerse.note: Abimelech means “my father is king”, a name at odds with Gideon’s refusal of kingship (8:23).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: From Mount Gerizim Jotham tells of the trees seeking a king: olive, fig and vine decline, and the bramble accepts, threatening fire (vv. 7-15). He applies the fable to Shechem (vv. 16-20) and flees (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: Jotham does not argue with Shechem; he tells them a story and lets them recognise themselves in it, as the prophet Nathan later does with David (2 Sam. 12:1-7).
verseByVerse.examples: Satire can be a faithful weapon. Jotham's fable has kept its force for three thousand years because it tells the truth about power in a form people remember.

verseByVerse.quote: When it was told to Jotham, he went and stood on top of Mount Gerizim and cried aloud and said to them, "Listen to me, you leaders of Shechem, that God may listen to you. The trees once went out to anoint a king over them, and they said to the olive tree, 'Reign over us.' But the olive tree said to them, 'Shall I leave my abundance, by which gods and men are honored, and go hold sway over the trees?' And the trees said to the fig tree, 'You come and reign over us.' But the fig tree said to them, 'Shall I leave my sweetness and my good fruit and go hold sway over the trees?' And the trees said to the vine, 'You come and reign over us.' But the vine said to them, 'Shall I leave my wine that cheers God and men and go hold sway over the trees?' Then all the trees said to the bramble, 'You come and reign over us.' And the bramble said to the trees, 'If in good faith you are anointing me king over you, then come and take refuge in my shade, but if not, let fire come out of the bramble and devour the cedars of Lebanon.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The surviving son climbs a mountain and shouts. Gerizim is the mountain of blessing, the one half the nation faced while the law was read in Joshua 8. It stands directly above Shechem, and it is often said that a voice from its slopes carries down to the town. Jotham chooses the place where blessings were pronounced, to pronounce a curse.

What follows is the first fable in the Bible, and it is very funny in a bleak way.

The trees want a king and go looking for one. They ask the olive first, which is the most valuable tree in the country — its oil lit the lamps of the tabernacle and anointed the priests. The olive declines, and its reason is the whole point of the fable: shall I leave my abundance... and go hold sway over the trees?

The fig says the same, and so does the vine. Three times over, the trees that are actually producing something ask why they would stop doing it in order to wave about above everybody else. Each refusal has the same shape: the productive have work to do, and the work is better than the position.

Then comes the bramble, which says yes immediately.

Two things about a bramble, and a Palestinian audience would have laughed at both. First, the offer of shade. A bramble is a thorn scrub that grows a foot or two off the ground; there is no shade under it, and anybody who tried to take refuge there would be cut to pieces. The one thing it promises is the one thing it cannot give.

Second, the threat. A dry bramble on a hillside is the most flammable thing in the country — it is what starts the fires that burn out whole slopes. The bramble cannot shelter anybody and it can burn everybody, and the cedars of Lebanon, the tallest and most magnificent trees there are, are precisely what it threatens.

The fable's argument is not that kingship is wrong. It is that the people most fit to lead will not usually want the job, and the person who wants it most is frequently the one with nothing to leave.
verseByVerse.note: The bramble of the fable is probably a kind of buckthorn or boxthorn, a low thorny shrub common in the hill country.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now therefore, if you acted in good faith and integrity when you made Abimelech king, and if you have dealt well with Jerubbaal and his house and have done to him as his deeds deserved— for my father fought for you and risked his life and delivered you from the hand of Midian, and you have risen up against my father's house this day and have killed his sons, seventy men on one stone, and have made Abimelech, the son of his female servant, king over the leaders of Shechem, because he is your relative— if you then have acted in good faith and integrity with Jerubbaal and with his house this day, then rejoice in Abimelech, and let him also rejoice in you. But if not, let fire come out from Abimelech and devour the leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo; and let fire come out from the leaders of Shechem and from Beth-millo and devour Abimelech." And Jotham ran away and fled and went to Beer and lived there, because of Abimelech his brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jotham drops the story and speaks plainly, and the case he makes is about debt.

His father fought for Shechem. He risked his life for them — the Hebrew is stronger, something like "threw his life out in front of him" — and delivered them from Midian. That is what they owed, and the killing of his sons is what they paid. He states the two facts side by side and lets the arithmetic stand, and he names the reason they gave: because he is your relative.

The conditional is heavy with sarcasm, and it is also a real offer: if this was honourable, then enjoy each other and live with what you have chosen.

The curse is precise and it runs both ways: fire out of Abimelech to consume Shechem; fire out of Shechem to consume Abimelech. He does not ask for an army or a judgment from outside. He asks that the two parties destroy each other, which is what people who have made an alliance like this one generally do.

The bramble threatened fire in the fable, and here it is applied. Everything Jotham asks for in this verse happens before the chapter ends, and verse 57 will name him when it does.

Then he runs. He does not stay to see it, does not raise a faction, and never appears again. The last surviving son of the man who saved Israel spends the rest of his life in Beer, out of his brother's reach.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–29 — God Sent an Evil Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God sends discord between Abimelech and Shechem, and a newcomer named Gaal stirs the city against its king.
verseByVerse.theology: God's justice in this chapter works slowly. Three years pass between the murders and the first sign of judgment, and the guilty may have thought they had got away with it. God's silence is not his indifference.
verseByVerse.examples: Alliances built on shared guilt rarely hold. What united Shechem and Abimelech was a crime, and a crime makes a poor foundation for trust.

verseByVerse.quote: Abimelech ruled over Israel three years. And God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem, and the leaders of Shechem dealt treacherously with Abimelech, that the violence done to the seventy sons of Jerubbaal might come, and their blood be laid on Abimelech their brother, who killed them, and on the men of Shechem, who strengthened his hands to kill his brothers. And the leaders of Shechem put men in ambush against him on the mountaintops, and they robbed all who passed by them along that way. And it was told to Abimelech. And Gaal the son of Ebed moved into Shechem with his relatives, and the leaders of Shechem put confidence in him. And they went out into the field and gathered the grapes from their vineyards and trod them and held a festival; and they went into the house of their god and ate and drank and reviled Abimelech. And Gaal the son of Ebed said, "Who is Abimelech, and who are we of Shechem, that we should serve him? Is he not the son of Jerubbaal, and is not Zebul his officer? Serve the men of Hamor the father of Shechem; but why should we serve him? Would that this people were under my hand! Then I would remove Abimelech. I would say to Abimelech, 'Increase your army, and come out.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three years pass, and then the alliance begins to come apart, and the narrator will not let us call it politics.

God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem. Whatever precisely that means, and the phrase is deliberately unsettling, the writer's point is the agency. The suspicion that grows up between these two parties is not accidental, and it is not merely the natural fate of a conspiracy. It was sent.

Verse 24 is the engine of everything that follows, and it is placed here so that no reader can mistake the mechanism for the cause.

Two parties are named, and the second is the one that ordinarily escapes. Abimelech killed them. The men of Shechem strengthened his hands to kill them — they did not swing anything, they wrote a cheque out of a temple and let a hired gang do the work. The book holds both accountable in one sentence, and the financiers are not treated as bystanders.

The first symptom of the breakdown is banditry. Shechem's leaders start robbing travellers on the roads — which is exactly the condition Deborah's song described as the mark of oppression (5:6), and it is now being organised by Israelites against anybody who passes.

A newcomer arrives and the city takes to him at once, which is what a city does when it has already stopped trusting the man it crowned.

The scene is a harvest festival in the temple of their god, with the wine flowing and the talk turning against the king — and the god in question is the one whose treasury paid for his coronation.

Listen to the argument that finishes Abimelech, because it is the argument that made him.

Shechem crowned him on the grounds that he was their relative, their bone and their flesh. Gaal's whole case is that he is not — he is Jerubbaal's son, an outsider from Ophrah, and Shechem should be serving its own ancient line instead.

Nothing has changed about Abimelech. The city has simply applied its own principle in the other direction, which is what happens to every arrangement built on being one of us.

Does God send evil? He sent a spirit of discord as judgment on men who were already guilty of murder (v. 24), working through their own free and guilty choices, as with Saul (1 Samuel 16:14) and Ahab (1 Kings 22:22). God is never the author of sin (James 1:13), but he rules even the evil of the wicked and turns it to justice.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zebul betrays Gaal to an ambush, and Gaal is driven out (vv. 30-41). Abimelech razes Shechem and sows it with salt (vv. 42-45), then burns about a thousand people inside the stronghold of El-berith (vv. 46-49).
verseByVerse.theology: The violence grows: from seventy brothers on one stone to a whole city razed and a thousand people burned. Evil that is not repented of rarely stays the same size.
verseByVerse.examples: Abimelech's men do whatever he does, as Gideon's once did. Following a leader is only as good as the leader followed, and Christians are called to imitate others only as they imitate Christ (1 Cor. 11:1).

verseByVerse.quote: When Zebul the ruler of the city heard the words of Gaal the son of Ebed, his anger was kindled. And he sent messengers to Abimelech secretly, saying, "Behold, Gaal the son of Ebed and his relatives have come to Shechem, and they are stirring up the city against you. Now therefore, go by night, you and the people who are with you, and set an ambush in the field. Then in the morning, as soon as the sun is up, rise early and rush upon the city. And when he and the people who are with him come out against you, you may do to them as your hand finds to do." So Abimelech and all the men who were with him rose up by night and set an ambush against Shechem in four companies. And Gaal the son of Ebed went out and stood in the entrance of the gate of the city, and Abimelech and the people who were with him rose from the ambush. And when Gaal saw the people, he said to Zebul, "Look, people are coming down from the mountaintops!" And Zebul said to him, "You mistake the shadow of the mountains for men." Gaal spoke again and said, "Look, people are coming down from the center of the land, and one company is coming from the direction of the Diviners' Oak."
