Then Zebul said to him, "Where is your mouth now, you who said, 'Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him?' Are not these the people whom you despised? Go out now and fight with them." And Gaal went out at the head of the leaders of Shechem and fought with Abimelech. And Abimelech chased him, and he fled before him. And many fell wounded, up to the entrance of the gate. And Abimelech lived at Arumah, and Zebul drove out Gaal and his relatives, so that they could not dwell at Shechem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abimelech has a man inside. Zebul governs Shechem for him, keeps his position through the whole festival of insults, and sends a message out by night.

The plan he proposes is a night march and a dawn ambush — and it is the plan Gideon used, minus everything that made Gideon's work God's.

Now a small scene of pure malice, and it is the best-written thing in the chapter.

Gaal is standing in the gate at dawn and sees movement on the hills. He says so. And Zebul — who arranged the ambush, who knows exactly what is coming, and who is standing beside him — tells him he is seeing shadows.

He keeps him talking until the companies are too close to escape.

Then he drops the pretence and quotes the man's own festival speech back at him. Where is your mouth now?

Gaal has to go out and fight, in front of the city, on ground he has not chosen, with the men he talked into it the night before. He is beaten to the gate, many fall, and Zebul drives him out of the city.

That is the whole career of Gaal son of Ebed. He arrives, is trusted, makes a speech at a party, and is gone within two verses of the fighting starting.

verseByVerse.quote: On the following day, the people went out into the field, and Abimelech was told. He took his people and divided them into three companies and set an ambush in the fields. And he looked and saw the people coming out of the city. So he rose against them and killed them. Abimelech and the company that was with him rushed forward and stood at the entrance of the gate of the city, while the two companies rushed upon all who were in the field and killed them. And Abimelech fought against the city all that day. He captured the city and killed the people who were in it, and he razed the city and sowed it with salt. When all the leaders of the Tower of Shechem heard of it, they entered the stronghold of the house of El-berith. Abimelech was told that all the leaders of the Tower of Shechem were gathered together. And Abimelech went up to Mount Zalmon, he and all the people who were with him. And Abimelech took an axe in his hand and cut down a bundle of brushwood and took it up and laid it on his shoulder. And he said to the men who were with him, "What you have seen me do, hurry and do as I have done." So every one of the people cut down his bundle and following Abimelech put it against the stronghold, and they set the stronghold on fire over them, so that all the people of the Tower of Shechem also died, about 1,000 men and women.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next morning the townspeople go out to work, and Abimelech is waiting for them.

He takes the gate first so that nobody can get back inside, and kills the people in the open — farmers, in the fields, in the morning.

Then follow a day of street fighting, the killing of the population, and the town pulled down and sown with salt. Sowing a site with salt is a formal act. It is not agriculture; the amounts involved could never sterilise a field. It is a curse performed in public, declaring that nothing will ever grow here again and no one will ever live here.

The man is destroying the city that made him king, in the ceremonial language reserved for places under a curse, three years after they crowned him at the oak.

The last of them shut themselves into the temple stronghold. Where else would they go? It is the strongest building in the city and it belongs to their god — the same treasury that paid the seventy pieces of silver.

Here is a sentence that ought to stop any reader who has just come through chapter 7. What you have seen me do, hurry and do as I have done. That echoes what Gideon said to the three hundred on the edge of the Midianite camp: look at me, and do likewise... when I blow the trumpet... then blow the trumpets also (7:17-18).

The same idea, the same posture, one generation later. Gideon's men copied him and an army destroyed itself in the dark. Abimelech's men copy him and carry firewood up to a temple full of their own countrymen.

A thousand people are burned inside the house of their god, and the first half of Jotham's curse is now complete, and it happened exactly as he said it: let fire come out from Abimelech and devour the leaders of Shechem. The bramble has burned what asked it to reign.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Thebez a woman on a tower ends Abimelech's life, and the narrator states what God has been doing all along.
verseByVerse.theology: He dies doing the thing that killed Shechem, at a door with fire in his hand, and the second half of Jotham's curse arrives from the last direction he was watching — from above, and from a woman he never saw.
verseByVerse.examples: Abimelech spent his dying breath on his reputation. It is worth asking what we are spending our lives to have said about us, and whether it matters more to us to be known by God (1 Cor. 8:3).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Abimelech went to Thebez and encamped against Thebez and captured it. But there was a strong tower within the city, and all the men and women and all the leaders of the city fled to it and shut themselves in, and they went up to the roof of the tower. And Abimelech came to the tower and fought against it and drew near to the door of the tower to burn it with fire. And a certain woman threw an upper millstone on Abimelech's head and crushed his skull. Then he called quickly to the young man his armor-bearer and said to him, "Draw your sword and kill me, lest they say of me, 'A woman killed him.'" And his young man thrust him through, and he died. And when the men of Israel saw that Abimelech was dead, everyone departed to his home. Thus God returned the evil of Abimelech, which he committed against his father in killing his seventy brothers. And God also made all the evil of the men of Shechem return on their heads, and upon them came the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He moves on to the next town, and it goes the same way — the city taken, the population shut into the tower. He has done this before, and it worked.

He walks up to the door with fire in his hand, personally, because it is what he did at Shechem and there is no reason to think it will fail twice.

An upper millstone is the top wheel of a hand mill — the stone a woman turned every morning to grind the day's flour. It is round and heavy, yet a woman could lift it, and from the roof of a tower it is a perfectly adequate weapon.

She is not named, and she is not a soldier. She is somebody on a roof with the household equipment, and she ends the career of the first man in Israel to call himself king.

His last recorded thought is about his reputation. He has minutes to live with a crushed skull, and what occupies him is the sentence people will say afterwards. So he arranges an alternative version and has his armour-bearer stab him to secure it — which is a fair summary of the whole life. Everything he ever did was about what would be said about him.

It did not work. The story is told here, in full, with the millstone in it. And it was still being told generations later: when Joab briefs a messenger on how to report a death at a wall, he expects the king to interrupt with who killed Abimelech the son of Jerubbesheth? Did not a woman cast an upper millstone on him from the wall? (2 Sam. 11:21).

Soldiers in Israel evidently knew it. The one thing he spent his dying breath preventing is the one detail that survived.

The army goes home. There is no succession, no mourning, no burial recorded, and no rest for the land at the end of this cycle — because this was never a deliverance. Abimelech is the one man in this book who is said only to have ruled Israel and is never said to have saved anybody.

Then the narrator, who has told fifty-five verses of politics and ambushes without a word of comment, states the meaning in two sentences. God returned it. Both halves, to both parties — to the man who killed his brothers, and to the men who paid for it out of a temple — and the writer names the mechanism as the curse of a youngest son who shouted from a mountainside and then went and lived quietly in Beer.

Nothing in this chapter looks like the hand of God while it is happening. It looks like a squalid provincial coup coming apart in the usual way: a rigged question, hired men, a conspiracy, a drunken speech, an ambush, a betrayal, a siege, a woman on a roof. That is exactly how it looked to everybody in it.

The blood of seventy brothers had been crying out from one stone in Ophrah for three years, and it was answered by a millstone and a bramble and a piece of bad advice at a city gate. God is not mentioned once between verses 25 and 55. He is named in verse 23 and again in verse 56, and those two verses hold everything in between.

Abel's blood cried from the ground in the same way (Genesis 4:10), and Scripture's last answer to such blood is not judgment alone. Hebrews speaks of the blood of Jesus, which speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (Hebrews 12:24): mercy for the guilty, bought by the one brother who let himself be killed for the rest.

9.theology:
The financiers are not bystanders. Verse 24 repays both the man who killed and the men who paid for the killing, and puts them in the same sentence.

The bramble. The fable's warning is that the one with nothing to give is often the one who wants to rule. It also waits for a king who reverses it. The olive would not leave its abundance to reign; the Son of God left the glory he shared with the Father, not to hold sway but to serve and to give his life (Philippians 2:6-8; Mark 10:45). Abimelech killed seventy brothers to take a throne. Jesus is not ashamed to call his people brothers, and he died to bring them to his (Hebrews 2:11).

The argument that makes you can unmake you. Shechem crowned Abimelech because he is our brother, and Gaal turned the city against him by claiming he was not one of them after all (v. 28). Any loyalty built on being one of us can be dismantled with the same tool.

Providence that looks like nothing. Most of the chapter reads as an ordinary coup coming apart, and that is how it looked to everybody in it. The narrator brackets it with two sentences about God, who sent the spirit (v. 23) and returned the evil (vv. 56-57).
9.examples:
Then: A man bought a crown with temple money at a rate of one silver piece per brother, ruled three years, burned a thousand of his own supporters inside their sanctuary, and died at a tower door because a woman dropped the top half of her kitchen mill on his head. His last request was that nobody should be able to say a woman killed him.

Now: Two things carry straight across. The first is verse 24 and the men who strengthened his hands: the people who fund, vote for, excuse or quietly enable what they would never do themselves, and who are named in the same sentence as the man who did it. Anyone who sees himself there need not wait for the millstone; the blood of Jesus speaks a better word than the blood of the seventy, and it is spoken over those who confess. The second is the fable: the person campaigning hardest for the position is very often the one with no fruit to leave behind, and the olive, the fig and the vine are usually busy.

10.title: Tola, Jair, and Renewed Apostasy
10.text: <sup>1</sup>After Abimelech there arose to save Israel Tola the son of Puah, son of Dodo, a man of Issachar, and he lived at Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim.<sup>2</sup>And he judged Israel twenty-three years. Then he died and was buried at Shamir.<sup>3</sup>After him arose Jair the Gileadite, who judged Israel twenty-two years.<sup>4</sup>And he had thirty sons who rode on thirty donkeys, and they had thirty cities, called Havvoth-jair to this day, which are in the land of Gilead.<sup>5</sup>And Jair died and was buried in Kamon.<sup>6</sup>The people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baals and the Ashtaroth, the gods of Syria, the gods of Sidon, the gods of Moab, the gods of the Ammonites, and the gods of the Philistines. And they forsook the LORD and did not serve him.<sup>7</sup>So the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of the Philistines and into the hand of the Ammonites,<sup>8</sup>and they crushed and oppressed the people of Israel that year. For eighteen years they oppressed all the people of Israel who were beyond the Jordan in the land of the Amorites, which is in Gilead.<sup>9</sup>And the Ammonites crossed the Jordan to fight also against Judah and against Benjamin and against the house of Ephraim, so that Israel was severely distressed.<sup>10</sup>And the people of Israel cried out to the LORD, saying, "We have sinned against you, because we have forsaken our God and have served the Baals."<sup>11</sup>And the LORD said to the people of Israel, "Did I not save you from the Egyptians and from the Amorites, from the Ammonites and from the Philistines?<sup>12</sup>The Sidonians also, and the Amalekites and the Maonites oppressed you, and you cried out to me, and I saved you out of their hand.<sup>13</sup>Yet you have forsaken me and served other gods; therefore I will save you no more.<sup>14</sup>Go and cry out to the gods whom you have chosen; let them save you in the time of your distress."<sup>15</sup>And the people of Israel said to the LORD, "We have sinned; do to us whatever seems good to you. Only please deliver us this day."<sup>16</sup>So they put away the foreign gods from among them and served the LORD, and he became impatient over the misery of Israel.<sup>17</sup>Then the Ammonites were called to arms, and they encamped in Gilead. And the people of Israel came together, and they encamped at Mizpah.<sup>18</sup>And the people, the leaders of Gilead, said one to another, "Who is the man who will begin to fight against the Ammonites? He shall be head over all the inhabitants of Gilead."
10.overview:
Tola judges twenty-three years and Jair twenty-two, and forty-five years pass in five verses with nothing going wrong.

Then the formula returns with the longest list in the book, the gods of every neighbour on every border, and two oppressors at once. Israel prays a real confession, and God refuses: I will save you no more, the only such refusal in the book. They accept the sentence, ask anyway, and put away the foreign gods with nothing promised them, and his soul can bear their misery no longer. The chapter ends with the elders of Gilead advertising for anybody to lead them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Tola of Issachar arose to save Israel and judged twenty-three years (vv. 1-2); Jair the Gileadite judged twenty-two, with thirty sons on thirty donkeys holding thirty towns (vv. 3-5).
verseByVerse.theology: Quiet years are a gift, even when nothing in them seems worth writing down. Faithfulness that makes no headlines is still faithfulness.
verseByVerse.examples: Jair's thirty sons on thirty donkeys is a display of rank — a donkey was what a man of standing rode — and it is Gideon's seventy sons in miniature. The judges have begun to look like dynasties, and Ibzan and Abdon will do the same thing again (12:9, 14).

verseByVerse.quote: After Abimelech there arose to save Israel Tola the son of Puah, son of Dodo, a man of Issachar, and he lived at Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim. And he judged Israel twenty-three years. Then he died and was buried at Shamir. After him arose Jair the Gileadite, who judged Israel twenty-two years. And he had thirty sons who rode on thirty donkeys, and they had thirty cities, called Havvoth-jair to this day, which are in the land of Gilead. And Jair died and was buried in Kamon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the fire and the millstone, two verses about a man who did nothing worth reporting.

Tola is given a father, a grandfather, a tribe, an address, a length of service and a grave. There is no oppression named, no battle, no crisis, no failure. He arose to save Israel — from what, we are not told — and then he judged for twenty-three years and was buried where he lived.

Jair gets one detail, and it is about status. Thirty sons, thirty donkeys, thirty towns. The towns were already called Havvoth-jair, the villages of Jair, in Numbers 32:41, after an earlier Jair of Manasseh; this judge was perhaps his descendant, or the old name was renewed in his day.

A donkey was what a man of rank rode in that country, and thirty sons each with his own mount and his own town is a display, a family that has arranged the map to suit itself. The office is quietly becoming a family business, and nobody says a word against it.

Before the criticism, though, notice what these five verses actually contain: forty-five years in which nothing goes wrong.

No apostasy is recorded, no raiders come, and nobody has to be rescued. Two men do their work for a working lifetime each and are buried in their own towns, and the writer has almost nothing to say about either of them.

Coming immediately after a chapter in which a thousand people burned inside a temple, that is not a dull passage. It is a mercy: a long stretch of unbroken quiet, and the reason there is nothing to tell is that nothing was wrong.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel serves the gods of every neighbour and forsook the LORD (v. 6), and God sells them to the Philistines and the Ammonites at once, who oppress Gilead eighteen years and then cross into Judah, Benjamin and Ephraim (vv. 7-9).
verseByVerse.theology: Idolatry is rarely content with one god. Once the LORD is no longer enough for a people, nothing else is either.
verseByVerse.examples: This is also the first oppression that comes from two directions at once. Ammon holds Gilead in the east and the Philistines press from the west, and the two threats will run on into the next six chapters — Jephthah against Ammon, Samson against the Philistines.

verseByVerse.quote: The people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baals and the Ashtaroth, the gods of Syria, the gods of Sidon, the gods of Moab, the gods of the Ammonites, and the gods of the Philistines. And they forsook the LORD and did not serve him. So the anger of the LORD was kindled against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of the Philistines and into the hand of the Ammonites, and they crushed and oppressed the people of Israel that year. For eighteen years they oppressed all the people of Israel who were beyond the Jordan in the land of the Amorites, which is in Gilead. And the Ammonites crossed the Jordan to fight also against Judah and against Benjamin and against the house of Ephraim, so that Israel was severely distressed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Count the entries in that list. First come the Baals and the Ashtaroth, the usual charge in this book; then the gods of Syria to the north, Sidon on the coast, Moab and Ammon across the Jordan, and the Philistines to the south-west. Seven in all, and between them they are every neighbour Israel has, in every direction.

This is not a nation drifting into one local cult because the rain matters. It is a nation that has collected the full set, taking up the religion of every people on every border, and kept them all.

The summary at the end of the verse is the flattest sentence in the book: they forsook the LORD and did not serve him. There is no qualification and no partial credit: not that they served him badly or now and then, but that they did not serve him.

Seven gods bring two oppressors at once. Every previous cycle had one main enemy: Cushan, Eglon, Jabin, Midian. Now Israel is worked from two sides, Ammon across the Jordan in the east and the Philistines on the western plain.

Then it spreads. Gilead had been taking it for eighteen years on the east bank, and now the Ammonites cross the river and go for the heartland: Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim.

That is a fair picture of what tolerated evil eventually does. The trouble that could be lived with while it stayed on the far side of the water does not stay there.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–14 — I Will Save You No More
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel confesses its sin, and for the only time in the book God refuses to save them, sending them instead to the gods they have chosen.
verseByVerse.theology: A confession can be honest and still be only the first word. God's refusal tests whether Israel wants him, or only his help (see vv. 15-16).
verseByVerse.examples: If you have ever felt that God has said no to you, notice that this chapter does not end at verse 14.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel cried out to the LORD, saying, "We have sinned against you, because we have forsaken our God and have served the Baals." And the LORD said to the people of Israel, "Did I not save you from the Egyptians and from the Amorites, from the Ammonites and from the Philistines? The Sidonians also, and the Amalekites and the Maonites oppressed you, and you cried out to me, and I saved you out of their hand. Yet you have forsaken me and served other gods; therefore I will save you no more. Go and cry out to the gods whom you have chosen; let them save you in the time of your distress."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the best prayer Israel has prayed in the book so far.

Every earlier cycle records only that they cried out. This time the cry has content, and the content is a confession: we have sinned against you. They name the offence, they name the party offended, and they specify what they did. Nobody is asking for the raiders to stop without mentioning why they came.

By any ordinary reckoning this is exactly what God has been waiting for. Yet his answer begins with a list, and the list is the point: Egyptians, Amorites, Ammonites, Philistines, Sidonians, Amalekites, Maonites. Seven oppressors, seven rescues — against the seven sets of gods in verse 6. (The Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, reads Midianites for Maonites, which would recall Gideon; the Hebrew has Maonites, probably a people of the south.)

The arithmetic is not accidental, and the argument is unanswerable: here is the list of everyone you have worshipped. Here is the list of everyone I have saved you from. They are the same length, and some of the names appear on both.

That last point is the sharpest thing in the passage. Israel is serving the gods of the Ammonites and the gods of the Philistines — and God's list of past rescues includes the Ammonites and the Philistines. They have adopted the religion of people God delivered them from.

The recurring clause in his summary is the one they have just used again: you cried out to me, and I saved you. He is quoting their own history of crying out.

Then comes the refusal. Nowhere else in this book is a cry for help answered with a refusal. There is no precedent for it and no softening after it, and it is spoken in answer to the most honest confession Israel has managed in ten chapters.

The force of the last verse is that it is not a threat. He is referring them elsewhere. You have been paying seven other departments for years; take the request to them. Let them save you in the time of your distress: the very thing they are advertised as doing.

The judgment is Bochim's, made explicit. There God said he would no longer drive out the nations Israel had declined to remove. Here he says he will no longer answer prayers a people have not really addressed to him. In both cases the sentence is that they may keep what they chose, and the horror of it is that God does not have to do anything at all.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–16 — They Put Away the Gods
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel accepts the verdict and asks anyway (v. 15), puts away the foreign gods and serves the LORD, and God can bear their misery no longer (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: The last clause of verse 16 is hard to translate and worth the effort: literally, his soul was shortened over the misery of Israel. It is the idiom used of a man at the end of his endurance, and it is used again of Samson when nagging "shortened his soul to death" (16:16; ESV "his soul was vexed to death").
verseByVerse.examples: For anyone who fears they have used up God's patience: in this book his patience runs out only once, and when it does, it runs out in the direction of mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel said to the LORD, "We have sinned; do to us whatever seems good to you. Only please deliver us this day." So they put away the foreign gods from among them and served the LORD, and he became impatient over the misery of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel does not argue with the verdict. God has said he will not save them, and they do not protest, bargain, or point out how long they have served him. They agree with the sentence, do to us whatever seems good to you, and ask anyway. It is a prayer with no claim in it: they have conceded that they deserve nothing and asked for everything.

Then a clause that has not appeared once in ten chapters. They went home and got rid of all seven sets and served the LORD instead. Every earlier repentance in this book is a noise. This one has furniture moving in it.

The order matters. Nothing has been promised; God has said no; they have accepted it and asked anyway; and with no assurance of any kind they clear out the shrines. That is not repentance bought by a guarantee. It is repentance performed in the dark.

So the last clause says that God could not stand it any longer. Not that he changed his mind about their guilt, and not that they had earned anything in the two verses since he refused them. He looked at the misery of a people who deserved every bit of it, and his patience gave way. Everything the book has said about him since 2:18 is in that clause. He was moved by their groaning then. Here, having formally declined to save them, he cannot watch.

Did God go back on his word? No. The refusal was real, and it exposed whether Israel wanted God or only relief. When they put the idols away with nothing promised, they were no longer the people he had refused, and God's warnings are always spoken so that sinners will turn (Jeremiah 18:7-8). His compassion does not cancel his justice; at the cross he would bear the misery himself. The God whose soul was shortened over Israel came near in his Son, who saw the crowds harassed and helpless and had compassion on them (Matthew 9:36).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ammon camps in Gilead and Israel at Mizpah (v. 17), and the leaders of Gilead ask who is the man who will fight, offering him the headship (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: The leaders' question, who will lead us, is one Israel keeps asking through Judges and Samuel. The Bible's final answer is a King whom God himself provides.
verseByVerse.examples: When nobody will step forward, God is not short of servants. He often finds them where respectable people were not looking.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Ammonites were called to arms, and they encamped in Gilead. And the people of Israel came together, and they encamped at Mizpah. And the people, the leaders of Gilead, said one to another, "Who is the man who will begin to fight against the Ammonites? He shall be head over all the inhabitants of Gilead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two armies face each other, and the chapter has one problem left to solve: Israel has no leader. Read the scene as it stands. The elders of Gilead are standing in a camp, in front of an enemy, asking each other a question, and the question is not what is the plan but who is the man. Nobody steps forward. They are reduced to advertising the post, and the salary offered is the highest office in the region: whoever will begin the fight becomes head over all Gilead.

In chapter 4 God had already commissioned Barak and he had to be sent for. In chapter 6 God had to go and find a man threshing in a pit. Here there is no commission recorded at all, and a committee is offering a promotion to anybody who will volunteer.

Weigh also what they are prepared to pay. Gideon was offered the crown after he won; this man is offered the headship before he starts, by men who have run out of alternatives.

The answer to their advertisement, in the next chapter, will be a man they had already thrown out of town. The leaders of Gilead are about to discover that the only person willing to take the job is somebody they had personally disqualified.

10.theology:
Seven and seven. The list of gods in verse 6 and the list of rescues in verses 11-12 are the same length, and the argument runs on the comparison. Israel has adopted the religion of the people God saved them from.

The refusal. Therefore I will save you no more (v. 13) is the one refusal in the book, and like the sentence at Bochim (2:3) it lets Israel keep what it chose.

Repentance performed in the dark. Every earlier cycle records a cry; this one records a clear-out (v. 16), after God has said no and nothing has been promised.

His soul was shortened. Israel had earned nothing since the refusal, yet God's patience gave way in the direction of mercy, as 2:18 said of him and as the cross would show again.
10.examples:
Then: A nation that had collected the gods of all seven of its neighbours finally said so out loud, was told to go and ask them for help, agreed that it deserved the answer, asked anyway, and then went home and threw the idols out before anyone had promised it a thing.

Now: Verse 16 is the model and verse 15 is the hard part. They made no claim, do to us whatever seems good to you, and cleared the house without any assurance that it would make a difference. Most repentance waits for terms. It is not a way of earning his help: the clear-out came after a lifetime of rescues they had done nothing to deserve, and the honesty to say we have sinned and mean it is itself the Spirit's work. And verse 14 is the warning underneath it all: the worst thing God can say to a person is not no. It is "go and ask the thing you have actually been serving, and see what it can do for you". If that sentence frightens you, read verse 16 again: a people who came with nothing but we have sinned were not finally turned away, and Jesus has promised that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37).

11.title: Jephthah
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty warrior, but he was the son of a prostitute. Gilead was the father of Jephthah.<sup>2</sup>And Gilead's wife also bore him sons. And when his wife's sons grew up, they drove Jephthah out and said to him, "You shall not have an inheritance in our father's house, for you are the son of another woman."<sup>3</sup>Then Jephthah fled from his brothers and lived in the land of Tob, and worthless fellows collected around Jephthah and went out with him.<sup>4</sup>After a time the Ammonites made war against Israel.<sup>5</sup>And when the Ammonites made war against Israel, the elders of Gilead went to bring Jephthah from the land of Tob.<sup>6</sup>And they said to Jephthah, "Come and be our leader, that we may fight against the Ammonites."<sup>7</sup>But Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, "Did you not hate me and drive me out of my father's house? Why have you come to me now when you are in distress?"<sup>8</sup>And the elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, "That is why we have turned to you now, that you may go with us and fight against the Ammonites and be our head over all the inhabitants of Gilead."<sup>9</sup>Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, "If you bring me home again to fight against the Ammonites, and the LORD gives them over to me, I will be your head."<sup>10</sup>And the elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, "The LORD will be witness between us, if we do not do as you say."<sup>11</sup>So Jephthah went with the elders of Gilead, and the people made him head and leader over them. And Jephthah spoke all his words before the LORD at Mizpah.<sup>12</sup>Then Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites and said, "What do you have against me, that you have come to me to fight against my land?"<sup>13</sup>And the king of the Ammonites answered the messengers of Jephthah, "Because Israel on coming up from Egypt took away my land, from the Arnon to the Jabbok and to the Jordan; now therefore restore it peaceably."<sup>14</sup>Jephthah again sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites<sup>15</sup>and said to him, "Thus says Jephthah: Israel did not take away the land of Moab or the land of the Ammonites,<sup>16</sup>but when they came up from Egypt, Israel went through the wilderness to the Red Sea and came to Kadesh.<sup>17</sup>Israel then sent messengers to the king of Edom, saying, 'Please let us pass through your land,' but the king of Edom would not listen. And they sent also to the king of Moab, but he would not consent. So Israel remained at Kadesh.<sup>18</sup>"Then they journeyed through the wilderness and went around the land of Edom and the land of Moab and arrived on the east side of the land of Moab and camped on the other side of the Arnon. But they did not enter the territory of Moab, for the Arnon was the boundary of Moab.<sup>19</sup>Israel then sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, king of Heshbon, and Israel said to him, 'Please let us pass through your land to our country,'<sup>20</sup>but Sihon did not trust Israel to pass through his territory, so Sihon gathered all his people together and encamped at Jahaz and fought with Israel.<sup>21</sup>And the LORD, the God of Israel, gave Sihon and all his people into the hand of Israel, and they defeated them. So Israel took possession of all the land of the Amorites, who inhabited that country.<sup>22</sup>And they took possession of all the territory of the Amorites from the Arnon to the Jabbok and from the wilderness to the Jordan.<sup>23</sup>So then the LORD, the God of Israel, dispossessed the Amorites from before his people Israel; and are you to take possession of them?<sup>24</sup>Will you not possess what Chemosh your god gives you to possess? And all that the LORD our God has dispossessed before us, we will possess.<sup>25</sup>Now are you any better than Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab? Did he ever contend against Israel, or did he ever go to war with them?<sup>26</sup>While Israel lived in Heshbon and its villages, and in Aroer and its villages, and in all the cities that are on the banks of the Arnon, 300 years, why did you not deliver them within that time?<sup>27</sup>I therefore have not sinned against you, and you do me wrong by making war on me. The LORD, the Judge, decide this day between the people of Israel and the people of Ammon."<sup>28</sup>But the king of the Ammonites did not listen to the words of Jephthah that he sent to him.<sup>29</sup>Then the Spirit of the LORD was upon Jephthah, and he passed through Gilead and Manasseh and passed on to Mizpah of Gilead, and from Mizpah of Gilead he passed on to the Ammonites.<sup>30</sup>And Jephthah made a vow to the LORD and said, "If you will give the Ammonites into my hand,<sup>31</sup>then whatever comes out from the doors of my house to meet me when I return in peace from the Ammonites shall be the LORD's, and I will offer it up for a burnt offering."<sup>32</sup>So Jephthah crossed over to the Ammonites to fight against them, and the LORD gave them into his hand.<sup>33</sup>And he struck them from Aroer to the neighborhood of Minnith, twenty cities, and as far as Abel-keramim, with a great blow. So the Ammonites were subdued before the people of Israel.<sup>34</sup>Then Jephthah came to his home at Mizpah. And behold, his daughter came out to meet him with tambourines and with dances. She was his only child; besides her he had neither son nor daughter.<sup>35</sup>And as soon as he saw her, he tore his clothes and said, "Alas, my daughter! You have brought me very low, and you have become the cause of great trouble to me. For I have opened my mouth to the LORD, and I cannot take back my vow."<sup>36</sup>And she said to him, "My father, you have opened your mouth to the LORD; do to me according to what has gone out of your mouth, now that the LORD has avenged you on your enemies, on the Ammonites."<sup>37</sup>So she said to her father, "Let this thing be done for me: leave me alone two months, that I may go up and down on the mountains and weep for my virginity, I and my companions."<sup>38</sup>So he said, "Go." Then he sent her away for two months, and she departed, she and her companions, and wept for her virginity on the mountains.<sup>39</sup>And at the end of two months, she returned to her father, who did with her according to his vow that he had made. She had never known a man, and it became a custom in Israel<sup>40</sup>that the daughters of Israel went year by year to lament the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite four days in the year.
11.overview:
Gilead's elders, desperate for anyone who will fight Ammon, hire the man their own community had thrown out: the son of a prostitute, living by raiding with a band of empty men. Before he fights, he does what no other judge does: he argues Israel's case to the king of Ammon from history and hands the verdict to God.

Then the Spirit of the LORD comes upon him, and in the very next verse he vows to burn whatever comes out of his house to meet him. God gives him the victory, which was never for sale, and his only child comes out of the door with tambourines.
11.theology:
Grace that cannot be bought. The Spirit came first, and the victory in v. 32 answers the Spirit in v. 29, not the bargain in v. 30 (see vv. 29-31). Trading a life for a battle is how the neighbouring nations prayed, and of such offerings God says they never came into his mind (Jer. 7:31).

Knowing God's word. Jephthah knows Israel's history well enough to lecture a king from it, yet he does not know what his own God's law says about vows. The law offered a way to redeem a person vowed to the LORD, and it forbade burning children outright, so I cannot take back my vow was sincere and it was wrong (see vv. 39-40).

Did he kill her? The old reading that he dedicated her to lifelong virginity rests on a possible or in v. 31 and the triple stress on her virginity. It is not foolish, but it is the weaker case: olah never means anything but a whole burnt sacrifice, v. 35 is unintelligible if the outcome is religious service, Israel had no order of celibate women, and the daughters go out to lament her. Either way the vow was faithless, unnecessary and pagan in shape when he made it.

Hebrews 11:32. Jephthah is named for faith alongside Gideon, Barak and Samson. Hebrews commends what these men did by faith (Heb. 11:33-34), not everything they did.
11.examples:
Then: A man his family had written off argued Israel's case better than any leader in the book, referred the verdict to God, went out with the Spirit of the LORD upon him, and then offered to pay for a victory he had already been given.

Now: Look at the promises you have made to God in a crisis. If a vow was made to secure something, ask whether God had not already promised it, and whether what you call devotion is really a payment plan for grace. Nothing is owed for what Christ has already bought; what is left is thanks, which the Spirit works in us freely. Notice too what destroyed Jephthah's house: not unbelief, but sincerity working on a law he had never read. God has given his word so that his people need not grope in the dark, and his Spirit opens it to those who ask. And if you have already spoken a rash word or made a vow God never asked for, the way back is not to pay it at any cost but to bring it to him, confess it, and be released by the one whose vow was kept perfectly for us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — The Son of a Prostitute
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The man who will deliver Gilead starts as its outcast: a proven fighter, disinherited by his half-brothers because of his mother, and leading a band of drifters in the land of Tob.
verseByVerse.theology: God's choice of deliverers keeps passing over the respectable: a left-handed Benjamite, a woman judging under a palm tree, the least man of the weakest clan, and now a prostitute's son.
verseByVerse.examples: The book is about to make a great deal turn on a man his own family had written off. Scripture repeats that shape, from Joseph to David, and it reaches its height in the stone the builders rejected that became the cornerstone, words Jesus took for himself (Ps. 118:22; Matt. 21:42). Jephthah is a dim and flawed instance of it, but it is the same God at work.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty warrior, but he was the son of a prostitute. Gilead was the father of Jephthah. And Gilead's wife also bore him sons. And when his wife's sons grew up, they drove Jephthah out and said to him, "You shall not have an inheritance in our father's house, for you are the son of another woman." Then Jephthah fled from his brothers and lived in the land of Tob, and worthless fellows collected around Jephthah and went out with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two facts in one sentence, and the second had already decided his life. He is a mighty warrior, the phrase the angel used of Gideon in the winepress, and in Jephthah's case demonstrably true. And he is the son of a prostitute, which in that society settled where he could live, what he could inherit and who would speak to him.

What his brothers say is a legal formula, not an insult: a ruling on the estate, on the grounds of his mother's occupation. He is evicted from his father's house for something that happened before he was born, by the respectable half of the family, protecting an inheritance they had done nothing to earn.

Tob is outside Israel, up towards Syria, and what forms around him there is a band of worthless fellows, empty men, the same class of word used of the crew Abimelech hired with temple silver (9:4). On paper, the man Gilead is about to make its head has Abimelech's exact profile: an irregular son, thrown out by his brothers, living off raiding.

The difference between them will not be their backgrounds. It will be that in verse 29 the Spirit of the LORD comes on this one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–11 — Hiring the Man They Threw Out
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The elders who drove Jephthah out now come to Tob to hire him, and he makes them admit what they did before he agrees to lead them.
verseByVerse.theology: This is a negotiation, not a call. Othniel, Ehud, Deborah, Gideon: God raised them up or spoke to them. Here a committee that has run out of options hires a man on terms, and the terms are settled before the fighting starts.
verseByVerse.examples: There is something here for anyone who has been valued only for what they could do. Jephthah's bitterness is understandable, and he is right about the elders. But God does not love his people for their usefulness: the son who came home hoping to be taken on as a hired servant was given a robe and a ring instead (Luke 15:19-22).

verseByVerse.quote: After a time the Ammonites made war against Israel. And when the Ammonites made war against Israel, the elders of Gilead went to bring Jephthah from the land of Tob. And they said to Jephthah, "Come and be our leader, that we may fight against the Ammonites." But Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, "Did you not hate me and drive me out of my father's house? Why have you come to me now when you are in distress?" And the elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, "That is why we have turned to you now, that you may go with us and fight against the Ammonites and be our head over all the inhabitants of Gilead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the answer to the advertisement at the end of chapter 10 (10:18). The leaders of Gilead have worked through the respectable candidates, and the man they come to find is the one their own community legally expelled.

He does not make it easy for them, and he is not wrong. Did you not hate me: a formal disinheritance is a public act, and the elders signed off on it. Why have you come to me now when you are in distress: we both know you would not be in Tob if Ammon were quiet. There is bitterness in it, and complete accuracy. He is being valued for his usefulness by people who never valued him for anything else.

They concede the whole charge. They do not deny driving him out or apologise; they say, in effect, yes, and that is exactly why we are here. And they raise the offer: verse 6 asked for a battlefield leader; verse 8 offers head over all the inhabitants of Gilead, the permanent office they had advertised. The price has gone up in two verses because they can see he might say no.

verseByVerse.quote: Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, "If you bring me home again to fight against the Ammonites, and the LORD gives them over to me, I will be your head." And the elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, "The LORD will be witness between us, if we do not do as you say." So Jephthah went with the elders of Gilead, and the people made him head and leader over them. And Jephthah spoke all his words before the LORD at Mizpah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He accepts, and he gets it in writing. The middle clause is the best thing in the sentence: and the LORD gives them over to me. Jephthah is not promising to win; if there is a victory it will be God's doing. The outcast raider has better theology in his contract than the elders have in their crisis. Yet he is still bargaining, for the headship, in advance, on terms.

Then he takes the contract before God, repeating the whole agreement out loud before the LORD at Mizpah. This is a man who believes that words spoken to God are binding. Hold that thought. When he says in his doorway I have opened my mouth to the LORD, and I cannot take back my vow, it will not be a sudden scruple but the same right conviction, running all the way through the chapter.

Notice the order, though: the arrangement is ratified at Mizpah after it has been agreed. God will honour it anyway (v. 29), but nobody in the chapter asked him first.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–28 — A History Lesson to a King
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before he fights, Jephthah writes. Ammon claims land Israel took on the way up from Egypt, and Jephthah answers with history, with precedent, and with an appeal to God as Judge. Ammon does not listen.
verseByVerse.theology: It is the longest speech by any judge in the book, and its instinct is right: settle the facts, establish the claim, and put the verdict in God's hands rather than seize it.
verseByVerse.examples: Sixteen verses of careful history, three arguments and a formal appeal to God changed nothing (v. 28). Jephthah did everything right here, and the war happened anyway. A good case, well made, does not always end a quarrel; sometimes it only shows who was in the right when the quarrel turned violent. That is worth remembering when patient, honest reasoning seems to have been wasted.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites and said, "What do you have against me, that you have come to me to fight against my land?" And the king of the Ammonites answered the messengers of Jephthah, "Because Israel on coming up from Egypt took away my land, from the Arnon to the Jabbok and to the Jordan; now therefore restore it peaceably." Jephthah again sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites and said to him, "Thus says Jephthah: Israel did not take away the land of Moab or the land of the Ammonites,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The raider's first act as head of Gilead is to open negotiations. Everything in his background predicts a fight; instead he sends a letter asking what the actual grievance is. Deuteronomy 20:10 requires exactly this, offering terms of peace before a siege, and whether Jephthah knows the statute or is simply being sensible, he does what the law asks and what no one else in this half of the book bothers with.

The answer is a territorial claim with a date on it, and it deserves to be heard properly. The king is not saying that Israel is offensive or that the borders are inconvenient. He is saying: that land was ours, you took it on the way up from Egypt, give it back. It is the kind of claim made in every century, and he evidently believes it.

The reply is not a threat but an argument. Thus says Jephthah borrows the formula a prophet uses, and there is some swagger in a border chieftain adopting it, but what follows is a serious piece of work.

verseByVerse.quote: but when they came up from Egypt, Israel went through the wilderness to the Red Sea and came to Kadesh. Israel then sent messengers to the king of Edom, saying, 'Please let us pass through your land,' but the king of Edom would not listen. And they sent also to the king of Moab, but he would not consent. So Israel remained at Kadesh. "Then they journeyed through the wilderness and went around the land of Edom and the land of Moab and arrived on the east side of the land of Moab and camped on the other side of the Arnon. But they did not enter the territory of Moab, for the Arnon was the boundary of Moab. Israel then sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, king of Heshbon, and Israel said to him, 'Please let us pass through your land to our country,' but Sihon did not trust Israel to pass through his territory, so Sihon gathered all his people together and encamped at Jahaz and fought with Israel. And the LORD, the God of Israel, gave Sihon and all his people into the hand of Israel, and they defeated them. So Israel took possession of all the land of the Amorites, who inhabited that country. And they took possession of all the territory of the Amorites from the Arnon to the Jabbok and from the wilderness to the Jordan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The defence opens with what Israel asked for and did not get. Twice Israel requested passage, from Edom and from Moab; twice it was refused, and twice Israel accepted the refusal and stayed at Kadesh. A nation that took land by force whenever it was told no would not have waited. They went the long way round rather than cross a border they had no right to cross, and camped beyond the Arnon, the river that marked Moab's boundary. Jephthah is arguing from a survey.

A third request went to Sihon, king of the Amorites, and this time the refusal came with an army: Sihon mobilised and marched out to Jahaz to attack. Everything turns on that, and the answer to Ammon's claim is one word: Amorites.

Compare the two descriptions. Ammon claimed the land from the Arnon to the Jabbok and to the Jordan (v. 13). Jephthah says Israel took from the Amorites the territory from the Arnon to the Jabbok and from the wilderness to the Jordan (v. 22). The boundaries match to the mile, but the previous owner is different. The land was not Ammonite when Israel arrived. It was Sihon's, and Sihon had taken it from Moab a generation earlier (Num. 21:26). Israel took it from the man who attacked them, in a war they did not start, having asked first. Ammon is claiming compensation for a loss somebody else suffered.

verseByVerse.quote: So then the LORD, the God of Israel, dispossessed the Amorites from before his people Israel; and are you to take possession of them? Will you not possess what Chemosh your god gives you to possess? And all that the LORD our God has dispossessed before us, we will possess.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having proved the case in court, he moves it to a higher one. So far the argument has been legal and historical. Now Jephthah says what actually settles it: the Amorites were not evicted by Israelite arms. The LORD, the God of Israel, dispossessed them, and what God has granted, a king of Ammon cannot reassign.

Then comes a verse that has troubled readers for a long time, because it sounds as though Jephthah thinks Chemosh is real. Take the difficulty at full strength first. He appears to be saying: your god gives you land, our God gives us land, and each nation keeps what its own deity provides. That is the belief that each people has its own god, and it falls short of what Israel was taught. Deuteronomy 4:39 says the LORD is God in heaven above and on the earth beneath; there is no other.

Two things can be said. The first is that this is diplomacy. Jephthah writes to a foreign king in that king's own terms, arguing from a premise his correspondent already holds: by your principles, you keep what Chemosh gives; by the same principle, leave alone what the LORD has given. It is a form of argument, not necessarily the writer's creed.

The second is more uncomfortable and may also be true. Chemosh was the god of Moab; Ammon's god was Milcom. Perhaps the king of Ammon was claiming old Moabite land as overlord of both peoples, so that Jephthah answers him in Moab's terms, and Moab runs through the whole letter (vv. 15, 17-18, 25). But if Jephthah has simply run the two peoples together, his theology is roughly right and careless in its details, and a man who can lecture a king from the national archive yet blur which god he is talking about is exactly the man who is about to make this vow.
verseByVerse.note: Ammon's god appears in Kings both as Milcom and as Molech (1 Kings 11:5, 7), the god to whom the law forbids Israel to give its children (Lev. 18:21).

verseByVerse.quote: Now are you any better than Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab? Did he ever contend against Israel, or did he ever go to war with them? While Israel lived in Heshbon and its villages, and in Aroer and its villages, and in all the cities that are on the banks of the Arnon, 300 years, why did you not deliver them within that time? I therefore have not sinned against you, and you do me wrong by making war on me. The LORD, the Judge, decide this day between the people of Israel and the people of Ammon." But the king of the Ammonites did not listen to the words of Jephthah that he sent to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A last argument from precedent, and a good one. Balak, king of Moab, had every reason to fight for that land and never did. He was frightened enough of Israel to hire a prophet to curse them from a hilltop (Num. 22), which tells you what he thought of his chances in the field, yet he never disputed the title. If the rightful owner did not press the claim, why is Ammon pressing it now?

Then comes the length of settled possession: three hundred years without one attempt to recover the land. Any lawyer would reach for this: if it was yours, you have had three centuries to say so. Jephthah even names the towns, Heshbon, Aroer and the villages along the Arnon, so the king can check the roll himself.

The figure also bears on the date of the exodus. Taken exactly, it fits the earlier date (about 1446 BC) and the 480 years of 1 Kings 6:1, once we allow that some judges ruled at the same time in different regions, and it puts Jephthah around 1100 BC. Christians who date the exodus later, about 1260 BC, take three hundred as a round number or a diplomat's generous claim. Faithful scholars differ here, and Jephthah's argument stands either way.

He ends by refusing to judge his own case. He has made his argument, but he does not declare himself the winner. He hands the file upward: the LORD, the Judge, decide this day. In a book where every strong man has so far settled his quarrels with his own hands, a leader who submits a dispute to God for a verdict is doing something the others never thought of.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–33 — The Spirit, and Then the Vow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Spirit of the LORD comes upon Jephthah, and in the very next verse he makes his vow. Those two verses, side by side, are the heart of the chapter.
verseByVerse.theology: Vows as such were lawful in Israel, and many were freely and rightly made (Num. 30; Ps. 116:14). What is wrong here is not that Jephthah vowed, but what he vowed and why.
verseByVerse.examples: The shape of the bargain is not Israelite. Offering a life in exchange for a victory is what the neighbours did: the king of Moab offers his eldest son on his own city wall when a battle turns against him (2 Kings 3:27).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Spirit of the LORD was upon Jephthah, and he passed through Gilead and Manasseh and passed on to Mizpah of Gilead, and from Mizpah of Gilead he passed on to the Ammonites. And Jephthah made a vow to the LORD and said, "If you will give the Ammonites into my hand, then whatever comes out from the doors of my house to meet me when I return in peace from the Ammonites shall be the LORD's, and I will offer it up for a burnt offering."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Read verse 29, then verse 30, and let nothing soften what stands between them. The Spirit of the LORD comes upon Jephthah, the book's formula for Othniel: God taking hold of a man and equipping him for the work. Whatever the elders negotiated, God has now put his own hand on the appointment. The commission is settled.

Then, with the Spirit of God already upon him, he tries to buy what he has just been given. Verse 29 is grace: unasked, unpriced, already granted. Verse 30 is a purchase offer for the same goods. If you will give the Ammonites into my hand: he is negotiating for a thing he is already carrying. A man who has survived by getting everything in writing has brought that habit into the presence of God, and God does not do business on those terms.

Consider what he offers. Houses in that country were not full of livestock waiting at the door. What comes out of a man's house to meet him when he comes home in triumph is his household. People have tried hard to make this a promise about a goat, but the text does not read that way.

Of offerings like this, Israel's God says he never commanded them and they never came into his mind (Jer. 7:31). Jephthah has learned the history, but he prays like a man who picked up his religion in Tob.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV note gives “whoever” as a possible rendering of “whatever comes out” in v. 31.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jephthah crossed over to the Ammonites to fight against them, and the LORD gave them into his hand. And he struck them from Aroer to the neighborhood of Minnith, twenty cities, and as far as Abel-keramim, with a great blow. So the Ammonites were subdued before the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD gave Ammon into Jephthah's hand, twenty cities, and the oppression of chapter 10 was broken. The narrator never says what God thought of the vow, and that silence is the hardest thing in the chapter. But the order of the verses points one way: the victory in verse 32 answers the Spirit in verse 29, not the bargain in verse 30. It was not a payment God had agreed to.

Jephthah does not see that, and he rides home from the greatest day of his life convinced that he owes for it. That is not confined to the Iron Age. A man can receive something entirely by grace and spend the rest of his life paying for it. He will call that gratitude, and it will look like devotion, and it will do damage in his house, because underneath it is the settled belief that God gave on terms, and the terms are now due.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The victory march ends at Jephthah's own door. What follows is the darkest scene in the book so far, and the narrator tells it with great restraint.
verseByVerse.theology: There is no word from God in these verses, neither rebuke nor approval. The reader is left to weigh the father's words against the daughter's, and to see what the text grieves over.
verseByVerse.examples: Read these verses with the daughter as well as the father. If you are reading them alongside someone who has been hurt by another person's religion, the comment at vv. 39-40 speaks to them directly.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jephthah came to his home at Mizpah. And behold, his daughter came out to meet him with tambourines and with dances. She was his only child; besides her he had neither son nor daughter. And as soon as he saw her, he tore his clothes and said, "Alas, my daughter! You have brought me very low, and you have become the cause of great trouble to me. For I have opened my mouth to the LORD, and I cannot take back my vow."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The behold makes us stand in the road with him. What comes out of the house is exactly what should come out of a house on such a day: a girl with a tambourine, doing what Miriam did at the sea and what the women would later do for Saul and David. Israel's victories were met with dancing daughters. She has no idea. She is first out of the door because she is the gladdest person in Gilead.

The narrator stops the story to tell us that she was his only child, and says it twice over: he had no other son or daughter. Jephthah was thrown out of his father's house with the words you shall not have an inheritance. He has fought his way to the headship of all Gilead, and this girl is everything he has to leave it to.

The grief is real, and the sentence is monstrous. Look at the pronouns. You have brought me very low. You have become the cause of great trouble to me. She has done nothing but come home to meet her father, and in his first words she is the agent, he is the victim, and the trouble is his own. Not once in the verse does he say what have I done.

Then the reason: I have opened my mouth to the LORD, and I cannot take back my vow. Here is the terrible part, because he is half right. Vows to God are not disposable; Ecclesiastes says it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay (Eccl. 5:5). Jephthah's reverence is real, and that is why it kills. What he is wrong about is I cannot (see vv. 39-40).

verseByVerse.quote: And she said to him, "My father, you have opened your mouth to the LORD; do to me according to what has gone out of your mouth, now that the LORD has avenged you on your enemies, on the Ammonites." So she said to her father, "Let this thing be done for me: leave me alone two months, that I may go up and down on the mountains and weep for my virginity, I and my companions." So he said, "Go." Then he sent her away for two months, and she departed, she and her companions, and wept for her virginity on the mountains.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The person with the least to gain speaks better than anyone else in the chapter. She does not argue or run, and she does not point out that she is not the one who opened his mouth. She takes her father's premise more seriously than he does, that a word given to God must be kept, and she gives God's victory over Ammon as the reason. The LORD has done his part, she says; do yours.

Nobody has taught her badly, and that is the awful thing. She has been raised to believe that God is to be taken at his word and honoured at cost, and she is about to be destroyed by a man who half believes the same thing.

She asks for two months, not for a reprieve. Notice exactly what she grieves: not, in the first place, her life, but her virginity, that she will never marry, never bear a child, never carry her father's name into another generation. In that world a woman's future was her children, and the loss is total: the family ends, and she ends with it. She spends those two months on the hills with her friends, weeping, and then she walks back down. In all of this her father says only one word to her: Go.

verseByVerse.quote: And at the end of two months, she returned to her father, who did with her according to his vow that he had made. She had never known a man, and it became a custom in Israel that the daughters of Israel went year by year to lament the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite four days in the year.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrator will not describe it. One clause for the thing itself, who did with her according to his vow that he had made, and then a sentence about her, not him: she had never known a man. The writer who gave us the tent peg through Sisera's temple and the fat closing over Ehud's blade turns his face away here.

Now the question every reader asks, and it deserves a straight answer: did Jephthah kill her?

There is a long-standing view that he did not, but dedicated her to lifelong service at the sanctuary, so that what she and Israel mourned was her perpetual virginity. Two things are urged for it. The Hebrew connective in verse 31 can sometimes be read as "or": whatever comes out shall be the LORD's, "or" I will offer it up. And the passage stresses her virginity three times in four verses, which would be an odd thing to stress if the point were her death.

It is not a foolish reading, and serious interpreters have held it. But it is the less likely one, and honesty requires saying so. A burnt offering (in Hebrew, olah) is something killed and wholly burned on an altar; the word never means dedicated service anywhere in the Old Testament. Verse 35 makes no sense if the outcome is a religious vocation: a man does not tear his clothes and cry that he has been brought very low because his daughter is going to serve at the tabernacle. There was no order of celibate women in Israel for her to join. And the daughters of Israel do not visit her four days a year; they go out to lament her.

The plain reading is that he burned her, and the plain reading is almost certainly right. Either way, the vow was faithless, unnecessary and pagan in shape when he made it, for the victory had already been given.

There was a way out, too. Leviticus 27:1-8 lets a person vowed to the LORD be redeemed for a fixed sum of silver paid to the sanctuary, and she comes home. That law may not have been written with a burnt-offering vow in mind, but another law settles the matter: the LORD had forbidden his people to burn their sons and daughters (Deut. 12:31; 18:10), and a vow to do what God forbids binds no one, as the Westminster Confession, a classic Reformed statement of faith, also says (22.7). This is not a loophole; it is God's law making room for exactly the situation Jephthah was standing in. He could quote three hundred years of history to a foreign king, and he did not know what his own God's book said about vows. That is what ignorance of Scripture costs when a sincere man is the one who is ignorant.

The book gives her no name. Her father has a name, a family line, a tribe, a hometown, an office and a long speech. She has four days a year and a description: the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite. The girls of Israel kept her memory when the record did not.

If you were harmed by a parent's religion, by vows, rules or fears laid on you that God never asked for, see whose side the text takes. It offers no word in the father's defence; it grieves with the daughter, and it set the whole nation grieving with her every year. God does not want children offered up to anyone's piety, and if such harm is still going on, seek safety and tell someone you trust.

One more question deserves an answer here. Jephthah is named in Hebrews 11 among those commended for faith (Heb. 11:32), so how does this chapter stand in that list? Consider his company there: Gideon, Barak, Samson. Hebrews is not certifying those lives; it names men who, at particular moments, believed God and acted on it, and the verses that follow describe what they did: conquered kingdoms... were made strong out of weakness... put foreign armies to flight (Heb. 11:33-34). Jephthah went out against Ammon trusting the LORD, the Judge, to decide the case, and God honoured that. Hebrews commends a man for the faith he had. It has never said that everything the man did was faith.

Now set this chapter beside the one other place in Scripture where a father takes his only child up a mountain for a burnt offering. On Moriah God commanded it, then stopped it with a shout, and provided a ram caught in the thicket, and the mountain was named the LORD will provide (Gen. 22:12-14). At Mizpah God commanded nothing, no voice came from heaven, and no substitute was found, because nobody had asked God for any of this. It was a man's own idea from beginning to end, and man's own religion has never yet produced a ram.

So God, in the end, brought his own only Son up a hill and did not stop it. There was no substitute that day either, for the opposite reason: he was the substitute. Jephthah's daughter died for nothing, because of a word her father should never have spoken and could have redeemed for a few shekels. The Son of God died for everything, because of a word the Father had spoken before the world began.

No unnamed girl need ever again walk down off a mountain to pay for a victory. It has been paid for.
verseByVerse.note: Leviticus 27:4-5 sets the redemption price at thirty shekels for a woman aged twenty to sixty and ten shekels for a girl aged five to twenty.

12.title: Jephthah's Conflict and the Minor Judges
12.text: <sup>1</sup>The men of Ephraim were called to arms, and they crossed to Zaphon and said to Jephthah, "Why did you cross over to fight against the Ammonites and did not call us to go with you? We will burn your house over you with fire."<sup>2</sup>And Jephthah said to them, "I and my people had a great dispute with the Ammonites, and when I called you, you did not save me from their hand.<sup>3</sup>And when I saw that you would not save me, I took my life in my hand and crossed over against the Ammonites, and the LORD gave them into my hand. Why then have you come up to me this day to fight against me?"<sup>4</sup>Then Jephthah gathered all the men of Gilead and fought with Ephraim. And the men of Gilead struck Ephraim, because they said, "You are fugitives of Ephraim, you Gileadites, in the midst of Ephraim and Manasseh."<sup>5</sup>And the Gileadites captured the fords of the Jordan against the Ephraimites. And when any of the fugitives of Ephraim said, "Let me go over," the men of Gilead said to him, "Are you an Ephraimite?" When he said, "No,"<sup>6</sup>they said to him, "Then say Shibboleth," and he said, "Sibboleth," for he could not pronounce it right. Then they seized him and slaughtered him at the fords of the Jordan. At that time 42,000 of the Ephraimites fell.<sup>7</sup>Jephthah judged Israel six years. Then Jephthah the Gileadite died and was buried in his city in Gilead.<sup>8</sup>After him Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel.<sup>9</sup>He had thirty sons, and thirty daughters he gave in marriage outside his clan, and thirty daughters he brought in from outside for his sons. And he judged Israel seven years.<sup>10</sup>Then Ibzan died and was buried at Bethlehem.<sup>11</sup>After him Elon the Zebulunite judged Israel, and he judged Israel ten years.<sup>12</sup>Then Elon the Zebulunite died and was buried at Aijalon in the land of Zebulun.<sup>13</sup>After him Abdon the son of Hillel the Pirathonite judged Israel.<sup>14</sup>He had forty sons and thirty grandsons, who rode on seventy donkeys, and he judged Israel eight years.<sup>15</sup>Then Abdon the son of Hillel the Pirathonite died and was buried at Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites.
12.overview:
Ephraim crosses the Jordan with the complaint they once made to Gideon, why did you not call us, and a threat of arson. Jephthah answers with the record, every word true, and forty-two thousand Israelites die at the fords, sorted by a one-word dialect trap: say Shibboleth.

Jephthah dies after six years, and for the first time the land does not rest. Three more judges follow in eight verses, with sons, marriages and donkeys but no oppressor named, and the chapter ends with a judge of Israel buried in Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites.
12.theology:
Right, and wrong. Every sentence Jephthah speaks in vv. 2-3 is true, and forty-two thousand men die for it, where Gideon's gentler answer to the same complaint ended the quarrel (8:2-3).

Shibboleth. At Christ's crossing there is no test of accent: everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved, because there is no distinction (Rom. 10:12-13).

The missing rest. The land had rest closed the accounts of Othniel, Ehud, Deborah and Gideon, and is never said again in the book. Hebrews says even Joshua did not give the true rest, which remains for the people of God (Heb. 4:8-10). Christ gives it (Matt. 11:28), and he won it by laying down his own life, not by taking his brothers'.

Amalek on the map. A district in Israel's heartland bears the name of the people God swore to blot out (Ex. 17:14), and nobody thinks it needs explaining (see vv. 11-15).
12.examples:
Then: A tribe too proud to fight the war showed up in force to argue about the credit, was answered with the plain facts, and lost forty-two thousand men at a river crossing to a test that examined nothing but their accent.

Now: Two things to take away. First, in the next disagreement where you are demonstrably in the right, ask what it would cost to give away credit you had actually earned, because Gideon did that and the quarrel ended, and Jephthah proved his case and buried the dead. Jephthah's own best sentence makes it possible: the LORD gave them into my hand. Credit that was a gift to begin with can be given away, and the Spirit who produces gentleness (Gal. 5:22-23) makes the soft answer more than a technique. Where we have already been Jephthah, harsh and right, Christ was the one who did not insist on his rights, and the way back is to confess it and go to the brother. Second, name your own shibboleths. Every congregation has a word, a translation, a position on a secondary matter that quietly decides who is one of us. Test it honestly: is this the gospel, or is it an accent? The Lord asks nobody at his ford to prove himself by pronunciation.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ephraim crosses the Jordan and threatens to burn Jephthah's house for not calling them (v. 1). He answers that he did call, they did not come, and the LORD gave them into my hand (vv. 2-3).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the second time Ephraim has made this complaint (8:1), and the two answers it receives carry the chapter's lesson: how a true thing is said can decide what follows.
verseByVerse.examples: Many quarrels, in churches and in families, are not about what they claim to be about. Ephraim's complaint about procedure was really a complaint about credit.

verseByVerse.quote: The men of Ephraim were called to arms, and they crossed to Zaphon and said to Jephthah, "Why did you cross over to fight against the Ammonites and did not call us to go with you? We will burn your house over you with fire." And Jephthah said to them, "I and my people had a great dispute with the Ammonites, and when I called you, you did not save me from their hand. And when I saw that you would not save me, I took my life in my hand and crossed over against the Ammonites, and the LORD gave them into my hand. Why then have you come up to me this day to fight against me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ephraim has said this before, almost word for word, to Gideon (8:1): a complaint about credit dressed as a complaint about procedure, from the proudest tribe in the north. But to Gideon they only accused him fiercely. To Jephthah they promise arson with the family inside. And Ammon had been crushing Gilead since 10:8 without Ephraim crossing the river once. They cross it now, in force, because somebody else won.

His answer is entirely accurate, and it is the wrong answer. Ephraim says he did not call; he says he did, and they did not come, and nothing in chapter 11 suggests he is the one lying. I took my life in my hand is the phrase of a man who went out without support and knew it. And the centre of the reply is right: the LORD gave them into my hand. The argument about credit is beside the point, because neither party won it.

So why is it wrong? Because Gideon had the same complaint from the same tribe and gave away credit he had earned, with flattery that was not strictly true, and their anger subsided. A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger (Prov. 15:1). Jephthah stands on the record, right about the facts and right about the theology, and in the next three verses forty-two thousand Israelites are killed.

Being right is not the same as being wise, and the man who insists on his accuracy in a quarrel may win the argument and bury the consequences.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Taunted as Ephraimite runaways, Gilead fights and seizes the fords, and every man who asks to cross must say Shibboleth; those who say Sibboleth are killed. Forty-two thousand fell (vv. 4-6).
verseByVerse.theology: Civil war is the darkest kind of war in Judges, and here it grows out of a quarrel over honour between tribes who should have stood together as brothers.
verseByVerse.examples: Divisions among God's people rarely begin with doctrine. They often begin with wounded pride and an insult, as this one did (v. 4).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jephthah gathered all the men of Gilead and fought with Ephraim. And the men of Gilead struck Ephraim, because they said, "You are fugitives of Ephraim, you Gileadites, in the midst of Ephraim and Manasseh." And the Gileadites captured the fords of the Jordan against the Ephraimites. And when any of the fugitives of Ephraim said, "Let me go over," the men of Gilead said to him, "Are you an Ephraimite?" When he said, "No," they said to him, "Then say Shibboleth," and he said, "Sibboleth," for he could not pronounce it right. Then they seized him and slaughtered him at the fords of the Jordan. At that time 42,000 of the Ephraimites fell.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The insult that starts the killing is about status. Ephraim's taunt is that the Gileadites are nobodies: runaways and leftovers of Ephraim and Manasseh, living out east on land nobody wanted, with no proper standing among the tribes. It is an old sneer directed at people on the far side of the river.

Of all the men in Israel to say that to, they say it to Jephthah, a man who was thrown out of his father's house as the wrong sort of son, told he would have no inheritance, and who has spent his whole life being the outsider that respectable people call in when they are desperate.

Seizing the fords of the Jordan is a manoeuvre this book has praised twice. Ehud took the fords against Moab and not a man escaped (3:28-29). Gideon sent to Ephraim to take the waters against Midian, and they did it and killed Oreb and Zeeb (7:24). It is the standard way of finishing a beaten enemy in this country: hold the crossings and let the retreat come to you.

Here it is Israelites holding the river against Israelites, and the tribe manning the checkpoint learned the tactic from the tribe now trying to get through it.

Then the word. Shibboleth means an ear of grain, or a flowing stream, and it is not a password: there is nothing to guess and no secret to betray. It is a dialect trap. The Ephraimite pronunciation of that first consonant was different, and a man from the western hills simply could not make the sound, however hard he tried, however loudly he swore he was not an Ephraimite.

He was condemned by an accent he had never chosen and could not hear.

As for the figure of forty-two thousand, the Hebrew word for thousand can also mean a clan unit, and some think the figure counts units rather than men; large numbers in these books are a known puzzle. On any reading, a great many Israelites died at that river.
