Set that figure beside the rest of the book. Not one of them was killed by Ammon, Moab, Midian, Canaan or Philistia. They were killed by other Israelites, one at a time, at a river crossing, after a hearing that lasted one word.

It is not even the worst the book has to show. The civil war of chapters 20-21 will cost more than sixty thousand, and it will be fought by mustered armies over three days for a reason everyone could state. This was a queue at a ford.

The man who ran that checkpoint had written sixteen verses of patient history to a foreign king in an effort to prevent a war. To his own countrymen he sent nothing at all.

The church has kept the practice, which is why the word is still in the language. A shibboleth is a test of belonging that has nothing to do with the truth being tested: the phrase you must use, the version you must carry, the position on a secondary question that marks you as one of us. It sorts people efficiently. It also puts on one side of the river a great many who love the Lord Jesus and merely say it with a different accent.

The Judge himself sets no such test at his crossing. Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved, and Paul's whole point in writing it is that there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, no dialect that disqualifies (Rom. 10:12-13). He knows his own, and he has never once asked a man to prove it by his pronunciation.
verseByVerse.note: The fords were the few shallow crossing places of the Jordan, and whoever held them controlled all movement between the east and west banks.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–15 — Six Years, No Rest, and Seventy Donkeys
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jephthah's six years end with no rest for the land, and three more judges follow, remembered for their families rather than their deeds.
verseByVerse.theology: Not every period of a nation's life is dramatic. These brief notices ask whether we can see God's people drifting even when nothing seems to be happening.
verseByVerse.examples: It is worth asking what in our own lives has stopped looking like an enemy simply because we have lived with it for a long time.

verseByVerse.quote: Jephthah judged Israel six years. Then Jephthah the Gileadite died and was buried in his city in Gilead. After him Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel. He had thirty sons, and thirty daughters he gave in marriage outside his clan, and thirty daughters he brought in from outside for his sons. And he judged Israel seven years. Then Ibzan died and was buried at Bethlehem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jephthah judged six years, and the land had no rest; both halves of that matter. Six years is the shortest tenure of any major judge in the book (Othniel had forty, Ehud eighty, Deborah forty, Gideon forty), and the formula that closed all four of those accounts is missing here. The land had rest. It is not said of Jephthah, and it will not be said again.

He broke Ammon, but the reason for the missing rest is in the verses just above: the peace was spent on a civil war. A deliverer who kills forty-two thousand of the people he delivered has not given anybody rest.

He is buried in his own city in Gilead, in the country he was driven out of, as its head. He got everything he negotiated for and lost the only person he had.

Ibzan arranged sixty marriages, in both directions. (His Bethlehem is probably the town in Zebulun, Joshua 19:15, rather than David's town in Judah, though some take it as the southern one.)

That is the whole record of the man, and it reads as exactly what it is: a description of a political operation. Thirty daughters sent out to other clans and thirty daughters brought in for his sons is a network of sixty families tied to his house by marriage. It is how dynasties were built.

No oppressor is named in his notice: no enemy, no battle, no deliverance, no cry to God. He judged seven years and consolidated.

Here is what the office has become. Othniel, Ehud, Deborah and Gideon were raised up against an enemy. Ibzan is raised up against nobody, and spends his term arranging weddings.

verseByVerse.quote: After him Elon the Zebulunite judged Israel, and he judged Israel ten years. Then Elon the Zebulunite died and was buried at Aijalon in the land of Zebulun. After him Abdon the son of Hillel the Pirathonite judged Israel. He had forty sons and thirty grandsons, who rode on seventy donkeys, and he judged Israel eight years. Then Abdon the son of Hillel the Pirathonite died and was buried at Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Elon judged ten years, and the writer has nothing whatever to report: not one act, word or enemy, only his name, tribe, term and grave. The verse tells us where he was buried and nothing about what he did there while he was alive.

Abdon's notice ends with seventy donkeys, and the count has been rising all through this section. Jair had thirty sons on thirty donkeys (10:4). Ibzan had thirty sons and sixty marriage alliances. Abdon has forty sons and thirty grandsons, and seventy mounts for them. A donkey was a mark of rank in that country, so this is a family that rides out in a body, seventy strong, and everybody in the district knows who they are.

Seventy is also the number of Gideon's sons, and the number of brothers Abimelech killed on one stone. The book does not press the point. It simply keeps counting.

The writer sets down the last phrase of the chapter without comment and walks away. Pirathon is in Ephraim, the heartland: Joshua's own tribe, the centre of the promised inheritance, as far from the frontier as it is possible to get. And a district in those hills is called after the Amalekites.

Amalek was the people who attacked Israel first, at Rephidim, before Sinai, before the law, picking off the stragglers at the back (Ex. 17:8; Deut. 25:17-18). God swore that day to blot out their memory from under heaven. Three hundred years later there is countryside in the middle of Israel that carries their name on the map, and a judge of Israel is buried in it, and nobody in the chapter thinks it worth a comment.

That is how a compromise ends: not with a decision, but with a place name that nobody notices any more. The thing you failed to remove stops being an enemy and becomes an address.

So the chapter closes: twenty-five years, three judges, no oppression named, no deliverance recorded, one hundred sons and grandsons, seventy donkeys, sixty marriages, and a stretch of Amalekite hill country in the middle of the promised land.

Israel has leaders, and no one is leading it anywhere.

13.title: Samson's Birth
13.text: <sup>1</sup>And the people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, so the LORD gave them into the hand of the Philistines for forty years.<sup>2</sup>There was a certain man of Zorah, of the tribe of the Danites, whose name was Manoah. And his wife was barren and had no children.<sup>3</sup>And the angel of the LORD appeared to the woman and said to her, "Behold, you are barren and have not borne children, but you shall conceive and bear a son.<sup>4</sup>Therefore be careful and drink no wine or strong drink, and eat nothing unclean,<sup>5</sup>for behold, you shall conceive and bear a son. No razor shall come upon his head, for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb, and he shall begin to save Israel from the hand of the Philistines."<sup>6</sup>Then the woman came and told her husband, "A man of God came to me, and his appearance was like the appearance of the angel of God, very awesome. I did not ask him where he was from, and he did not tell me his name,<sup>7</sup>but he said to me, 'Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son. So then drink no wine or strong drink, and eat nothing unclean, for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb to the day of his death.'"<sup>8</sup>Then Manoah prayed to the LORD and said, "O Lord, please let the man of God whom you sent come again to us and teach us what we are to do with the child who will be born."<sup>9</sup>And God listened to the voice of Manoah, and the angel of God came again to the woman as she sat in the field. But Manoah her husband was not with her.<sup>10</sup>So the woman ran quickly and told her husband, "Behold, the man who came to me the other day has appeared to me."<sup>11</sup>And Manoah arose and went after his wife and came to the man and said to him, "Are you the man who spoke to this woman?" And he said, "I am."<sup>12</sup>And Manoah said, "Now when your words come true, what is to be the child's manner of life, and what is his mission?"<sup>13</sup>And the angel of the LORD said to Manoah, "Of all that I said to the woman let her be careful.<sup>14</sup>She may not eat of anything that comes from the vine, neither let her drink wine or strong drink, or eat any unclean thing. All that I commanded her let her observe."<sup>15</sup>Manoah said to the angel of the LORD, "Please let us detain you and prepare a young goat for you."<sup>16</sup>And the angel of the LORD said to Manoah, "If you detain me, I will not eat of your food. But if you prepare a burnt offering, then offer it to the LORD." (For Manoah did not know that he was the angel of the LORD.)<sup>17</sup>And Manoah said to the angel of the LORD, "What is your name, so that, when your words come true, we may honor you?"<sup>18</sup>And the angel of the LORD said to him, "Why do you ask my name, seeing it is wonderful?"<sup>19</sup>So Manoah took the young goat with the grain offering, and offered it on the rock to the LORD, to the one who works wonders, and Manoah and his wife were watching.<sup>20</sup>And when the flame went up toward heaven from the altar, the angel of the LORD went up in the flame of the altar. Now Manoah and his wife were watching, and they fell on their faces to the ground.<sup>21</sup>The angel of the LORD appeared no more to Manoah and to his wife. Then Manoah knew that he was the angel of the LORD.<sup>22</sup>And Manoah said to his wife, "We shall surely die, for we have seen God."<sup>23</sup>But his wife said to him, "If the LORD had meant to kill us, he would not have accepted a burnt offering and a grain offering at our hands, or shown us all these things, or now announced to us such things as these."<sup>24</sup>And the woman bore a son and called his name Samson. And the young man grew, and the LORD blessed him.<sup>25</sup>And the Spirit of the LORD began to stir him in Mahaneh-dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol.
13.overview:
The cycle turns for the sixth time, and one clause is missing. Israel does evil and is given into Philistine hands for forty years, the longest oppression in the book, and this time nobody cries out. God sends a deliverer to a people who never asked for one.

The angel of the LORD comes to a barren woman in a border village of the failing tribe of Dan. Her son is to be a Nazirite from the womb (no vine, no razor, no corpse) and she must keep the food restrictions herself while she carries him. And the commission has a ceiling written into it from the start: he shall begin to save Israel. David finishes that war about a century later.

Manoah prays to be taught how to raise the child, and God answers by sending the angel back to his wife. Manoah asks about the boy's mission and is told only to keep the vow. He offers the visitor a meal and is told to offer a sacrifice instead, asks his name and is told it is wonderful, and watches him ascend in the flame of the burnt offering. Then Manoah says they will die, and his unnamed wife shows him why they will not.
13.theology:
Grace to people who did not send for it. Forty years without one recorded prayer, and God raises up a deliverer anyway. Through all four Samson chapters the initiative is entirely God's, towards a nation too comfortable in its captivity to want rescuing.

A vow broken one part at a time. Samson is a Nazirite for life, bound by the three restrictions of Numbers 6. He will break all three, and the razor comes last, when the other two are long gone.

Begin, not finish. No other judge is given a limited brief. Samson is announced as a start before he is conceived, and someone else will finish the work. That is a hard word for anyone who wants a completed work to show, and a true one.

The one called Wonderful. The visitor speaks as God, accepts a burnt offering made to the LORD, keeps his name beyond reach, and goes up in the altar flame. The chapter points beyond itself to the Son, in whom the one who receives the offering becomes the offering.

Reasoning from grace already given. Manoah's doctrine is right and his conclusion is wrong. His wife reasons from what God has already done to what he must therefore intend, and that is the logic of Christian assurance.
13.examples:
Then: A childless couple in a frontier village were told they would have a son who would only begin the work, were refused any account of his mission, and were given instead a set of instructions for the next nine months. Then the messenger went up in the fire of their own sacrifice, and the husband concluded they were about to die and the wife proved they were not.

Now: Manoah asked what this is for and where it is going, and got today's obedience with the future left in God's hands. Many of us ask the same of an illness, a job or a child, and are given the same answer. The Spirit who stirred Samson now lives in believers to make that daily obedience possible (Gal. 5:16). And when the fear comes that God has shown you kindness in order to destroy you afterwards, use his wife's method rather than his: list what God has already done. He accepted the offering. He has shown you these things. He has told you what is coming. Nobody pays a price like Calvary and then changes his mind.

verseByVerse.ref: v. 1 — The Cycle With No Cry
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The sixth turn of the cycle, and the sentence stops.
verseByVerse.theology: Five times the next clause has been a cry to the LORD. This time nobody cries.
verseByVerse.examples: They are not groaning under the Philistines. They have learned to live with them.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, so the LORD gave them into the hand of the Philistines for forty years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Read the next verse and see what is not in it. Five times this book has followed the oppression with the same clause: Israel cried out to the LORD (3:9, 3:15, 4:3, 6:6, 10:10). Here, nothing.

Forty years is the longest oppression in the book. Cushan had eight, Eglon eighteen, Jabin twenty, Midian seven, Ammon eighteen. This one runs twice as long and produces not a single recorded groan.

Two chapters on, Judah will explain it. When Samson is hiding in a rock and three thousand men of Judah come out, not to fight the Philistines but to hand him over, and their opening words are: do you not know that the Philistines are rulers over us? (15:11). That is the language of a people who have decided the arrangement is survivable and are annoyed with the man disturbing it.

Israel is not oppressed enough to pray, and God sends a deliverer anyway. Nobody asked for him, which is what grace has always looked like: while we were still weak, at the right time, Christ died for the ungodly (Rom. 5:6). Not for people who sent for him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 2–7 — To a Woman Who Is Never Named
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A barren woman is promised a son who will be a Nazirite from the womb, with the vow laid on her first and a limit written into his commission (vv. 2-5). She reports it all to her husband (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: The angel comes to her, not to him, and the book never tells us what she was called. Manoah is named again and again in this chapter. His wife is the woman throughout, and she is the one who sees, listens, reports accurately and works out what it means.
verseByVerse.examples: Scripture has walked this road before: a barren woman, an announced son. The deliverer is God's gift, not something his parents achieved.

verseByVerse.quote: There was a certain man of Zorah, of the tribe of the Danites, whose name was Manoah. And his wife was barren and had no children. And the angel of the LORD appeared to the woman and said to her, "Behold, you are barren and have not borne children, but you shall conceive and bear a son. Therefore be careful and drink no wine or strong drink, and eat nothing unclean, for behold, you shall conceive and bear a son. No razor shall come upon his head, for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb, and he shall begin to save Israel from the hand of the Philistines."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Zorah sits on the western edge of the hill country, right on the frontier where Israel's land runs down into the Philistine plain. Dan is the tribe that failed to take its allotted territory (1:34) and will shortly abandon it altogether (ch. 18). This is a family on the losing edge of a losing tribe.

Scripture has taught us to read barrenness as the beginning of something: Sarah and Isaac, Rebekah and Jacob, Rachel and Joseph, Hannah and Samuel, Elizabeth and John. Each time God opens a closed womb, the child belongs to God in a way no ordinary child does, and the parents know they did not produce him.

If you are childless and longing, these stories are not a promise that every closed womb will open, and they are not a verdict on you. They are the places God chose to bring his deliverers into the world. And the same God sought out a woman with no name in a village on the edge of things, spoke to her first, and said her sorrow out loud before anything else. He has not overlooked yours.

The vow arrives before the child does, and it is laid on the mother first.

A Nazirite vow is set out in Numbers 6, and it has three parts. Nothing from the vine: no wine, no strong drink, no grapes, not even the skins or the seeds. No razor on the head, the hair left uncut as the visible sign. And no contact with a dead body, not even a parent's (Num. 6:3-7). It was normally something a person chose, for a set period, and then ended with a sacrifice.

Nothing about Samson's is normal. He does not choose it, it is not temporary, and it starts before he is conceived: a Nazirite to God from the womb. His mother takes the food restrictions on herself for the pregnancy so that the boy is under the vow from his first cell.

Fix the three parts in your mind, because this is the last time in the story that all three are intact. Samson will hold a seven-day "drinking feast" at his wedding; the Hebrew word for the party is built on the verb to drink (14:10). He will scoop honey out of a lion's carcass and eat it and give it to his parents (14:8-9). And the razor will come at last in Delilah's lap (16:19).

Then the commission, and it has a ceiling built into it. He shall begin to save Israel from the hand of the Philistines.

Begin. Not finish. God tells this couple, before the child is conceived, that their son's life work will be incomplete. No other judge is given a limited brief; the others are simply raised up to save. Samson is announced as a start.

The Philistine war he begins is not won until David, about a century later, breaks them at Baal-perazim and again in the valley of Rephaim and subdues them (2 Sam. 5:17-25; 8:1). Samson is the first crack in a wall somebody else pulls down.
verseByVerse.note: Zorah lay in the Shephelah, the lowlands between Judah’s hills and Philistia.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the woman came and told her husband, "A man of God came to me, and his appearance was like the appearance of the angel of God, very awesome. I did not ask him where he was from, and he did not tell me his name, but he said to me, 'Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son. So then drink no wine or strong drink, and eat nothing unclean, for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb to the day of his death.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
She is exact about what she does not know. She calls him a man of God, which is the term for a prophet: the safe, sober description of what she can be sure of. Then she says his appearance was like the appearance of the angel of God, and she does not push the comparison further than that. And she volunteers the two gaps in her information: she did not ask where he came from, and he did not say who he was.

She has met something overwhelming and is not exaggerating about it. Very awesome is her one phrase for the impression, and it is a word for holy fear, not for admiration.

She adds a phrase: to the day of his death.

The angel had said from the womb, and she says from the womb to the day of his death. It may be that she was told more than verse 5 records. It may be that she has understood correctly what a lifelong vow means and said so. Either way it is not carelessness: she has thought about the length of this thing and grasped that there is no end date and no releasing sacrifice at the finish.

She also leaves something out. The angel had said the boy would begin to save Israel from the Philistines, and she does not repeat it.

The text does not tell us why, and it would be easy to make too much of it. But look at what she has kept and what she has dropped. She has held on to every word about the vow (the part that is her responsibility, starting today) and said nothing about the national mission, which is God's business and years away.

That is not a bad instinct in a person who has just been handed something enormous. She has been given a promise and a duty, and she goes home talking about the duty.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — Teach Us What We Are to Do
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Manoah prays to be taught, and God listens, but sends the angel back to the woman (vv. 8-9). Manoah asks about the boy's mission, and is answered with the vow (vv. 10-14).
verseByVerse.theology: It is a prayer for instruction rather than rescue, and God listens to it. He simply does not answer in the way Manoah expected.
verseByVerse.examples: The instruction that comes back is not about the boy's career but about the mother's diet.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Manoah prayed to the LORD and said, "O Lord, please let the man of God whom you sent come again to us and teach us what we are to do with the child who will be born." And God listened to the voice of Manoah, and the angel of God came again to the woman as she sat in the field. But Manoah her husband was not with her. So the woman ran quickly and told her husband, "Behold, the man who came to me the other day has appeared to me." And Manoah arose and went after his wife and came to the man and said to him, "Are you the man who spoke to this woman?" And he said, "I am."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the best prayer prayed by a man in the book of Judges.

He does not ask for a sign to test the message, as Gideon did twice with the fleece. He does not bargain, as Jephthah did. He does not ask for the Philistines to be dealt with, which is nearly the only thing anyone in this book asks for.

He asks to be taught. Teach us what we are to do with the child who will be born: a man who has been told he is going to be a father to somebody set apart for God, and whose first reaction is that he does not know how to do this and needs instructing.

He believes the message completely. He does not ask whether it is true; he asks to be taught how to carry it out. And he prays for both of them: teach us.

God listened, and then arranged the meeting exactly as before. It is nearly comic and entirely deliberate. Manoah prays that the man of God would come again to us. God grants the request: the messenger comes back, but he comes back to the woman, sitting alone in a field, with her husband somewhere else.

Heaven has now twice chosen to speak to the wife and twice arranged for the husband not to be there. God answers Manoah's prayer, and answers it in a way that says quietly whose word is to be trusted in that house.

She runs, because she knows what this is, and he goes after his wife to be shown. She leads him to the place. And his first words are a verification question: are you the man who spoke to this woman?

There is nothing wrong with the question. But note that she never asked one. She has believed the message since verse 3, and has spent this whole scene as the person who knows.

verseByVerse.quote: And Manoah said, "Now when your words come true, what is to be the child's manner of life, and what is his mission?" And the angel of the LORD said to Manoah, "Of all that I said to the woman let her be careful. She may not eat of anything that comes from the vine, neither let her drink wine or strong drink, or eat any unclean thing. All that I commanded her let her observe."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two questions, and the second one is the one every parent secretly wants answered.

What is to be the child's manner of life: how is he to be raised, what is the rule for him. Fair enough; that is what Manoah prayed for. But then: what is his mission? What is he going to do? What is this boy for?

The angel answers the first question and passes over the second entirely: nothing about the Philistines, nothing about what the boy will grow up to do. He simply repeats the instructions already given, and repeats them, twice over, as instructions given to her. Of all that I said to the woman. All that I commanded her.

He even expands the detail slightly: not merely no wine, but anything that comes from the vine, which is the full Numbers 6 restriction. He is making sure she has it exactly.

So the answer to "what is he for?" is: keep the vow, and wait. That is how God often deals with people who want the plan. It is not a refusal to answer. It is the answer: your job is the vow, not the mission.

There is an irony coming that neither of them can see. The one thing they were told to guard is the one thing that will finally matter. Samson's whole story turns on the vow: not on strategy, not on armies, but on whether the hair is cut. The parents were told to watch the very thing the son eventually threw away.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hospitality redirected to worship, a name refused, and a visitor who ascends in the altar flame (vv. 15-21).
verseByVerse.theology: Manoah still takes his visitor for a prophet. The reader is being shown, step by step, that he is far more than that.
verseByVerse.examples: Manoah asked for a name to honor (v. 17), and was given a fire instead.

verseByVerse.quote: Manoah said to the angel of the LORD, "Please let us detain you and prepare a young goat for you." And the angel of the LORD said to Manoah, "If you detain me, I will not eat of your food. But if you prepare a burnt offering, then offer it to the LORD." (For Manoah did not know that he was the angel of the LORD.) And Manoah said to the angel of the LORD, "What is your name, so that, when your words come true, we may honor you?" And the angel of the LORD said to him, "Why do you ask my name, seeing it is wonderful?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Feeding a visitor is what a decent man does. Abraham did exactly this at Mamre: ran to the herd, took a calf, and stood by while three strangers ate under the tree (Gen. 18:7-8). Manoah is offering ordinary hospitality to someone he still takes to be a prophet.

The visitor firmly turns the offer from a meal to an altar. I will not eat your food, he says. If you want to bring that goat, bring it as a burnt offering, and bring it to the LORD. He will not receive as a guest what should be given as worship, and the narrator steps in with a parenthesis to make sure we notice the point Manoah is missing: he did not know who he was talking to.

So the visitor has just told a man to sacrifice to the LORD, standing in front of him, and will in a moment go up in that sacrifice's flame.

Manoah's request for a name has a good motive, and it cannot be granted. He wants to know whom to thank. When the baby is born and the promise is proved, he intends to honour the man who brought the news, and for that he needs a name.

Jacob asked the same question at the Jabbok and got the same non-answer (Gen. 32:29). Moses asked it at the bush and was given I am who I am, which is a name that cannot be used as a handle (Ex. 3:14).

The word here is pele': wonderful, and not in the weak modern sense. Pele' is the word for what only God does, the category of the miraculous. Verse 19 will call the LORD the one who works wonders, from the same root, in the very next breath. The KJV renders it secret; the sense is a name beyond human grasp, too wonderful to be handled.

It is also the word Isaiah reaches for when he needs a name for the child who is to be born: and his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace (Isa. 9:6).

So gather what is standing on this hillside: a person who appears in the form of a man, speaks as God and is called the angel of the LORD, refuses food but accepts a burnt offering made to the LORD, keeps his name beyond asking, and in a moment will ascend to heaven in fire.

Manoah wanted a name so that he might honour him when the words came true. He was not given one. It would be another eleven hundred years or so before the name was given, and then it was given to another couple, in another small town, by another angel: you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins (Matt. 1:21).

Not begin to save. Save.

Who is the angel of the LORD? He speaks as God himself and is called “the LORD”. Some take him as a created angel speaking with God’s full authority. The best reading, held by many in the Reformed tradition, is that he is the LORD appearing in person, most likely the Son before his incarnation.

verseByVerse.quote: So Manoah took the young goat with the grain offering, and offered it on the rock to the LORD, to the one who works wonders, and Manoah and his wife were watching. And when the flame went up toward heaven from the altar, the angel of the LORD went up in the flame of the altar. Now Manoah and his wife were watching, and they fell on their faces to the ground. The angel of the LORD appeared no more to Manoah and to his wife. Then Manoah knew that he was the angel of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He does as he was told, on a rock, with no priest and no tabernacle. The visitor said his name was wonderful; Manoah offers to the God who works wonders. The writer joins the two before Manoah has worked it out.

Stand in that field for a moment. The goat is on the rock, the flame climbs, and the man who has been talking to them steps into the column of fire and rises with it. They are, the text says twice, watching, and then their faces are in the dirt.

The one who receives the offering is carried up inside the offering. He is not standing beside the altar taking delivery; he is in the flame, going up with the smoke, as though the sacrifice and the one it is made to were going home together.

There is a mystery here that the Old Testament keeps circling and cannot resolve, and it is resolved at Calvary. The one to whom the offering is made turned out to be the offering. He has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself (Heb. 9:26).

Manoah worked it out at the last possible moment, one moment too late to ask anything. The narrator has been telling us since verse 3. Manoah has been in the presence of the angel of the LORD through two conversations, has asked his name and been refused, has been told to offer a sacrifice, and has understood none of it until the fire took him away. Then Manoah knew.

That is description, not criticism. God is often recognised in the rear-view mirror. The two on the Emmaus road knew who had been walking with them at the exact moment he vanished from their sight (Luke 24:31).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–25 — She Reasons Better Than He Fears
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Manoah fears death; his wife reasons from what God has done (vv. 22-23). The son is born, blessed and stirred by the Spirit (vv. 24-25).
verseByVerse.theology: The husband knows the right doctrine; the wife reads the evidence. The accepted sacrifice is the proof that God does not intend their death.
verseByVerse.examples: The place named in v. 25 is where he will be buried (16:31).

verseByVerse.quote: And Manoah said to his wife, "We shall surely die, for we have seen God." But his wife said to him, "If the LORD had meant to kill us, he would not have accepted a burnt offering and a grain offering at our hands, or shown us all these things, or now announced to us such things as these."
verseByVerse.commentary:
His theology is correct and his conclusion is wrong.

He is quoting the settled understanding of Israel, and it is right: man shall not see me and live (Ex. 33:20). Gideon said the same thing when he realised who had been sitting under his terebinth (6:22). But he has reasoned from a true principle straight to despair.

Then the woman with no name reasons better than anyone else in Judges. She does not deny his premise. She tests his fear against the evidence, and produces three pieces.

First: he would not have accepted a burnt offering and a grain offering at our hands. God took the sacrifice and went up in its flame. A God who intends to destroy you does not first accept your offering.

Second: or shown us all these things. He revealed himself: twice to her, once in the fire to both of them. Revelation is not how executions begin.

Third: or now announced to us such things as these. He has promised them a son who will begin to deliver Israel. You do not tell a dead couple about the future of their child.

She reasons forward from grace received to grace to come, precisely the logic of Christian assurance: he who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things? (Rom. 8:32).

The argument is the same, and the sacrifice is infinitely greater. If God has already accepted an offering on your behalf (and he has, and it was his Son), then whatever else is coming, it is not your condemnation. That question was settled at the altar. You may be as much in the dark about the future as Manoah was. But God did not accept that offering in order to destroy you afterwards.

Manoah looked at the fire and saw his death in it. His wife looked at the same fire and saw that their offering had been received. She was right.

verseByVerse.quote: And the woman bore a son and called his name Samson. And the young man grew, and the LORD blessed him. And the Spirit of the LORD began to stir him in Mahaneh-dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She names him, and the name is usually connected with the Hebrew word for the sun.

It is an odd, bright, hopeful name for a boy born on the Philistine frontier, and there is something poignant in it, because the village of Beth-shemesh, the house of the sun, was just down the valley. A mother who had waited years for a child very likely named him for the sun.

The LORD blessed him. Whatever comes later, that is the sentence over his childhood.

The verb for the Spirit's stirring is a strong one: to thrust or impel, to push at something until it moves. So the picture at the end of this chapter is of a young man being made restless by the Spirit of God. Not yet sent anywhere, not yet doing anything, but stirred: something in him will not settle, and it is God who is doing the unsettling. The great strength has not yet appeared. The first thing the Spirit produces in him is discontent.

Then the place: Mahaneh-dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol. Hold on to those two village names.

Three chapters from now, when the temple has come down at Gaza and his brothers have carried the body up out of Philistine country, the last verse of his story reads: and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of Manoah his father (16:31).

He is buried where the Spirit first stirred him. Everything in between (the riddle, the foxes, the jawbone, the harlot, the lap, the mill, the shaven head) happens away from those two villages, and in the end he is carried back to them. Whatever we make of the next twenty years, that is where he starts: an answered prayer, a kept promise, and the Spirit of God stirring a boy on the edge of enemy territory.

14.title: Samson's Marriage
14.text: <sup>1</sup>Samson went down to Timnah, and at Timnah he saw one of the daughters of the Philistines.<sup>2</sup>Then he came up and told his father and mother, "I saw one of the daughters of the Philistines at Timnah. Now get her for me as my wife."<sup>3</sup>But his father and mother said to him, "Is there not a woman among the daughters of your relatives, or among all our people, that you must go to take a wife from the uncircumcised Philistines?" But Samson said to his father, "Get her for me, for she is right in my eyes."<sup>4</sup>His father and mother did not know that it was from the LORD, for he was seeking an opportunity against the Philistines. At that time the Philistines ruled over Israel.<sup>5</sup>Then Samson went down with his father and mother to Timnah, and they came to the vineyards of Timnah. And behold, a young lion came toward him roaring.<sup>6</sup>Then the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and although he had nothing in his hand, he tore the lion in pieces as one tears a young goat. But he did not tell his father or his mother what he had done.<sup>7</sup>Then he went down and talked with the woman, and she was right in Samson's eyes.<sup>8</sup>After some days he returned to take her. And he turned aside to see the carcass of the lion, and behold, there was a swarm of bees in the body of the lion, and honey.<sup>9</sup>He scraped it out into his hands and went on, eating as he went. And he came to his father and mother and gave some to them, and they ate. But he did not tell them that he had scraped the honey from the carcass of the lion.<sup>10</sup>His father went down to the woman, and Samson prepared a feast there, for so the young men used to do.<sup>11</sup>As soon as the people saw him, they brought thirty companions to be with him.<sup>12</sup>And Samson said to them, "Let me now put a riddle to you. If you can tell me what it is, within the seven days of the feast, and find it out, then I will give you thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes,<sup>13</sup>but if you cannot tell me what it is, then you shall give me thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes." And they said to him, "Put your riddle, that we may hear it."<sup>14</sup>And he said to them, "Out of the eater came something to eat. Out of the strong came something sweet." And in three days they could not solve the riddle.<sup>15</sup>On the fourth day they said to Samson's wife, "Entice your husband to tell us what the riddle is, lest we burn you and your father's house with fire. Have you invited us here to impoverish us?"<sup>16</sup>And Samson's wife wept over him and said, "You only hate me; you do not love me. You have put a riddle to my people, and you have not told me what it is." And he said to her, "Behold, I have not told my father nor my mother, and shall I tell you?"<sup>17</sup>She wept before him the seven days that their feast lasted, and on the seventh day he told her, because she pressed him hard. Then she told the riddle to her people.<sup>18</sup>And the men of the city said to him on the seventh day before the sun went down, "What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?" And he said to them, "If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have found out my riddle."<sup>19</sup>And the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and he went down to Ashkelon and struck down thirty men of the town and took their spoil and gave the garments to those who had told the riddle. In hot anger he went back to his father's house.<sup>20</sup>And Samson's wife was given to his companion, who had been his best man.
14.overview:
Samson goes down to Timnah, sees a Philistine girl, and comes home with an instruction rather than a request. His parents object on exactly the right grounds (Deut. 7:3-4) and he does not answer the argument; he repeats the order and gives his reason: she is right in my eyes. That phrase is the book's own verdict on the whole period (17:6; 21:25), and here the deliverer says it about himself.

On the road he kills a lion bare-handed when the Spirit rushes on him. Later he eats honey from its carcass, feeds his parents with it, and tells nobody, and before the wedding is over only the razor is left of his vow. He wagers on a riddle nobody could solve, loses it when his bride is threatened, and pays the debt with the clothes of thirty men he kills in Ashkelon. His wife is given to the best man.
14.theology:
Right in my eyes. Yashar b'einay (v. 3) is the phrase the book uses for the anarchy of the whole period. Samson is not merely living in that age; he is its portrait. The Deliverer Israel needed would say the opposite, in a garden, with far more at stake: not my will, but yours, be done (Luke 22:42), and by that one man's obedience the many who trust him are made righteous (Rom. 5:19).

God rules a sin he does not author. Verse 4 says the marriage was from the LORD, and not one word of the parents' objection is withdrawn. God works his purpose through human wrongdoing while the wrongdoer remains answerable for all of it.

The strength was never in the hair. It was the Spirit's. The uncut hair is the sign of the vow, not its source.

Gifts are not certificates. The same Spirit who gave strength against the lion gives it at Ashkelon, where Samson kills thirty strangers over a bet. What God does through a person is no verdict on that person's heart.

He was shown the method and did not learn it. The tears, the pressing and the betrayed secret at his wedding all come back, in almost the same words, in Delilah's house.
14.examples:
Then: A man raised up to deliver Israel married into the enemy because she looked good to him, broke his vow at a carcass and hid it, cheated thirty villagers with an unanswerable riddle, and murdered thirty strangers in another city to cover the loss, and God used the whole squalid business to begin breaking the Philistine grip on a nation that had never asked him to.

Now: The chapter leaves two questions. Is there something you would rather not say where you got, as Samson hid where the honey came from (v. 9)? Then bring it into the light; God forgives what is confessed. And if God has used you, in a word that landed or a work that prospered, do not read it as a verdict on your walk with him (v. 19). He struck the first blow for Israel through a man settling a gambling debt.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A demand, a right objection left unanswered, and a narrator's note his parents could not have known (vv. 1-4).
verseByVerse.theology: Samson's appetite overrides his parents' plea from Scripture, and God is at work behind it all.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 4 does not excuse a word of it. God governs the sin he never authors, and the sinner is answerable for every bit of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Samson went down to Timnah, and at Timnah he saw one of the daughters of the Philistines. Then he came up and told his father and mother, "I saw one of the daughters of the Philistines at Timnah. Now get her for me as my wife." But his father and mother said to him, "Is there not a woman among the daughters of your relatives, or among all our people, that you must go to take a wife from the uncircumcised Philistines?" But Samson said to his father, "Get her for me, for she is right in my eyes." His father and mother did not know that it was from the LORD, for he was seeking an opportunity against the Philistines. At that time the Philistines ruled over Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two verbs, and the whole man is in them: he went down, and he saw.

Zorah sits up in the hills; Timnah lies four miles away in the valley, on the Philistine side of the line. The writer uses went down again and again in this chapter, and the geography is accurate every time. It is also doing other work: every step down takes him further from where he belongs.

Then he saw. The Spirit had begun to stir him at Mahaneh-dan (13:25); the first recorded result is that he walked into enemy territory and looked at a girl.

He does not ask. There is no please, no case made. The sentence is get her for me, addressed to the two people who had waited years for him and kept a vow through a pregnancy on his behalf.

They are entirely right, and they say so gently.

The law was explicit about marrying into the nations of the land: you shall not intermarry with them... for they would turn away your sons from following me (Deut. 7:3-4). And the reason given is not racial but spiritual: the danger is to the worship. His parents put it as a question, offer an alternative, and appeal to the covenant sign: these people are uncircumcised. They are not being snobs. They are being Israelites.

The argument goes unanswered. He repeats the order and supplies a reason, and the reason is the most important sentence in the chapter.

She is right in my eyes. In Hebrew it is yashar b'einay, the phrase the book will use twice more, in the last five chapters, as its whole diagnosis of the period: everyone did what was right in his own eyes (17:6; 21:25).

The book's summary judgment on the age is spoken here by the man God raised up to deliver it. Be honest about what the phrase covers. He is not making a case for missionary marriage, or claiming a leading, or arguing that the girl fears the LORD. He looked at her, and she suited him. That is the entire justification offered, and it is offered to godly parents quoting Scripture, and it wins.

Then comes the verse that gives readers the most trouble, dropped in by the narrator as an aside: it was from the LORD. Behind Samson's appetite, unknown to his parents and unknown to Samson, God was working: he was seeking an occasion against the Philistines, and this marriage was going to provide it.

Be careful with what that does and does not say. It does not say God gave Samson the lust, or approved the marriage, or suspended the commandment in Deuteronomy 7. Every criticism his parents made stands, and God's use of the episode removes not one ounce of Samson's guilt in it.

What it says is that God is not blocked by human sin, and does not wait for it to finish before he acts. Joseph's brothers meant evil and God meant good (Gen. 50:20). Christ was crucified by the hands of lawless men, according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God (Acts 2:23). The last clause of the verse explains why God was seeking an occasion at all: at that time the Philistines ruled over Israel, and nobody in Israel had asked him to do anything about it.

Does this apply to Christians? The law forbade marrying the Canaanites because they would turn Israel to their gods (Deut. 7:3-4). The New Testament carries the principle forward: a believer must marry only in the Lord (1 Cor. 7:39; 2 Cor. 6:14). If you are already married to someone who does not share your faith, Paul's word to you is different and kind: do not leave; your marriage is not unclean, and your spouse may yet be won (1 Cor. 7:12-16; 1 Pet. 3:1-2).
verseByVerse.note: Timnah lay in Philistine territory. The Philistines had probably come from the Aegean world (Scripture says from Caphtor, Amos 9:7) and controlled the coastal plain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–9 — The Lion and the Honey
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A lion killed in the Spirit's strength and kept secret; a carcass visited, honey eaten, and that kept secret too (vv. 5-9).
verseByVerse.theology: The strength comes from the Spirit; the secrets come from Samson.
verseByVerse.examples: Each secret is worse than the one before.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Samson went down with his father and mother to Timnah, and they came to the vineyards of Timnah. And behold, a young lion came toward him roaring. Then the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and although he had nothing in his hand, he tore the lion in pieces as one tears a young goat. But he did not tell his father or his mother what he had done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Note the address before the lion arrives: the vineyards of Timnah.

Samson is a Nazirite. The first restriction in Numbers 6 is not merely no wine, but nothing from the vine at all: no grapes, fresh or dried, not the skins, not the seeds (Num. 6:3-4). And here he is, walking through the vineyards on the road to his Philistine wedding.

The writer does not comment. He just tells us where the man was standing.

Then comes the first display of the strength, and its source needs stating precisely. The strength is not in his muscles and not in his hair. The Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him (the verb is violent, a sudden seizing), and the narrator adds that he had nothing in his hand so that no one can suppose a weapon did it. What happens next is that a man tears a lion the way an ordinary man might tear a kid goat for the pot.

The hair, when we come to chapter 16, is not a battery. It is a sign. The power was always the Spirit's, and the uncut hair was the visible token of the vow that marked him as God's.

The first of this chapter's three secrets: he tells nobody, not even the parents who would have understood better than anyone alive. The habit runs right through him. He does not tell them about the lion (v. 6). He does not tell them about the honey (v. 9). He boasts to his wife that he has not told his father or mother the riddle (v. 16). Samson is a man who holds things back, and in the end the one secret he cannot keep is the only one that mattered.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he went down and talked with the woman, and she was right in Samson's eyes. After some days he returned to take her. And he turned aside to see the carcass of the lion, and behold, there was a swarm of bees in the body of the lion, and honey. He scraped it out into his hands and went on, eating as he went. And he came to his father and mother and gave some to them, and they ate. But he did not tell them that he had scraped the honey from the carcass of the lion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrator repeats the phrase, and this time he says it himself. In verse 3 it was Samson's excuse. Here it is the writer's flat description of the state of affairs: she was right in his eyes, and that is all there is to say about the courtship. He went down, he talked with her, and she suited him.

He turned aside: it was a deliberate detour, and nobody made him do it. He was on the road to his wedding, and he went out of his way to look at a dead animal, and a Nazirite is forbidden to go near a dead body at all. The restriction is severe and explicit: he may not make himself unclean even for his father, his mother, his brother or his sister, when they die (Num. 6:6-7). Samson is not caught out by a corpse on the path. He walks over to it.

Familiarity has worn the shock off. He is scooping honey out of the body of a rotting lion, in his palms, walking along and licking his fingers. Under the law he is unclean from the moment he touches it. Under his own vow he is a Nazirite handling the dead, and there is a whole procedure in Numbers 6:9-12 for what a Nazirite must do when this happens: shave the head, bring offerings, start the count again.

He does none of it. He eats and keeps walking.

Then he makes his parents unclean too. That is the second secret, and it is worse than the first. Withholding the story of the lion was pride, or reticence. This is deception with a consequence: two people who had ordered their whole lives around this vow are handed food out of a carcass by their son and eat it, and are defiled, and do not know.

The concealment is the thing that convicts him. A man who did not know he had done wrong would have said where the honey came from; it is a marvellous story. He says nothing, because he knows exactly what he has done.

The same test works on us: what you have to keep quiet is usually what you already know is wrong. And the way out is the one Samson never took: say it to God, who promises to forgive what is confessed and not covered (Ps. 32:5; 1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–18 — A Riddle Nobody Could Answer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A drinking-feast, a riddle nobody could solve, a threatened bride and a secret given away (vv. 10-18).
verseByVerse.theology: The wedding becomes a contest Samson has rigged, and then a threat on his bride's life.
verseByVerse.examples: He survives the pressure here. He will not survive it in Delilah's house.

verseByVerse.quote: His father went down to the woman, and Samson prepared a feast there, for so the young men used to do. As soon as the people saw him, they brought thirty companions to be with him. And Samson said to them, "Let me now put a riddle to you. If you can tell me what it is, within the seven days of the feast, and find it out, then I will give you thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes, but if you cannot tell me what it is, then you shall give me thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes." And they said to him, "Put your riddle, that we may hear it." And he said to them, "Out of the eater came something to eat. Out of the strong came something sweet." And in three days they could not solve the riddle.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Hebrew word for the feast is mishteh, and it is built on the verb "to drink".

The text does not say that Samson drank, and it is fair to say so. It says a Nazirite made a seven-day drinking-feast in Philistine Timnah and presided over it.

Line up where he now stands with the vow. He has broken the rule about corpses outright, twice over. He has walked through the vineyards and is hosting the drinking. Only the razor is still intact. Two of the three are compromised long before Delilah appears, and nobody has noticed, including him.

The thirty men who appear may be more than groomsmen. The phrasing is careful: as soon as they saw him, they brought thirty companions. This is a Philistine town looking at a very large Israelite and deciding he needs an escort. They look very like a guard, arranged on the spot.

The stake is sixty garments, two for each of the thirty, far beyond what ordinary men could raise. Linen garments and changes of clothes were serious property in that world: the sort of thing given as a reward or taken as spoil. He is proposing a wager thirty villagers cannot cover, at his own wedding, with his bride's people.

The riddle is a good line and a dishonest game. A riddle is meant to be solvable. It hides an answer in an image, and a clever hearer can work it out. This one cannot be worked out by anybody, because the answer is not an image at all: it is a private memory of a dead lion in a field that only Samson has ever seen inside. He has staked sixty garments on a question with no route to the answer, against thirty men who cannot pay.

Something else is in the riddle that he cannot see and we can. He has made a joke out of the fact that sweetness came out of a killer, and life came out of a carcass. It is the one moment in his life when he says something larger than himself, the true and terrible pattern by which God brings food out of death, and he uses it to win clothes off villagers.

Christians have long heard more in that line than Samson meant. It is not a prophecy, and the lion is not a symbol. But the shape it names, sweetness out of the strong and food out of death, is the shape of the gospel, where life for the world comes out of the death of the strongest one of all (John 6:51; 12:24).

verseByVerse.quote: On the fourth day they said to Samson's wife, "Entice your husband to tell us what the riddle is, lest we burn you and your father's house with fire. Have you invited us here to impoverish us?" And Samson's wife wept over him and said, "You only hate me; you do not love me. You have put a riddle to my people, and you have not told me what it is." And he said to her, "Behold, I have not told my father nor my mother, and shall I tell you?" She wept before him the seven days that their feast lasted, and on the seventh day he told her, because she pressed him hard. Then she told the riddle to her people. And the men of the city said to him on the seventh day before the sun went down, "What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?" And he said to them, "If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have found out my riddle."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wedding turns into a hostage situation on day four. They cannot pay. Have you invited us here to impoverish us is the complaint of men who know exactly what sixty garments would cost them, and who have concluded that the bride's family set them up. So they threaten to burn her alive, with her father's household, unless she gets the answer.

She is a girl caught between a husband she has known for days and a town that has just promised to kill her. Whatever she does next, remember where she is standing.

Her weapon is tears and an accusation about love; his defence is a boast about secrecy. He does not say the riddle is not hers to have; he says he has not even told his parents, so why should she rank above them? It is the third secret of the chapter, produced as a trophy. He is proud of what he withholds.

On the seventh day he gives way, and the scene will happen again. Two chapters from here, Delilah says: how can you say, "I love you," when your heart is not with me? And the narrator writes, when she pressed him hard with her words day after day, and urged him, his soul was vexed to death (16:15-16). Identical method. Nearly identical words. The same man.

Nothing at Timnah deceives him that he could not have foreseen. He is shown the whole method in week one, at his own wedding, at a cost of thirty lives, and years later he walks into it again.

They put the answer as two questions, a taunt in his own rhythm, minutes before the deadline. His answer is coarse, and it blames her. It is an ugly thing to call a woman, said in public, at the feast that was supposed to be her wedding, and it is not even the right target. Nobody ploughed with anybody. Thirty men threatened to burn her alive and she believed them, and the only reason she had anything to tell was that Samson gave it to her.

He has lost a wager he designed to be unloseable, and his instinct is that somebody else has cheated.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Spirit, Ashkelon, thirty dead strangers, and a debt paid in their clothes (vv. 19-20).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the deliverance beginning, and it looks like a tantrum.
verseByVerse.examples: The wife he demanded is the one who pays.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and he went down to Ashkelon and struck down thirty men of the town and took their spoil and gave the garments to those who had told the riddle. In hot anger he went back to his father's house. And Samson's wife was given to his companion, who had been his best man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not soften either half of the verse. The Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, the same phrase as the lion. And what he does with it is walk over twenty miles to a city on the coast, kill thirty men who were not at his wedding, had never heard his riddle and owed him nothing, strip the clothes off their bodies, and carry them back to settle a bet.

Both things are in the sentence, and the sentence does not blush. The Spirit's coming upon a man is not God's endorsement of the man. It is God equipping him for a purpose that belongs to God. Ashkelon is the first blow of the deliverance announced in 13:5 (the Philistine oppression has begun to be answered), and it is struck by a furious young man in the middle of a private grudge, and the two facts sit in one verse.

Do not build a doctrine of your own soundness on what God has done through you. Some will list their mighty works in his name on the last day and hear I never knew you (Matt. 7:22-23). Gifts prove God's power. They prove nothing else.

He goes home without his wife, a bleak comedy. The man who told his father and mother get her for me, who overrode their objection with she is right in my eyes, is back in their house within days in a temper, without the bride, having killed thirty strangers to pay for a joke.

She has been threatened with fire, used as a lever, publicly called a heifer, abandoned at her own wedding feast, and married off to one of the thirty. She is not named. She will be dead within a chapter, burned along with her father by the Philistines, just as the thirty threatened here (15:6), and the reason will be something else Samson did.

Everyone in this chapter is doing what is right in his own eyes, and it is the woman nobody names who pays for it. That is what the phrase costs when it is finally totalled up, and it is why the book keeps repeating it.

15.title: Samson's Vengeance
15.text: <sup>1</sup>After some days, at the time of wheat harvest, Samson went to visit his wife with a young goat. And he said, "I will go in to my wife in the chamber." But her father would not allow him to go in.<sup>2</sup>And her father said, "I really thought that you utterly hated her, so I gave her to your companion. Is not her younger sister more beautiful than she? Please take her instead."<sup>3</sup>And Samson said to them, "This time I shall be innocent in regard to the Philistines, when I do them harm."<sup>4</sup>So Samson went and caught 300 foxes and took torches. And he turned them tail to tail and put a torch between each pair of tails.<sup>5</sup>And when he had set fire to the torches, he let the foxes go into the standing grain of the Philistines and set fire to the stacked grain and the standing grain, as well as the olive orchards.<sup>6</sup>Then the Philistines said, "Who has done this?" And they said, "Samson, the son-in-law of the Timnite, because he has taken his wife and given her to his companion." And the Philistines came up and burned her and her father with fire.<sup>7</sup>And Samson said to them, "If this is what you do, I swear I will be avenged on you, and after that I will quit."<sup>8</sup>And he struck them hip and thigh with a great blow, and he went down and stayed in the cleft of the rock of Etam.<sup>9</sup>Then the Philistines came up and encamped in Judah and made a raid on Lehi.<sup>10</sup>And the men of Judah said, "Why have you come up against us?" They said, "We have come up to bind Samson, to do to him as he did to us."<sup>11</sup>Then 3,000 men of Judah went down to the cleft of the rock of Etam, and said to Samson, "Do you not know that the Philistines are rulers over us? What then is this that you have done to us?" And he said to them, "As they did to me, so have I done to them."<sup>12</sup>And they said to him, "We have come down to bind you, that we may give you into the hands of the Philistines." And Samson said to them, "Swear to me that you will not attack me yourselves."<sup>13</sup>They said to him, "No; we will only bind you and give you into their hands. We will surely not kill you." So they bound him with two new ropes and brought him up from the rock.<sup>14</sup>When he came to Lehi, the Philistines came shouting to meet him. Then the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and the ropes that were on his arms became as flax that has caught fire, and his bonds melted off his hands.<sup>15</sup>And he found a fresh jawbone of a donkey, and put out his hand and took it, and with it he struck 1,000 men.<sup>16</sup>And Samson said, "With the jawbone of a donkey, heaps upon heaps, with the jawbone of a donkey have I struck down a thousand men."<sup>17</sup>As soon as he had finished speaking, he threw away the jawbone out of his hand. And that place was called Ramath-lehi.<sup>18</sup>And he was very thirsty, and he called upon the LORD and said, "You have granted this great salvation by the hand of your servant, and shall I now die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?"<sup>19</sup>And God split open the hollow place that is at Lehi, and water came out from it. And when he drank, his spirit returned, and he revived. Therefore the name of it was called En-hakkore; it is at Lehi to this day.<sup>20</sup>And he judged Israel in the days of the Philistines twenty years.
15.overview:
Samson comes back to Timnah with a goat, expecting to resume a marriage he had walked out on, and finds his wife given to the best man. He declares himself innocent in advance and burns the Philistine harvest, and the Philistines answer by burning the woman and her father alive.

Then three thousand men of Judah march out, not against the raiders camped in their territory, but to arrest their own deliverer and hand him over bound. Their words, do you not know that the Philistines are rulers over us?, explain why nobody cried out at 13:1: they are not in agony, only irritated. At Lehi the Spirit rushes on him, the ropes fall away and a thousand men fall to a donkey's jawbone. He sings about himself; then thirst brings him to his first recorded prayer, and God splits open the ground and gives him water.
15.theology:
Marking your own paper. A wronged person who decides alone that his revenge is justified is grading his own work. Scripture takes the pen away, because we are not the judge. The Judge has already dealt with our own wrongs at the cross, and his Spirit makes it possible to leave the rest with him.

The chain that killed her. An unwinnable riddle, a threat of fire, a betrayal made to escape it, an insult, an abandonment, a burnt harvest, and at last the fire itself. Every link is someone doing what was right in his own eyes, and the person who dies is the one with the fewest choices. Sin is never as private as the sinner supposes.

Judah's quiet sin. Samson's failures are loud, and you can see each one coming. Judah's is sensible, collective and unremarkable: three thousand reasonable men who had made their peace with the thing God sent a deliverer to destroy. It is the easier sin to miss, and the more common.

Power without holiness. The strength keeps coming while the vow lies in ribbons, because it was always the Spirit's and never the man's. That is mercy, and it is also a trap: a man who goes on succeeding while disobeying concludes that the disobedience does not matter. Chapter 16 is what happens when he finds out.

The spring of him who called. God gives water to a man who has earned none, without a word of rebuke. Many Christians have set this thirst beside another: the thirst Christ endured on the cross (John 19:28-34), which is why the thirsty may now come to him and drink.
15.examples:
Then: A deliverer burned a nation's harvest to settle a private score and got a woman killed by it; his own tribe mustered three thousand men to arrest him rather than fight the occupier; he killed a thousand of the enemy with a corpse's jawbone and sang about himself; and then he got thirsty, prayed for the first time the book records, and God gave him water without one word of reproach.

Now: Watch for the two sins in this chapter, because they are opposites and most of us lean towards one of them. Samson's is the private verdict: deciding alone that what you are about to do is justified because of what was done to you. Judah's is the settled arrangement: making your peace with the thing God means to destroy, and coming to resent whoever disturbs it. Then take En-hakkore with you. When you come to pray after a day you are not proud of, the spring is not named for the deserving. It is named for the man who called.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Samson returns to a wife already given away, refuses the sister, and declares himself innocent in advance (vv. 1-3).
verseByVerse.theology: Samson builds a legal case for a revenge he has already decided on.
verseByVerse.examples: The grievance is real: his wife has been given to another man. But it became possible because he walked out of his own wedding feast in a temper (14:19-20).

verseByVerse.quote: After some days, at the time of wheat harvest, Samson went to visit his wife with a young goat. And he said, "I will go in to my wife in the chamber." But her father would not allow him to go in. And her father said, "I really thought that you utterly hated her, so I gave her to your companion. Is not her younger sister more beautiful than she? Please take her instead." And Samson said to them, "This time I shall be innocent in regard to the Philistines, when I do them harm."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He arrives with a present and an assumption. He has offered no apology and sent no message since he walked out in a rage. His temper has cooled, and he expects the door to open.

The father is frightened, and not unreasonable. His daughter's bridegroom lost a wager at his own wedding, called her a heifer in front of the whole town, disappeared, and was next heard of killing thirty men in Ashkelon. I really thought that you utterly hated her. Anybody would have thought so.

So he did what a father in that position did: he gave her to the best man rather than leave her abandoned. And now, faced with the man himself at the door, he offers the younger daughter as a substitute, which tells you how badly he wants this settled without violence.

He pronounces himself not guilty before he has done anything, and that shows how his conscience works. He is not reacting in blind fury. He is reasoning, in advance, with a formula: this time I shall be innocent, implying he knows the Ashkelon business was another matter, and therefore what follows is permitted.

He has drawn up the charge, heard the case, delivered the verdict and licensed the sentence, and every one of those offices is his own. Nobody else in the chapter has been consulted, least of all God.

The habit is not confined to strong men with a grudge. The most dangerous thing a person can do with a wrong done to him is to establish, quietly and alone, that his response is now justified. The reasoning is always available and always convincing, and the reason it convinces is that it is being marked by the person who wrote it.

Scripture takes the pen out of his hand: never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, "Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord" (Rom. 12:19). The prohibition is not that revenge is unjust. It is that you are not the judge.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–8 — Foxes, Fire, and a Woman Burned
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The harvest burned, the woman burned, and one more round of vengeance (vv. 4-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Revenge answers revenge, and the fire threatened at the wedding comes at last.
verseByVerse.examples: The victims are farmers and a frightened young woman, not soldiers.

verseByVerse.quote: So Samson went and caught 300 foxes and took torches. And he turned them tail to tail and put a torch between each pair of tails. And when he had set fire to the torches, he let the foxes go into the standing grain of the Philistines and set fire to the stacked grain and the standing grain, as well as the olive orchards. Then the Philistines said, "Who has done this?" And they said, "Samson, the son-in-law of the Timnite, because he has taken his wife and given her to his companion." And the Philistines came up and burned her and her father with fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three hundred foxes, caught alive, one at a time: this is not a flash of rage but long, patient trapping, carried out cold. Verse 1 told us the season: wheat harvest.

Three things burn, and the order is the order of ruin. The stacked grain is what is already cut and gathered, this year's food. The standing grain is the rest of the same year, still in the field. And the olive orchards are not a year at all. An olive tree takes a decade to come into bearing and a lifetime to mature. Burning the orchards takes food out of the mouths of children not yet born.

These are farmers, the growers of Timnah, not the lords of the five cities or the men at his wedding.

Turn back to 14:15. The threat to burn her and her father's house is why she wept at him for seven days; it is why she betrayed the riddle to her people; it is the reason for everything she did that Samson took as treachery. She was a girl trying not to be burned alive.

She is burned alive, by the Philistines, in the manner the thirty had promised. And the thing that finally brought it on her was not her betrayal; it was Samson's revenge for losing her.

Follow the chain, because the writer means us to. He designs an unwinnable riddle; they threaten her with fire; she gives them the answer; he calls her a heifer and abandons her; her father marries her to somebody else; he burns their harvest for it; and they burn her for that. Every link is a man doing what was right in his own eyes, and the one who dies is the girl who had the fewest choices of anybody in the story.

She has no name in this book. She is "Samson's wife", and then "the Timnite's" daughter, and then ash.

verseByVerse.quote: And Samson said to them, "If this is what you do, I swear I will be avenged on you, and after that I will quit." And he struck them hip and thigh with a great blow, and he went down and stayed in the cleft of the rock of Etam.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After that I will quit is the oldest sentence in the history of grudges, and it has never once been true, because a feud does not end when one side is satisfied: the other side is now owed as well, and the reckoning has no natural stopping place.

Note also that his sworn purpose has quietly changed. In verse 3 the harm was to be his compensation. Now it is his answer to their answer. He is no longer setting a price; he is taking a turn.

Hip and thigh is an idiom, probably from wrestling, meaning comprehensively: he took them apart.

Then the judge of Israel, at the height of his strength, hides in a crevice in the hills, and the next thing that happens is that his own countrymen come to fetch him out.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–13 — Judah Comes Out Three Thousand Strong
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Philistines camp in Judah, and Judah arrests its own deliverer and hands him over bound (vv. 9-13).
verseByVerse.theology: Here at last is the explanation of the missing cry at 13:1.
verseByVerse.examples: The tribe of the coming king acts as the occupier's police.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Philistines came up and encamped in Judah and made a raid on Lehi. And the men of Judah said, "Why have you come up against us?" They said, "We have come up to bind Samson, to do to him as he did to us." Then 3,000 men of Judah went down to the cleft of the rock of Etam, and said to Samson, "Do you not know that the Philistines are rulers over us? What then is this that you have done to us?" And he said to them, "As they did to me, so have I done to them." And they said to him, "We have come down to bind you, that we may give you into the hands of the Philistines." And Samson said to them, "Swear to me that you will not attack me yourselves." They said to him, "No; we will only bind you and give you into their hands. We will surely not kill you." So they bound him with two new ropes and brought him up from the rock.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An occupying army camps inside Judah, and Judah's response is not to muster or to cry to the LORD as their fathers had done, but to ask a polite question. When they are told the trouble, they organise the arrest.

Judah can put three thousand fighting men into the field within days. Ehud had only a hastily gathered levy. Gideon beat Midian with three hundred. Shamgar killed six hundred Philistines with an ox goad. Three thousand armed men of Judah went out, in force, and marched in the wrong direction.

Then the sentence that explains the whole Samson cycle: do you not know that the Philistines are rulers over us?

Here is why forty years produced no cry. Judah is not in anguish. Judah has looked at the occupation, judged it liveable, and is angry with the one man who will not leave it alone. What then is this that you have done to us? It is as if the trouble in the land were Samson.

Consider who is talking. This is Judah, the tribe God named when Israel asked who should go up first against the Canaanites (1:1-2). The tribe of the lion, of the sceptre, of David, and at long last of Christ. That tribe is out here as the occupier's police force, arresting the deliverer God sent them.

Nothing in the chapter is more uncomfortable than this. Judah's sin is quiet, sensible, and shared by three thousand men who all thought they were being reasonable. They had made their peace with the thing God had sent a man to destroy, and their only complaint was that he was making life difficult.

Samson's whole defence, as they did to me, so have I done to them, is the same accounting as verse 3.

He surrenders, and asks only that they will not kill him themselves. That is the extent of what he expects from his own people, and they give him exactly that and nothing more.

The man God raised up to begin saving Israel from the Philistines is delivered to the Philistines, bound, by his own countrymen, who are afraid of what the rulers will do if they do not. Centuries later, at another handing-over, the words will be: we have no king but Caesar (John 19:15). The pattern of a people surrendering their deliverer to the occupying power to keep the peace is older than Pilate.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–20 — Heaps upon Heaps, and Then a Drink
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A thousand men fall to a jawbone, a song with no God in it, and then thirst, a first prayer and a split-open spring (vv. 14-20).
verseByVerse.theology: The song and the prayer are two verses apart and say opposite things. Thirst taught him in an afternoon what a thousand dead men had not.
verseByVerse.examples: God's answer to a flawed prayer is water, not a lecture.

verseByVerse.quote: When he came to Lehi, the Philistines came shouting to meet him. Then the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him, and the ropes that were on his arms became as flax that has caught fire, and his bonds melted off his hands. And he found a fresh jawbone of a donkey, and put out his hand and took it, and with it he struck 1,000 men. And Samson said, "With the jawbone of a donkey, heaps upon heaps, with the jawbone of a donkey have I struck down a thousand men." As soon as he had finished speaking, he threw away the jawbone out of his hand. And that place was called Ramath-lehi.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They came shouting, which means they thought it was over.

Then the Spirit of the LORD rushed on him, and the image the writer chooses is exact: flax that has caught fire. Two new ropes, strong enough that three thousand men were satisfied with them, going the way a bundle of dry linen fibre goes when a spark touches it. Not snapped but melted off his hands.

A fresh jawbone means recently dead; an old sun-dried bone would have shattered. So the animal has not long been a carcass, and it is a donkey, an unclean animal, and Samson picks it up in his hand without a moment's hesitation.

He is a Nazirite, forbidden to go near a dead body (Num. 6:6-7). He has now handled a corpse to get honey and a corpse to get a weapon, and in between hosted a seven-day drinking feast. Two of the three strands of his vow are in ribbons, and the strength keeps coming anyway. God went on using him. The power did not depend on Samson's faithfulness, and it never had: it was the Spirit of the LORD, rushing upon a man who was in no condition to deserve it.
