Which is a mercy, and also a trap, because a man who keeps succeeding while disobeying will conclude that the disobedience does not matter. Chapter 16 is what happens when he finds out.

His victory song is a pun, and it has no God in it. The Hebrew plays on two words that sound almost identical (the word for donkey and the word for heap), so the line runs something like: with the jaw of an ass, I have assed them in heaps. It is clever. It is also two lines long, and its subject is a jawbone and the man swinging it.

Set it beside the other victory song in this book. Deborah and Barak sang for thirty-one verses and the song begins bless the LORD, and it is about him from end to end: his marching from Seir, his stars fighting from heaven, his people offering themselves willingly (5:2-5, 20). Samson sings two lines about his weapon.

The place is named after the bone: Ramath-lehi. The map now carries the memory of the weapon, and the next four verses will put another name on the same ground, and that one will remember something else entirely.
verseByVerse.note: “Ramath-lehi” means “the hill of the jawbone” (ESV note). A pun: the Hebrew words for “donkey” and “heap” are spelled alike, hamor.

verseByVerse.quote: And he was very thirsty, and he called upon the LORD and said, "You have granted this great salvation by the hand of your servant, and shall I now die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?" And God split open the hollow place that is at Lehi, and water came out from it. And when he drank, his spirit returned, and he revived. Therefore the name of it was called En-hakkore; it is at Lehi to this day. And he judged Israel in the days of the Philistines twenty years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A thousand men are dead on the ground and Samson is beaten by thirst. The man who tore a lion cannot get through the afternoon. The body that God had made irresistible still needed a drink of water. It is the first thing in his life he has not been able to do for himself, and it is what finally puts him on his knees.

This is the first prayer of Samson's that the book records. Everything until now has been demand, riddle, insult, threat and song. And it is better theology than anything else he has said.

You have granted this great salvation. Not "I have struck down a thousand men", which is what he sang two verses ago. Now the victory is God's grant. And by the hand of your servant: the first humble word out of his mouth in three chapters. Not the strong man, not the son-in-law of the Timnite. The servant.

Be honest about the rest of it, though. The second half of the prayer is a complaint with an edge: shall I now die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised? There is concern for his own dignity in it, and a hint that this would reflect badly on the arrangement. It is not a model prayer. It is a real one, from a man who has just discovered he is not self-sufficient and is not sure he likes it.

God does not lecture him; he splits open the ground.

The KJV reads that God clave a hollow place that was in the jaw, so the water seems to come from the jawbone itself. Lehi means jaw, so the place and the bone share a name; modern translations take it as the hollow at Lehi, which fits the naming of the spring that follows.

There is no rebuke in the answer, no interrogation about the vineyards or the carcasses or the song. He asked for water and water came, immediately, out of the ground where he was standing. His spirit returned, and he revived: the phrase is used of a man coming back from the point of collapse.

The place gets a second name, after the cry rather than the weapon: not the spring of the faithful Nazirite but the spring of the man who called. And the man who called had that same day broken his vow on a corpse, taken a thousand lives in a private feud, and sung a song in which God did not appear. He called, and God gave him water.

Israel had drunk from a split rock before, in the wilderness, and Paul says the Rock that followed them was Christ (Ex. 17:6; 1 Cor. 10:4).

Many Christians have set one more thirst beside this one, as an echo rather than the meaning of Lehi. At Lehi a strong man cried out that he was dying of thirst, and God split open the ground and gave him water and he revived. At Calvary another man said I thirst, and no spring came. He was handed sour wine on a sponge, and he died (John 19:28-30).

Then a soldier put a spear into his side, and at once there came out blood and water (John 19:34). At Lehi God split open the ground to save his servant. At Golgotha God let his Son be split open to save his enemies, and the water came out of him.

He had said what he intended to do with it: if anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (John 7:37).

In the days of the Philistines holds the whole assessment: after twenty years of judging, these are still the Philistines' days. The oppression named in 13:1 has not lifted. Ehud gave the land eighty years of rest and Deborah forty; Samson's twenty years end with the enemy exactly where they were when he started.

That is what the angel said would happen: he would begin to save Israel (13:5). God announced the limit before the man was conceived, and the limit held.
verseByVerse.note: “En-hakkore” means “the spring of him who called” (ESV note).

16.title: Samson and Delilah
16.text: <sup>1</sup>Samson went to Gaza, and there he saw a prostitute, and he went in to her.<sup>2</sup>The Gazites were told, "Samson has come here." And they surrounded the place and set an ambush for him all night at the gate of the city. They kept quiet all night, saying, "Let us wait till the light of the morning; then we will kill him."<sup>3</sup>But Samson lay till midnight, and at midnight he arose and took hold of the doors of the gate of the city and the two posts, and pulled them up, bar and all, and put them on his shoulders and carried them to the top of the hill that is in front of Hebron.<sup>4</sup>After this he loved a woman in the Valley of Sorek, whose name was Delilah.<sup>5</sup>And the lords of the Philistines came up to her and said to her, "Seduce him, and see where his great strength lies, and by what means we may overpower him, that we may bind him to humble him. And we will each give you 1,100 pieces of silver."<sup>6</sup>So Delilah said to Samson, "Please tell me where your great strength lies, and how you might be bound, that one could subdue you."<sup>7</sup>Samson said to her, "If they bind me with seven fresh bowstrings that have not been dried, then I shall become weak and be like any other man."<sup>8</sup>Then the lords of the Philistines brought up to her seven fresh bowstrings that had not been dried, and she bound him with them.<sup>9</sup>Now she had men lying in ambush in an inner chamber. And she said to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" But he snapped the bowstrings, as a thread of flax snaps when it touches the fire. So the secret of his strength was not known.<sup>10</sup>Then Delilah said to Samson, "Behold, you have mocked me and told me lies. Please tell me how you might be bound."<sup>11</sup>And he said to her, "If they bind me with new ropes that have not been used, then I shall become weak and be like any other man."<sup>12</sup>So Delilah took new ropes and bound him with them and said to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" And the men lying in ambush were in an inner chamber. But he snapped the ropes off his arms like a thread.<sup>13</sup>Then Delilah said to Samson, "Until now you have mocked me and told me lies. Tell me how you might be bound." And he said to her, "If you weave the seven locks of my head with the web and fasten it tight with the pin, then I shall become weak and be like any other man."<sup>14</sup>So while he slept, Delilah took the seven locks of his head and wove them into the web. And she made them tight with the pin and said to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" But he awoke from his sleep and pulled away the pin, the loom, and the web.<sup>15</sup>And she said to him, "How can you say, 'I love you,' when your heart is not with me? You have mocked me these three times, and you have not told me where your great strength lies."<sup>16</sup>And when she pressed him hard with her words day after day, and urged him, his soul was vexed to death.<sup>17</sup>And he told her all his heart, and said to her, "A razor has never come upon my head, for I have been a Nazirite to God from my mother's womb. If my head is shaved, then my strength will leave me, and I shall become weak and be like any other man."<sup>18</sup>When Delilah saw that he had told her all his heart, she sent and called the lords of the Philistines, saying, "Come up again, for he has told me all his heart." Then the lords of the Philistines came up to her and brought the money in their hands.<sup>19</sup>She made him sleep on her knees. And she called a man and had him shave off the seven locks of his head. Then she began to torment him, and his strength left him.<sup>20</sup>And she said, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" And he awoke from his sleep and said, "I will go out as at other times and shake myself free." But he did not know that the LORD had left him.<sup>21</sup>And the Philistines seized him and gouged out his eyes and brought him down to Gaza and bound him with bronze shackles. And he ground at the mill in the prison.<sup>22</sup>But the hair of his head began to grow again after it had been shaved.<sup>23</sup>Now the lords of the Philistines gathered to offer a great sacrifice to Dagon their god and to rejoice, and they said, "Our god has given Samson our enemy into our hand."<sup>24</sup>And when the people saw him, they praised their god. For they said, "Our god has given our enemy into our hand, the ravager of our country, who has killed many of us."<sup>25</sup>And when their hearts were merry, they said, "Call Samson, that he may entertain us." So they called Samson out of the prison, and he entertained them. They made him stand between the pillars.<sup>26</sup>And Samson said to the young man who held him by the hand, "Let me feel the pillars on which the house rests, that I may lean against them."<sup>27</sup>Now the house was full of men and women. All the lords of the Philistines were there, and on the roof there were about 3,000 men and women, who looked on while Samson entertained.<sup>28</sup>Then Samson called to the LORD and said, "O Lord GOD, please remember me and please strengthen me only this once, O God, that I may be avenged on the Philistines for my two eyes."<sup>29</sup>And Samson grasped the two middle pillars on which the house rested, and he leaned his weight against them, his right hand on the one and his left hand on the other.<sup>30</sup>And Samson said, "Let me die with the Philistines." Then he bowed with all his strength, and the house fell upon the lords and upon all the people who were in it. So the dead whom he killed at his death were more than those whom he had killed during his life.<sup>31</sup>Then his brothers and all his family came down and took him and brought him up and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of Manoah his father. He had judged Israel twenty years.
16.overview:
Samson goes into Gaza, the chief Philistine city, to visit a prostitute, and leaves at midnight carrying the city gate towards Hebron. Then comes Delilah, bribed by the five Philistine lords. She asks him openly where his strength lies; three times he lies, and three times she tries to have him taken in front of his eyes, and he stays.

Worn down at last, he tells her all his heart, and what he gives away is the vow itself. He wakes expecting to shake himself free as at other times, but he did not know that the LORD had left him. They blind him and put him on the mill in Gaza. Then one word turns: but the hair of his head began to grow again. When a temple full of Philistines credits Dagon with a victory over the God of Israel, a blind man asks to be remembered, and brings the house down.
16.theology:
He did not know. This is the heart of the whole Samson cycle. The strength was never in the hair, which was only the sign of a vow; every display of strength is credited to the Spirit (14:6, 14:19, 15:14). What Samson lost was the LORD, and he lost him without noticing, because he had gone on succeeding for years while the vow came apart.

He was not deceived. Delilah states her purpose to his face and carries it out in front of him before he gives anything away. This is not a trap sprung on an innocent but a man who no longer believes in consequences, and whose lies drift steadily towards the truth.

Why the last scene happens. Not because Samson has earned anything, but because God will not let Dagon have his glory. The hair growing back is a sign restored where nobody is watching, on a man who can ask for nothing, and that is the sort of place God begins again.

Heard, though the prayer is mixed. Samson's last prayer is about his own eyes, and God answers it. That is why Hebrews lists him among those made strong out of weakness (Heb. 11:32-34).

Where the parallel breaks. Samson's death is a flawed and partial pattern of the deliverer who conquers by dying, and it is clearest where it fails: he pulled the house down on his enemies, and Christ let it fall on himself.
16.examples:
Then: A man who had watched a woman try three times to hand him to his enemies went back a fourth, handed over the vow that had marked him for God since before he was born, woke expecting to be strong as usual, and found God had gone without telling him. He lost the eyes that had led him everywhere, ground grain in the dark, and prayed twice that we are told of, once for water and once for strength, and was heard both times.

Now: The warning is v. 20, and it is not mainly about lust. Ask whether anything in your life is running on momentum: the gift working, the reputation holding, the ministry going on, while faithfulness quietly comes apart in private. Where the vow has come apart, Christ kept faith perfectly in our place, and his faithfulness is counted to all who come back to him (Rom. 5:19). The comfort is v. 22, and it is for people who have already fallen: the hair grew back where nobody could see it, on a man who could not have asked for it, and God was not finished with him. If you can still say remember me, you are not past the point Samson prayed from.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A prostitute in Gaza, an ambush at the gate, and the gate carried off (vv. 1-3).
verseByVerse.theology: Samson leaves the enemy capital standing open, as a joke on his way home from a brothel.
verseByVerse.examples: It is a magnificent feat, and God's name is nowhere near it.

verseByVerse.quote: Samson went to Gaza, and there he saw a prostitute, and he went in to her. The Gazites were told, "Samson has come here." And they surrounded the place and set an ambush for him all night at the gate of the city. They kept quiet all night, saying, "Let us wait till the light of the morning; then we will kill him." But Samson lay till midnight, and at midnight he arose and took hold of the doors of the gate of the city and the two posts, and pulled them up, bar and all, and put them on his shoulders and carried them to the top of the hill that is in front of Hebron.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He walks deep into enemy country, to their chief city, for this. Gaza is the greatest of the five Philistine capitals, and the judge of Israel goes there alone, for one reason, and the verb is the one that has run through his whole story: he saw. He saw the woman at Timnah; he sees this one. Twenty years of judging have not touched the eyes.

The text makes nothing of it: no Spirit rushing, no divine occasion sought, no mitigating clause. Just a man, a city, and a purchase.

The whole city knows quickly, and they are perfectly sensible about it. They do not attack him in the dark; they lock the only way out and wait for daylight, when they can see what they are fighting. It is good planning against a man they have every reason to fear.

He does not break out. He takes the door with him. A city gate was the strongest thing the town possessed: massive doors, hung on posts sunk into the wall, barred at night. It was also the place where the elders sat, where cases were heard and business transacted; the gate was the city's authority in one structure. Boaz went to the gate to settle a legal matter (Ruth 4:1).

The hill in front of Hebron is not down the road. If, as most think, it lies near Hebron itself, it is a long climb up out of the coastal plain into the hill country, carrying a gate. (Some read it as a hill nearer Gaza looking towards Hebron; the insult to Judah stands either way.)

Gaza wakes to find its front wall has a hole in it. Now note what the writer leaves out and what he puts in. He leaves out the Spirit. Every other feat has the clause attached: the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him at the lion (14:6), at Ashkelon (14:19), at Lehi (15:14). Here, nothing. Samson is now doing this on his own account, for his own amusement, and the narrator declines to put God's name anywhere near it.

He puts in the destination: the hill that is in front of Hebron. Hebron is in Judah. Judah is the tribe that had just come down three thousand strong to tie him up and hand him to the Philistines (15:11-13). So the gates of the enemy capital are dumped on the doorstep of the men who would not fight for them.

It is a magnificent, pointless, contemptuous act, and it is the last free thing he does.
verseByVerse.note: Gaza to Hebron is about 40 miles, uphill.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–14 — A Game He Thought He Could Win
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Delilah, a bribe from the five lords, and three false answers, each tested in front of him (vv. 4-14).
verseByVerse.theology: Samson plays a game he is sure he cannot lose.
verseByVerse.examples: Sin that is managed rather than killed keeps moving closer.

verseByVerse.quote: After this he loved a woman in the Valley of Sorek, whose name was Delilah. And the lords of the Philistines came up to her and said to her, "Seduce him, and see where his great strength lies, and by what means we may overpower him, that we may bind him to humble him. And we will each give you 1,100 pieces of silver."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the first time the book says Samson loved anyone. Of the girl at Timnah it said only that she was right in his eyes.

Delilah is also the only woman in Samson's story who is given a name. His mother is the woman. His wife is "Samson's wife", and then "the Timnite's" daughter, and then ash. The prostitute in Gaza is a prostitute. The one who is named is the one who destroys him.

The Valley of Sorek runs down from the hills to the plain, past Zorah where he was born. He has not gone far. He is in the borderland he grew up in, and so is she.

The Philistine confederation had five cities, Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, Gath, and all five lords make the journey to a woman's house in a border valley because one Israelite is beyond their army.

Eleven hundred pieces of silver each makes five and a half thousand shekels for a man's life, a fortune several times over, offered to a woman who evidently did not have to think about it very long.

Read their brief carefully, because she follows it to the letter and he watches her do it. Find where the strength lies. Find how we can overpower him. So that we may bind him: to humble him. They do not say to kill him. They want him brought low, and in the end they get exactly that: blind, shackled, grinding grain, and brought out to be laughed at.

Money has bought a man's betrayal before and since, and the price is never the point. Judas took thirty pieces of silver for the Son of God, which is a fraction of what Delilah was paid, and the smallness of that sum is part of its horror (Matt. 26:15). What Delilah's price shows is something else: the Philistines had learned, over twenty years, exactly what Samson could not be beaten by, and exactly what he could.
verseByVerse.note: Eleven hundred shekels from each lord was a huge sum: over 25 pounds of silver each.

verseByVerse.quote: So Delilah said to Samson, "Please tell me where your great strength lies, and how you might be bound, that one could subdue you." Samson said to her, "If they bind me with seven fresh bowstrings that have not been dried, then I shall become weak and be like any other man." Then the lords of the Philistines brought up to her seven fresh bowstrings that had not been dried, and she bound him with them. Now she had men lying in ambush in an inner chamber. And she said to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" But he snapped the bowstrings, as a thread of flax snaps when it touches the fire. So the secret of his strength was not known. Then Delilah said to Samson, "Behold, you have mocked me and told me lies. Please tell me how you might be bound." And he said to her, "If they bind me with new ropes that have not been used, then I shall become weak and be like any other man." So Delilah took new ropes and bound him with them and said to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" And the men lying in ambush were in an inner chamber. But he snapped the ropes off his arms like a thread.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She does not disguise it in the slightest: no pretext, no clever indirection. It is the lords' brief, repeated to his face almost word for word.

He knows what she is asking. Note who appears in his answer: if they bind me. He has not been told there is a they. He has worked it out, and says so, and plays on.

So now he has seen it done. She got the materials from somewhere, which means she is in contact with them. She tied him up while he lay there and let her. There were armed men behind the door. And she shouted the alarm that was meant to be the last thing he ever heard.

He snapped the strings and stayed. Her complaint is that he lied to her, a brazenness that is almost admirable: she has just tried to hand him to his enemies and her grievance is his dishonesty. She reproaches him for not cooperating in his own destruction, and he accepts the reproach as reasonable.

His second answer is new ropes, the same thing Judah used on him at the rock of Etam (15:13), which came off at Lehi like flax in a fire. He is now naming methods that have already failed in living memory. He is not even trying to be plausible; he is enjoying it.

Be clear about what is going on, because the chapter is often told as though Samson were seduced into an unwitting slip. He is not tricked. He has been told her purpose, has watched her carry it out twice, has heard the alarm shouted twice with men waiting in the next room, and he goes back for a third round.

This is a man who believes he can hold something lethal and put it down whenever he chooses. He has survived so much for so long that he has stopped believing in consequences. Every previous escape has taught him the wrong lesson.

That is how sin destroys strong people. It waits while they prove to themselves, over and over, that they can handle it, and the proof is the trap. Let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall (1 Cor. 10:12).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Delilah said to Samson, "Until now you have mocked me and told me lies. Tell me how you might be bound." And he said to her, "If you weave the seven locks of my head with the web and fasten it tight with the pin, then I shall become weak and be like any other man." So while he slept, Delilah took the seven locks of his head and wove them into the web. And she made them tight with the pin and said to him, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" But he awoke from his sleep and pulled away the pin, the loom, and the web.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third answer brings his hair into it. Bowstrings and ropes had nothing to do with him; the seven locks of his head are still a lie, but a lie built out of the truth. He has moved from things that have no connection to his vow to the one thing that does.

She now knows the hair is somewhere in this. He has handed her the field.

The strongest man alive lies asleep while a woman who has twice tried to have him taken works on the sign of his consecration with a weaving pin. This is the shape of every gradual fall. He is not being dragged; he is drifting inward, one concession at a time, and every concession feels small because it is only slightly worse than the one before.

Nobody gives away the centre in one movement. He gives away the outer things first, discovers he survived, and moves in.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The vow told, the head shaved, the LORD gone without his knowing, the eyes, the mill, and then one word turns (vv. 15-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The razor only finished what twenty years of small surrenders had begun.
verseByVerse.examples: Samson tells the truth at last, and it costs him everything.

verseByVerse.quote: And she said to him, "How can you say, 'I love you,' when your heart is not with me? You have mocked me these three times, and you have not told me where your great strength lies." And when she pressed him hard with her words day after day, and urged him, his soul was vexed to death. And he told her all his heart, and said to her, "A razor has never come upon my head, for I have been a Nazirite to God from my mother's womb. If my head is shaved, then my strength will leave me, and I shall become weak and be like any other man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now go back and read 14:16.

You only hate me; you do not love me. You have put a riddle to my people, and you have not told me what it is.

That was his bride at Timnah, years earlier. The same accusation about love, the same complaint about a secret withheld, the same aim. He knows this speech. He has heard it before, in almost these words, from a woman in the pay of the same people, and thirty men in Ashkelon died the last time he gave in to it.

Day after day: this is not a moment of weakness but a siege. Take the Hebrew of the last clause exactly: his soul was "shortened" to death. It is the idiom for an endurance that has come to its end: a man worn down to the point where he will pay anything to make it stop.

That same idiom has appeared once before in this book, at 10:16. There it is used of God: when Israel put away their foreign gods, "his soul was shortened" over the misery of Israel: he could bear it no longer.

The same phrase, and the two ends of the book's whole meaning. God's patience runs out, and what comes out of it is mercy for people who deserved nothing. Samson's endurance runs out, and what comes out of it is a shaved head and a millstone. It is one thing to be worn down by love for someone else's misery. It is another to be worn down by a woman who is being paid to do it.

All his heart, the narrator says twice. Weigh what the secret actually is. It is not a fact about hair. It is a vow: I have been a Nazirite to God from my mother's womb. The one thing in Samson's life that had been about God, kept since before he was conceived, guarded by a mother who went without wine to carry him, and he hands it to a woman on the Philistine payroll to buy an hour's peace.

He has been giving away pieces of that vow for twenty years. The razor was all that was left, and he gives it away in words: not overpowered, not drugged, not deceived. He told her.

verseByVerse.quote: When Delilah saw that he had told her all his heart, she sent and called the lords of the Philistines, saying, "Come up again, for he has told me all his heart." Then the lords of the Philistines came up to her and brought the money in their hands. She made him sleep on her knees. And she called a man and had him shave off the seven locks of his head. Then she began to torment him, and his strength left him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She knew immediately that this time it was true, because the first three answers were about equipment and this one was about God. A man does not invent a childhood vow and a mother's abstinence to get a woman off his back. She heard the difference at once, and sent for the lords.

They came with the money in their hands: a man asleep inside, and outside the door his price being counted.

She made him sleep on her knees contains no violence at all, and no sentence in the chapter is more terrible. The posture is trust. His head is in her lap, and he is asleep, the deepest thing a strong man can offer, and that is the position from which she calls in the barber.

Note that the shaving is not her own hand. She calls a man, so that the work is done carefully while Samson lies still. Twenty years of Philistine warfare ended by a man with a razor and a steady hand.

Then she began to torment him: testing, before she raises the alarm, and this time there is no snapping of anything.

Here the narrator writes the clause the whole chapter has been moving towards: his strength left him. Not "the hair was gone, therefore he was weak". Something left him. The next verse will say who.

verseByVerse.quote: And she said, "The Philistines are upon you, Samson!" And he awoke from his sleep and said, "I will go out as at other times and shake myself free." But he did not know that the LORD had left him. And the Philistines seized him and gouged out his eyes and brought him down to Gaza and bound him with bronze shackles. And he ground at the mill in the prison. But the hair of his head began to grow again after it had been shaved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fourth time she shouts it, he expects it to go like the first three. As at other times is a man's whole life in four words. It has always worked before; it will work now. He stands up out of her lap, shakes himself, and reaches for what has never once failed him.

Few sentences in the Old Testament are sadder, and everything in these four chapters has been driving at it. First: the LORD had left him. Not his hair, not his strength. The LORD. The strength was always the Spirit of the LORD rushing upon him. The hair was the visible token of a vow; the power was a Person, and the Person has gone.

Second: he did not know. He had lost God and could not tell. He got up and expected to perform, because he had been performing for years while the vow came apart in pieces (the carcass, the feast, the jawbone, and now the razor), and nothing had ever visibly changed. Every unpunished breach had taught him that the vow was decorative.

So the departure was not sudden. What was sudden was the discovery.

This reaches people who will never go near a Delilah. A man can lose the presence of God and go on preaching, leading the family prayers, running the meeting, being admired for his gift, because the gift is not the presence, and the gift can outlive it for a long time. The Spirit gave Samson victories in a year when he was breaking his vow on a corpse. God is generous like that, and his generosity is not an audit.

So you cannot measure your standing with God by whether things are still working. Samson's things were still working right up to the morning they were not.

Four verbs, the exact shape of what sin does. They seized him, who had never been held. They gouged out his eyes, and consider which organ they took. It was seeing that ruined him: he saw a woman at Timnah, he saw a prostitute in Gaza, and everything was right in his own eyes. He is now blind, and the punishment is a picture of the sin.

They brought him down to Gaza: back to the city where this chapter began, back to the scene of his last free act, in chains. And he ground at the mill, which was the work of women and animals. The strongest man in Israel, walking in a circle in the dark, turning a stone, on the same treadmill until he dies.

That is what sin offers everyone in the end. It shows you what you want, takes what you see with, brings you back where you started, and puts you to work going round in circles.

One word turns this chapter: but. Verse 22 is not saying that the power was in the hair after all and is regrowing with it, like a battery on charge. God is not bound by follicles, and the writer has never once said the strength was in the hair.

What is growing back is the sign: the visible mark of a man set apart to God from his mother's womb, coming back on a head that is blind, shaved, shackled and grinding. The vow is being restored on a man in no position to restore anything.

Nobody in Gaza is watching a prisoner's hair. It happens where only God can see it, on a man who has nothing and can do nothing. God is not finished with people who are finished with themselves, and the proof of it, in this chapter, is a quiet biological fact noticed by no one and written down for ever.

Can a believer lose the Spirit? In the Old Testament the Spirit came on judges and kings to empower them for their office, and that empowering could be withdrawn (1 Sam. 16:14). In the new covenant the Spirit dwells in every believer for ever (John 14:16) as the seal of salvation (Eph. 1:13-14). Samson lost his strength, not necessarily his salvation; Hebrews counts him among those who had faith (Heb. 11:32). And if you are a Christian afraid that you have lost God without knowing it, your fear is not Samson's condition: he did not know and did not care. A troubled conscience over sin is a mark of the Spirit's presence, not his absence (Eph. 4:30). David prayed take not your Holy Spirit from me (Ps. 51:11), and he was heard.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–31 — Let Me Die with the Philistines
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Dagon credited, the blind man brought out for sport, a last prayer, the house brought down, and a burial at home (vv. 23-31).
verseByVerse.theology: From verse 23 the question is no longer what Samson deserves but whose glory is at stake.
verseByVerse.examples: A ruined man calls on God, and is heard.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the lords of the Philistines gathered to offer a great sacrifice to Dagon their god and to rejoice, and they said, "Our god has given Samson our enemy into our hand." And when the people saw him, they praised their god. For they said, "Our god has given our enemy into our hand, the ravager of our country, who has killed many of us." And when their hearts were merry, they said, "Call Samson, that he may entertain us." So they called Samson out of the prison, and he entertained them. They made him stand between the pillars.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With the Philistines' song the whole matter changes, because it is no longer about Samson. They do not say "we caught him", but Our god has given Samson our enemy into our hand. Dagon is being publicly credited with a victory over the God of Israel, at a great sacrifice, by the assembled rulers of a nation.

Nothing in the Old Testament is older or more serious than that issue. When Israel is beaten, the watching nations do not conclude that Israel was unfaithful; they conclude that Israel's God is weak. Moses argued with God on exactly that ground (what will the Egyptians say?), and God himself says he acts for the sake of my name, so that the nations shall know he is the LORD (Num. 14:13-16; Ezek. 36:22-23).

So the reason the last scene of this chapter happens is not that Samson has earned another chance. It is that a temple full of people is giving God's glory to Dagon, and God will not have it.

The ravager of our country is a fair description from where they stand. He burned their harvest at harvest time and their olive groves with it. He killed thirty men in Ashkelon over a bet and a thousand at Lehi. From a Philistine farmer's side of the line, Samson is a terrorist, and the relief in this room is genuine.

They send for him as the after-dinner amusement, to make sport of him: whatever a blind, shaved strongman could be prodded into doing to make a hall laugh. The man who tore a lion is now the act, and he is led out by the hand for it.

This is what the lords commissioned at the beginning: bind him to humble him (v. 5). They have got everything they paid for.
verseByVerse.note: Dagon was the chief god of the Philistines.

verseByVerse.quote: And Samson said to the young man who held him by the hand, "Let me feel the pillars on which the house rests, that I may lean against them." Now the house was full of men and women. All the lords of the Philistines were there, and on the roof there were about 3,000 men and women, who looked on while Samson entertained.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A boy is leading him, and he asks the boy for a favour. The whole position is in that one image. The strongest man in the world is holding a child's hand, because he cannot cross a room alone, and has to ask permission to lean on something. And his request is the request of a tired old man: let me lean.

The boy does it. There is no reason not to. The prisoner has been safe for a long time.

The narrator stops and counts the house before anything happens. Every one of the five lords is inside: the entire ruling class of Philistia in one building. The floor is full. And on the flat roof, three thousand more, pressed to the edges, looking down into the courtyard at the show.

So the weight of three thousand people is resting on the roof, and the roof is resting on those pillars, and the pillars are what a blind man has just been allowed to put his hands on.

Could two pillars really hold such a building? Excavated Philistine temples, such as one at Tell Qasile near modern Tel Aviv, had their roofs carried on two central wooden pillars set on stone bases about two metres apart, close enough for one man to reach both. The narrator describes a building of the kind archaeologists have found.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Samson called to the LORD and said, "O Lord GOD, please remember me and please strengthen me only this once, O God, that I may be avenged on the Philistines for my two eyes." And Samson grasped the two middle pillars on which the house rested, and he leaned his weight against them, his right hand on the one and his left hand on the other. And Samson said, "Let me die with the Philistines." Then he bowed with all his strength, and the house fell upon the lords and upon all the people who were in it. So the dead whom he killed at his death were more than those whom he had killed during his life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In his second and last recorded prayer he uses three names for God in one breath, like someone reaching for every handle he can find.

Please remember me. That is the prayer of a man who has every reason to think he has been forgotten and would deserve it. It is very like the dying thief's prayer, centuries early: Jesus, remember me (Luke 23:42).

Only this once. He is not asking for restoration or a career. One more time, and then nothing.

Now be honest about the last clause, because the chapter is: that I may be avenged on the Philistines for my two eyes.

Not a word about Israel is in it, or about the God whose name is being handed to Dagon in that very room. To the end, the account he is settling is his own. And God answers him.

Hold both of those together and do not tidy either one. The prayer is self-interested, and the prayer is real; the motive is mixed, and the man is genuinely calling on the LORD; and the God who had left him in verse 20 does not say no in verse 28. Samson prays as what he is, a ruined, blinded man with nothing left and no illusions about his own record, and heaven does not require him to pray better before it listens.

That is why Hebrews can put his name in the roll of faith (Heb. 11:32), among those who were made strong out of weakness (Heb. 11:34): an exact description of a blind prisoner asking the God of Israel for strength one last time and staking his life on the answer.

Let me die with the Philistines is not despair, and it is not suicide in the ordinary sense; it is a soldier choosing to go down with the objective. He is between the two pillars, with three thousand on the roof, and there is no version of this where he walks out.

The narrator's verdict, that his death accomplished more than his life, is sad and true. Twenty years of judging, and the greatest blow struck for Israel was struck by a blind man in a heathen temple in the last thirty seconds he had.

Now set that sentence, carefully, beside another death. Scripture never calls Samson a picture of Christ, and he was too wilful to be a clean one. But the deliverer who conquers by dying is a shape the whole Bible moves towards, and here it appears in flawed and partial form, which makes the place where it breaks all the clearer.

Another deliverer was seized by his enemies, mocked as entertainment, blindfolded and struck and told to prophesy, and who accomplished more by dying than by living. So far the shapes match.

Here is where they part. Samson prayed let me die with the Philistines, and pulled the house down on the heads of his enemies. Jesus prayed Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do (Luke 23:34), and let the house fall on himself instead.

Samson killed more in his death than in his life; Christ saved more in his death than in his life, and every one of those saved was on the roof.

Was Samson’s death suicide? It is not held up as a model for taking one’s own life. Samson prayed for strength to bring judgment on God’s enemies, God answered, and he died in the act, like a soldier in battle; the three thousand on the roof were the Philistine rulers and people gathered to celebrate Dagon over the LORD (vv. 23–27). It was a unique moment of judgment. It gives no warrant for suicide, or for killing others for a cause; life is God’s to give and take. If you have lost someone to suicide, this chapter is no verdict on them or on you; bring that grief to the Lord who was himself a man of sorrows. If you are thinking of ending your own life, please tell someone today, a pastor, a friend, a doctor or an emergency line. Your life is precious to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Then his brothers and all his family came down and took him and brought him up and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of Manoah his father. He had judged Israel twenty years.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His family come for the body. Nobody else does: no national mourning, no song like Deborah's. His brothers and his father's household walk down to Gaza, dig him out of the rubble of a Philistine temple, and carry him home.

They lay him between Zorah and Eshtaol.

Turn back three chapters. And the Spirit of the LORD began to stir him in Mahaneh-dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol (13:25).

Exactly the same ground. That is where the Spirit first made a young man restless, and it is where they put him in the earth. Everything in between (the girl at Timnah, the lion, the riddle, the foxes, the jawbone, the gates of Gaza, the lap, the razor, the mill, the pillars) happened away from those two villages, and in the end he was carried back to them.

He is buried in the tomb of Manoah his father: the man who prayed teach us what we are to do with the child who will be born, and was told to keep the vow and wait.

He had judged Israel twenty years. And the Philistines are still there. Chapter 13 said he would only begin, and he only began; the war he opened is not finished until David (2 Sam. 5:17-25; 8:1).

So the last word on Samson is not a triumph, and the book is not embarrassed about it. He is the deliverer who did what was right in his own eyes and destroyed himself doing it; who was given more raw power than perhaps any other man in Scripture and used most of it on private quarrels; who lost God and did not notice; and who at the very end, blind and shaved and mocked, called on the LORD and was heard. He asked to be remembered, and he was. The God who left him in verse 20 answered him in verse 28, not because the man had improved, but because a temple full of people were crediting Dagon with a victory over the living God, and the living God had one servant left in the building.

17.title: Micah's Idol
17.text: <sup>1</sup>There was a man of the hill country of Ephraim, whose name was Micah.<sup>2</sup>And he said to his mother, "The 1,100 pieces of silver that were taken from you, about which you uttered a curse, and also spoke it in my ears, behold, the silver is with me; I took it." And his mother said, "Blessed be my son by the LORD."<sup>3</sup>And he restored the 1,100 pieces of silver to his mother. And his mother said, "I dedicate the silver to the LORD from my hand for my son, to make a carved image and a metal image. Now therefore I will restore it to you."<sup>4</sup>So when he restored the money to his mother, his mother took 200 pieces of silver and gave it to the silversmith, who made it into a carved image and a metal image. And it was in the house of Micah.<sup>5</sup>And the man Micah had a shrine, and he made an ephod and household gods, and ordained one of his sons, who became his priest.<sup>6</sup>In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.<sup>7</sup>Now there was a young man of Bethlehem in Judah, of the family of Judah, who was a Levite, and he sojourned there.<sup>8</sup>And the man departed from the town of Bethlehem in Judah to sojourn where he could find a place. And as he journeyed, he came to the hill country of Ephraim to the house of Micah.<sup>9</sup>And Micah said to him, "Where do you come from?" And he said to him, "I am a Levite of Bethlehem in Judah, and I am going to sojourn where I may find a place."<sup>10</sup>And Micah said to him, "Stay with me, and be to me a father and a priest, and I will give you ten pieces of silver a year and a suit of clothes and your living." And the Levite went in.<sup>11</sup>And the Levite was content to dwell with the man, and the young man became to him like one of his sons.<sup>12</sup>And Micah ordained the Levite, and the young man became his priest, and was in the house of Micah.<sup>13</sup>Then Micah said, "Now I know that the LORD will prosper me, because I have a Levite as priest."
17.overview:
A man of Ephraim named Micah admits to his mother that he stole the eleven hundred pieces of silver she cursed the thief for taking, and he admits it because he is under the curse, not because he is sorry. She cancels the curse with a blessing in the LORD's name, and then dedicates the money to the LORD to have a carved image and a metal image made. That sentence is the whole chapter: the covenant name and a breach of the second commandment in one breath.

Micah then assembles a homemade religion in his own house, with one of his sons as priest, and the narrator states the thesis of the book's last five chapters: in those days there was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes. Then a young Levite comes past looking for a place to land, Micah hires him, and concludes that the LORD will now prosper him.
17.theology:
Not apostasy but devotion done wrong. Nobody in this house has abandoned the LORD. They use his name constantly and mean the images as piety. That is what makes it more dangerous than open idolatry: a family worshipping the true God in a manner he forbade, and feeling generous about the cost.

Words used as mechanisms. A curse, a confession to escape it, a blessing to cancel it: nothing in the exchange is addressed to God, and his name is in every line of it.

Right in his own eyes. These are not people knowingly doing evil but people who have each become the final authority on what is good, and every one of them is satisfied.

You cannot hire a father. Once a salary is attached, the man whose task is to tell you the truth is the man whose keep depends on you. Micah wants a priest's authority and a servant's compliance.

Religion as a machine. Micah's confidence in verse 13 is superstition in flawless orthodox vocabulary. Every element is a true and good thing; the relationship is upside down, with God treated as the output of a correctly configured system. Chapter 18 shows what becomes of such a system.

The priest nobody hires. Against Micah's hired Levite stands the priest God himself appointed, who holds his office for ever, cannot be bought and cannot be carried away.
17.examples:
Then: A man returned stolen money to escape a curse, his mother dedicated it to the LORD to have an idol cast, he built a chapel in his front room and ordained his own son, and then hired a wandering Levite on a small annual salary and concluded that his prospects were now secure.

Now: Micah's vocabulary was faultless, so the chapter's question is not whether you believe the right things but whether you are using them to secure a result. The difference shows the day the machinery is taken away. And the mother's arithmetic is worth checking against our own: what we pledge out loud and what we actually give are not always the same.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Eleven Hundred Pieces of Silver
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A theft confessed under a curse, a blessing to cancel it, and silver dedicated to the LORD for an idol (vv. 1-4).
verseByVerse.theology: Confession, blessing and dedication all happen here, and none of them is what it seems.
verseByVerse.examples: The narrator reports the figures and lets the reader notice the gap.

verseByVerse.quote: There was a man of the hill country of Ephraim, whose name was Micah. And he said to his mother, "The 1,100 pieces of silver that were taken from you, about which you uttered a curse, and also spoke it in my ears, behold, the silver is with me; I took it." And his mother said, "Blessed be my son by the LORD." And he restored the 1,100 pieces of silver to his mother. And his mother said, "I dedicate the silver to the LORD from my hand for my son, to make a carved image and a metal image. Now therefore I will restore it to you." So when he restored the money to his mother, his mother took 200 pieces of silver and gave it to the silversmith, who made it into a carved image and a metal image. And it was in the house of Micah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eleven hundred pieces of silver is what each Philistine lord offered Delilah (16:5): a distinctive sum, twice in adjoining chapters, both times buying something that should never have been for sale.

See why Micah confesses. Not because he has been caught, and not because he is sorry. His mother uttered a curse over the thief and spoke it in my ears: he was standing there when she cursed him, and he has been living under it ever since.

He is not repenting; he is trying to get out from under a curse. Her reply is not forgiveness either but a countermeasure: a blessing in the covenant name put into the air to cancel the curse. Mother and son are both handling words as though they were mechanisms. Something has been said that might damage him, so something must be said to undo it.

Nothing here is about God at all, and both of them are talking about him constantly.

Verse 3 holds the whole chapter: the covenant name of the God of Israel, and the direct breach of his second commandment, in one breath, with no sense of any difficulty.

The commandment could hardly be plainer: you shall not make for yourself a carved image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath (Ex. 20:4). She is not turning to Baal. She is not renouncing the LORD. She intends this as an act of piety, in his honour, funded by recovered money, on behalf of her son.

Nobody in this house has decided to abandon God. They have decided to worship him in a way he forbade, and to feel good about the expense.

She said eleven hundred. She spent two hundred. She had declared the whole sum dedicated to the LORD from my hand, and then she took less than a fifth of it to the silversmith. Perhaps the rest went on the shrine and the ephod; the text does not say she kept it. But the narrator lets the gap stand in plain sight.

There is a kind of religion that is generous in its language and careful with its money, and the question to ask is whether anyone has ever seen the gap between what was pledged out loud and what actually went. Nobody audited this woman.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A homemade religion, and the sentence the last five chapters are built on (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: Nothing in Micah's religion was received or commanded; all of it came from inside his own household.
verseByVerse.examples: The writer's verdict is not that Israel chose wrong, but that everyone chose for himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And the man Micah had a shrine, and he made an ephod and household gods, and ordained one of his sons, who became his priest. In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything in this verse is homemade. The building is his own house of gods, not the tabernacle. The ephod is the priestly garment used for seeking God's guidance, and the exact thing Gideon made out of the Midianite gold, which became a snare to him and his household (8:27). The household gods are teraphim, the family figurines Rachel stole from Laban. And the priest is his own son, ordained by his own father, from the tribe of Ephraim.

The Hebrew for ordained is the technical term for installing a priest. Micah uses the correct word for something he has no right whatever to do. Not one item was received; the whole assembly is in his own front room, where he can get at it.

The sentence in verse 6 will be said again before the end (in full at 21:25, and in shorter form at 18:1 and 19:1), and it is the writer's verdict on everything from here to the last verse.

Take the two halves separately. There was no king in Israel: no central authority, no one to enforce the covenant, no one over the tribes. The book is arguing for a monarchy, and it is doing so honestly: what follows in these five chapters is what happens without one.

But the second half is the deeper diagnosis, because a king would not have cured it. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes: not what was wrong in his own eyes, but what was right. This is not a nation of people knowingly doing evil. It is a nation of people each of whom has become his own final authority on what is good, and every one of them is satisfied.

Micah is a case in point. He has restored stolen money, honoured his mother, built a place of worship, made provision for the LORD's service and installed a priest. If you asked him, he would tell you he was a religious man doing his best, and he would be sincere.

You met the phrase three chapters ago: She is right in my eyes (14:3). The writer has taken that private sentence from the deliverer's mouth and laid it over the whole nation. Samson was not the exception to his generation. He was the specimen.
verseByVerse.note: “Ordained” is literally “filled the hand of” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — A Priest for Ten Pieces a Year
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A wandering Levite hired as a father and a priest, and Micah's confident conclusion (vv. 7-13).
verseByVerse.theology: A Levite with no post meets a householder who wants a priest, and each gets what he wants.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 13 gives away what the whole apparatus is for.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a young man of Bethlehem in Judah, of the family of Judah, who was a Levite, and he sojourned there. And the man departed from the town of Bethlehem in Judah to sojourn where he could find a place. And as he journeyed, he came to the hill country of Ephraim to the house of Micah. And Micah said to him, "Where do you come from?" And he said to him, "I am a Levite of Bethlehem in Judah, and I am going to sojourn where I may find a place."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A Levite living in Bethlehem is the first thing wrong. The tribe of Levi had no territory of its own. That was deliberate: the LORD himself was to be their inheritance, and in place of land they were given forty-eight cities scattered through every other tribe, so that the whole nation would have men among them who knew the law and could teach it (Num. 18:20; Josh. 21). Bethlehem was not one of the forty-eight.

So this young man is away from his post before the story starts. His whole ambition is somewhere to land: walking north with no destination, he arrives at Micah's door because that is the door he happened to reach. Asked who he is, he leads with his qualification and, in the same sentence, his availability. Micah, whose priest at present is one of his own sons, is listening very carefully.

A Levite “of the family of Judah” was a Levite by descent who lived among Judah’s clans; Levites had no tribal land and lived in towns among the other tribes.

verseByVerse.quote: And Micah said to him, "Stay with me, and be to me a father and a priest, and I will give you ten pieces of silver a year and a suit of clothes and your living." And the Levite went in. And the Levite was content to dwell with the man, and the young man became to him like one of his sons. And Micah ordained the Levite, and the young man became his priest, and was in the house of Micah. Then Micah said, "Now I know that the LORD will prosper me, because I have a Levite as priest."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the offer, and the two halves of it do not belong in the same sentence.

Be to me a father is a title of respect for a spiritual guide, someone whose counsel you submit to. And then come the terms of employment: ten pieces of silver a year, one suit of clothes, and board.

A father cannot be hired. The moment a salary is attached, the man who is supposed to tell you the truth is the man whose keep depends on you, and everyone in the arrangement knows it. Micah wants the authority of a priest and the compliance of a servant, and he thinks the two can be bought together.

Eleven hundred for the images; ten a year for the priest. Micah's budget tells you what he thinks he is buying.

Content is the writer's word, and it is the most damning thing said about him.

He does not argue about the images. He does not ask whose shrine this is, or point out that a carved image in a private house in Ephraim is not what Levites were scattered through Israel to maintain. He belongs to the tribe set apart to teach the law of Moses, and he settles down.

Micah "filled his hand", the technical phrase again, and the Levite lets him. An Ephraimite householder has now installed a priest by his own authority, which belonged to nobody but God, and the priest so installed had every reason to know it and said nothing.

Verse 13 shows what all of it was for. Weigh the shape of the sentence. Now I know is certainty, at last. That the LORD will prosper me is the desired outcome. Because I have a Levite as priest is the lever, the thing that makes the outcome follow.

Micah has assembled a machine. Shrine, ephod, images, and now a genuine Levite to work the controls, and with that last component fitted he is confident of results. God has become the predictable output of a correctly configured system, and the system stands in his house where he can maintain it.

Everything in Micah's sentence is a true and good thing in itself. He has got the words right and the whole relationship upside down. The danger is a live one for anyone who takes religion seriously, in a way that open idolatry never is. The question is not whether a person believes the right things. It is whether he is using them. Do I read, pray, attend, give and serve because God is God, or because the practices are the mechanism by which I expect life to come out well? The second one feels like faith and behaves like machinery, and the tell is the word because. Now I know it will go well for me, because I have got the arrangement right. But God's favour was never a result to be secured. He gives it freely, through the priest he himself appointed, and the practices are his gifts for those already welcomed.

The next chapter is God's answer to Micah's sentence. Six hundred armed men will walk into his house, take the images, take the ephod, take the household gods and take the Levite, and leave him standing in the road with nothing. It turns out that a mechanism you can build is a mechanism somebody else can carry away.

Set beside Micah's Levite the priest nobody hires. No one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God. Christ did not exalt himself to be made a high priest; his Father appointed him (Heb. 5:4-5). He holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever, and therefore he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them (Heb. 7:24-25).

He cannot be bought for ten pieces of silver a year, and he cannot be taken off you by six hundred men.

18.title: The Danites Steal the Idol
18.text: <sup>1</sup>In those days there was no king in Israel. And in those days the tribe of the people of Dan was seeking for itself an inheritance to dwell in, for until then no inheritance among the tribes of Israel had fallen to them.<sup>2</sup>So the people of Dan sent five able men from the whole number of their tribe, from Zorah and from Eshtaol, to spy out the land and to explore it. And they said to them, "Go and explore the land." And they came to the hill country of Ephraim, to the house of Micah, and lodged there.<sup>3</sup>When they were by the house of Micah, they recognized the voice of the young Levite. And they turned aside and said to him, "Who brought you here? What are you doing in this place? What is your business here?"<sup>4</sup>And he said to them, "This is how Micah dealt with me: he has hired me, and I have become his priest."<sup>5</sup>And they said to him, "Inquire of God, please, that we may know whether the journey on which we are setting out will succeed."<sup>6</sup>And the priest said to them, "Go in peace. The journey on which you go is under the eye of the LORD."<sup>7</sup>Then the five men departed and came to Laish and saw the people who were there, how they lived in security, after the manner of the Sidonians, quiet and unsuspecting, lacking nothing that is in the earth and possessing wealth, and how they were far from the Sidonians and had no dealings with anyone.<sup>8</sup>And when they came to their brothers at Zorah and Eshtaol, their brothers said to them, "What do you report?"<sup>9</sup>They said, "Arise, and let us go up against them, for we have seen the land, and behold, it is very good. And will you do nothing? Do not be slow to go, to enter in and possess the land.<sup>10</sup>As soon as you go, you will come to an unsuspecting people. The land is spacious, for God has given it into your hands, a place where there is no lack of anything that is in the earth."<sup>11</sup>So 600 men of the tribe of Dan, armed with weapons of war, set out from Zorah and Eshtaol,<sup>12</sup>and went up and encamped at Kiriath-jearim in Judah. On this account that place is called Mahaneh-dan to this day; behold, it is west of Kiriath-jearim.<sup>13</sup>And they passed on from there to the hill country of Ephraim, and came to the house of Micah.<sup>14</sup>Then the five men who had gone to scout out the country of Laish said to their brothers, "Do you know that in these houses there are an ephod, household gods, a carved image, and a metal image? Now therefore consider what you will do."<sup>15</sup>And they turned aside there and came to the house of the young Levite, at the home of Micah, and asked him about his welfare.<sup>16</sup>Now the 600 men of the Danites, armed with their weapons of war, stood by the entrance of the gate.<sup>17</sup>And the five men who had gone to scout out the land went up and entered and took the carved image, the ephod, the household gods, and the metal image, while the priest stood by the entrance of the gate with the 600 men armed with weapons of war.<sup>18</sup>And when these went into Micah's house and took the carved image, the ephod, the household gods, and the metal image, the priest said to them, "What are you doing?"<sup>19</sup>And they said to him, "Keep quiet; put your hand on your mouth and come with us and be to us a father and a priest. Is it better for you to be priest to the house of one man, or to be priest to a tribe and clan in Israel?"<sup>20</sup>And the priest's heart was glad. He took the ephod and the household gods and the carved image and went along with the people.<sup>21</sup>So they turned and departed, putting the little ones and the livestock and the goods in front of them.<sup>22</sup>When they had gone a distance from the home of Micah, the men who were in the houses near Micah's house were called out, and they overtook the people of Dan.<sup>23</sup>And they shouted to the people of Dan, who turned around and said to Micah, "What is the matter with you, that you come with such a company?"<sup>24</sup>And he said, "You take my gods that I made and the priest, and go away, and what have I left? How then do you ask me, 'What is the matter with you?'"<sup>25</sup>And the people of Dan said to him, "Do not let your voice be heard among us, lest angry fellows fall upon you, and you lose your life with the lives of your household."<sup>26</sup>Then the people of Dan went their way. And when Micah saw that they were too strong for him, he turned and went back to his home.<sup>27</sup>But the people of Dan took what Micah had made, and the priest who belonged to him, and they came to Laish, to a people quiet and unsuspecting, and struck them with the edge of the sword and burned the city with fire.<sup>28</sup>And there was no deliverer because it was far from Sidon, and they had no dealings with anyone. It was in the valley that belongs to Beth-rehob. Then they rebuilt the city and lived in it.<sup>29</sup>And they named the city Dan, after the name of Dan their ancestor, who was born to Israel; but the name of the city was Laish at the first.<sup>30</sup>And the people of Dan set up the carved image for themselves, and Jonathan the son of Gershom, son of Moses, and his sons were priests to the tribe of the Danites until the day of the captivity of the land.<sup>31</sup>So they set up Micah's carved image that he made, as long as the house of God was at Shiloh.
18.overview:
The tribe of Dan, which never took the land God gave it, goes looking for somewhere easier. Five scouts lodge at Micah's house, get an instant blessing from his hired Levite, and find at Laish a peaceable town that cannot defend itself.

Six hundred armed men march north, strip Micah's shrine, and buy his priest with a bigger post. Micah is left asking what he has left. Laish, which had no deliverer, is put to the sword and renamed Dan, the stolen image is set up there, and the priest turns out to be Moses' own grandson. And all this while the house of God was at Shiloh.
18.theology:
A failure rewritten as a shortage. What Dan refused to fight for becomes, in their telling, what was never offered, and the rewritten history licenses the raid.

The hired oracle. The Levite fetches no ephod, waits for nothing and asks no one, and gives an answer that is soothing and cannot be tested. A man whose keep depends on his hearers will find over time that the word of the LORD agrees with them, and he will never experience it as dishonesty. That the journey then succeeds proves nothing about him.

Providence read backwards. The Danites call an easy target God's gift, and the reason for their confidence is that the victims will not see them coming. Ease is not the same as God's will, and the test is whether we would still call a thing God's will if it were hard or costly.

Gods that can be carried. A god you can make is a god stronger men can take from you. Micah's loss shows what he had really been trusting, and the prophets make the same point with something close to laughter.

The hired hand and the good shepherd. Content when he found a post and glad when a bigger one came, the Levite carries the stolen images out himself. Jesus drew the contrast: the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11). The Levite took a better living; the Shepherd gave his life.

Three generations from Sinai. The priest is Moses' own grandson, and the shrine he serves outlasts everyone in the chapter. Faithfulness is not inherited; it can be lost in a single lifetime, even in the best family in Israel.

And the house of God was at Shiloh. The real tabernacle stood in the same hill country the entire time, and nobody went, because the real thing was near, free, and impossible to manage. The New Testament carries this to its end. God's dwelling is now his Son, the temple raised on the third day (John 2:19-21), and the Father is worshipped neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem but in spirit and truth (John 4:21-24). He is nearer than Shiloh ever was, freely given, and no more open to management than the ark.
18.examples:
Then: A tribe that would not fight for the land God gave it marched north instead, chose a town for the sole reason that it could not defend itself, called that God's gift, robbed a private chapel on the way, bought the chaplain with a bigger job, and founded a shrine that lasted until the exile, all in the same hill country as the tabernacle.

Now: The chapter puts three questions to us. Am I calling something God's will because it is right, or because it is easy? If what I rely on were taken from me by force, what would I have left? And is there a substitute I prefer to the real thing, not because it is closer but because I can manage it? The genuine thing is nearer than Shiloh ever was: God has come to us in his Son, freely given to people who could never earn him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — A Tribe Looking for Somewhere Easier
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Dan looks for an inheritance; five scouts meet the Levite at Micah's house and get the answer they wanted (vv. 1-6).
verseByVerse.theology: Dan did have an inheritance (Josh. 19:40-48). The grievance in v. 1 is worded as though God had left them out.
verseByVerse.examples: The priest consults nothing, and puts the LORD's name on the answer his questioners came for.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days there was no king in Israel. And in those days the tribe of the people of Dan was seeking for itself an inheritance to dwell in, for until then no inheritance among the tribes of Israel had fallen to them. So the people of Dan sent five able men from the whole number of their tribe, from Zorah and from Eshtaol, to spy out the land and to explore it. And they said to them, "Go and explore the land." And they came to the hill country of Ephraim, to the house of Micah, and lodged there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The refrain again, and then a claim that is not quite true. Read on its own, it sounds as though Dan had been overlooked in the division of the land, as though the lot came round and there was nothing left for them.

Turn to Joshua 19. Dan was allotted a territory, and it is named town by town: Zorah, Eshtaol, Aijalon, Timnah, Ekron and more, out to the border over against Joppa: good country on the coastal plain, some of the best in the land. It fell to them exactly as the others did.

What happened is recorded in the first chapter of this book. The Amorites pressed the people of Dan back into the hill country, for they did not allow them to come down to the plain (1:34). They had the deed and never took possession. It was too hard, and the enemy was too settled, and they gave up and stayed in the hills.

So the grievance in verse 1 is a piece of careful editing. Not "we would not fight for what God gave us", but "nothing had fallen to us". The failure has been rewritten as a shortage, and the shortage justifies what they are about to do. People do the same with their own histories, and it is worth asking where we have done it.

Zorah and Eshtaol are Samson's two villages. He was born at Zorah, the Spirit first stirred him between them, and his brothers buried him between them two chapters ago (13:2, 13:25, 16:31). This scouting party sets out from the ground where God's deliverer for this tribe is lying in his father's tomb.

They are going the other way. Samson went down to the Philistine plain to begin taking what Dan had abandoned; his tribe now sends five men north, to look for somewhere easier.

verseByVerse.quote: When they were by the house of Micah, they recognized the voice of the young Levite. And they turned aside and said to him, "Who brought you here? What are you doing in this place? What is your business here?" And he said to them, "This is how Micah dealt with me: he has hired me, and I have become his priest." And they said to him, "Inquire of God, please, that we may know whether the journey on which we are setting out will succeed." And the priest said to them, "Go in peace. The journey on which you go is under the eye of the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They knew his voice. The Levite is from Bethlehem in Judah and they are men of Dan, and it may be that the moment he speaks they place him by his accent: a southern voice a long way north, in a private house in Ephraim. This book has already shown what an accent could do at a river crossing (12:6). Here it simply makes a stranger recognisable.

Their three questions are the right ones. A Levite belongs in one of the forty-eight cities given to his tribe, teaching the law. He is a long way from any of them and everyone can see it.

He answers with the terms of his employment, and hears nothing wrong in it. He has hired me is the whole account of his calling.

Having established that he is for hire, they ask him for an oracle. The request is polite and the theology behind it is old and good: before a campaign, ask God. Israel asked at the start of this very book (who shall go up first for us against the Canaanites?), and got an answer (1:1-2). Joshua's mistake with Gibeon came from not asking (Josh. 9:14).

He answers immediately, and he consults nothing. There is an ephod in the house, the very instrument used for enquiring of God, and he does not go and get it. He does not withdraw, or wait, or pray, or say he will have an answer in the morning. There is no pause of any kind between the question and the reply.

What he gives them is a blessing with no content. It is soothing, it is unfalsifiable, and it is precisely what five armed men on their way to look for a soft target wanted to hear.

That is what a hired oracle is for, and it is why the arrangement in chapter 17 was rotten from the first day. A man whose keep depends on the goodwill of his hearers will simply never find himself with anything uncomfortable to say.

Paul saw the same market and named it: the time is coming when people will not endure sound teaching, but having itching ears they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions (2 Tim. 4:3). Note who is doing the accumulating. The demand comes first; the supply always arrives.

The Danites will get a hundred miles up the country on the strength of that sentence, and it will turn out to have been true: the journey succeeds. That is the most sobering thing here. A false prophet's word coming true proves nothing at all. Moses had already said so: even if the sign comes to pass, if he leads you after other gods, do not listen (Deut. 13:1-3).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A soft target found at Laish, called God's gift, and six hundred men on the march (vv. 7-13).
verseByVerse.theology: The scouts choose by weakness, then use the language of faith.
verseByVerse.examples: Easy is not the same as right.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the five men departed and came to Laish and saw the people who were there, how they lived in security, after the manner of the Sidonians, quiet and unsuspecting, lacking nothing that is in the earth and possessing wealth, and how they were far from the Sidonians and had no dealings with anyone. And when they came to their brothers at Zorah and Eshtaol, their brothers said to them, "What do you report?" They said, "Arise, and let us go up against them, for we have seen the land, and behold, it is very good. And will you do nothing? Do not be slow to go, to enter in and possess the land. As soon as you go, you will come to an unsuspecting people. The land is spacious, for God has given it into your hands, a place where there is no lack of anything that is in the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every detail in that report is an assessment of how easy it would be. They live in security, with no defences worth the name. Quiet and unsuspecting means no watch and no expectation of attack. Lacking nothing... possessing wealth means worth taking. Far from the Sidonians means their nearest kin are too far off to come, and no dealings with anyone means no allies and nobody who owes them anything.

Not one word about whether the land was promised to Israel. Not one word about the people's wickedness, which is the ground on which Canaan was to be dispossessed (Gen. 15:16; Deut. 9:4-5). The five men have found a prosperous, peaceable, isolated town that cannot defend itself, and that is the entire case.

The speech is stirring, and every phrase in it is borrowed: the vocabulary of Caleb and Joshua at Kadesh, urging a frightened nation into the country God had sworn to their fathers (Num. 13:30; 14:7-9). It is the language of faith, used here to recruit a raiding party.

God has given it into your hands is the conquest formula. It is what the LORD said to Joshua about Jericho and Ai, and it means that God has determined an outcome and Israel is to act on his word. Here it is being used of a town nobody asked God about, chosen for the single reason that it could not fight back.

Weigh the sentence structure, because the two halves give the game away. You will come to an unsuspecting people, and then, in the very next breath, for God has given it into your hands. The reason for the confidence is stated first, and it is not God. It is that the victims will not see them coming.

This is the chapter's most religious sentence and there is nothing in it. Providence is being read backwards off an opportunity: the thing is easy, therefore God must intend it. Men have justified a great deal that way, and the test is simple enough: would you still call it God's will if it were hard, or costly, or if the people concerned could defend themselves?

verseByVerse.quote: So 600 men of the tribe of Dan, armed with weapons of war, set out from Zorah and Eshtaol, and went up and encamped at Kiriath-jearim in Judah. On this account that place is called Mahaneh-dan to this day; behold, it is west of Kiriath-jearim. And they passed on from there to the hill country of Ephraim, and came to the house of Micah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The writer counts them here and twice more (vv. 16, 17), because the number is the argument. Everything that happens from now on happens because six hundred men with weapons want it to.

Mahaneh-dan is where the Spirit of the LORD began to stir Samson (13:25). The writer names it here without comment, and the two uses could hardly be further apart: at the first, God moving on one man to begin saving Israel; at the second, six hundred of that man's own tribe camped on the road north, leaving the fight behind them.

They stop at Micah's house, which the five had told them about.
verseByVerse.note: “Mahaneh-dan” means “camp of Dan” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–20 — Is It Better to Serve One House or a Tribe?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The shrine stripped while the priest stands at the gate, and the priest bought with a bigger post (vv. 14-20).
verseByVerse.theology: A promotion offer works instantly on a man who was hired in the first place.
verseByVerse.examples: The words Micah used to hire him (17:10) are used to buy him away.
