verseByVerse.quote: Then the five men who had gone to scout out the country of Laish said to their brothers, "Do you know that in these houses there are an ephod, household gods, a carved image, and a metal image? Now therefore consider what you will do." And they turned aside there and came to the house of the young Levite, at the home of Micah, and asked him about his welfare. Now the 600 men of the Danites, armed with their weapons of war, stood by the entrance of the gate. And the five men who had gone to scout out the land went up and entered and took the carved image, the ephod, the household gods, and the metal image, while the priest stood by the entrance of the gate with the 600 men armed with weapons of war. And when these went into Micah's house and took the carved image, the ephod, the household gods, and the metal image, the priest said to them, "What are you doing?" And they said to him, "Keep quiet; put your hand on your mouth and come with us and be to us a father and a priest. Is it better for you to be priest to the house of one man, or to be priest to a tribe and clan in Israel?" And the priest's heart was glad. He took the ephod and the household gods and the carved image and went along with the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consider what you will do is as close as anyone comes to saying it out loud.

They do not propose a theft; they mention an inventory and leave a pause. Everyone understands perfectly. It is the way men arrange to do something they would rather not have anybody name.

Consider what they want: not the silver, not the livestock, not the house, but the religious equipment. A tribe on its way to take a city by surprise has decided it would like some gods to travel with.

They ask after the Levite's health while the army fills the doorway: a friendly conversation at the front, six hundred armed men at the gate, and the five scouts walking past both into the shrine.

The priest is not overpowered. He stands at the gate with the soldiers while his sanctuary is emptied behind him, and when he speaks it is a question rather than a refusal. The answer is a threat, and a promotion.

Put your hand on your mouth is not a request. Six hundred men are at the gate, and the instruction is to stop talking. And then, in the same breath, comes the offer, in Micah's exact words. Be to us a father and a priest; Micah had said be to me a father and a priest (17:10). The men stealing him know precisely what he was bought with.

The argument is put as a career question: is it better to be priest to one man's house, or to a whole tribe? Not whether it is right, or whose gods these are, only which is the bigger position. No hesitation is recorded. His heart is glad, and he picks up the stolen gods with his own hands and carries them out, so that the theft is completed by the clergyman.

He came looking for a place to sojourn (17:8) and was content when he found one (17:11). Now a better offer has arrived and he is glad. Every word the narrator gives him is about his own comfort, and not one is about God.

A man who takes a post for the living will leave it for a better living, and he will not regard the second move as a betrayal any more than he regarded the first as a compromise. The Lord drew the line exactly here: the hired hand is not the shepherd and the sheep are not his own, so when he sees the wolf coming he leaves them and runs, because he is a hired hand and cares nothing for the sheep (John 10:12-13).

Teraphim were household images used for divination and as tokens of family inheritance (Gen. 31:19; 1 Sam. 19:13). They were always on the wrong side of the law.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–26 — My Gods That I Made
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Micah pursues, says the truest thing in the story, and goes home empty (vv. 21-26).
verseByVerse.theology: Micah pleads for his gods and is threatened into silence.
verseByVerse.examples: His confidence of chapter 17 ends in a bare shelf.

verseByVerse.quote: So they turned and departed, putting the little ones and the livestock and the goods in front of them. When they had gone a distance from the home of Micah, the men who were in the houses near Micah's house were called out, and they overtook the people of Dan. And they shouted to the people of Dan, who turned around and said to Micah, "What is the matter with you, that you come with such a company?" And he said, "You take my gods that I made and the priest, and go away, and what have I left? How then do you ask me, 'What is the matter with you?'" And the people of Dan said to him, "Do not let your voice be heard among us, lest angry fellows fall upon you, and you lose your life with the lives of your household." Then the people of Dan went their way. And when Micah saw that they were too strong for him, he turned and went back to his home.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They put the vulnerable at the front, which is sound tactics: the pursuit will come from behind.

Micah and a handful of Ephraimite farmers have caught up with a war party, which asks him, mildly, with six hundred armed men behind the question, what he is making a fuss about.

My gods that I made: he says it in his own defence, in front of witnesses, and hears nothing wrong with it. "My gods" are possessions, listed like furniture. "That I made" is the manufacturer's claim, produced as proof of ownership.

He has just given the complete case against idolatry in five words, and he is using it as an argument.

The prophets go after this with something close to laughter. Isaiah watches Babylon's great gods loaded onto beasts of burden: Bel bows down, Nebo stoops... these things you carry are borne as burdens on weary beasts... they cannot save the burden (Isa. 46:1-2). The god has to be loaded onto an animal, and the animal is tired. And the psalm says what such gods are: silver and gold, the work of human hands, with mouths that do not speak and eyes that do not see: those who make them become like them (Ps. 115:4-8).

A god you can make is a god that can be taken away from you by men stronger than you. That is not a flaw in Micah's particular idols. It is the definition.

Then the rest of his sentence, which is the truest thing anybody says in these two chapters: and what have I left?

Nothing. He had assembled the entire apparatus and concluded, in so many words, now I know that the LORD will prosper me (17:13). The system was complete. And it walked up the road with somebody else.

Ask the question of anything you are relying on: if six hundred men came and took it, what would be left? Whatever answers that question is your actual god, and the point of the story is that Micah's could be carried.

The threat is put with a kind of courtesy, which makes it worse: not "we will kill you" but "there are men in this column with tempers, and you have a family".

Nothing more is said of Micah. He does not pray, or repent, or go to Shiloh, or do anything at all. He looks at the size of the column, works out that he cannot win, and walks back to a house with a bare shelf in it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–31 — Laish, and a Shrine That Lasted
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Laish destroyed and renamed, the image set up, the priest named, and the house of God at Shiloh all along (vv. 27-31).
verseByVerse.theology: The word in v. 28 for what Laish did not have is the book's own word for its deliverers (3:9, 15).
verseByVerse.examples: The last verse is the sharpest: the real thing was available, and nobody went near it.

verseByVerse.quote: But the people of Dan took what Micah had made, and the priest who belonged to him, and they came to Laish, to a people quiet and unsuspecting, and struck them with the edge of the sword and burned the city with fire. And there was no deliverer because it was far from Sidon, and they had no dealings with anyone. It was in the valley that belongs to Beth-rehob. Then they rebuilt the city and lived in it. And they named the city Dan, after the name of Dan their ancestor, who was born to Israel; but the name of the city was Laish at the first.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrator repeats the phrase from the scouting report, and the repetition is the judgment.

A people quiet and unsuspecting. In verse 7 that was a strategic assessment, the reason the town was chosen. Here it is set immediately beside struck them with the edge of the sword and burned the city with fire, so that we cannot miss what the assessment meant in practice.

Was this the conquest God had commanded? No. That war was against peoples whose wickedness had come to its full measure (Gen. 15:16), in the territory God allotted. Laish lay far outside Dan's allotment, was chosen for its weakness, and is told here as a sign of how far the age had fallen. Scripture records it without approving it.

A deliverer, a saviour, is what this whole book has been about. God raised up deliverers for Israel when they cried out: Othniel, Ehud, Shamgar, Deborah, Gideon, Jephthah. Samson was announced before his birth as the one who would begin to deliver.

Here, in the tribe of Samson's own account, the phrase turns up for the people on the other end of the sword. Laish had nobody. No ally near enough, no treaty, no rescuer, no one who would even hear about it. In a book about deliverance, the last conquest recorded is Israelites destroying a town that had no deliverer.

They put their own name on it, and the name lasts. From Dan to Beersheba becomes the standard phrase for the whole length of Israel, north to south, for the rest of the Old Testament, and the northern end of it is this town, taken from a peaceable people by a tribe that would not fight for the land God actually gave it.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Dan set up the carved image for themselves, and Jonathan the son of Gershom, son of Moses, and his sons were priests to the tribe of the Danites until the day of the captivity of the land. So they set up Micah's carved image that he made, as long as the house of God was at Shiloh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Levite gets a name at last, and it is the last name anyone expected.

Jonathan, son of Gershom, son of Moses. Gershom was Moses' firstborn, named for a man who was a sojourner in a foreign land (Ex. 2:22), and the grandson has spent this whole story sojourning wherever he could find a place.

The young man hired to tend a private idol is Moses' own grandson.

Ancient scribes tried to spare the lawgiver's name from this verse with a suspended letter (see the note below). The ESV prints Moses; the KJV and NKJV follow the scribes' mark and print Manasseh. Men who loved the Scriptures found this sentence hard enough to want to soften it, and yet they kept the true letters on the page.

Sinai to a shrine in Dan in three generations. That is how fast it can go, and it went that fast in the best family in Israel.

The name also tells us when this happened. If the line is complete, a grandson of Moses was a young man early in the time of the judges, so these closing chapters are probably not the last events in the book but an appendix from its first generations, placed at the end to show what the whole age was like.

Until the day of the captivity of the land. The shrine is not a passing episode. Most likely it runs for centuries, all the way to the Assyrian deportation of the north (2 Kings 15:29), though some take the captivity as the loss of the ark in Eli's day (1 Sam. 4), which would fit the Shiloh line that follows. And when the kingdom divides, Jeroboam will put one of his two golden calves at Dan and tell Israel behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt (1 Kings 12:28-30), on ground that had been consecrated to this business long before he got there.

A carved image made from a mother's dedicated silver, in a private house in Ephraim, ends up as the northern shrine of a whole kingdom's apostasy.

With the last line the writer quietly condemns everybody in the chapter. The tabernacle, the real one, with the ark and the mercy seat and the appointed priesthood, was standing at Shiloh the entire time. It was in the hill country of Ephraim, the same hills as Micah's house. The five spies and the six hundred passed through that country. The Levite had lived in its shadow.

Nobody went. Nobody in two chapters, not the mother, not Micah, not the Danites, not Moses' grandson, made the journey to the place where God had said he would meet with his people.

It was not ignorance. Shiloh was where the nation assembled; everyone knew what was there. They preferred a shrine they could carry, a priest they could pay, and an oracle that agreed with them. The genuine thing was near, and free, and unavailable to be managed, and that last quality is why they left it alone.

That is the whole indictment: two chapters of religion, expensive and busy and constantly invoking the name of the LORD, conducted in the same hill country as the place where God actually was.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes the alternative “Manasseh”: Hebrew scribes raised one letter above the line so the name could be read that way, probably to protect Moses’ name.

19.title: The Levite's Concubine
19.text: <sup>1</sup>In those days, when there was no king in Israel, a certain Levite was sojourning in the remote parts of the hill country of Ephraim, who took to himself a concubine from Bethlehem in Judah.<sup>2</sup>And his concubine was unfaithful to him, and she went away from him to her father's house at Bethlehem in Judah, and was there some four months.<sup>3</sup>Then her husband arose and went after her, to speak kindly to her and bring her back. He had with him his servant and a couple of donkeys. And she brought him into her father's house. And when the girl's father saw him, he came with joy to meet him.<sup>4</sup>And his father-in-law, the girl's father, made him stay, and he remained with him three days. So they ate and drank and spent the night there.<sup>5</sup>And on the fourth day they arose early in the morning, and he prepared to go, but the girl's father said to his son-in-law, "Strengthen your heart with a morsel of bread, and after that you may go."<sup>6</sup>So the two of them sat and ate and drank together. And the girl's father said to the man, "Be pleased to spend the night, and let your heart be merry."<sup>7</sup>And when the man rose up to go, his father-in-law pressed him, till he spent the night there again.<sup>8</sup>And on the fifth day he arose early in the morning to depart. And the girl's father said, "Strengthen your heart and wait until the day declines." So they ate, both of them.<sup>9</sup>And when the man and his concubine and his servant rose up to depart, his father-in-law, the girl's father, said to him, "Behold, now the day has waned toward evening. Please, spend the night. Behold, the day draws to its close. Lodge here and let your heart be merry, and tomorrow you shall arise early in the morning for your journey, and go home."<sup>10</sup>But the man would not spend the night. He rose up and departed and arrived opposite Jebus (that is, Jerusalem). He had with him a couple of saddled donkeys, and his concubine was with him.<sup>11</sup>When they were near Jebus, the day was nearly over, and the servant said to his master, "Come now, let us turn aside to this city of the Jebusites and spend the night in it."<sup>12</sup>And his master said to him, "We will not turn aside into the city of foreigners, who do not belong to the people of Israel, but we will pass on to Gibeah."<sup>13</sup>And he said to his young man, "Come and let us draw near to one of these places and spend the night at Gibeah or at Ramah."<sup>14</sup>So they passed on and went their way. And the sun went down on them near Gibeah, which belongs to Benjamin,<sup>15</sup>and they turned aside there, to go in and spend the night at Gibeah. And he went in and sat down in the open square of the city, for no one took them into his house to spend the night.<sup>16</sup>And behold, an old man was coming from his work in the field at evening. The man was from the hill country of Ephraim, and he was sojourning in Gibeah. The men of the place were Benjaminites.<sup>17</sup>And he lifted up his eyes and saw the traveler in the open square of the city. And the old man said, "Where are you going? And where do you come from?"<sup>18</sup>And he said to him, "We are passing from Bethlehem in Judah to the remote parts of the hill country of Ephraim, from which I come. I went to Bethlehem in Judah, and I am going to the house of the LORD, but no one has taken me into his house.<sup>19</sup>We have straw and feed for our donkeys, with bread and wine for me and your female servant and the young man with your servants. There is no lack of anything."<sup>20</sup>And the old man said, "Peace be to you; I will care for all your wants. Only, do not spend the night in the square."<sup>21</sup>So he brought him into his house and gave the donkeys feed. And they washed their feet, and ate and drank.<sup>22</sup>As they were making their hearts merry, behold, the men of the city, worthless fellows, surrounded the house, beating on the door. And they said to the old man, the master of the house, "Bring out the man who came into your house, that we may know him."<sup>23</sup>And the man, the master of the house, went out to them and said to them, "No, my brothers, do not act so wickedly; since this man has come into my house, do not do this vile thing.<sup>24</sup>Behold, here are my virgin daughter and his concubine. Let me bring them out now. Violate them and do with them what seems good to you, but against this man do not do this outrageous thing."<sup>25</sup>But the men would not listen to him. So the man seized his concubine and made her go out to them. And they knew her and abused her all night until the morning. And as the dawn began to break, they let her go.<sup>26</sup>And as morning appeared, the woman came and fell down at the door of the man's house where her master was, until it was light.<sup>27</sup>And her master rose up in the morning, and when he opened the doors of the house and went out to go on his way, behold, there was his concubine lying at the door of the house, with her hands on the threshold.<sup>28</sup>He said to her, "Get up, let us be going." But there was no answer. Then he put her on the donkey, and the man rose up and went away to his home.<sup>29</sup>And when he entered his house, he took a knife, and taking hold of his concubine he divided her, limb by limb, into twelve pieces, and sent her throughout all the territory of Israel.<sup>30</sup>And all who saw it said, "Such a thing has never happened or been seen from the day that the people of Israel came up out of the land of Egypt until this day; consider it, take counsel, and speak."
19.overview:
This is one of the darkest chapters in Scripture, and it is told so that it will not be forgotten. A Levite goes to Bethlehem to win back the concubine who has left him, and her father's hospitality keeps them until too late in the day. Refusing to lodge in a Canaanite town, the Levite presses on to Gibeah of Benjamin, where nobody takes them in except an old man who is not from there.

In the night the men of the town surround the house, as the men of Sodom did, and there is no angel to rescue anyone. The Levite puts his concubine out of the door to save himself, and in the morning she lies dead with her hands on the threshold. He sends her body through Israel in twelve pieces, and the nation is told: consider it, take counsel, and speak.
19.theology:
Gibeah has become Sodom. The parallel with Genesis 19 is exact and deliberate: Israel has become the city God destroyed, and this time there is no rescue.

The label is not the safeguard. Membership of God's people has never in itself made a community safe. The Levite trusted the name "Israelite" and was wrong about his own side.

Where "right in his own eyes" ends. Every person in the chapter had a reason, and not one of them thought he was the villain. The book's refrain, followed all the way down, ends not in a homemade shrine but in a body on a doorstep.

She is unnamed here, but not with God. Scripture does not explain this away and does not leave it out. Nothing done to her in the dark was dark to him (Ps. 139:11-12).

The sentence that was never kept, and the one that was. The Levite came to speak to her heart and handed her over to save himself. Christ came to a people who had left him and, when the mob was at the door, gave himself up so that his own would go free.
19.examples:
Then: A woman was refused shelter by a whole Israelite town, offered to a mob by the man who had taken her in, pushed through the door by the man who had come to win her back, abused until dawn, and found dead on the threshold by a husband whose first words were an instruction to hurry.

Now: The chapter ends with a command rather than a moral, consider it, take counsel, and speak, and the command still stands. Reasonable men, each doing what looked right to him, produced this between them; and God put it in his book, so that she would not be forgotten. That is part of the answer to anyone who has wondered whether he was watching. If you have suffered sexual violence, hear this plainly: what was done to her was evil, it was not her fault, and God’s own law counts a woman forced in this way innocent and her attacker as a murderer (Deuteronomy 22:25–27). Abuse is never to be tolerated or hidden. If you are in danger, seek safety at once, tell someone you trust and the police, and let your church’s elders help you. The God who wrote her down has not forgotten you.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A concubine leaves, a Levite goes after her, and her father's welcome will not let him go (vv. 1-9).
verseByVerse.theology: The narrator slows the story almost to a stop, and every delay matters.
verseByVerse.examples: Bethlehem's warmth will be set against Gibeah's coldness.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days, when there was no king in Israel, a certain Levite was sojourning in the remote parts of the hill country of Ephraim, who took to himself a concubine from Bethlehem in Judah. And his concubine was unfaithful to him, and she went away from him to her father's house at Bethlehem in Judah, and was there some four months. Then her husband arose and went after her, to speak kindly to her and bring her back. He had with him his servant and a couple of donkeys. And she brought him into her father's house. And when the girl's father saw him, he came with joy to meet him. And his father-in-law, the girl's father, made him stay, and he remained with him three days. So they ate and drank and spent the night there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is another Levite, and again the hill country of Ephraim and Bethlehem in Judah, the same two places as chapter 17, and again the word sojourning: a man of the priestly tribe living wherever he happens to have settled.

A concubine was a wife of the second rank: joined to a man, bound to him, with a wife's duties and very little of a wife's standing or protection. She is his, and she has almost no claim on him.

Does Scripture approve of concubines? It records the custom, as it records polygamy, without commending it, and the stories in which it appears are nearly all stories of grief. God’s pattern from the beginning is one man and one woman (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4–6).

There is a real difficulty in verse 2. The Hebrew word means she was unfaithful. The ancient Greek translation (followed by the ESV's footnote, "became angry with him"), probably made from a Hebrew text older than our oldest complete manuscripts, says she was angry with him and left. And the behaviour recorded fits the second better than the first: a woman who had committed adultery could expect no shelter in her father's house, and this father receives his son-in-law with open delight, which is not how a man greets the husband of a daughter who has disgraced him.

Beyond that we do not know, and the narrator does not tell us because he is not interested in grading her. She will not speak a single word in this chapter. Everything that happens to her is done by men, and every judgment passed on her is passed by men, and the writer declines to add his own.

He went, literally, "to speak to her heart", the phrase used of a man wooing, of comfort spoken to the grieving, of God himself promising to bring Israel into the wilderness and speak tenderly to her (Hos. 2:14). It is the best sentence anybody says about this man.

Hold on to it, because before this chapter ends he will push her through a door into the hands of a mob. She brought him into her father's house: whatever the trouble was, she is the one who opens the door to him. The father is delighted, and the narrator deliberately lets the scene feel safe.

verseByVerse.quote: And on the fourth day they arose early in the morning, and he prepared to go, but the girl's father said to his son-in-law, "Strengthen your heart with a morsel of bread, and after that you may go." So the two of them sat and ate and drank together. And the girl's father said to the man, "Be pleased to spend the night, and let your heart be merry." And when the man rose up to go, his father-in-law pressed him, till he spent the night there again. And on the fifth day he arose early in the morning to depart. And the girl's father said, "Strengthen your heart and wait until the day declines." So they ate, both of them. And when the man and his concubine and his servant rose up to depart, his father-in-law, the girl's father, said to him, "Behold, now the day has waned toward evening. Please, spend the night. Behold, the day draws to its close. Lodge here and let your heart be merry, and tomorrow you shall arise early in the morning for your journey, and go home."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The delays pile up. On the fourth day the father presses a morsel of bread on him, and the bread becomes a meal and the meal another night. On the fifth day he does it a third time, and then a fourth (v. 9), which is nearly a plea: the old man is running out of arguments and points to the lengthening shadows. Look how late it is; one more night, and go at dawn.

Why does the writer spend five verses on this? He never wastes words (he tells the whole story of the judge Shamgar in one verse, 3:31), and here he gives us four separate rounds of a man being persuaded to stay for another meal. There are two reasons.

The first is that this hospitality is what puts them on the road at the wrong hour. They leave on the afternoon of the fifth day, with nowhere near enough light to reach home, and everything that follows happens because they are looking for a bed after dark. The kindest man in the story sets the trap without meaning to.

The second is contrast. Bethlehem, in Judah, cannot stop feeding a stranger. Gibeah, in Benjamin, will not take him in at all. The writer is measuring one Israelite town against another, and he wants us to have five verses of open-handed generosity in mind when the Levite sits down in an empty square with nobody looking at him.

One more thing before they leave. Count the speeches in this passage: the father, the father, the father, the father. She has been the subject of the entire journey and has not said a word.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–15 — We Will Not Turn Aside Into the City of Foreigners
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Levite passes by Canaanite Jebus for Israelite Gibeah, and in Gibeah nobody opens a door (vv. 10-15).
verseByVerse.theology: The decision that leads to her death is made for the sake of safety.
verseByVerse.examples: Gibeah has told us what it is before the horror begins.

verseByVerse.quote: But the man would not spend the night. He rose up and departed and arrived opposite Jebus (that is, Jerusalem). He had with him a couple of saddled donkeys, and his concubine was with him. When they were near Jebus, the day was nearly over, and the servant said to his master, "Come now, let us turn aside to this city of the Jebusites and spend the night in it." And his master said to him, "We will not turn aside into the city of foreigners, who do not belong to the people of Israel, but we will pass on to Gibeah." And he said to his young man, "Come and let us draw near to one of these places and spend the night at Gibeah or at Ramah." So they passed on and went their way. And the sun went down on them near Gibeah, which belongs to Benjamin, and they turned aside there, to go in and spend the night at Gibeah. And he went in and sat down in the open square of the city, for no one took them into his house to spend the night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They get about six miles before the light starts to go.

Jebus is Jerusalem, and it is not yet Israelite. Benjamin had been given it and had not driven out the Jebusites who lived there (1:21); it will not belong to Israel until David takes it, centuries later. Tonight it is a Canaanite town on the road north.

The servant, who has no standing at all in this story, gives the only piece of good advice anybody offers. The Levite's refusal is the decision that leads to her death, and there is nothing stupid in it. He will not put his household in a pagan city overnight. These people are not God’s covenant people; they do not fear the God of Israel; who knows what a Canaanite town does to travellers after dark. Better to press on a few more miles to Gibeah, where the men are Benjaminites, sons of Jacob, circumcised, under the law of Moses.

Nothing in the chapter is more sensible. It is spoken by a Levite, a man trained to know the difference between the holy and the common. And it is wrong in every particular, because the Israelite town turns out to be the one where they meet the mob.

This needs saying carefully and not as a slogan: belonging outwardly to God’s covenant people does not guarantee how anyone will behave. Being God’s people by name has never, in itself, made a community safe; and a town can be full of the circumcised and be Sodom by nightfall. The Levite made the mistake of assuming that the label secured the behaviour, and he made it about his own side.

The sunset is reported as a plain fact, and it falls on the story like a sentence of judgment. Then nobody opens a door. Hospitality to a traveller was not a nicety; it was close to a sacred duty, and a stranger sitting in the open square at nightfall was a standing accusation against the whole town. Abraham ran to meet three strangers and pressed food on them. This man is a Levite, of the priestly tribe, plainly not a threat, travelling with a woman and a servant and two donkeys, and Gibeah looks at him and goes indoors.

The horror of this chapter has not begun yet, and the town has already told us what it is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–21 — The Only Man Who Offers a Bed Is Not From There
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: An old man from Ephraim, sojourning in Gibeah, takes the travellers in (vv. 16-21).
verseByVerse.theology: A stranger in the town does what the town would not.
verseByVerse.examples: He knows what his neighbours are, and the rest of the chapter shows that knowing was not enough.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, an old man was coming from his work in the field at evening. The man was from the hill country of Ephraim, and he was sojourning in Gibeah. The men of the place were Benjaminites. And he lifted up his eyes and saw the traveler in the open square of the city. And the old man said, "Where are you going? And where do you come from?" And he said to him, "We are passing from Bethlehem in Judah to the remote parts of the hill country of Ephraim, from which I come. I went to Bethlehem in Judah, and I am going to the house of the LORD, but no one has taken me into his house. We have straw and feed for our donkeys, with bread and wine for me and your female servant and the young man with your servants. There is no lack of anything." And the old man said, "Peace be to you; I will care for all your wants. Only, do not spend the night in the square." So he brought him into his house and gave the donkeys feed. And they washed their feet, and ate and drank.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrator has put two sentences side by side on purpose: the old man was from Ephraim, and the men of the place were Benjaminites. The only person in the town who behaves like an Israelite is not from the town. He is an outsider, living there, coming in tired from a day's work in somebody else's fields, and he is the one who notices a stranger in the square when every householder in Gibeah has managed not to.

He lifted up his eyes and saw him; that is all it took. The Levite mentions the house of the LORD, and it does him no good. The Greek translation reads my house here, which may be the original. Whether he means the sanctuary at Shiloh or his own home, he is identifying himself as a man in God's service. And he ends the sentence with the complaint that matters: no one has taken me into his house. He is not asking. He is stating the fact and letting it stand.

He is careful to say he is not begging: they have their own fodder, bread and wine, enough for all of them. He needs only a roof.

The old man's last clause matters most. He does not say "you would be more comfortable indoors". He says: whatever happens, do not sleep out there. He has lived in Gibeah long enough to know exactly what is on those streets after dark, and he gets three travellers off them as fast as he can.

He is right about the danger and wrong about the safety of his house, and by morning both will be clear.

Feed for the animals, water for their feet, food and wine. Every duty of a host, done properly, by an outsider, in a town that would not do any of it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sodom in Israel: the mob, the host's offer, and the Levite's own hand on the door (vv. 22-26).
verseByVerse.theology: Every element of the scene matches Sodom (Gen. 19:4-8), except the rescue.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 25 must be read exactly as it stands: it says who opened the door.

verseByVerse.quote: As they were making their hearts merry, behold, the men of the city, worthless fellows, surrounded the house, beating on the door. And they said to the old man, the master of the house, "Bring out the man who came into your house, that we may know him." And the man, the master of the house, went out to them and said to them, "No, my brothers, do not act so wickedly; since this man has come into my house, do not do this vile thing. Behold, here are my virgin daughter and his concubine. Let me bring them out now. Violate them and do with them what seems good to you, but against this man do not do this outrageous thing."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Making their hearts merry is the same phrase as at Bethlehem, and this time it is the last quiet moment.

The men are called worthless fellows, literally sons of Belial, sons of worthlessness. The English is the same as for the gang Abimelech hired and the crew that gathered around Jephthah in Tob (9:4; 11:3), though the Hebrew here is harsher. And chapter 20 will show that the city stood behind them.

You have read the mob’s demand before, almost word for word. Two visitors come to Lot in Sodom, and before they lie down the men of the city surround the house and call out: where are the men who came to you tonight? Bring them out to us, that we may know them (Gen. 19:4-5).

The writer is laying one scene on top of the other, and every element will match: the mob at the door, the demand for the guest, the host going out to them, the address my brothers, the plea not to do this wicked thing, and the daughters offered in the guest's place.

One thing in Genesis is not here. In Sodom, the angels reached out, pulled Lot back inside, and struck the men at the door with blindness (Gen. 19:10-11). There is no angel in this house.

The old man goes out to them, which takes courage, and he calls them my brothers.

His argument is the right one as far as it goes: this man is under my roof, and what you are proposing is wickedness and outrage. He knows right from wrong, and he names the thing correctly.

Then he says the unspeakable thing. He offers them his own daughter. He offers them his guest's wife. He tells a mob it may rape two women and do with them what seems good to you, and he does it in the same breath in which he is defending the honour of the household.

Lot did this too (Gen. 19:8), and it was monstrous there as well. Scripture reports it; it does not commend it. There is a way of reading these stories that treats the host as the hero because his intention was to protect a guest, and it will not do. Two women are being offered to a rape gang by the man responsible for them, and no calculation about ancient hospitality makes that anything other than what it plainly is.

Hear the phrase he uses, though. Do with them what seems good to you is, in Hebrew, "what is good in your eyes", a near echo of the sentence stamped across these last five chapters, “Everyone did what was right in his own eyes” (17:6; 21:25), spoken here to a mob about two women, by a decent man, as the best solution he can think of.

“That we may know him” is sexual, as verse 25 shows. The men of Gibeah demanded the gang rape of a guest, as Sodom did (Gen 19:5). It is violent, humiliating evil, and it shows how far Israel had become like Canaan. Scripture’s teaching on same-sex relations rests on wider texts (Lev 18:22; Rom 1:26–27), not on this scene alone.
verseByVerse.note: The scene deliberately echoes Sodom: Israel has become like Canaan.

verseByVerse.quote: But the men would not listen to him. So the man seized his concubine and made her go out to them. And they knew her and abused her all night until the morning. And as the dawn began to break, they let her go. And as morning appeared, the woman came and fell down at the door of the man's house where her master was, until it was light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man here is not the old host. The host's offer was refused; the mob would not listen to him. What follows is done by the Levite. He seized his own concubine, and he made her go out.

Every word in that sentence is against him. Seized: she did not go willingly. His concubine: his own, the woman he had travelled all that way to fetch home, to speak to her heart. Made her go out: he opened the door and put her through it, and then it was shut behind her.

He did it to save himself. There is no other reading available: the mob had asked for him, and he sent her out in his place. And when the tribes assemble in the next chapter and he tells the story, he will describe the night at some length and leave this detail out entirely (20:5).

It went on all night: not a moment of violence but hours of it, by a crowd, until the sky began to lighten and they had finished. Then they let her go, as one might release something no longer of use.

Inside the house a man slept.

The most terrible detail in the chapter is that she got back to the door. However far they had taken her, and in whatever state they left her, she crossed Gibeah in the half-dark and reached the house, and got as far as the door, and fell there.

The word for the man inside is her master. The narrator does not call him her husband here.

She could not open it, or nobody heard her, or nobody came. She lay against it until it was light.

Nothing in Scripture asks us to explain this away, and there is no explanation. What Scripture does is refuse to leave it out. This account is in the word of God because God would not have it forgotten, and the men who did it and the man who opened the door have not been allowed the last word on that night. What they did has been read, by strangers, in many languages, for millennia.

She has no name in the book. She has one with God, who keeps count of tossings and puts tears in his bottle and writes them in his book (Ps. 56:8), and who has never yet mislaid a single person that the world discarded.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–30 — Consider It, Take Counsel, and Speak
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The morning on the threshold, the twelve pieces, and a command to the nation (vv. 27-30).
verseByVerse.theology: The morning brings no grief from the Levite, only haste.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter ends by handing the reader an assignment rather than a conclusion.

verseByVerse.quote: And her master rose up in the morning, and when he opened the doors of the house and went out to go on his way, behold, there was his concubine lying at the door of the house, with her hands on the threshold. He said to her, "Get up, let us be going." But there was no answer. Then he put her on the donkey, and the man rose up and went away to his home.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three ordinary clauses, and every one of them is an accusation. He slept. He got up in the morning. And he was leaving: the sentence tells us his intention before it tells us what he found, which means he had not been out to look for her.

With her hands on the threshold.

She had reached the door of the house where he was and put her hands on the step, and that is where she stopped. The last thing she did was try to get in.

Get up, let us be going are the worst words in the chapter. No cry. No kneeling beside her. No question about who did this, no rage, no grief, not one syllable of tenderness from the man who had come to speak to her heart. He looks at what is lying across his doorstep and tells it to get up because he wants to leave.

But there was no answer.

That is how we learn she is dead. Not from a physician, not from a lament, not from the writer telling us plainly, but from a silence where a reply should have been. She never spoke in this chapter, and the moment we notice it is the moment she cannot.

Then he loads her onto the donkey like the rest of the baggage and goes home. The verse gives her the same treatment the animals get.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he entered his house, he took a knife, and taking hold of his concubine he divided her, limb by limb, into twelve pieces, and sent her throughout all the territory of Israel. And all who saw it said, "Such a thing has never happened or been seen from the day that the people of Israel came up out of the land of Egypt until this day; consider it, take counsel, and speak."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He butchers her in his own house. The language is the language of the altar: taking hold of the body, dividing it limb by limb, into pieces. It is what you do to a sacrificial animal, and he does it to a woman on his floor, and there is no indication that it occurred to him to bury her.

Twelve pieces, for twelve tribes. It is not madness; it is a calculated summons, and it works. Generations later Saul, a Benjaminite from this same Gibeah, will send a yoke of oxen through Israel cut into pieces to muster the nation against the Ammonites (1 Sam. 11:7), and the echo of this night is probably part of the message. Everyone knew what the twelve pieces meant.

Yet look at what he has done, in order to get the tribes to act about a woman's murder. He has mutilated her body. His response to what was done to her is one more thing done to her.

When he explains it all in chapter 20, he will not mention that he was the one who put her out of the door (20:5).

Consider it, take counsel, and speak. Three commands. Set your heart on this thing; talk it over; say something. The narrator will not tell us what to think. He puts the pieces on the table and hands us the assignment, and that is the most uncomfortable thing he could have done.

So consider it. Every person in this chapter had a reason. The father-in-law was being generous. The Levite was avoiding a pagan town for the sake of safety, and later he was saving his own life. The old man was protecting a guest under his roof, which was a sacred obligation. The men of Gibeah were doing what seemed good to them. Not one of them thought of himself as the villain of the story, and between them they left a woman dead on a doorstep with her hands on the step.

That is what everyone did what was right in his own eyes comes to when it is followed all the way down. It does not stop at a private shrine and a hired priest. It ends here.

Now consider one thing more, because the chapter has one good sentence in it, a promise the Levite did not keep.

A man came from a far country to a woman who had left him, to speak to her heart and bring her home. That is how it starts, and it is a beautiful sentence, and he betrayed it before the week was out. When the mob was at the door he handed her over and saved himself.

Another came from further, to a people who had left him, to speak to their hearts and bring them home. And when the mob was at the door, he did not put anybody through it. If you seek me, let these men go: he said it in the garden, with the torches on his face, and John notes that he said it so that the word he had spoken would be fulfilled: of those whom you gave me I have lost not one (John 18:8-9).

The Levite went out of the door in the morning and found her on the step. Christ went out in the night to meet the armed crowd himself, and stood between it and his own.

No one who comes to that door and lays a hand on the threshold will ever be told to get up and be going. Whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37).

20.title: Civil War Against Benjamin
20.text: <sup>1</sup>Then all the people of Israel came out, from Dan to Beersheba, including the land of Gilead, and the congregation assembled as one man to the LORD at Mizpah.<sup>2</sup>And the chiefs of all the people, of all the tribes of Israel, presented themselves in the assembly of the people of God, 400,000 men on foot that drew the sword.<sup>3</sup>(Now the people of Benjamin heard that the people of Israel had gone up to Mizpah.) And the people of Israel said, "Tell us, how did this evil happen?"<sup>4</sup>And the Levite, the husband of the woman who was murdered, answered and said, "I came to Gibeah that belongs to Benjamin, I and my concubine, to spend the night.<sup>5</sup>And the leaders of Gibeah rose against me and surrounded the house against me by night. They meant to kill me, and they violated my concubine, and she is dead.<sup>6</sup>So I took hold of my concubine and cut her in pieces and sent her throughout all the country of the inheritance of Israel, for they have committed abomination and outrage in Israel.<sup>7</sup>Behold, you people of Israel, all of you, give your advice and counsel here."<sup>8</sup>And all the people arose as one man, saying, "None of us will go to his tent, and none of us will return to his house.<sup>9</sup>But now this is what we will do to Gibeah: we will go up against it by lot,<sup>10</sup>and we will take ten men of a hundred throughout all the tribes of Israel, and a hundred of a thousand, and a thousand of ten thousand, to bring provisions for the people, that when they come they may repay Gibeah of Benjamin for all the outrage that they have committed in Israel."<sup>11</sup>So all the men of Israel gathered against the city, united as one man.<sup>12</sup>And the tribes of Israel sent men through all the tribe of Benjamin, saying, "What evil is this that has taken place among you?<sup>13</sup>Now therefore give up the men, the worthless fellows in Gibeah, that we may put them to death and purge evil from Israel." But the Benjaminites would not listen to the voice of their brothers, the people of Israel.<sup>14</sup>Then the people of Benjamin came together out of the cities to Gibeah to go out to battle against the people of Israel.<sup>15</sup>And the people of Benjamin mustered out of their cities on that day 26,000 men who drew the sword, besides the inhabitants of Gibeah, who mustered 700 chosen men.<sup>16</sup>Among all these were 700 chosen men who were left-handed; every one could sling a stone at a hair and not miss.<sup>17</sup>And the men of Israel, apart from Benjamin, mustered 400,000 men who drew the sword; all these were men of war.<sup>18</sup>The people of Israel arose and went up to Bethel and inquired of God, "Who shall go up first for us to fight against the people of Benjamin?" And the LORD said, "Judah shall go up first."<sup>19</sup>Then the people of Israel rose in the morning and encamped against Gibeah.<sup>20</sup>And the men of Israel went out to fight against Benjamin, and the men of Israel drew up the battle line against them at Gibeah.<sup>21</sup>The people of Benjamin came out of Gibeah and destroyed on that day 22,000 men of the Israelites.<sup>22</sup>But the people, the men of Israel, took courage, and again formed the battle line in the same place where they had formed it on the first day.<sup>23</sup>And the people of Israel went up and wept before the LORD until the evening. And they inquired of the LORD, "Shall we again draw near to fight against our brothers, the people of Benjamin?" And the LORD said, "Go up against them."<sup>24</sup>So the people of Israel came near against the people of Benjamin the second day.<sup>25</sup>And Benjamin went against them out of Gibeah the second day, and destroyed 18,000 men of the people of Israel. All these were men who drew the sword.<sup>26</sup>Then all the people of Israel, the whole army, went up and came to Bethel and wept. They sat there before the LORD and fasted that day until evening, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the LORD.<sup>27</sup>And the people of Israel inquired of the LORD (for the ark of the covenant of God was there in those days,<sup>28</sup>and Phinehas the son of Eleazar, son of Aaron, ministered before it in those days), saying, "Shall we go out once more to battle against our brothers, the people of Benjamin, or shall we cease?" And the LORD said, "Go up, for tomorrow I will give them into your hand."<sup>29</sup>So Israel set men in ambush around Gibeah.<sup>30</sup>And the people of Israel went up against the people of Benjamin on the third day and set themselves in array against Gibeah, as at other times.<sup>31</sup>And the people of Benjamin went out against the people and were drawn away from the city. And as at other times they began to strike and kill some of the people in the highways, one of which goes up to Bethel and the other to Gibeah, and in the open country, about thirty men of Israel.<sup>32</sup>And the people of Benjamin said, "They are routed before us, as at the first." But the people of Israel said, "Let us flee and draw them away from the city to the highways."<sup>33</sup>And all the men of Israel rose up out of their place and set themselves in array at Baal-tamar, and the men of Israel who were in ambush rushed out of their place from Maareh-geba.<sup>34</sup>And there came against Gibeah 10,000 chosen men out of all Israel, and the battle was hard, but the Benjaminites did not know that disaster was close upon them.<sup>35</sup>And the LORD defeated Benjamin before Israel, and the people of Israel destroyed 25,100 men of Benjamin that day. All these were men who drew the sword.<sup>36</sup>So the people of Benjamin saw that they were defeated. The men of Israel gave ground to Benjamin, because they trusted the men in ambush whom they had set against Gibeah.<sup>37</sup>Then the men in ambush hurried and rushed against Gibeah; the men in ambush moved out and struck all the city with the edge of the sword.<sup>38</sup>Now the appointed signal between the men of Israel and the men in the main ambush was that when they made a great cloud of smoke rise up out of the city<sup>39</sup>the men of Israel should turn in battle. Now Benjamin had begun to strike and kill about thirty men of Israel. They said, "Surely they are defeated before us, as in the first battle."<sup>40</sup>But when the signal began to rise out of the city in a column of smoke, the Benjaminites looked behind them, and behold, the whole of the city went up in smoke to heaven.<sup>41</sup>Then the men of Israel turned, and the men of Benjamin were dismayed, for they saw that disaster was close upon them.<sup>42</sup>Therefore they turned their backs before the men of Israel in the direction of the wilderness, but the battle overtook them. And those who came out of the cities were destroying them in their midst.<sup>43</sup>Surrounding the Benjaminites, they pursued them and trod them down from Nohah as far as opposite Gibeah on the east.<sup>44</sup>Eighteen thousand men of Benjamin fell, all of them men of valor.<sup>45</sup>And they turned and fled toward the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon. Five thousand men of them were cut down in the highways. And they were pursued hard to Gidom, and 2,000 men of them were struck down.<sup>46</sup>So all who fell that day of Benjamin were 25,000 men who drew the sword, all of them men of valor.<sup>47</sup>But 600 men turned and fled toward the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon and remained at the rock of Rimmon four months.<sup>48</sup>And the men of Israel turned back against the people of Benjamin and struck them with the edge of the sword, the city, men and beasts and all that they found. And all the towns that they found they set on fire.
20.overview:
No other muster in the book brings every tribe out: from Dan to Beersheba, four hundred thousand men, as one man. Against Jabin, Midian, Ammon and the Philistines only some tribes ever came. They come for this, and the enemy is Israel.

The Levite tells a true story that leaves out his own part. The assembly makes exactly the right demand, in the law's own words, and Benjamin refuses, choosing the tribe over the law.

Israel goes to war, asks God the wrong questions, and loses forty thousand men in two days. Only at the third asking, after weeping, fasting and sacrifice, does it ask whether to stop, and that is the question God answers with a promise.

The ambush works, twenty-five thousand of Benjamin fall and six hundred escape to a rock in the wilderness. Then the last verse: Israel goes back through Benjamin killing men, women, children and cattle, and burning every town.
20.theology:
Benjamin's choice (v. 13). Loyalty to one's own, right or wrong, binds a whole community to the worst thing done inside it. Benjamin is destroyed not for the crime at Gibeah but for standing behind it.

The three enquiries. "Who goes first?" (v. 18) assumed the war and asked about the marching order. "Shall we go again against our brothers?" (v. 23) at least named them as kin. Only the third, or shall we cease? (v. 28), puts the whole thing back in God's hands with a refusal genuinely possible, and that is the one he answers with tomorrow I will give them into your hand. Such prayer is not doubt about God, who has already bound himself to his people; it is trust that he may know better than we do.

Right, and terrible (v. 48). The crime was real, the demand lawful, and the LORD himself gave the victory; and by nightfall a tribe was destroyed. When we are certain we are right, we stop weighing what we do.

With, or instead. Benjamin put itself between guilty men and the justice they had earned and was destroyed in their place, and deserved it, because it was covering sin, not bearing it. One other stood in that position, not to hide sin but to carry its punishment: he himself bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Pet. 2:24). Benjamin perished with the guilty because it took their side; Christ perished instead of them because he took their place, and only one of those leaves anybody alive.
20.examples:
Then: A nation that would not raise an army against any of its enemies raised four hundred thousand men against one of its own tribes, was right about everything, lost forty thousand men before it asked God whether to fight at all, and then burned every town in Benjamin.

Now: Two things. First, watch how you tell the story of something that went wrong with your help. The Levite got every fact right and left himself out of the one sentence that mattered, and four hundred thousand men acted on it. We can afford to put ourselves back in the story, because the God who laid our sins on Christ forgives what is confessed (1 John 1:9). Second, and harder: when you are certain you are in the right, notice whether you have stopped asking. Israel's prayers improved as its army shrank, and the only prayer God answered with a promise was the one that offered him the word cease. A cause that cannot be halted by God is not being held before him; it is being announced to him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel assembles as one man at Mizpah, from Dan to Beersheba, four hundred thousand swordsmen (vv. 1-2). The Levite tells his story: the leaders of Gibeah meant to kill him, they violated his concubine, she is dead (vv. 4-6). The assembly vows not to go home until it is dealt with, and sends to Benjamin with a demand that is exactly right: hand over the worthless fellows of Gibeah, to be put to death (v. 13). Benjamin will not listen.
verseByVerse.theology: Unity is not the same as being right. The first thing the whole nation ever does together is go to war with itself.
verseByVerse.examples: Before acting on someone's account of a wrong, ask what part the teller played. Israel asked the Levite how it happened (v. 3) and asked nothing further.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the people of Israel came out, from Dan to Beersheba, including the land of Gilead, and the congregation assembled as one man to the LORD at Mizpah. And the chiefs of all the people, of all the tribes of Israel, presented themselves in the assembly of the people of God, 400,000 men on foot that drew the sword. (Now the people of Benjamin heard that the people of Israel had gone up to Mizpah.) And the people of Israel said, "Tell us, how did this evil happen?" And the Levite, the husband of the woman who was murdered, answered and said, "I came to Gibeah that belongs to Benjamin, I and my concubine, to spend the night. And the leaders of Gibeah rose against me and surrounded the house against me by night. They meant to kill me, and they violated my concubine, and she is dead. So I took hold of my concubine and cut her in pieces and sent her throughout all the country of the inheritance of Israel, for they have committed abomination and outrage in Israel. Behold, you people of Israel, all of you, give your advice and counsel here."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel is finally united, and no other muster in the book manages it: Dan in the far north to Beersheba in the far south, Gilead across the Jordan too, the chiefs of every tribe, as one man.

Can the numbers be right? The Hebrew word for thousand (’eleph) can also mean a clan or a military unit, and some careful conservative scholars think the figures in these chapters count units rather than individual men, which would make the armies much smaller. Others take them at face value. Either way the writer’s point is the contrast: this is the largest army in the book.

Set that against the rest of the book. Barak could not get Reuben, Dan or Asher to leave their sheepfolds and their ships (5:16-17). Gideon was left with three hundred. Jephthah faced Ammon with Gilead alone. Judah turned out three thousand men to arrest Samson (15:11). For forty years of Philistine rule, nobody mustered at all. Four hundred thousand men can be raised in this country; they have simply never been raised against an enemy.

The Levite's statement is true in every fact, and it is not honest. He says the leaders of Gibeah; chapter 19 said worthless fellows of the city. They meant to kill me is a reasonable inference from what they demanded, not what they said. They violated my concubine, and she is dead is exactly what happened.

What he leaves out is the door: that the mob asked for him, that the old man offered two women in his place, and that he himself took hold of his concubine and put her outside (19:25). He is perfectly willing to describe how he took hold of her and cut her in pieces; only the earlier taking hold is missing. Four hundred thousand men are about to go to war on an account whose one missing detail is the speaker's part.

This is not lying, and it is worse for not being lying. It is a true account arranged so that the man giving it does not appear in the part he would have to answer for, and it is exactly what any of us produces when we tell the story of a disaster we helped cause.
verseByVerse.note: “From Dan to Beersheba” means the whole land, north to south.

verseByVerse.quote: And all the people arose as one man, saying, "None of us will go to his tent, and none of us will return to his house. But now this is what we will do to Gibeah: we will go up against it by lot, and we will take ten men of a hundred throughout all the tribes of Israel, and a hundred of a thousand, and a thousand of ten thousand, to bring provisions for the people, that when they come they may repay Gibeah of Benjamin for all the outrage that they have committed in Israel." So all the men of Israel gathered against the city, united as one man. And the tribes of Israel sent men through all the tribe of Benjamin, saying, "What evil is this that has taken place among you? Now therefore give up the men, the worthless fellows in Gibeah, that we may put them to death and purge evil from Israel." But the Benjaminites would not listen to the voice of their brothers, the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their oath not to go home is the first of three in these two chapters that will cost them dearly. They organise properly, a tenth of the men set aside to bring food for the rest, and at this point the response is aimed at one town: what we will do to Gibeah.

The demand to Benjamin is entirely right. They do not attack first. They send messengers, state the charge, and ask for the guilty men: not the tribe, not the town, the men. Purge evil from Israel echoes the formula Deuteronomy attaches to the gravest offences, purge the evil from your midst (Deut. 13:5; 17:7; 19:19; 22:21). This is a lawful demand, correctly worded, made through the proper channel, about a real crime. Israel in this verse is doing exactly what God required of it.

Benjamin refuses. Everything turns on that, and there is no defending it. They were not asked to surrender their independence or pay tribute or give up territory. They were asked to hand over a gang of rapists and murderers from one of their towns, by their own brothers, under their own law. They chose the tribe over the law. Whatever the men of Gibeah had done, they were Benjaminites, and Israel was not going to touch them.

It is the oldest and most respectable form of corruption there is, always defended in the language of loyalty: ours, right or wrong; we do not hand our own over to outsiders. What it produces, every time, is a whole community bound to the worst thing done inside it, because to condemn the man is now to betray the family. Benjamin is about to be almost wiped off the map, not for the crime at Gibeah, which was the act of a mob, but for the decision to stand behind it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Benjamin musters twenty-six thousand, with seven hundred left-handed slingers (vv. 14-16). At Bethel Israel asks who shall go up first and is told Judah (v. 18). Benjamin kills twenty-two thousand Israelites on the first day (v. 21). Israel weeps, asks again, and loses eighteen thousand more (vv. 22-25).
verseByVerse.theology: Victory is not a verdict. Israel loses twice in a just cause, so the outcome of a battle cannot tell anyone who is in the right.
verseByVerse.examples: Most of us know the first two prayers well: asking God's help with a decision already made. The answer is not to pray less but to bring him the decision itself.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the people of Benjamin came together out of the cities to Gibeah to go out to battle against the people of Israel. And the people of Benjamin mustered out of their cities on that day 26,000 men who drew the sword, besides the inhabitants of Gibeah, who mustered 700 chosen men. Among all these were 700 chosen men who were left-handed; every one could sling a stone at a hair and not miss. And the men of Israel, apart from Benjamin, mustered 400,000 men who drew the sword; all these were men of war. The people of Israel arose and went up to Bethel and inquired of God, "Who shall go up first for us to fight against the people of Benjamin?" And the LORD said, "Judah shall go up first."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Twenty-six thousand against four hundred thousand, outnumbered fifteen to one, and Benjamin comes anyway, without hesitating. Whatever else is true of this tribe, they are not cowards, and the writer takes a moment to tell us what their speciality is.

Seven hundred left-handed slingers, each able to hit a hair. The name Benjamin means "son of the right hand" (ESV note, Gen. 35:18), and its elite troops are all left-handed. Ehud was a left-handed Benjaminite too, and it made him deadly against Eglon, since a left-handed man could carry a blade where nobody thought to look (3:15-16). The sling will be famous again when a shepherd boy from Judah brings down a Philistine with one (1 Sam. 17:49).

Israel's question at Bethel, and God's answer, are almost word for word the first two verses of the book (1:1-2). The book has come round in a complete circle. The difference is who is standing on the other side of the valley: in chapter 1 the Canaanites, here Benjamin. Everything between those two verses is the story of how a nation that could not be bothered to fight its enemies ended up able to fight nobody but itself.

And look at what they actually asked: who shall go up first, the order of march. They did not ask whether God wanted this war fought at all, or whether four hundred thousand men should be marching against twenty-six thousand of their own countrymen, or what he thought of the case. The campaign was decided at Mizpah before anyone came to Bethel, and God was asked only about the marching order.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the people of Israel rose in the morning and encamped against Gibeah. And the men of Israel went out to fight against Benjamin, and the men of Israel drew up the battle line against them at Gibeah. The people of Benjamin came out of Gibeah and destroyed on that day 22,000 men of the Israelites. But the people, the men of Israel, took courage, and again formed the battle line in the same place where they had formed it on the first day. And the people of Israel went up and wept before the LORD until the evening. And they inquired of the LORD, "Shall we again draw near to fight against our brothers, the people of Benjamin?" And the LORD said, "Go up against them." So the people of Israel came near against the people of Benjamin the second day. And Benjamin went against them out of Gibeah the second day, and destroyed 18,000 men of the people of Israel. All these were men who drew the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Twenty-two thousand dead on the first day, and Israel had the just cause, the lawful demand, the numbers and a word from God. This is the difficulty in the chapter that will not go away. Everything they had done was correct. God had told them Judah should go first. And they lost more men in one day than Gideon ever took into battle.

The second question is better than the first, and the phrase that makes it better is our brothers. They weep this time and name Benjamin as kin; the war has stopped being the arrest of criminals and become what it is, a war between brothers. But the question is still "shall we go again", and the answer is go up, with no promise attached.

Why did they lose, having asked God twice and been told to go? The easy answers are all false. God did not deceive them; he told them the truth both times. He simply did not promise them anything, and they did not notice.

Many commentators add a second answer, and it is fair to the book. The whole nation, not Benjamin alone, had been tolerating idols (the shrine at Dan was still standing, 18:30-31), and the defeats humbled all Israel before the victory came. God was punishing Gibeah’s crime and, at the same time, humbling the tribes he used to punish it.

What was wrong was not the cause but the assumption underneath it: that God's agreement could be taken for granted because their case was good, and that only the arrangements were left to settle with him. Four hundred thousand men marched on a resolution passed at Mizpah, and came to Bethel to ask who should lead. Forty thousand of them die before anybody asks a question that leaves God free to say no.

This is a warning for people who are right, not a warning against being right. It is exactly when our cause is good that we stop asking God and start telling him, because when a thing is obviously just, asking whether to do it feels like weakness.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The whole army goes to Bethel, weeps, fasts until evening, and offers burnt offerings and peace offerings, with Phinehas ministering before the ark (vv. 26-28). This time the question is different: or shall we cease? Now God answers with a promise (v. 28). The third day is fought with an ambush, and the LORD defeats Benjamin (vv. 29-36).
verseByVerse.theology: Repentance comes before the promise: weeping, fasting and offerings, and then a question that leaves God free to say no.
verseByVerse.examples: When a cause you were sure of goes badly wrong, the third day is the pattern: stop, grieve, come to God, and let him decide whether you go on.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the people of Israel, the whole army, went up and came to Bethel and wept. They sat there before the LORD and fasted that day until evening, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before the LORD. And the people of Israel inquired of the LORD (for the ark of the covenant of God was there in those days, and Phinehas the son of Eleazar, son of Aaron, ministered before it in those days), saying, "Shall we go out once more to battle against our brothers, the people of Benjamin, or shall we cease?" And the LORD said, "Go up, for tomorrow I will give them into your hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third time the whole army goes, and they weep, sit, fast the entire day, and bring burnt offerings and peace offerings. They had wept once before (v. 23); the fasting and the offerings are new. The war council has become a nation in mourning.

The narrator stops to tell us who was at the altar, and the name dates these chapters. Phinehas, son of Eleazar and grandson of Aaron, stopped the plague at Peor with a spear in Moses' own lifetime (Num. 25:7-11). If he is still ministering, this is very near the beginning of the time of the judges, within a generation or two of Joshua. These last five chapters are not the final collapse after Samson. The writer has gathered the worst of the age and placed it at the end as a summary, and the point is not "look what Israel came to" but "look what Israel was, from the start". The private shrine, the priest for hire, the migration, Gibeah: all of it within living memory of the conquest.

Or shall we cease. It took forty thousand deaths to get to the question. For the first time Israel comes to God with the possibility of stopping in its hand: tell us whether to do this at all, and we will abide by it. Twice he had said go up and nothing more. Now: go up, for tomorrow I will give them into your hand.

Nothing about their case has changed. What has changed is that they are asking rather than assuming, prepared to be told no. Prayer genuinely willing to receive a refusal is a different thing from prayer that has already decided, and God treats the two differently.

The ark is at Bethel here, though the tabernacle was at Shiloh (18:31). It had probably been brought to Bethel, about ten miles south, for the war, as it was later carried into battle (1 Sam 4:4). The KJV translates the place as the house of God in these chapters (20:18, 26; 21:2), which is what Bethel means; modern versions take it as the town.
verseByVerse.note: Burnt offerings were given wholly to God; peace offerings were shared in a meal, a sign of fellowship restored.

verseByVerse.quote: So Israel set men in ambush around Gibeah. And the people of Israel went up against the people of Benjamin on the third day and set themselves in array against Gibeah, as at other times. And the people of Benjamin went out against the people and were drawn away from the city. And as at other times they began to strike and kill some of the people in the highways, one of which goes up to Bethel and the other to Gibeah, and in the open country, about thirty men of Israel. And the people of Benjamin said, "They are routed before us, as at the first." But the people of Israel said, "Let us flee and draw them away from the city to the highways." And all the men of Israel rose up out of their place and set themselves in array at Baal-tamar, and the men of Israel who were in ambush rushed out of their place from Maareh-geba. And there came against Gibeah 10,000 chosen men out of all Israel, and the battle was hard, but the Benjaminites did not know that disaster was close upon them. And the LORD defeated Benjamin before Israel, and the people of Israel destroyed 25,100 men of Benjamin that day. All these were men who drew the sword. So the people of Benjamin saw that they were defeated. The men of Israel gave ground to Benjamin, because they trusted the men in ambush whom they had set against Gibeah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The plan is Joshua's plan at Ai, and it works the same way (Josh. 8:3-22): hide a force behind the city, offer the main army as bait, run when the garrison comes out, and let the ambush take the town from behind.

The phrase as at other times runs through this passage, and it is the trap. Benjamin has beaten this army twice on this ground, and the third morning looks exactly like the first two: thirty men down, the line giving way. They have seen this before and they know what it means. Their own experience is what kills them. Because the same opening has twice ended in victory, they follow it a third time without looking, straight into the ambush.

The LORD defeated Benjamin before Israel. The narrator will not let the ambush have the credit. The plan was well carried out and the ten thousand chosen men fought hard, yet the sentence that explains the day names God. He had said tomorrow I will give them into your hand, and this is that word being kept.

Verse 35 counts 25,100 Benjaminites killed; verses 44–46 give the round total, 25,000. Benjamin had mustered 26,700 (v. 15) and 600 escaped (v. 47), so about a thousand are not accounted for; some Greek manuscripts give a lower figure at verse 15, and others suppose some Benjaminites fell in the first two days.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 37–48 — What a Just War Became
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The ambush fires the city, and Benjamin, looking behind them, sees the whole town burning (vv. 37-40). Twenty-five thousand fall; six hundred escape to the rock of Rimmon and stay there four months (vv. 44-47). Then Israel turns back through Benjamin and burns every town they come to (v. 48).
verseByVerse.theology: What was demanded at v. 13 was the surrender of the guilty men of one town. What is done at v. 48 is the destruction of a tribe, its women, children, animals and towns, in language borrowed from the conquest of Canaan.
verseByVerse.examples: Anger that begins as justice for a victim can end by making many new victims. Notice how far v. 48 has travelled from v. 13.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the men in ambush hurried and rushed against Gibeah; the men in ambush moved out and struck all the city with the edge of the sword. Now the appointed signal between the men of Israel and the men in the main ambush was that when they made a great cloud of smoke rise up out of the city the men of Israel should turn in battle. Now Benjamin had begun to strike and kill about thirty men of Israel. They said, "Surely they are defeated before us, as in the first battle." But when the signal began to rise out of the city in a column of smoke, the Benjaminites looked behind them, and behold, the whole of the city went up in smoke to heaven. Then the men of Israel turned, and the men of Benjamin were dismayed, for they saw that disaster was close upon them. Therefore they turned their backs before the men of Israel in the direction of the wilderness, but the battle overtook them. And those who came out of the cities were destroying them in their midst. Surrounding the Benjaminites, they pursued them and trod them down from Nohah as far as opposite Gibeah on the east. Eighteen thousand men of Benjamin fell, all of them men of valor. And they turned and fled toward the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon. Five thousand men of them were cut down in the highways. And they were pursued hard to Gidom, and 2,000 men of them were struck down. So all who fell that day of Benjamin were 25,000 men who drew the sword, all of them men of valor. But 600 men turned and fled toward the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon and remained at the rock of Rimmon four months. And the men of Israel turned back against the people of Benjamin and struck them with the edge of the sword, the city, men and beasts and all that they found. And all the towns that they found they set on fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The men of Benjamin turn round in the middle of a battle they think they are winning and see their town going up in smoke, and when the fleeing army turns to fight, they understand everything at once.

Twice the writer says it: all of them men of valor. He will not let them go down as a rabble. These were brave men, and their bravery was spent defending the indefensible. He says so over their bodies. Six hundred are left, out of twenty-six thousand, and the whole tribe of Benjamin is now this: men with no wives, no towns and no children, sitting on a crag in the desert for four months, waiting to see whether anyone is still hunting them.

The last verse undoes everything the chapter began with. In verse 13 Israel demanded the surrender of the men, the worthless fellows in Gibeah: one town, the guilty, under the law. In verse 48 it marches back through the whole territory of Benjamin killing everything it finds and burning every town. That takes in the women who never went near Gibeah, the children, the livestock, and villages that had nothing to do with any of it.

Did God command this? No. He promised the defeat of Benjamin’s army (v. 28); nowhere did he order the killing of its women and children or the burning of its towns. The narrator records it, as he records everything in these chapters, without approving it.

The language is borrowed, too: striking a city with the edge of the sword, men and beasts, burning the towns, is the vocabulary of the conquest of Canaan, now applied by Israelites to a tribe of Israel.

Hold the two facts together, because separating them is how this chapter gets misread. Israel was right. The crime at Gibeah was real and monstrous, the demand lawful, Benjamin's refusal indefensible. Israel wept, fasted, sacrificed and asked whether to stop, and God himself gave the victory. By nightfall they had destroyed a tribe.

This is the danger of a just cause, and nobody feels it while he is in it. Being in the wrong makes a man cautious; he knows he can be challenged. Being demonstrably in the right takes the brake off, because every further step is carried by the same certainty that justified the first one. Israel never had to ask whether burning the villages was warranted; they had settled who was righteous days earlier, and after that there was nothing left to weigh.
