The next chapter opens with the whole nation at Bethel weeping over what it has just done.

Benjamin died for sheltering guilty men, covering their sin rather than bearing it. There is one who stood between guilty men and the justice they had earned, and was destroyed in their place, not to hide their sin but to pay for it. He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Pet. 2:24). Benjamin perished with the guilty because it took their side. Christ perished instead of the guilty because he took their place. Everything turns on that difference, and only one of the two leaves anybody alive.

21.title: Benjamin's Survival and the Final Verdict
21.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the men of Israel had sworn at Mizpah, "No one of us shall give his daughter in marriage to Benjamin."<sup>2</sup>And the people came to Bethel and sat there till evening before God, and they lifted up their voices and wept bitterly.<sup>3</sup>And they said, "O LORD, the God of Israel, why has this happened in Israel, that today there should be one tribe lacking in Israel?"<sup>4</sup>And the next day the people rose early and built there an altar and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings.<sup>5</sup>And the people of Israel said, "Which of all the tribes of Israel did not come up in the assembly to the LORD?" For they had taken a great oath concerning him who did not come up to the LORD to Mizpah, saying, "He shall surely be put to death."<sup>6</sup>And the people of Israel had compassion for Benjamin their brother and said, "One tribe is cut off from Israel this day.<sup>7</sup>What shall we do for wives for those who are left, since we have sworn by the LORD that we will not give them any of our daughters for wives?"<sup>8</sup>And they said, "What one is there of the tribes of Israel that did not come up to the LORD to Mizpah?" And behold, no one had come to the camp from Jabesh-gilead, to the assembly.<sup>9</sup>For when the people were mustered, behold, not one of the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead was there.<sup>10</sup>So the congregation sent 12,000 of their bravest men there and commanded them, "Go and strike the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead with the edge of the sword; also the women and the little ones.<sup>11</sup>This is what you shall do: every male and every woman that has lain with a male you shall devote to destruction."<sup>12</sup>And they found among the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead 400 young virgins who had not known a man by lying with him, and they brought them to the camp at Shiloh, which is in the land of Canaan.<sup>13</sup>Then the whole congregation sent word to the people of Benjamin who were at the rock of Rimmon and proclaimed peace to them.<sup>14</sup>And Benjamin returned at that time. And they gave them the women whom they had saved alive of the women of Jabesh-gilead, but they were not enough for them.<sup>15</sup>And the people had compassion on Benjamin because the LORD had made a breach in the tribes of Israel.<sup>16</sup>Then the elders of the congregation said, "What shall we do for wives for those who are left, since the women are destroyed out of Benjamin?"<sup>17</sup>And they said, "There must be an inheritance for the survivors of Benjamin, that a tribe not be blotted out from Israel.<sup>18</sup>Yet we cannot give them wives from our daughters." For the people of Israel had sworn, "Cursed be he who gives a wife to Benjamin."<sup>19</sup>So they said, "Behold, there is the yearly feast of the LORD at Shiloh, which is north of Bethel, on the east of the highway that goes up from Bethel to Shechem, and south of Lebonah."<sup>20</sup>And they commanded the people of Benjamin, saying, "Go and lie in ambush in the vineyards<sup>21</sup>and watch. If the daughters of Shiloh come out to dance in the dances, then come out of the vineyards and snatch each man his wife from the daughters of Shiloh, and go to the land of Benjamin.<sup>22</sup>And when their fathers or their brothers come to complain to us, we will say to them, 'Grant them graciously to us, because we did not take for each man of them his wife in battle, neither did you give them to them, else you would now be guilty.'"<sup>23</sup>And the people of Benjamin did so and took their wives, according to their number, from the dancers whom they carried off. Then they went and returned to their inheritance and rebuilt the towns and lived in them.<sup>24</sup>And the people of Israel departed from there at that time, every man to his tribe and family, and they went out from there every man to his inheritance.<sup>25</sup>In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
21.overview:
Israel sits at Bethel and weeps all day, and asks God why has this happened in Israel, that today there should be one tribe lacking? They had just killed everything they found in Benjamin. The grief is entirely real and no sentence in it begins with we.

Two rash oaths sworn at Mizpah now drive everything: no daughter to Benjamin, and death to any town that missed the muster. Neither is reconsidered. The question becomes how to get round them, and the answers are a massacre at Jabesh-gilead and an abduction at a festival of the LORD at Shiloh.

It works, after a fashion. Benjamin rebuilds, everyone goes home, and the book ends with its diagnosis: no king, and everyone his own judge of what is right.
21.theology:
Grief is not repentance (v. 3). The tears are real, but the wording leaves out who did it: why has this happened, not “what have we done”.

Jephthah's error, held nationally (v. 7). Since we have sworn is Jephthah's conviction again (11:35), now held by a whole people, with the same refusal to look at what the law provided for a rash oath.

Providence made to carry it (vv. 3, 15). Twice the destruction of Benjamin is laid at God's door. He gave the victory; he never told them to burn the towns, swear the oath, or destroy Jabesh-gilead.

Verse 22 is the whole book in one piece of legal advice. You did not give them to them, else you would now be guilty. Every word of the oath survives and its entire purpose is defeated. This is not lawlessness but rule-keeping to the letter that throws away what the rule was for, the instinct the Lord named in his own day (Mark 7:11-13; Matt. 23:24).

The ending is a need, not an answer. No judge, no enemy defeated, no repentance, no rebuke, no word from God, and no the land had rest. Ruth follows in English Bibles, in the days when the judges ruled, beginning at Bethlehem and ending with the line of David (Ruth 1:1; 4:21-22). And David was not the last word either. The book is finally answered by the other man from Bethlehem (Mic. 5:2), whose rest does not end after forty years, and whose name is written King of kings and Lord of lords (Rev. 19:16).
21.examples:
Then: A nation wept all day over a tribe it had destroyed, asked God why he had let it happen, and then, rather than reconsider two oaths it had never asked him about, wiped out an Israelite town for its virgins and staged an abduction at a festival of the LORD, so that no man present would technically be guilty.

Now: Two questions and a hope. First, listen to how you grieve over damage you have done: why has this happened and what have I done are not the same prayer, and only the second can be answered with forgiveness: the God who has already provided the sacrifice forgives what is owned before him (Psalm 32:5). Second, look for verse 22 in your own reasoning: the arrangement that keeps every rule intact while defeating everything the rule was for, and costs somebody who is not in the room. And then the hope, which is why the book ends where it does. It leaves you in a country with no king and does not pretend to fix it. Ruth begins on the next page in Bethlehem and ends with David, and David was not enough either. In those days there was no king in Israel. There is one now. And to anyone who has been taken, forced or abused as the women of Jabesh-gilead and Shiloh were: Scripture records it here and condemns it elsewhere, for God’s law made kidnapping a capital crime (Exodus 21:16; Deuteronomy 24:7) and declared the forced woman innocent (Deuteronomy 22:25–27). It was never your fault. If you are in danger, seek safety at once and tell someone who can help; the King who reigns now never asks anyone to stay in harm’s way.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The men of Israel had sworn at Mizpah that none of them would give a daughter to Benjamin (v. 1). Now they sit at Bethel until evening and weep bitterly, and ask God: why has this happened in Israel, that today there should be one tribe lacking? (vv. 2-3). They build an altar, then turn to the practical problem: six hundred men, no wives, and an oath in the way (vv. 4-7).
verseByVerse.theology: An oath sworn in anger and never brought to God becomes the master of everything that follows. They asked him nothing before swearing it, and they ask him nothing about keeping it.
verseByVerse.examples: Their compassion for Benjamin (v. 6) is not play-acting. It is the second half of the sentence that dooms everybody: they will not reconsider the vow.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the men of Israel had sworn at Mizpah, "No one of us shall give his daughter in marriage to Benjamin." And the people came to Bethel and sat there till evening before God, and they lifted up their voices and wept bitterly. And they said, "O LORD, the God of Israel, why has this happened in Israel, that today there should be one tribe lacking in Israel?" And the next day the people rose early and built there an altar and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrator reaches back to an oath we had not heard before, sworn at Mizpah in the first heat of the outrage, and it made sense at the time. A tribe that would shelter the men of Gibeah was not a tribe you married your daughters into.

Nobody asked God about it. The whole business of the last two chapters has been men resolving first and enquiring afterwards, and this vow was never brought to Bethel at all.

The weeping is real. They do not celebrate the victory or count the spoil; the whole army sits on the ground before God until dark and cries out loud, and there is nothing false about it. They have destroyed their own brother and they know it.

Then they ask God why he did it, and everything that follows grows out of the question. Why has this happened in Israel? As though it had simply happened, with nobody doing it. As though a tribe had gone missing overnight and nobody could account for it.

They did it. They marched on Benjamin, burned every town, and killed everything they found in it (20:48). There is no mystery about why there is one tribe lacking in Israel.

Sorrow and repentance are not the same thing, and this is the difference between them. Everything in this scene looks like the real thing. What is missing is one sentence beginning we. Nobody says "we have done this". They say why has this happened, and the wording has quietly left out the people who did it.

A man can be genuinely broken-hearted about a situation he created and never once own it. He will usually be sincere: he grieves over the result and asks God why, but he never says “I did this”.

They build an altar and sacrifice. The instinct is right and it goes nowhere, because in a moment they will turn from the altar to the problem and solve it entirely by themselves. God is worshipped in this chapter and never consulted. They weep at him, sacrifice to him, and then hold a committee.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel said, "Which of all the tribes of Israel did not come up in the assembly to the LORD?" For they had taken a great oath concerning him who did not come up to the LORD to Mizpah, saying, "He shall surely be put to death." And the people of Israel had compassion for Benjamin their brother and said, "One tribe is cut off from Israel this day. What shall we do for wives for those who are left, since we have sworn by the LORD that we will not give them any of our daughters for wives?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A second oath. At Mizpah they swore two things: no daughter to Benjamin, and death to any town that stayed away. Neither was commanded. Neither was brought to God. And between them, over the next twenty verses, they will produce a massacre and a mass abduction.

The book has shown us this before. Jephthah stood in his doorway and said I have opened my mouth to the LORD, and I cannot take back my vow (11:35), and his daughter died for it, and the law he was appealing to had made provision to redeem her. The same conviction is at work here, held by a whole nation: a word given to God is unbreakable, therefore whatever it costs must be paid.

As with Jephthah, nobody goes and looks. There is no attempt to bring the vow to the priest, no enquiry whether a rash oath sworn in fury binds a man to catastrophe. Leviticus 5:4-6 provides for exactly that case: a man who swears rashly with his lips, when he realises it, is guilty, and brings a sin offering, and is forgiven. There was an altar standing in front of them, and they had just been sacrificing on it.

Compassion for Benjamin their brother. The word is warm and it is meant; the enemy of the battle is their brother again, and their hearts are pointing the right way.

The second half of the sentence is where it all goes wrong: since we have sworn. The oath is treated as the one fixed object in the room. Compassion may move, the tribe may be saved, the plan may be anything at all, but the vow does not come up for discussion.

So the question they set themselves is not "was that oath righteous?" but "how do we get round it?" And a nation that has decided it must keep the letter of a bad promise will find a way, and the way will cost somebody who is not in the room.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second oath, death to any town that missed the muster, falls on Jabesh-gilead (vv. 5-9). The town is destroyed and four hundred girls are spared for Benjamin (vv. 10-14). It is not enough.
verseByVerse.theology: This is a massacre carried out to repair the damage of a massacre, and the arithmetic is the whole reason for it: they needed wives, and the only lawful-seeming source was a town already under a death sentence by their own oath.
verseByVerse.examples: Remember Jabesh-gilead. Generations later a Benjaminite king will ride to its rescue in his first act as king (1 Sam. 11:1-11), and its men will risk their lives to recover his body from a Philistine wall (1 Sam. 31:11-13). The bond between that town and that tribe starts here, in blood.

verseByVerse.quote: And they said, "What one is there of the tribes of Israel that did not come up to the LORD to Mizpah?" And behold, no one had come to the camp from Jabesh-gilead, to the assembly. For when the people were mustered, behold, not one of the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead was there. So the congregation sent 12,000 of their bravest men there and commanded them, "Go and strike the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead with the edge of the sword; also the women and the little ones. This is what you shall do: every male and every woman that has lain with a male you shall devote to destruction." And they found among the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead 400 young virgins who had not known a man by lying with him, and they brought them to the camp at Shiloh, which is in the land of Canaan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They go looking for a town under sentence, and they find one. Follow the logic, because it is careful and it is monstrous. We may not give our daughters to Benjamin. But we swore that any town which missed the muster should die. If such a town exists, its people are already condemned to die, and its unmarried girls are not given by anyone; they are taken as spoil. The oath is untouched. Jabesh-gilead, east of the Jordan, had not come.

Also the women and the little ones. The order is explicit, and it is given not by a mob but by the assembly of Israel, just after it wept before God and built an altar, in a formal resolution, with twelve thousand picked men detailed to carry it out.

The phrase devote to destruction is the herem, the ban, by which a city was given wholly over to God in destruction: the word used of Jericho (Josh. 6:17).

God had commanded that against the Canaanites, for their wickedness, after four centuries of patience. Israel now pronounces it on an Israelite town, on its own authority, to solve a shortage of brides.

Four hundred girls are marched to Shiloh over the bodies of their families. The writer records it flatly, as he does throughout these chapters. The whole town was killed so that four hundred of its daughters could be handed to the survivors of the tribe that had sheltered the rapists of Gibeah.

A woman was violated at Gibeah, and the nation went to war over it. In two chapters that war has produced the extermination of a tribe and the systematic abduction of four hundred girls, and every step of it was taken by men who believed they were putting things right.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the whole congregation sent word to the people of Benjamin who were at the rock of Rimmon and proclaimed peace to them. And Benjamin returned at that time. And they gave them the women whom they had saved alive of the women of Jabesh-gilead, but they were not enough for them. And the people had compassion on Benjamin because the LORD had made a breach in the tribes of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peace is proclaimed after four months on the rock (20:47), and the last men of Benjamin walk back into a nation that destroyed them.

But they were not enough. Six hundred men, four hundred women. The whole of Jabesh-gilead has been put to the sword and the sum still does not work, and the narrator states the shortfall as flatly as a storekeeper counting stock.

Verse 15 says the LORD had made a breach, a gap where a tribe should be. Twice now in this chapter the destruction of Benjamin has been laid at God's door as something that simply befell the nation (cf. v. 3). And there is a sense in which it is true: God did give Israel the victory, and said he would (20:28). But he never told them to burn the towns, or kill the women and children, or swear the oath, or destroy Jabesh-gilead.

Providence, God’s rule over everything that happens, gets the blame for the results of decisions God was never asked about. It is one of the most common things people do with that truth, and this chapter shows exactly how it works: you take the part he did, and quietly extend it to cover the part you did.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two hundred short, the elders send Benjamin to seize girls dancing at the yearly feast of the LORD at Shiloh, and prepare the answer they will give the fathers (vv. 16-22). Everyone goes home, and the book ends with its verdict (vv. 23-25).
verseByVerse.theology: The scheme protects the men from guilt and does nothing at all for the girls. Rules kept for their own sake end by caring only for the people who keep them.
verseByVerse.examples: When you find yourself working out how to keep the wording of a promise while defeating its purpose, stop and ask who is paying for it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the elders of the congregation said, "What shall we do for wives for those who are left, since the women are destroyed out of Benjamin?" And they said, "There must be an inheritance for the survivors of Benjamin, that a tribe not be blotted out from Israel. Yet we cannot give them wives from our daughters." For the people of Israel had sworn, "Cursed be he who gives a wife to Benjamin." So they said, "Behold, there is the yearly feast of the LORD at Shiloh, which is north of Bethel, on the east of the highway that goes up from Bethel to Shechem, and south of Lebonah." And they commanded the people of Benjamin, saying, "Go and lie in ambush in the vineyards and watch. If the daughters of Shiloh come out to dance in the dances, then come out of the vineyards and snatch each man his wife from the daughters of Shiloh, and go to the land of Benjamin. And when their fathers or their brothers come to complain to us, we will say to them, 'Grant them graciously to us, because we did not take for each man of them his wife in battle, neither did you give them to them, else you would now be guilty.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The elders take over, and the problem is now purely technical: two hundred short. They hold two things with equal firmness: a tribe must not be blotted out, and we cannot give them our daughters.

The oath has hardened since verse 1. It is no longer only we will not give; it is cursed be he who gives. Anybody who solves this the obvious way brings a curse on himself.

Notice where their plan is set. Shiloh is where the house of God was, with the tabernacle and the appointed priesthood, the place everyone in chapters 17 and 18 ignored (18:31). And this is the yearly feast of the LORD, one of the appointed festivals, with the young women of the town out dancing as they did every year in perfect safety.

The elders of Israel station armed men in the vineyards around a worship festival and instruct them to seize the girls as they come out.

The word is snatch.

Verse 22 holds the whole book. Take it apart. You did not give them to them: so the oath is intact, because giving was the forbidden act and no father gave anything. Else you would now be guilty: and there it is, the only thing they actually care about. Not the girls, not the fathers: only that no man should be guilty.

The whole scheme exists so that no Israelite man has to be technically in breach of a vow he should never have sworn. Every word of the oath survives untouched. Its entire purpose is defeated, since two hundred daughters of Israel end up in Benjamin exactly as if they had been handed over. The only difference is a form of words the elders have prepared in advance.

This is what religion becomes when it has nothing left in it but rules. It is not lawlessness but the opposite: scrupulous, worked out with care by the elders at a feast of the LORD, and it produces an outcome so obviously wicked that no argument is needed; you only have to picture the vineyards.

The Lord met this exact instinct in his own day and named it. Men would not lift a finger to help a parent, having declared the money given to God, and he told them that they had made void the word of God by their tradition, and were straining out gnats and swallowing camels (Mark 7:11-13; Matt. 23:24).

Israel here strains out a gnat, and the camel goes down whole.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Benjamin did so and took their wives, according to their number, from the dancers whom they carried off. Then they went and returned to their inheritance and rebuilt the towns and lived in them. And the people of Israel departed from there at that time, every man to his tribe and family, and they went out from there every man to his inheritance. In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It works. Benjamin goes home, rebuilds the burnt towns and settles in them, and the nation has achieved its object: no tribe is blotted out of Israel. Two hundred girls from Shiloh and four hundred from Jabesh-gilead never saw it coming, and nobody asked them anything at any point.

Everybody goes home, and that is the whole conclusion. No judge is raised up. No enemy is defeated. Nobody repents, and nobody is rebuked, and God says nothing at all. Four hundred thousand men who mustered as one man disperse to their own inheritances, and the writer does not tell us that the land had rest, because it did not.

There the book stops. The no king line has appeared four times in these five chapters and the full sentence twice, and this is the only one with nothing after it. There is no closing prayer, no summary of the period, no promise. The last sentence of the book of Judges is a diagnosis.

Look back down the whole length of it from here. Othniel, and the land had rest forty years. Ehud, and eighty. Deborah, and forty. Gideon, and forty, and then an ephod that became a snare, and seventy sons murdered on one stone. Jephthah, and no rest recorded at all. Samson, who only began to save Israel (13:5). And then a private shrine, a priest for hire, a tribe that took the easy land, a woman dead on a doorstep, a war that destroyed a brother, and elders arranging an ambush at a festival of the LORD.

The line runs downhill from the first chapter to the last, and the writer's explanation never changes: no king, and every man his own authority on what was good. So the book ends by asking for something it cannot supply.

The judges could not supply it. Every one of them was temporary, local and flawed, and the best of them left a nation that reverted the moment he was buried. What Israel needed was not another deliverer for another crisis. It was a king: someone permanently over them, someone whose word settled what was right, so that a man's own eyes were no longer the final court.

Turn the page in your Bible and the next words are: in the days when the judges ruled, there was a famine in the land, and a man of Bethlehem in Judah went to sojourn in the country of Moab (Ruth 1:1).

The same period and the same wretched conditions, and a story that begins in Bethlehem, the town these closing chapters keep returning to (17:7; 19:1), and ends with a genealogy: Boaz fathered Obed, Obed fathered Jesse, and Jesse fathered David (Ruth 4:21-22).

Ruth is the answer to Judges 21:25, and in English Bibles, which follow the order of the Greek Old Testament, it stands immediately after it. (The Hebrew Bible places Ruth later, among the Writings.)

But David was not the last word either. He was Israel's best king and he had a man killed to cover his adultery, and his own house never recovered from it. The book that ends everyone did what was right in his own eyes is not finally satisfied by a man from Bethlehem with a crown and a harp.

It is satisfied by the other one from Bethlehem. You, O Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are too little to be among the clans of Judah, from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel (Mic. 5:2). He came, and he was born under that same sky and buried in a borrowed grave and raised on the third day, and there is no verse anywhere that says his rest came to an end after forty years.

Judges leaves us in a country where men who mean well produce catastrophe after catastrophe because there is nobody over them, and that describes any life, and any age, that has no one on the throne. On leadership and order as God’s gift in every sphere, see on Ephesians 5:21.

The last book of the Bible answers the last verse of Judges directly. There is a name written on the robe and on the thigh of the rider on the white horse, and it is King of kings and Lord of lords (Rev. 19:16).

In those days there was no king in Israel. There is one now.

Is this an argument for monarchy? Samuel later treats the people’s demand for a king as a rejection of God (1 Sam 8:7), and Gideon refused a crown because the LORD should rule (8:23). Both are true. Israel needed a king, but the right king in the right way: God had planned one (Deut 17:14–20), and he chose David, whose Son is the King Israel finally needed.
verseByVerse.note: The book’s last words explain its chaos and point forward to the need for a godly king.
